evidence: “A randomization list was created using the ASELECT formula in Microsoft Excel 2007”; allocation used blocks of six, stratified by gender and HIV status (p. 10, Study design).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when a random component was used, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: The article describes randomization and placebo blinding (p. 10), and pharmacy repackaging/relabeling (p. 12), but does not describe who held the allocation list or how assignments were concealed until enrollment. Fixed blocks alone do not establish that recruiters could predict assignments.
guidance: §4.1.2 distinguishes concealment from subsequent blinding; §4.3.2 and Table 2 require an adequate allocation mechanism. §1.1 permits NI when neither PY nor PN is reasonably supported.

evidence: Table 1 (p. 3) includes all 150 randomized participants, 50 per arm. Age, weight, sex, HIV status, and baseline microbiology show no pattern indicating failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when observed imbalances are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 excludes chance imbalances from this domain.

evidence: Described as “double-blind” with two supplementary capsules in every arm: two placebos, one rifampin plus one placebo, or two rifampin capsules (p. 10). This supports participant blinding, although capsule appearance and blinding success are not explicitly documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 recognizes placebo blinding; §5.1.3 cautions that “double blind” alone does not identify everyone blinded. §1.1 supports a qualified, inferred response.

evidence: The double-blind, placebo-controlled regimen and pharmacy repackaging support personnel blinding (pp. 10, 12). No disclosure of assignments or dose-specific unblinding is reported, although individual staff roles are not specified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses personnel awareness; §5.1.3 requires assessing the reported blinding arrangements rather than assuming all roles from the label alone.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN, based on the blinding arrangements on p. 10.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask 2.3 only if either 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: No applicable preceding assessment of trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: No applicable preceding assessment of deviations affecting the outcome.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Tables 3–4 (p. 5) summarize safety by the original three dose groups, retaining denominators of 50 each. No safety exclusions or regrouping by treatment received are described. The five explicit exclusions concern bacteriological analysis, not this result (p. 5). An explicit safety ITT statement is absent.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept analysis in randomized groups; exclusion solely for missing outcomes belongs in D3. The evidence supports probable appropriateness without establishing complete follow-up.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is PY.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask only if 2.6 is N/PN/NI.

evidence: Tables 3–4 give randomized denominators, but do not report how many participants completed safety follow-up. The scheduled visits (p. 11) and recorded deaths (p. 5) support active surveillance, but there is no safety-specific accounting of withdrawals, missed assessments, or follow-up completeness. Culture-sampling losses (pp. 6, 9) cannot establish missingness for AEs.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires available outcome data, not merely inclusion in a denominator. §6.1.1 says even an ITT analysis may contain missing outcomes; §6.3(1) states that absent information about their extent usually leads to High risk.

evidence: No sensitivity analysis or method addressing missing grade 3 AE outcomes is reported in the safety results or statistical methods (pp. 4–5, 11–12).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses under plausible missingness assumptions. None is supplied.

evidence: If safety follow-up was incomplete, illness or adverse effects could plausibly influence attendance or withdrawal. The report documents severe events and deaths (pp. 4–5), but supplies no safety-specific reasons allowing such dependence to be excluded. Recorded deaths are not themselves treated as proof of missing grade 3 outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness could depend on the true outcome when loss or withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status.”

evidence: Arm-specific amounts and reasons for incomplete safety follow-up are not reported (pp. 4–5, 11). Consequently, the evidence cannot distinguish possible from likely dependence on grade 3 AE status.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely” using missingness proportions, reasons, and circumstances. Under Table 10, NI at this reached question maps to High; this is uncertainty, not evidence that informative loss occurred.

evidence: Severity, including laboratory abnormalities, was classified using “CTCAE; version 4.0” and reviewed by a data safety monitoring board (p. 11). Scheduled examinations, laboratory testing, and safety histories provided an appropriate ascertainment system.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns unsuitable or insufficiently sensitive measurement methods; §7.3 identifies absence of systems defining or detecting adverse outcomes as a potential problem. Such systems were present here.

evidence: The same examinations, laboratory tests, safety histories, and assessment schedule are described for all arms (p. 11). Hospital versus home treatment varied by site (p. 10), but outpatient proportions were similar across arms (Table 1, p. 3), with no reported dose-dependent ascertainment procedures.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable times; §7.3 focuses on systematic differences in opportunities for detection.

evidence: Investigator assessment occurred within the double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (pp. 10–11), supporting probable assessor unawareness. Separate blinding details for investigators and the monitoring board are absent.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 asks whether assessors knew intervention status; §7.3 requires examining assessor blinding. The placebo arrangements support PN, with the reporting limitation acknowledged.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. Table 4 contains both laboratory events and symptoms, but their susceptibility to judgement does not activate this branch when assessors were probably blinded.
guidance: Box 10 branching: ask only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached under the assessor-blinding branch.
guidance: Box 10 branching: ask only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The article specifies safety summaries by severity and relatedness, with patient counts for grade 3 events (p. 11), matching Tables 3–4. However, no dated advance analysis plan is supplied; the registry identifier on p. 1 does not establish its contents or timing.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require analysis intentions finalized before unblinded outcome data became available. Publication methods alone do not establish that timing.

evidence: Reporting all severity grades and relatedness categories in Table 3, alongside Table 4 and the abstract, provides evidence against obvious selective presentation. Nevertheless, no advance specification establishes all eligible safety definitions or reporting periods; the tables’ cutoff is unstated (pp. 1, 5, 11).
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and the domain could be measured in multiple ways. Multiplicity alone does not establish result-based selection.

evidence: Both event counts and affected-patient counts are reported consistently (pp. 4–5, 11). There is no direct evidence of selecting a favorable analysis, but no advance plan establishes the intended analysis population, missing-data handling, or complete set of eligible analyses.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible. §8.1.2 requires selection based on the results to establish selective-reporting bias.

evidence: A randomization list used “the ASELECT formula in Microsoft Excel 2007,” with stratification and blocks of six (p. 10, Study design).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers,” supports Y.

evidence: Double blinding and pharmacy repackaging/relabeling support concealment as a possibility (pp. 10, 12), but the article does not identify control of the allocation list, sequential dispensing, or the enrollment-to-assignment procedure. Pharmacy preparation does not establish pharmacy-controlled allocation.
guidance: §4.1.2 distinguishes allocation concealment from blinding; Table 2 identifies adequate allocation mechanisms. Under §1.1, NI applies when a probable answer cannot reasonably be established.

evidence: Table 1 (p. 3) presents 50 randomized participants per arm, with broadly comparable demographic and baseline characteristics. Differences do not suggest manipulation or failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer N when differences are “compatible with chance.” Baseline balance must not determine answers to 1.1 or 1.2.

evidence: “Double-blind” treatment used two supplementary capsules in every arm, combining rifampin and placebo according to allocation (p. 10). Participant blinding is probable, although appearance and blinding success are not explicitly documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 recognizes placebo blinding; §5.1.3 cautions that broad blinding terminology is insufficiently specific. The supporting regimen permits PN under §1.1.

evidence: Double-blind treatment, placebo capsules, and pharmacy repackaging support probable personnel blinding (pp. 10, 12). Personnel roles and code access are not individually specified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns personnel awareness; §5.1.3 requires considering actual blinding arrangements. Unknown concealment in D1 does not establish that allocation was disclosed.

evidence: Not reached because both awareness responses are PN, supported by the regimen on p. 10.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only if either 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: No applicable preceding finding of trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: No applicable preceding assessment of deviations affecting outcomes.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Tables 3–4 retain the three randomized dose groups and denominators of 50 each (p. 5). No safety exclusions or treatment-based regrouping are described. The five stated exclusions apply specifically to bacteriological analysis. An explicit safety ITT declaration is absent.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept analysis in randomized groups; missing-outcome exclusions are assessed separately in D3. Evidence supports probable appropriate grouping without proving complete observation.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is PY, based on Tables 3–4.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.6 is N/PN/NI.

evidence: Full randomized denominators, documented deaths, and scheduled safety surveillance favor completeness (pp. 5, 11). However, Table 4 explicitly labels its denominator “patients randomized”; neither table establishes complete safety observation. No safety-specific follow-up accounting or completion statement is provided.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 asks whether outcome data were available, not whether participants appeared in denominators. §6.1.1 warns that even ITT analyses may have missing outcomes; §6.3(1) addresses absent information about their extent.

evidence: The safety results and analysis methods provide no missing-data correction or sensitivity analysis establishing robustness (pp. 4–5, 11–12).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from appropriate analysis methods or sensitivity analyses under plausible missingness assumptions.

evidence: If safety observations were missing, illness or adverse effects could influence follow-up. Severe events are documented, but safety-specific reasons for incomplete observations are not (pp. 4–5, 11). This does not assert that withdrawals occurred.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: dependence is possible when loss or withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status.” Documented outcome-independent reasons could exclude it, but none are supplied.

evidence: The report does not provide arm-specific amounts or reasons for missing safety outcomes, preventing a judgement about likely dependence (pp. 4–5, 11). Recorded deaths and missing culture samples do not establish missing grade 3 AE outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence using proportions, reasons, and circumstances. Table 10 explicitly maps a reached NI response to High.

evidence: Severity, including laboratory abnormalities, followed CTCAE v4.0 and was reviewed by a data safety monitoring board. Examinations, laboratory testing, and safety histories supplied an ascertainment system (p. 11).
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns inappropriate measurement methods; §7.3 highlights lack of systems defining or detecting adverse outcomes. Such systems were present.

evidence: The same safety methods and visit schedule are described for all groups (p. 11). Hospital/home care varied by site (p. 10), but outpatient proportions were similar across arms (Table 1, p. 3), with no reported dose-dependent surveillance.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods, thresholds, and time points; §7.3 targets systematic differences in detection opportunities.

evidence: Assessments occurred within the double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (pp. 10–11). This supports probable assessor blinding, although separate investigator and monitoring-board masking details are absent.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 addresses assessor awareness; §7.3 requires evaluating assessor blinding. The regimen supports PN rather than an unequivocal N.

evidence: Not reached because assessors were probably unaware. Table 4 includes symptoms as well as laboratory abnormalities, but potential subjectivity alone does not activate the branch.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached under the preceding assessor-blinding response.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Published methods specify severity/relatedness summaries and grade 3 patient counts, matching Tables 3–4 (pp. 5, 11). However, no supplied document establishes that these analysis intentions preceded unblinded data. The registry identifier alone supplies no such evidence.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” establishing advance intentions; Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available.

evidence: Reporting all grades, relatedness categories, and grade 3 patient counts argues against obvious selection (p. 5). Nevertheless, no advance specification establishes all eligible definitions or reporting periods; the tables do not explicitly identify their cutoff.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficient and multiple measurements are possible. Absence of demonstrated selection does not establish that all intended measurements were reported.

evidence: Event and patient counts agree across the abstract, results, and tables (pp. 1, 4–5), and match published methods (p. 11). These are reassuring, but no advance plan establishes all intended analyses, populations, or missing-data procedures.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible; §8.1.2 requires result-based selection to establish selective-reporting bias.

evidence: Although §2.3 reports a “software-generated randomization plan,” it also describes consecutive coding with “the first 12” assigned to P-MPMP, the second 12 to SA-MPMP and the last 12 to SMC (p.1034). The discussion acknowledges possible “order effects” from these blocks (p.1042). Taken together, allocation probably followed a systematic sequence; the conflicting software statement prevents a definitive N.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer N when “the sequence is predictable,” including “any other systematic…method.” §4.1.1 describes valid blocked randomization as allocations assigned “in random order within each block.”

evidence: The consecutive treatment blocks described in §2.3 make forthcoming allocations probably predictable. Investigators and treatment staff “were not blinded to the randomization” (p.1034). No independent allocation service or other concealment safeguard is described. This judgement rests on the predictable scheme, rather than absent reporting alone.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer N where there is “reason to suspect” knowledge of forthcoming allocation. §4.1.2 includes the “ability to predict assignments successfully” as failure of concealment.

evidence: The demographic sample totals 33, whereas 36 were randomized (p.1034); Figure 1 likewise shows only 33 initially assessed (p.1035). Full randomized-group baseline information is unavailable. Among those reported, only anxiety differed significantly, p=0.047; other comparisons were nonsignificant (§3.1, p.1039). These observations do not establish abnormal imbalance.
guidance: §4.3.3: assessment “should be based on data for all randomized participants.” Box 4, 1.3 permits NI for inadequate baseline information and states that a small number of differences at 0.05 “should usually be considered…compatible with chance.”

evidence: The claim that participants were “blinded to their random assignment” (§2.3, p.1034) does not establish ignorance of treatment received. Participants attended sessions with spouses, attended without spouses, or received routine medical care (§§2.5.1–2.5.3, pp.1037–1038), making treatment awareness probable.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants knew their “assigned intervention during the trial.” §5.1.3 distinguishes intervention blinding from knowledge of randomization procedures.

evidence: “Investigators and treatment staff were not blinded” (§2.3, p.1034). Providers delivered the distinguishable treatment programmes.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness among “carers or people delivering the interventions.”

evidence: Both active programmes used the same professionals and manuals; sessions were filmed and reviewed for fidelity (pp.1037–1038). Authors state interventions were implemented “according to the study protocol” (p.1041). Reported attendance problems were practical; variable SMC services were part of intended routine care (Figure 1; p.1042). No trial-induced, non-protocol treatment change is identified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that the trial context caused non-protocol changes. It allows N/PN for non-adherence consistent with circumstances outside a trial.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; the implementation evidence is described above (pp.1037–1038, 1041).
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because no qualifying deviations were identified at 2.3.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: §2.6 states “intent-to-treat analyses, with dropouts included,” using baseline observations carried forward (p.1038). No reassignment by treatment received or exclusion of available outcomes for non-adherence is described. Participant counts and degrees of freedom do not fully reconcile with 36 randomized, limiting certainty; the documented omissions concern unavailable assessments.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept ITT and analyses excluding participants with missing outcomes for this domain; “bias because of the missing outcome data is addressed separately.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=PY. The reported analysis retains assigned groups (§2.6, p.1038).
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.7 only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Figure 1 shows follow-up assessments for 10 P-MPMP, 9 SA-MPMP and 10 SMC participants: 29/36, approximately 81% (p.1035). Seven missing assessments could materially affect these continuous outcomes. Baseline-carried-forward values are not observed follow-up data.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “‘Nearly all’” requires that missing outcomes could make “no important difference”; “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.”

evidence: “Pretreatment scores were moved forward to subsequent assessments” (§2.6, p.1038). No sensitivity analysis assessing plausible missing outcomes is reported. Similar demographic characteristics of completers and dropouts (§3.2, p.1039) do not establish comparable unobserved pain or disability.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires corrective methods or sensitivity analyses demonstrating robustness. §6.1.6 says baseline observation carried forward is “unlikely to remove” bias when missingness depends on the true outcome.

evidence: Figure 1 gives practical reasons for three early SA-MPMP withdrawals, but one SMC participant was “no longer interested,” and reasons for three additional losses before follow-up are absent (p.1035). Pain, disability or perceived recovery could have influenced these unexplained losses.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome; low risk requires documented outcome-independent reasons for all missing data.

evidence: Three SA-MPMP losses involved being busy, scheduling conflict and family obligations, arguing against direct symptom-driven withdrawal. However, the SMC loss of interest and subsequent losses remain unexplained. Follow-up missingness was 3/12 versus 2/12 in each other arm—a modest difference that does not establish outcome dependence. The evidence is insufficient to judge dependence likely or unlikely (Figure 1, p.1035).
guidance: §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient evidence to support PY or PN. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely…depended”; reasons and between-group differences inform that judgement. Table 10 explicitly maps NI at 3.4 to High when preceding answers are N/N/Y-PY.

evidence: RDQ is a 24-item disability checklist with reported validity and reliability (§2.4.1.1, pp.1035–1036). VAS measures pain intensity, with validity and responsiveness described (§2.4.1.2, p.1036). The 10-cm/0–100 description and Table 1’s 0–10 presentation do not demonstrate an unsuitable instrument.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns instruments insensitive to plausible effects or demonstrated to have “poor validity”; it does not question whether the selected outcome is sensible.

evidence: All groups completed the same questionnaire battery at baseline, post-treatment and 12-month follow-up (§2.4, pp.1034–1035). SMC explicitly received the “same battery of assessment instruments” at follow-up (§2.5.3, p.1038).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable collection as “the same measurement methods…used at comparable time points.”

evidence: Participants completed both measures themselves (§2.4, p.1035). Their exposure to spouse-assisted sessions, patient-only sessions or routine care made awareness probable despite the statement about blinding to random assignment (§2.3; §§2.5.1–2.5.3). No credible participant masking method is described.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “For participant-reported outcomes, the outcome assessor is the study participant.”

evidence: RDQ asks patients to judge limitations in daily activities; VAS asks them to rate pain (§2.4.1, pp.1035–1036). Both permit subjective interpretation influenced by treatment knowledge.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: knowledge “could influence participant-reported outcomes (such as level of pain).”

evidence: The active programmes explicitly trained interpretation and management of pain and disability, with ongoing home practice, versus routine medical care (pp.1037–1038). These distinguishable experiences make differential expectations likely to influence subjective reporting. Twelve-month timing and the authors’ suggestion of lower expectations for psychological treatment (p.1042) temper certainty, but do not eliminate this plausible differential reporting mechanism.
guidance: §§7.1 and 7.3 require assessing conscious and subconscious “interests” and “expectations”; risk is greater against usual care than another active intervention. §7.3 also requires considering assessment timing. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes likely influence from mere possibility.

evidence: The supplied source is the main article only. §2.6 describes analyses, and §3.1 explains adjustment for the observed anxiety imbalance (pp.1038–1039), but neither establishes a plan finalized before unblinded data were available.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require that finalization “precede availability of unblinded outcome data”; a date-stamped analysis intention is needed to verify this.

evidence: RDQ and VAS are identified as primary measures (§2.4, p.1035); Table 1 reports their scheduled time points. Three VAS ratings were collected (§2.4.1.2, p.1036), with other ratings described as nonsignificant (§3.3.1, p.1039). These findings argue against demonstrated significance-driven selection, but prospective measurement intentions are unavailable. The assessment remains restricted to the specified RDQ and current-week VAS results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 permits NI when intentions are unavailable and multiple measurements are possible; it restricts attention to measurements “eligible for consideration.” Multiplicity alone does not establish results-based selection.

evidence: The article describes several ANCOVA approaches and data-informed covariate adjustment (§2.6; §3.1). Table 1 reports analyses both with and without follow-up and explains this by differences in treatment length (p.1039). There is no clear evidence that favourable analyses were selectively retained, but no prospective plan establishes all intended eligible analyses.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3: answer NI when analysis intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and there is “more than one way” to analyse the measurement. High requires likely selection “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: The “software-generated randomization plan” supports randomness, but the operational description assigns consecutively coded patients in successive groups of 12 to P-MPMP, SA-MPMP and SMC (§2.3, p.1034). The acknowledged possibility of “order effects” supports interpreting these as sequential treatment blocks (p.1042). This conflicting account warrants PN rather than definitive N.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 includes a “predictable” sequence or “systematic…method” under N. §4.1.1 requires random ordering of allocations within conventional randomized blocks.

evidence: Consecutive treatment blocks probably made forthcoming assignments predictable (§2.3, p.1034). No safeguard against this is described. Staff being unblinded after allocation would not alone establish failed concealment; the sequential allocation description is the deciding evidence.
guidance: §4.1.2 identifies “ability to predict assignments successfully” as compromised concealment. Box 4, 1.2 permits N/PN where forthcoming allocation was probably known.

evidence: Baseline demographics describe 33 participants despite 36 randomized; Figure 1 shows 33 initially assessed (pp.1034–1035). Complete randomized-group baseline data are unavailable. The reported anxiety difference, p=0.047, and otherwise nonsignificant comparisons do not establish problematic imbalance (§3.1, p.1039).
guidance: §4.3.3 requires assessment based on “all randomized participants.” Box 4, 1.3 permits NI for insufficient baseline information and says isolated conventional significance is usually “compatible with chance.”

evidence: Participants were described as blinded to “random assignment,” but receiving spouse-assisted sessions, patient-only sessions or routine medical care would make their actual intervention apparent (§2.3, p.1034; §§2.5.1–2.5.3, pp.1037–1038).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness of the “assigned intervention during the trial”; §5.1.3 defines blinding in terms of interventions received.

evidence: “Investigators and treatment staff were not blinded to the randomization” (§2.3, p.1034); they delivered the distinguishable programmes.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether carers and intervention providers were aware of assignment.

evidence: Manuals, common professionals and filmed-session review support intended delivery (pp.1037–1038). Authors report implementation “according to the study protocol” (p.1041). Practical attendance difficulties and variable routine SMC do not establish trial-induced non-protocol changes (Figure 1; p.1042).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol changes. Non-adherence consistent with circumstances outside the trial supports N/PN.

evidence: Not reached after 2.3=PN; implementation evidence is in §§2.5.1–2.5.3 and the discussion (pp.1037–1038, 1041).
guidance: Box 6: answer only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is not applicable. No qualifying trial-context deviations were identified.
guidance: Box 6: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: The report specifies “intent-to-treat analyses, with dropouts included” and baseline observations carried forward (§2.6, p.1038). Counts do not fully reconcile, but no analysis by treatment received or exclusion of available outcomes for non-adherence is reported. Documented unavailable assessments belong in D3.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept ITT and analyses excluding missing outcomes; missing-data bias is “addressed separately.”

evidence: Not reached after 2.6=PY, supported by the reported assignment-based analysis (§2.6, p.1038).
guidance: Box 6: answer only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Figure 1 shows 29/36 assessed at follow-up: P-MPMP 10/12, SA-MPMP 9/12 and SMC 10/12 (p.1035). Seven missing assessments could materially affect these continuous outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires missing observations to be too few to make an important difference; “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.”

evidence: “Pretreatment scores were moved forward” (§2.6, p.1038). No sensitivity analysis establishes robustness to plausible missing outcomes. Similar dropout/completer demographics (§3.2, p.1039) do not establish comparable missing pain or disability scores.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from corrective methods or sensitivity analyses. §6.1.6 says baseline observation carried forward is unlikely to remove outcome-dependent missingness bias.

evidence: Three later follow-up losses lack reported reasons; one early SMC withdrawal was “no longer interested” (Figure 1, p.1035). Symptoms or recovery could have influenced these losses, despite practical explanations for the three SA-MPMP withdrawals.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal potentially related to “participants’ health status” permits outcome-dependent missingness. Documented unrelated reasons for all losses would support N/PN, but are absent here.

evidence: On reconsideration, the observed pattern supports a tentative negative judgement: SA-MPMP withdrawals were attributed to being busy, scheduling and family obligations; two occurred before treatment. Follow-up losses differed by only one participant across arms (Figure 1, p.1035). The remaining unexplained losses preserve possibility, but do not make symptom-dependent missingness probable. My earlier NI underweighted the available reasons and timing.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes missingness that “could depend” from that “likely…depended” on the outcome. §1.1 reserves NI for circumstances where a reasoned PY/PN is unreasonable. §6.1.4 requires considering both proportions and reasons.

evidence: RDQ assesses daily disability and has reported validity and reliability; VAS assesses pain intensity with reported validity and responsiveness (§2.4.1, pp.1035–1036). Neither instrument is demonstrated unsuitable.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns insensitive instruments or demonstrated “poor validity,” rather than whether another outcome would have been preferable.

evidence: All groups used the same questionnaire battery at comparable assessment points; SMC explicitly completed the “same battery” at 12 months (§2.4, pp.1034–1035; §2.5.3, p.1038).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable collection as the same methods at “comparable time points.”

evidence: Participants supplied the RDQ and VAS responses and probably recognized their treatment experience, notwithstanding the statement about blinding to random assignment (§§2.3–2.4, pp.1034–1035; §2.5, pp.1037–1038).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: for participant-reported outcomes, “the outcome assessor is the study participant.”

evidence: Judgements about daily limitations and pain intensity could be influenced by treatment knowledge (§2.4.1, pp.1035–1036).
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 explicitly includes participant-reported outcomes, “such as level of pain,” among susceptible assessments.

evidence: My earlier PY gave excessive weight to the intervention’s intended changes in coping and appraisal; those do not themselves demonstrate erroneous reporting. SMC provided active medical treatment, two arms received comparable active programmes, and the target includes a distant follow-up. Authors suggest lower expectations of psychological treatment, although this is speculative (pp.1037–1038, 1042). Post-treatment data also contribute to the ANCOVA, so timing alone is insufficient; collectively, the evidence supports possible rather than probable material reporting influence.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes “could have influenced” from “likely to influence.” §7.3 requires considering comparator, expectations and timing, including reduced influence at one year. §7.1 defines measurement bias through errors in measured outcomes, rather than intended treatment effects.

evidence: Only the main article is supplied. Its statistical methods and explanation of anxiety adjustment do not establish an analysis plan finalized before unblinded data became available (§2.6 and §3.1, pp.1038–1039).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require analysis intentions finalized before unblinded outcome data; the latter discusses a confirming “date-stamp.”

evidence: RDQ and VAS are named primary measures; scheduled RDQ and current-week VAS measurements appear in Table 1. Other VAS ratings are described as nonsignificant (§2.4, p.1035; §2.4.1.2, p.1036; §3.3.1, p.1039). This challenges selection based on significance, but prospective measurement intentions remain unavailable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 permits NI when intentions are unavailable and multiple measurements are possible. It restricts attention to measurements “eligible for consideration”; omitted alternative VAS ratings alone do not establish bias in this specified target.

evidence: Several ANCOVA approaches are described. Table 1 reports analyses with and without follow-up and explains the distinction through differences in treatment length (pp.1038–1039). These disclosures argue against demonstrated selective analysis reporting, but a prospective plan is absent.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 permits NI when analysis intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible. High requires likely selection “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: Article p.86, §2.2: “computer-generated randomization table.”
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when a random component was used, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: Article p.86, §2.2: “Serially numbered unopened, opaque envelopes were used to hide allocations”; subsequently described as “sealed.” These support concealment, although tamper-proof sealing and opening only after irreversible enrolment are not explicitly documented.

evidence: Article p.86, §§2.2–2.3 describes active RF cycles versus an inactive device, making operator awareness probable; explicitly blinded clinicians were those conducting follow-up. evidence: Article pp.86–87 describes a standardized procedure and planned rescue paracetamol “as required or whenever the NRS score was >5.” Figure 1 identifies technical failures of intra-articular dye spread, but provides no indication that these arose because of recruitment, allocation awareness, or other trial-context influences. guidance: Box 6, 2.3: answer Y/PY only with “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that deviations arose because of the trial context. Changes consistent with the protocol, or deviations consistent with ordinary practice outside the trial, support N/PN.

guidance: Box 6, 2.6: excluding participants who did not receive their assigned intervention is inappropriate; excluding participants solely because of missing outcomes is acceptable within D2. §5.3.1 distinguishes these situations.

evidence: Figure 1, p.88 identifies three technical-failure exclusions—2/34 Control and 1/34 RF. evidence: Figure 1, p.88 explicitly records two Control and three RF participants “lost to follow up”: at least 5/68, or 7.4%, lack follow-up data. guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §6.1.3.2 states that there is “no sensible threshold” applicable universally.

evidence: Article p.87, §2.8 and p.89, Table 2 report group comparisons without a missing-data correction or sensitivity analysis demonstrating robustness.

evidence: Figure 1, p.88 gives no reasons for the five losses beyond “lost to follow up.” Continuing pain or disability could affect attendance or willingness to provide scores; no documented outcome-independent explanation excludes that possibility.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Figure 1 shows similar loss proportions—2/34 versus 3/34—which argues against a pronounced differential-loss mechanism. However, reasons, timing, and preceding symptom trajectories are absent. The documents do not establish whether dependence on pain or disability was likely or unlikely.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible dependence from likely dependence using proportions, reasons, and circumstances. §1.1 supports NI when neither probability judgement is justified; Table 10 maps NI here to High.

evidence: Article Table 2, p.702: baseline RMDQ medians were both 15; pain was 6.7 versus 6.3. evidence: Article Figure 1, p.701: “new disc herniation” explains three losses in each arm; antibiotic losses also include side effects and new cancer. New herniation can directly relate to both disability and lumbar pain.

evidence: Article Figure 1, p.701: missingness differs between arms, 14.4% versus 6.9%, and includes outcome-related new herniation and differing reasons—four side-effect and two cancer losses only with antibiotics. guidance: Box 8, 3.4, reasons 1–3: differing missingness proportions, outcome-related reasons, and differing reasons between groups support likely dependence. §§6.1.4.1–6.1.4.2 distinguish this from proof of actual bias.

evidence: Figure 1 (p. 343) reports 15/90, 12/63, 18/87, 31/99, and 27/69 discontinuations. guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.” §§6.1.1 and 6.3: an ITT label or inclusion in analysis does not establish complete outcome ascertainment.

evidence: Classifying AE/inefficacy withdrawals as nonresponders retains them in the analysis, but does not demonstrate their actual week-13 pain response. guidance: Box 8, 3.2: evidence requires correction for bias or robustness under “a range of plausible assumptions.” §6.1.6: single imputation cannot be assumed to remove bias.

evidence: “Unsatisfactory response – efficacy” is a documented withdrawal reason (Figure 1, p. 343). Thus missing subsequent pain assessments could depend on pain response. AE-related withdrawal provides another health-related mechanism (p. 346).

evidence: Withdrawal proportions and reasons vary across groups: AE withdrawals were 5, 8, 7, 21, and 21; inefficacy withdrawals were 3, 1, 3, 1, and 0 (Figure 1). guidance: Box 8, 3.4, reasons 1–3: differing missingness proportions, outcome-related reasons, and differing reasons between groups support Y/PY. §6.1.4.2 discusses differential adverse-event and inefficacy withdrawal.

evidence: Participants recorded “overall pain over the last 24 hours” on a 0–10 NRS in electronic diaries; daily scores were averaged (p. 341). The response threshold was ≥50% reduction (p. 342). No evidence indicates an unsuitable measurement instrument.

evidence: Five multiply imputed datasets and repeated-measures models were used, and Little’s test was nonsignificant (P=.89). guidance: §6.1.6: multiple imputation does not remove bias unless outcome-dependent missingness is explained by measured variables. §6.1.7 requires sensitivity analyses to address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Most missing questionnaires followed early dropout. guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal potentially related to health status permits outcome-dependent missingness; exclusion requires documented reasons unrelated to outcome for all missing data.

evidence: Missingness was appreciably greater with placebo during treatment: day-6 data were missing for 9/24 versus 4/27. This differential dropout, alongside differing withdrawal trajectories, supports likely informative missingness. Against this concern, environmental dissatisfaction predominated and measured covariates/AEs did not significantly predict dropout; neither establishes independence from unobserved symptoms (A, pp. 284–286, Figure 2).
guidance: Box 8, 3.4, reason 1 identifies “differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data” as evidence; §§6.1.4.1 and 6.1.6 require consideration of outcome dependence despite modelling.

evidence: The CWS directly measures 19 withdrawal symptoms over the preceding 24 hours, each scored 0–10. guidance: Box 10, 4.1 identifies inappropriate methods through insensitivity or demonstrated poor validity; subjective measurement is not inherently inappropriate.

evidence: Both groups used the same CWS and daily assessment schedule, with the same symptom definitions (A, p. 283; Figure 2; S, eTable 1). Different completion rates concern missingness, not different measurement methods.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable measurement as the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points; §6.1 assigns missing measurements to D3.

evidence: Both groups used the same CWS, symptom groupings and daily assessment schedule (Article, p. 283; Figure 2, p. 286; Supplement, eTable 1). Unequal questionnaire completion is addressed in D3.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparability through the same methods and thresholds at comparable times; §6.1 addresses missing measurements separately.

evidence: The participants supplied the symptom ratings and were reportedly masked using matched placebo. Investigators and outcome assessors were also masked; reported intoxication and identification findings do not demonstrate failed masking (Article, pp. 283, 285).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: for participant-reported outcomes, “the outcome assessor is the study participant.” Probable assessor unawareness supports PN.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. Subjective CWS ratings could be influenced if assignment were known, but that hypothetical possibility does not establish awareness (Article, p. 283).
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI; §7.3 recognizes successful masking as protection against differential measurement error.

evidence: Not reached through 4.4; masking evidence is in Article, pp. 283 and 285.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The protocol is described as available on request, but is absent. The article supplies analysis methods and a registration identifier, not a dated plan verifying that these choices preceded access to unblinded outcomes (Article, pp. 281–284).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require intentions finalized before unblinded data were available; §8.3.1 calls for a confirming “date-stamp.”

evidence: Tables 2–3 report all listed symptom groupings, including nonsignificant findings, and eTable 1 explains their composition. This argues against selective measurement reporting. However, the complete intended set of eligible measurements and time summaries cannot be verified without prospective documentation (Article, pp. 286–288; Supplement, p. 3).
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI where intentions are unavailable or insufficient and multiple measurements are possible. Y/PY requires evidence of selection “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: Both adjusted and unadjusted results are disclosed. Depression becomes significant only after adjustment, but its nonsignificant unadjusted result remains available. Reporting both models argues against selective withholding; it does not verify all intended model, covariate and missing-data choices (Article, p. 284; Tables 2–3).
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when analysis intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible. §8.1.2 requires results-based selection, not merely multiple analyses.

evidence: Page 4, “Randomization and blinding”: “block randomization…four subjects per block,” performed by an “independent statistician.” These support intended randomization, but the random component used to order allocations within blocks is not described.
guidance: §4.3.1.1: when blocked allocation is reported “without an explicit statement that the order…within the blocks was random,” NI should generally be provided.

evidence: Page 4 reports an independent statistician, identical capsules, and blinding, but does not describe how forthcoming assignments were concealed from recruiters until enrollment and allocation. Independent sequence preparation does not establish independent control of allocation.
guidance: §4.1 distinguishes allocation concealment from subsequent blinding. Box 4, 1.2 requires concealment until assignment; §1.1 permits NI where details do not support PY or PN.

evidence: Page 6, Table 1 covers the ITT population: baseline pain was 7.78 versus 7.67, age 59.89 versus 58.56 years, and PDN duration 37.22 versus 35.32 months. Allocation was 55 versus 57 (page 4). The hypertension row has internally inconsistent counts/percentages/p-value, limiting certainty, but the available differences do not convincingly indicate failed randomization.
guidance: §4.3.3 requires assessment of all randomized participants. Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance” do not indicate bias; §4.3.3.2 requires substantial or implausible imbalances.

evidence: Page 4: “Trial participants…were unaware of treatment allocation until the end of the study”; capsules were “identical in appearance.” No reported evidence of participant unblinding.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding may prevent awareness; intervention-specific side effects can indicate awareness, but such recognition is not documented here.

evidence: Page 4 explicitly includes “treating physicians” among those unaware of allocation. Pages 6–7 report comparable adverse events, many attributed to pregabalin given in both groups; no personnel unblinding is reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding prevents awareness. Uncertainty about concealment in D1 is not evidence that allocation was actually disclosed.

evidence: Not reached: participants and treating physicians were reported blinded (page 4).
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask 2.3 only if either 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached; 2.3 is NA. Page 4 supplies the blinding evidence underlying this route.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask 2.4 only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached; 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask 2.5 only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Page 4: efficacy analyses included “all randomized patients”; all were entered in the final analysis despite nonadherence and withdrawal. Pages 4–5 report responder denominators of 57 and 55, matching randomized groups. LOCF addressed missing observations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 accepts ITT analyses. §6.1 assigns bias from missing data and procedures used to impute them to D3; nonadherence does not itself invalidate an assignment-effect analysis retaining randomized groups.

evidence: Not reached: all randomized participants were retained in their assigned-group analysis (pages 4–5).
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask 2.7 only if 2.6 is N/PN/NI.

evidence: Page 5, Fig. 1: six of 57 and five of 55 were lost to follow-up; only 101/112 completed treatment. Page 4 reports LOCF. Eleven missing week-8 outcomes are not negligible relative to the reported 27 versus 15 responders and could materially alter the comparison.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “imputed data should be regarded as missing data”; “nearly all” requires that missing outcomes could make no important difference. §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal percentage threshold.

evidence: Page 4 reports LOCF without sensitivity analyses or a justification establishing that it removes bias. Table 2 (page 6) shows pain continuing to change over follow-up, so stable outcomes after the last observation cannot simply be assumed.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: LOCF “should not be assumed to correct for bias.” §6.1.6 requires clear justification for low risk with single imputation.

evidence: Pages 4–5: missing outcomes followed nonadherence (four versus three) and intolerable adverse effects (two versus two). Nonadherence or withdrawal could relate to pain relief or continuing symptoms; reasons for nonadherence are not given.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” permits dependence on the true outcome. Not all reported reasons establish independence from pain response.

evidence: Fig. 1 (page 5) shows similar missingness proportions—10.5% versus 9.1%—and similar reason distributions. Page 7 identifies nausea/dizziness among withdrawal-related adverse effects; no withdrawals are explicitly attributed to inadequate pain relief or improvement. Outcome dependence remains possible, but the available pattern does not make it likely.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely…depended”; consider differences in proportions, reasons, and trial circumstances. Under §1.1, these details support a qualified judgement rather than NI; similar attrition does not establish absence of bias.

evidence: Page 3, “Efficacy assessment”: daily 0–10 pain NRS, weekly averages requiring at least four diary entries, and response defined by ≥50% reduction from baseline to week 8. No evidence indicates an unsuitable measurement instrument or insensitive range.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 targets methods unsuitable for the outcome, such as demonstrated poor validity or inability to detect relevant changes.

evidence: Page 3 describes the same diary procedure, assessment schedule, and ≥50% response threshold for both groups, with twice-weekly reminders to complete diaries.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses “the same measurement methods and thresholds…at comparable time points.”

evidence: Participants supplied the pain ratings (page 3), making them the relevant assessors. Page 4 explicitly states participants and outcome assessors remained unaware of allocation until study end; identical capsules support this.
guidance: §7.1 and Box 10, 4.3: for participant-reported outcomes, “the outcome assessor is the study participant”; answer N when assessors were blinded.

evidence: Not reached because the relevant assessors were blinded (pages 3–4). Pain’s subjective nature does not itself establish awareness.
guidance: Box 10 branching: ask 4.4 only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached; 4.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 10 branching: ask 4.5 only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Page 1 reports registration on 21 February 2021, before recruitment began in March 2021 (page 4). Pages 3–4 describe response and analysis methods, but no supplied dated registry contents, protocol, or SAP establish that this analysis was finalized before unblinded data became available.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” confirming prospective analysis intentions. Registration identification and retrospective article methods alone cannot verify the plan’s contents; §1.1 supports NI.

evidence: The week-8 ≥50% response definition in Methods (page 3) matches Results (pages 4–5), supporting consistency. However, without prospective intentions, it cannot be established whether this was the complete set of intended eligible response measurements or definitions. No affirmative evidence shows results-based selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 directs NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and the domain could be measured in more than one way. §8.3.2 permits comparison of Methods and Results, but consistency does not prove prospective specification.

evidence: Page 4 describes ITT, LOCF, and categorical testing; pages 4–5 give the responder result. No prospective plan establishes the intended responder analysis or missing-data strategy. Alternative analyses were possible, but the article does not demonstrate that multiple analyses were performed and selectively reported.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 explicitly includes different missing-data strategies and categorical cut-points; use NI when analysis intentions are insufficient. Y/PY requires evidence that selection was likely based on results.

evidence: Page 4 reports “block randomization…four subjects per block” by an independent statistician. This supports an intended random process, but does not specify random ordering within blocks or another random component.
guidance: §4.3.1.1 specifically recommends NI for blocked allocation reported “without an explicit statement that the order…within the blocks was random.”

evidence: Page 4 reports an independent statistician, identical capsules, and blinded participants/physicians. However, it does not establish who controlled access to forthcoming allocations or how enrollment preceded disclosure. I reconsidered whether independence justified PY, but the allocation procedure remains unspecified.
guidance: §4.1 distinguishes concealment from blinding. Box 4, 1.2 requires an allocation process controlled independently of enrollment personnel, or another adequate concealment procedure; §1.1 permits NI where PY/PN cannot reasonably be inferred.

evidence: Table 1, page 6: baseline pain 7.78 versus 7.67, age 59.89 versus 58.56, and PDN duration 37.22 versus 35.32 months. The hypertension row contains inconsistencies. Also, 57:55 allocation is not the exact balance expected from complete balanced blocks of four, but this small discrepancy does not establish prognostic selection or a substantial allocation imbalance.
guidance: §4.3.3 and Box 4, 1.3 require differences suggesting a randomization problem, rather than chance-compatible differences; §4.3.3.2 identifies “substantial differences” in group sizes and implausible prognostic imbalances.

evidence: Page 4 explicitly states participants were “unaware of treatment allocation until the end of the study”; capsules were identical in appearance. No recognized intervention-specific effects revealing assignment are reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 addresses awareness, including recognition of intervention-specific side effects. The reported blinding supports N.

evidence: Page 4 explicitly includes treating physicians among those unaware of allocation. Pages 6–7 describe comparable adverse events, many attributed to pregabalin received by both groups.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses personnel awareness. Unreported allocation-concealment details do not establish that concealment failed or personnel knew assignments.

evidence: Not reached because both participants and treating physicians were reported blinded (page 4).
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only if either 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached following 2.3 NA; page 4 provides the blinding evidence underlying this branch.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached following 2.4 NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Page 4 says efficacy analyses included “all randomized patients,” including those nonadherent or withdrawn. Responder denominators on pages 4–5 match randomized groups, 57 and 55. No exclusion or reassignment is identified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 accepts ITT analysis. §6.1 explicitly assigns bias introduced by imputation to missing outcome data, so LOCF does not independently invalidate D2.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is Y; pages 4–5 support retention of randomized participants in assigned groups.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.7 only if 2.6 is N/PN/NI.

evidence: Page 5, Fig. 1: six of 57 and five of 55 were lost to follow-up. Page 4 reports LOCF. Thus, inclusion of all 112 in the analysis does not mean all had observed week-8 outcomes. Eleven missing outcomes could materially affect the 27-versus-15 responder comparison.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.” “Nearly all” requires that missing outcomes could make no important difference; §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal percentage threshold.

evidence: Page 4 describes LOCF but no sensitivity analysis establishing robustness. Table 2, page 6, shows continuing pain improvement over time, undermining an unsupported assumption of unchanged outcomes after dropout.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: LOCF “should not be assumed to correct for bias.” §6.1.6 requires clear justification for low risk with single imputation.

evidence: Pages 4–5 attribute missingness to nonadherence and adverse effects. Reasons for nonadherence are not explained; continuing pain or perceived improvement could affect adherence and follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” permits dependence on the true outcome. Documented independence from pain response is absent.

evidence: Fig. 1, page 5: missingness was similar, 10.5% versus 9.1%, with nonadherence in four versus three and adverse-effect withdrawal in two versus two. Page 7 identifies nausea/dizziness; no withdrawal is explicitly attributed to pain improvement or lack of efficacy. This supports possible, rather than likely, dependence on pain response.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely…depended” using proportions, reasons, and circumstances. Similar patterns do not prove independence, but provide evidence supporting PN rather than an unsupported assumption of likely dependence.

evidence: Page 3: daily 0–10 pain NRS, weekly averages requiring at least four entries, and response defined as ≥50% reduction at week 8. No evidence establishes poor validity or inadequate sensitivity.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 targets unsuitable measurement methods, including demonstrated poor validity or inability to detect relevant changes.

evidence: Page 3 describes the same diary, averaging rule, response threshold, assessment schedule, and diary reminders for both groups.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable measurement as the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points.

evidence: Participants supplied pain ratings (page 3) and were explicitly blinded until study end (page 4). Identical capsules support the report; no evidence establishes unblinding.
guidance: §7.1 and Box 10, 4.3 identify the participant as assessor for participant-reported outcomes and direct N when assessors were blinded.

evidence: Not reached because participant-assessors were blinded (pages 3–4).
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI. Subjectivity alone does not activate this branch.

evidence: Not reached following 4.4 NA.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Registration reportedly preceded recruitment: 21 February 2021 (page 1), versus March 2021 (page 4). However, only the article is supplied; no dated registry contents, protocol, or SAP establish the prospective responder-analysis intentions.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires evidence that analysis intentions were finalized before unblinded data became available. A registration date alone does not verify those intentions.

evidence: The week-8 ≥50% definition in Methods (page 3) matches Results (pages 4–5), arguing against an obvious reporting discrepancy. Nevertheless, prospective intentions are unavailable and cannot establish the complete intended set of eligible response definitions or measurements.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 directs NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible. §8.3.2 allows Methods–Results comparison, but does not equate consistency with prospective specification.

evidence: Page 4 describes ITT, LOCF, and categorical tests. No prospective plan establishes the intended responder analysis or missing-data strategy. There is no evidence that competing analyses were performed and a favorable result selected.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 directs NI for insufficient analysis intentions; different missing-data strategies are eligible analytical alternatives. Y/PY requires evidence of likely selection based on results.

evidence: “A computerized random number generator” was used by a research nurse not otherwise involved in the study (p. 3, §2.3).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when a “random component” was used, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: Assignments were “concealed in envelopes,” with each participant choosing one of three after baseline assessment and consent (p. 3, §2.3). This supports attempted concealment, but opacity, sealing, and safeguards against identifying assignments are unreported. Independent sequence generation does not establish secure envelope handling.
guidance: §4.3.2 and Table 2 specify safeguards for envelope concealment; Box 4 permits judgement where details are incomplete. Under §1.1, NI applies when details do not support PY or PN. Missing safeguards in the report do not establish that concealment failed.

evidence: Tables 1–2 describe only the 53 analysed participants, rather than all 60 randomized (pp. 6–7; Figure 1, p. 4). Their characteristics show no compelling evidence of failed randomization, but cannot establish balance in the randomized population.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly permits NI for studies reporting “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis”; §4.3.3 requires assessment based on all randomized participants.

evidence: Although §2.3 says participants were blinded, treatment involved live video supervision, telephone-supported independent exercise, or usual care (pp. 3–5, §§2.3–2.5). Participants probably recognized the intervention they received; no credible masking procedure is described.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness “during the trial.” §5.1.3 states that an attempt at blinding “does not ensure successful blinding in practice.”

evidence: Therapists delivered real-time visual feedback in PT and daily telephone motivation/education in PE (pp. 4–5, §§2.5.1–2.5.2), necessarily distinguishing these assignments.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether “people delivering the interventions” were aware of assignment.

evidence: Surgery and postoperative rehabilitation were standardized (p. 3, §2.4). PT participants exercised more than PE participants (p. 10), and two discontinued because of intensity (p. 11), but these are consistent with ordinary adherence differences. Uncontrolled postoperative pain-medication use is acknowledged (p. 11), without evidence of trial-induced, non-protocol prescribing.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol changes; answer N/PN for non-adherence consistent with what could occur outside a trial. Lack of blinding alone is insufficient.

evidence: Not reached: 2.3=PN. The reported adherence differences do not establish qualifying trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6: 2.4 is asked only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached: 2.4=NA.
guidance: Box 6: 2.5 is asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Figure 1 identifies seven losses to follow-up and analyses of 18 PT, 17 PE, and 18 control participants; Table 2 uses those same groups (pp. 4, 7). This appears to be an available-case analysis retaining randomized assignments. No regrouping or exclusion of observed outcomes solely for non-adherence is reported.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 consider analyses “excluding participants with missing outcome data” appropriate for this domain; missing-data bias is assessed separately in D3.

evidence: Not reached: 2.6=PY.
guidance: Box 6: 2.7 is asked only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Only 53/60 participants (88.3%) contributed to the reported interaction. Losses were PT 2/20, PE 3/20, and control 2/20 (Figure 1, p. 4; Table 2, p. 7). Seven missing trajectories cannot reasonably be assumed incapable of materially affecting this small trial’s result.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” as missing outcomes that “could have made no important difference”; §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal numerical threshold.

evidence: The analysis section describes repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni testing, with no correction for informative missingness or sensitivity analysis (p. 6, §2.8). Table 2 reports n=53.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from methods correcting bias or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions.” No such evidence is supplied.

evidence: Losses involved intervention discontinuation, cancelled surgery, and a fall (Figure 1, p. 4). Discontinuation was attributed to high exercise intensity (p. 11). Exercise tolerance and a fall could relate to strength or functional status; surgery-cancellation reasons are unexplained.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: when withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome. These are not all documented outcome-independent losses.

evidence: PT losses followed inability or unwillingness to continue high-intensity exercise; a control loss followed a fall (pp. 4, 11). These reasons plausibly identify participants with different strength trajectories. Reasons also differed between groups, although total loss rates were fairly similar (10%, 15%, 10%).
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 identifies outcome-related reasons, differing reasons between groups, and trial circumstances as evidence supporting likely dependence. §6.1.4.2 explains why reasons matter beyond the proportions missing.

evidence: Strength was measured using a Biodex dynamometer, with reported reliability ICC 0.947–0.966, stabilization straps, joint-axis alignment, and averaging of three trials (p. 5, §2.6). Nothing indicates an unsuitable instrument or measurement range.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” such as poor validity or inadequate sensitivity. The reported method provides evidence against that concern.

evidence: A common dynamometry procedure and the same three assessment times are described for all groups; measurements occurred in an independent room (pp. 3, 5, §§2.3–2.6). No systematic difference in measurement procedures is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable assessment as the same methods used at “comparable time points.” Potential effects of awareness are considered separately below.

evidence: Examiners were explicitly unaware of allocation at every assessment (p. 3, §2.3). Nevertheless, this active strength test also involves the participant, who probably recognized video-supervised exercise, telephone-supported exercise, or usual care (pp. 4–5). Thus the participant–assessor measurement interaction was probably not fully blinded.
guidance: §7.3: for assessments involving participant–collector interaction, if either is unblinded, assessors should be considered aware “unless convincing evidence is available to the contrary.”

evidence: Dynamometry supplies an instrument-recorded torque value, but generating peak torque requires participant effort (p. 5, §2.6). Knowledge of treatment could influence that effort even when the examiner is blinded.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 asks whether knowledge “could” influence assessment. §7.3 requires consideration of the actual measurement interaction; an instrument reading does not eliminate participant-dependent influences.

evidence: Blinded examiners, standardized positioning, an independent assessment room, and averaging three trials reduce opportunities for differential measurement (pp. 3, 5). There is no reported differential encouragement or evidence of strong participant expectations affecting test effort. Possible influence is therefore not judged likely.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from influence judged likely. §7.3 directs consideration of assessor independence and conscious or subconscious expectations.

evidence: Registration was explicitly retrospective (p. 3, §2.2). The publication describes ANOVA (p. 6, §2.8), but no dated prospective analysis plan is available. Appendix A describes exercises, not analysis intentions.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available; §8.3.1 requires an appropriate “date-stamp.” A publication’s methods section cannot establish that timing.

evidence: For the specifically eligible 60°/s extension outcome, Table 2 reports all three stated measurement times and the joint interaction (p. 7; timing specified on p. 3). It also reports 180°/s extension. Although flexion was measured but not tabulated, flexion is outside this specified quadriceps-extension target. Prospective intentions remain unavailable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 restricts attention to measurements “eligible for consideration by the RoB 2 tool user.” §8.3.2 permits comparison of publication methods and results when prospective intentions are unavailable. Reporting all stated target time points supports PN rather than evidence of selection.

evidence: The reported interaction matches the repeated-measures ANOVA described in §2.8, and Table 2 also reports time and group effects (pp. 6–7). However, no prospective plan establishes whether other eligible models, adjustment strategies, or missing-data analyses were performed and selectively omitted.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when analysis intentions are unavailable or insufficient and there is “more than one way” to analyse the measurement. Statistical significance alone does not demonstrate selective reporting.

evidence: An independent research nurse used a “computerized random number generator” (p. 3, §2.3). Nothing contradicts random sequence generation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers,” supports Y.

evidence: Participants chose among three envelopes after consent and baseline assessment; assignments were described as “concealed in envelopes” (p. 3, §2.3). This supports attempted concealment, but opacity, sealing, and protection against identifying assignments are unspecified.
guidance: §4.3.2 and Table 2 give envelope safeguards. Box 4 permits PY/PN judgement with incomplete details, but §1.1 supports NI when neither inference is sufficiently supported. Missing reporting does not establish failed concealment.

evidence: Tables 1–2 report baseline characteristics for 53 analysed participants, not all 60 randomized (pp. 6–7; Figure 1, p. 4). Their apparent comparability is reassuring but incomplete.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly identifies studies reporting “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis” as a reason for NI; §4.3.3 calls for all randomized participants.

evidence: The statement that participants were blinded (p. 3) conflicts with readily distinguishable experiences: live video supervision, telephone-supported exercise, and usual care (pp. 4–5, §2.5). Participants probably recognized their treatment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness during treatment. §5.1.3: attempted blinding “does not ensure successful blinding in practice.”

evidence: Therapists provided video feedback in PT and daily telephone education/motivation in PE (pp. 4–5, §§2.5.1–2.5.2), necessarily knowing the intervention delivered.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among “people delivering the interventions.”

evidence: Postoperative care was standardized (p. 3, §2.4). More exercise in PT than PE (p. 10), intensity-related discontinuation (p. 11), and uncontrolled pain-medication use (p. 11) do not establish trial-context-induced departures from intended treatment. No compensatory treatment-seeking or deliberate unequal co-intervention is reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol changes. N/PN applies to ordinary non-adherence that could occur outside the trial.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; the reported adherence differences do not establish qualifying deviations.
guidance: Box 6: asked only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4=NA.
guidance: Box 6: asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Figure 1 labels seven participants as lost to follow-up and shows analyses of 18 PT, 17 PE, and 18 controls; Table 2 uses those groups (pp. 4, 7). There is no reported reassignment or exclusion of available outcomes solely because of non-adherence.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept analyses “excluding participants with missing outcome data” for this domain. Such missingness is assessed in D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=PY.
guidance: Box 6: asked only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Table 2’s interaction uses 53/60 randomized participants. Losses were 2/20 PT, 3/20 PE, and 2/20 controls (Figure 1, p. 4; Table 2, p. 7). Seven missing trajectories are not demonstrably immaterial.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by whether missing outcomes “could have made no important difference.” §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal percentage threshold.

evidence: §2.8 reports repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni testing, without a missingness correction or sensitivity analysis (p. 6); Table 2 reports n=53.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions.” No such evidence is available.

evidence: Losses followed exercise discontinuation, surgery cancellation, and a fall (Figure 1, p. 4). Discontinuation was “due to the high intensity” (p. 11). Exercise tolerance and falls can relate to strength; cancellation reasons are unspecified.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal potentially related to “participants’ health status” supports possible dependence on the true outcome. The losses are not all documented as outcome-independent.

evidence: Intensity-related withdrawal from the strengthening intervention and a control-group fall provide substantive reasons to expect different strength trajectories among some missing participants (pp. 4, 11). Reasons differ by group. Similar overall loss rates provide counterevidence, but do not neutralize those mechanisms.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 lists outcome-related reasons, different reasons between groups, and trial circumstances as grounds for Y/PY. §6.1.4.2 emphasizes the importance of differing reasons.

evidence: Biodex dynamometry used stabilization, joint-axis alignment, and averaging of three trials; reported reliability was ICC 0.947–0.966 (p. 5, §2.6). No evidence indicates unsuitable measurement.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” including poor validity or inadequate sensitivity.

evidence: The same measurement protocol and assessment schedule are described across groups, with measurements in an independent room (pp. 3, 5, §§2.3–2.6). No differential measurement procedure is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods and “comparable time points.” Awareness is addressed separately in subsequent questions.

evidence: Examiners were explicitly blinded at all assessments (p. 3, §2.3). However, participants actively generated the measured force and probably recognized their intervention (pp. 4–5). The measurement interaction was therefore probably not wholly blinded.
guidance: §7.3 says that for participant–collector interactions, assessors should be considered aware if either party is unblinded, “unless convincing evidence is available to the contrary.” This is an outcome-specific application, not automatic transfer from D2.

evidence: The dynamometer records torque objectively, but peak torque depends on participant effort during the test (p. 5, §2.6). Knowledge could affect test effort despite blinded recording.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 asks whether assessment “could” be influenced. §7.3 requires considering the measurement interaction; mechanical recording does not eliminate every participant-dependent influence.

evidence: Blinded examiners, standardized positioning, an independent room, and averaging three trials limit differential influence (pp. 3, 5). There is no reported differential encouragement or evidence that treatment expectations affected effort.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from influence judged likely. §7.3 identifies assessor independence and expectations as relevant considerations.

evidence: Registration was retrospective (p. 3, §2.2). The publication’s ANOVA description (p. 6, §2.8) has no demonstrated pre-unblinding date. No separate prospective analysis plan was supplied; Appendix A is an exercise protocol.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires intentions finalized before unblinded data were available. §8.3.1 calls for a confirming “date-stamp.”

evidence: Table 2 reports 60°/s extension values at all three stated times and their joint interaction (p. 7; schedule, p. 3). It also reports 180°/s extension. Unreported flexion measurements are outside this specified extension target. This supports PN despite unavailable prospective intentions.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 restricts assessment to measurements “eligible for consideration” by the assessor. §8.3.2 permits comparison of publication methods and results when prospective intentions are unavailable.

evidence: The interaction matches the described ANOVA, and Table 2 also reports time and group effects (pp. 6–7). Nevertheless, no prospective plan establishes whether alternative eligible models or missing-data analyses were undertaken and selectively omitted.
