Earlier versions and adequately detailed pre-unblinding intentions for these follow-up analyses are unavailable.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires evidence that intentions preceded availability of unblinded data; Box 11, 5.1 makes that timing essential. §1.1 supports NI where the available information cannot resolve it.

evidence: Follow-up through 12 months was planned and all scheduled time points are reported for pain and ODI (P pp.6,24; M Table 2). The plan allowed the single BPI item if highly correlated with the four-item mean; S2 p.4 reports approximately .90 correlations and explains the choice. ODI’s change from co-primary to secondary designation does not omit the targeted results (P pp.9,26; M p.16).
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection based on results, restricted to eligible measurements. §8.3.2 treats designation discrepancies as clues requiring assessment, not automatic proof of selection.

evidence: P pp.8–9 broadly specifies mixed models, adjustment and ITT/completer analyses. It does not fully specify the reported individual-follow-up change-score and bootstrap calculations (M p.16, Table 2; S2 p.6). There is insufficient information about alternative eligible analyses performed. The anomalous ODI “−0.23” entry alone does not show selective analysis reporting.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions lack sufficient detail and multiple analyses are possible; Y/PY requires evidence of selection “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: “Patients were randomized in blocks of 6” (p.228). The method generating the sequence or random order within blocks is absent.
guidance: §4.3.1.1: blocked allocation without confirmation of a random component should generally receive “No information.”

evidence: Assignment was “in a double-blind fashion,” with identical-looking capsules (p.228), but no central allocation, independently controlled dispensing, numbered containers, or equivalent concealment procedure is described.
guidance: §4.1 distinguishes allocation concealment from subsequent blinding; Box 4, 1.2 requires evidence of concealment until assignment. §1.1 permits NI when a probable answer cannot reasonably be inferred.

evidence: Table 2 includes all 25 randomized participants. Group sizes were 13 versus 12; baseline Likert scores were 6.45 versus 6.63 and VAS scores 58.9 versus 63.9. Age, BMI and race differences do not establish failed randomization in this small trial (p.229).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when observed imbalances are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 cautions that small trials can have appreciable chance imbalances.

evidence: The trial was double-blind, and zonisamide was double-encapsulated “so as to appear identical to the placebo” (p.228). One placebo participant opened the capsule and was withdrawn (p.230); adverse effects also occurred, but the report does not establish that participants learned their allocations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding can prevent awareness; side effects imply awareness when participants knew them to be specific to an intervention. That additional condition is not documented.

evidence: The double-blind design and matching capsules support probable staff blinding (pp.227–228). Staff monitored tolerability and adjusted doses, but no allocation disclosure or recognized intervention-specific toxicity is reported (pp.228, 230–231).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses actual or probable awareness, including toxicities personnel knew were intervention-specific; §5.1.3 cautions that “double blind” alone is imperfectly informative.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. Dose reduction for intolerance was expressly allowed (p.228); withdrawal and medication cessation are described on pp.230–232.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. It also specifies that toxicity-related cessation is not automatically a trial-context deviation.

evidence: No qualifying trial-context deviation identified through the applicable branch; see pp.228, 230–232.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached; the differing withdrawal rates in Figure 1 do not themselves activate this question (p.230).
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI; it concerns balance of qualifying deviations, not withdrawal rates generally.

evidence: ITT-E: included patients receiving drug with at least one efficacy evaluation, 11 versus 12 (p.228). The analysis included “each patient who had any treatment data” (p.229); no reassignment is reported. The two omissions appear to reflect unavailable efficacy data. Maintenance: inclusion required at least one maintenance week (p.228), excluding four zonisamide and one placebo participant whose efficacy data contributed to ITT-E (pp.230–231, Figure 3).
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept mITT exclusion for missing outcomes, assessed separately in D3. Analyses excluding eligible participants with available data after randomization are inappropriate for assignment effects.

evidence: ITT-E: included patients receiving drug with at least one efficacy evaluation, 11 versus 12 (p.228). The analysis included “each patient who had any treatment data” (p.229); no reassignment is reported. The two omissions appear to reflect unavailable efficacy data. Maintenance: inclusion required at least one maintenance week (p.228), excluding four zonisamide and one placebo participant whose efficacy data contributed to ITT-E (pp.230–231, Figure 3).
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept mITT exclusion for missing outcomes, assessed separately in D3. Analyses excluding eligible participants with available data after randomization are inappropriate for assignment effects.

evidence: ITT-E: not reached. Maintenance: excluding five additional participants changed the observed response comparison from 27% versus 0% to 43% versus 0%, with P changing from 0.09 to 0.04 (p.230; Figure 3, p.231). Selection depended on remaining through titration and was markedly unequal between groups.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact”; even small exclusions can matter when events are rare or exclusions relate to prognosis. Only three responders occurred.

evidence: ITT-E: not reached. Maintenance: excluding five additional participants changed the observed response comparison from 27% versus 0% to 43% versus 0%, with P changing from 0.09 to 0.04 (p.230; Figure 3, p.231). Selection depended on remaining through titration and was markedly unequal between groups.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact”; even small exclusions can matter when events are rare or exclusions relate to prognosis. Only three responders occurred.

evidence: Only 23/25 randomized participants had any efficacy evaluation; both absent participants were assigned zonisamide (p.228; Figure 1, p.230). Two unknown responses are material relative to three observed responders. Figure 3 additionally labels ITT as “analysis with imputation” (p.231). The five additional maintenance exclusions with earlier data are distinguished under D2.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: assess all randomized participants; for binary outcomes, completeness depends on missing numbers relative to events. “Imputed data should be regarded as missing data.”

evidence: LOCF is described on pp.228–229. Alternative population analyses are reported, but no sensitivity analysis tests plausible relationships between missingness and responder status. Figure 3's imputation description also leaves some ambiguity against the final-participation wording on p.230.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: LOCF “should not be assumed to correct for bias.” §6.1.7 requires sensitivity analyses addressing dependence of missingness on the true outcome.

evidence: Withdrawal included headache on day 2, rash, irritability/insomnia, other illness and death, alongside time constraints and a placebo protocol violation (p.230). Thus outcome availability could relate to health and treatment experience.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” dependence on the true outcome is possible.

evidence: Both participants without any efficacy evaluation were in the zonisamide arm; later attrition was also strongly unequal, with several drug-related withdrawals (Figure 1, p.230; pp.231–232). This supports probable informative missingness, although the report does not link both wholly absent evaluations individually to withdrawal reasons. Similar initial pain in zonisamide completers and noncompleters (p.229) does not establish similar subsequent responses.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 identifies unequal missingness proportions and differing withdrawal reasons as evidence supporting Yes/PY. §§6.1.4 and 6.1.6 explain why baseline similarity and earlier observations do not establish unbiased missing outcomes.

evidence: Daily VAS and Likert pain ratings were averaged weekly (pp.227–228); response was a ≥50% reduction, and both scales gave identical responder classifications (Figure 3, p.231). There is no evidence of an unsuitable instrument.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable collection methods, such as poor validity or inability to detect plausible effects; it does not judge whether the chosen outcome was sensible.

evidence: Both groups used the same daily logs, scales, assessment schedule and response threshold (Table 1, p.227; p.228; Figure 3, p.231). No separate ascertainment procedure by arm is described. Earlier final observations arose through withdrawal, whose consequences are considered in D3.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 assesses comparable “measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times. §7.3 targets systematic differences in collection or opportunities for detection.

evidence: Participants supplied the pain ratings and were therefore the assessors. Matching capsules and the double-blind design support probable lack of awareness (p.228). Capsule opening by one placebo participant and adverse effects create possible challenges, but do not demonstrate that allocation became known (pp.230–231).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: for participant-reported outcomes, “the outcome assessor is the study participant.” §§5.1.3 and 7.3 require considering whether blinding was compromised in practice.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. The endpoint is participant-reported pain (pp.227–228).
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI; subjectivity alone does not activate the question when assessors were probably blinded.

evidence: Not reached; no established awareness requiring assessment of its likely influence. See blinding methods, p.228.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The article explicitly calls this “a post hoc responder analysis” (p.230; also p.229). No dated analysis plan establishes that this analysis was finalized before unblinded results were available.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires analysis intentions finalized before availability of unblinded outcome data. Explicit post hoc designation supports N rather than merely NI.

evidence: Pain was collected using VAS, Likert and the Short Form McGill questionnaire at multiple times (pp.227–228). VAS and Likert yielded identical responder results (Figure 3), arguing against selection between those scales. However, no prospective specification establishes all eligible measurements or the intended responder time point.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: use NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible. Multiple measurements alone do not demonstrate result-based selection.

evidence: The ≥50% analysis was post hoc; continuous analyses and both responder populations were nevertheless reported, including nonsignificant results (pp.229–231). The article explains the cutoff as used in other pain studies (p.229). There is no record showing whether additional thresholds or analyses were tried and selectively omitted.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3: NI applies when analysis intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible. High risk requires evidence that a reported analysis was likely selected on the basis of its results, not simply that it was post hoc.

evidence: “Patients were randomized in blocks of 6” (p.228), without describing sequence generation or confirming random ordering within blocks.
guidance: §4.3.1.1: blocked allocation without an explicit random component generally warrants “No information.”

evidence: Double-blind assignment and matching capsules are reported (p.228), but allocation control, concealment procedures and who could access forthcoming assignments are absent.
guidance: §4.1 distinguishes concealment before assignment from subsequent blinding. Box 4, 1.2 requires evidence of concealment until enrolment and assignment.

evidence: Table 2 covers all 25 randomized participants. Allocation was 13 versus 12; baseline pain, age, BMI and demographic differences do not suggest a departure from chance in this small sample (p.229).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when differences are “compatible with chance.” §4.3.3.1 warns against interpreting ordinary small-trial imbalances as failed randomization.

evidence: Double-blinding was supported by capsules made to “appear identical” (p.228). One placebo participant opened a capsule and was withdrawn (p.230); this challenges blinding but does not establish knowledge of allocation. Adverse effects likewise do not establish recognized allocation.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: adverse effects justify awareness when participants knew them to be specific to an intervention. §1.1 permits a probable answer supported by the circumstances.

evidence: Double-blinding and matching capsules support probable personnel blinding (pp.227–228). Dose adjustments and adverse-event assessments occurred, but recognized allocation or code disclosure is not reported (pp.230–231).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness, including recognized intervention-specific toxicities. §5.1.3 cautions that the term “double blind” is imperfect evidence, considered here alongside matching capsules.

evidence: Not reached because both awareness answers are PN. Dose reduction for intolerance was permitted (p.228); the reported withdrawals do not themselves establish trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6: 2.3 applies only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. It expressly excludes ordinary toxicity-related cessation from automatically qualifying as a deviation.

evidence: Not reached; no qualifying deviation was established through 2.3. Intervention adjustments are described on pp.228 and 230.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only following Y/PY to 2.3.

evidence: Not reached. Unequal withdrawals in Figure 1 (p.230) are not automatically unequal trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only following Y/PY/NI to 2.4; the question concerns qualifying deviations.

evidence: ITT-E: included 23 participants with treatment and an efficacy evaluation (p.228); analysis covered “each patient who had any treatment data” (p.229), without reported reassignment. Maintenance: restricted analysis to participants providing a maintenance week, excluding four zonisamide and one placebo participant whose final-participation pain data contributed to ITT-E (pp.228, 230; Figure 3, p.231).
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept mITT exclusion because outcomes are missing, but reject post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants with available outcomes. The specified endpoint is final participation, not exclusively week 12.

evidence: ITT-E: included 23 participants with treatment and an efficacy evaluation (p.228); analysis covered “each patient who had any treatment data” (p.229), without reported reassignment. Maintenance: restricted analysis to participants providing a maintenance week, excluding four zonisamide and one placebo participant whose final-participation pain data contributed to ITT-E (pp.228, 230; Figure 3, p.231).
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept mITT exclusion because outcomes are missing, but reject post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants with available outcomes. The specified endpoint is final participation, not exclusively week 12.

evidence: ITT-E: not reached. Maintenance: five additional exclusions changed the response comparison from 27% versus 0% to 43% versus 0% (p.230). Their unequal distribution and dependence on continued participation can materially change the assignment-effect estimate.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact”; small numbers can matter for rare outcomes. The change in response proportion, rather than crossing P=0.05 alone, supports Y.

evidence: ITT-E: not reached. Maintenance: five additional exclusions changed the response comparison from 27% versus 0% to 43% versus 0% (p.230). Their unequal distribution and dependence on continued participation can materially change the assignment-effect estimate.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact”; small numbers can matter for rare outcomes. The change in response proportion, rather than crossing P=0.05 alone, supports Y.

evidence: Two of 25 randomized participants lacked any efficacy evaluation, both assigned zonisamide (p.228; Figure 1, p.230). Two unknown responses are not negligible against three observed responders. Figure 3 also labels ITT as using imputation (p.231). I do not count every withdrawal as missing at the stated final-participation endpoint or count the five available-data exclusions again here.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 assesses all randomized participants and relates missingness to event frequency; “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.” §6.1 separates unavailable outcomes from deliberate exclusions addressed in D2.

evidence: LOCF and alternative population analyses are reported (pp.228–230), but no analysis establishes robustness to plausible responder outcomes among participants with missing data. The Figure 3 imputation description does not resolve this (p.231).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: LOCF “should not be assumed to correct for bias.” §6.1.7 requires sensitivity analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Reported withdrawal reasons include early headache, rash, insomnia, other illness and death, alongside time constraints and a protocol violation (p.230). These circumstances permit a health-related missingness mechanism; the reasons for the two wholly absent evaluations are not individually identified.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” makes outcome-dependent missingness possible.

evidence: My earlier answer relied too heavily on all withdrawals. For this final-participation endpoint, many withdrawn participants supplied usable pain data. The report does not link the two wholly absent evaluations to individual withdrawal reasons or establish their relationship to pain response (pp.228–230). Both were in the active arm, but that alone does not establish the mechanism in these two people.
guidance: §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient evidence to justify a probable answer. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence. Table 10 explicitly includes NI at 3.4 on the High-risk route.

evidence: Daily VAS and Likert pain ratings were averaged weekly (pp.227–228). The ≥50% classifications agreed across both scales (Figure 3, p.231); there is no evidence of unsuitable measurement.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns unsuitable instruments, poor validity or insensitivity—not whether the chosen outcome or cutoff was desirable.

evidence: Both arms used the same daily logs, scales, scheduled assessments and responder threshold (Table 1, p.227; pp.228, 230–231). There is no separate arm-specific collection procedure. Different participation durations do not by themselves demonstrate different measurement procedures for this final-participation endpoint.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods, thresholds and timing; §7.3 targets systematic differences in ascertainment. Missing follow-up and imputation are separately addressed in D3.

evidence: Participants assessed their own pain. Matching capsules support probable blinding (p.228). Capsule opening and adverse effects are counterevidence to consider, but neither establishes that the pain assessors knew their allocations (pp.230–231).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: for participant-reported outcomes, “the outcome assessor is the study participant.” §7.3 requires assessment of actual or probable blinding.

evidence: Not reached after 4.3 PN. Pain is subjective (pp.227–228), but that does not establish awareness.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached; the matching-capsule evidence supports the preceding blinding branch (p.228).
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The analysis is explicitly “post hoc” (pp.229–230), strongly suggesting it was not prospectively fixed. However, the article does not specify exactly when it was formulated relative to access to unblinded data. My earlier definitive N overstated that timing evidence.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 specifically requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available. §1.1 distinguishes firm evidence from a probable judgement.

evidence: Multiple pain instruments and times were available (pp.227–228). Identical VAS and Likert responder classifications argue against selection between those scales (Figure 3), but prospective intentions are insufficient to establish the complete eligible measurement set.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible. Multiplicity alone does not establish selection based on results.

evidence: The post hoc cutoff and favorable discussion raise suspicion (pp.229–232). Against selective reporting, both responder analyses and nonsignificant continuous analyses are reported, and a rationale for ≥50% is given (pp.229–230). No document establishes that other eligible analyses were conducted and omitted because of their results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely result-based selection for Y/PY; it specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible. Post hoc analysis alone does not meet the High-risk criterion.

evidence: An independent pharmacist prepared a schedule that “randomly assigned the treatments in blocks of four to a consecutive series of numbers” (A, p557, Randomisation and masking).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when “a random component was used”; §4.3.1 accepts randomized blocked allocation.

evidence: Allocation followed a centralized schedule controlled by an independent pharmacist with no other study role; the code remained sealed until study end. Site pharmacists supplied indistinguishable preparations (A, pp556–557).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: centrally administered allocation controlled independently of enrolment personnel qualifies. §4.3.2: fixed blocks threaten concealment when preceding allocations are known; masking protected them here.

evidence: Table 1 shows broadly comparable characteristics, including baseline pain 6.5 versus 6.4, but describes only the 66 analysed participants, not all 68 randomized. Baseline information for the two excluded placebo participants is absent (A, pp558–559, Figure 1 and Table 1).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: NI applies when studies report “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis.” §4.3.3 requires assessment based on all randomized participants; observed chance-compatible differences do not establish faulty randomization.

evidence: Participants received “transparent and indistinguishable” solutions (A, p557). Treatment guesses reflected perceived improvement; no participant attributed identification to skin changes or injection pain (A, p562).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns actual awareness. §5.1.3 cautions that successful guessing can reflect efficacy “even when the blinding has been preserved.”

evidence: Pharmacists prepared syringes so injecting physicians “would not recognise the treatment”; investigators were masked (A, p557). No distinguishing skin changes were reported (A, pp562, 564). Pharmacists had no other trial role.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding can prevent personnel awareness; intervention-specific adverse effects would support awareness. Such distinguishing effects were not reported here.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. Withdrawal and missed second administrations are documented in Figure 1 (A, p558), but do not independently activate this question.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2.”

evidence: Not reached; 2.3 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached; 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: The responder analysis retained 34 versus 32 participants in their assigned groups, including those missing the second administration, using LOCF. Two randomized placebo participants were excluded after immediate withdrawal or failure to provide any pain diaries (A, pp558–559; S, p9). This appears to be missing-data exclusion, with no reported exclusion of observed responder outcomes because of nonadherence.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept “mITT analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data.” §6.1 assigns missing outcomes and imputation to D3. The article’s ITT label alone is insufficient (§1.3.1).

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is PY.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.7 only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Only 52/68 randomized participants completed follow-up: 29/34 active and 23/34 placebo. The reported 34/32 analysis denominators include imputation, not complete observed 24-week outcomes (A, pp558–559). S, p14 confirms missingness concentrated near week 24. The exact observed responder-data count is not separately tabulated.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.” For binary outcomes, missingness must be judged relative to event numbers; these losses are material relative to 15 ≥50% responders and 30 ≥30% responders.

evidence: LOCF was used for these secondary outcomes (A, p558). Supporting sensitivity analyses concern the continuous primary outcome, not either responder proportion (S, pp12–13). S, p14 claims MAR because baseline variables did not predict missingness, but this does not establish independence from unobserved subsequent pain. No responder-specific robustness analysis is supplied.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: LOCF “should not be assumed to correct for bias.” §6.1.7 requires sensitivity analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome; §6.1.6 explains limitations of imputation.

evidence: “Absence of efficacy” accounted for three active-group and seven placebo-group withdrawals across follow-up (A, p558, Figure 1). Three placebo participants classified as having ≥30% worsening “stopped the study prematurely” (S, p9).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: health-related withdrawal can make missingness depend on the true outcome. §6.1.4.2 specifically identifies “lack of efficacy” as outcome-related.

evidence: Efficacy-related withdrawals directly implicate pain response, and follow-up losses were greater with placebo: nine of 32 treated placebo participants versus five of 34 active participants, plus two initial placebo exclusions (A, pp558–559). S, p14 also reports more missing data with placebo. Other reasons—painful injections and one death—do not explain away the efficacy-related losses.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4, reasons 1–3: differing missingness proportions, outcome-related reasons, and differing reasons between groups support likely dependence. The supplied analyses do not demonstrate that this dependence was removed.

evidence: Pain was recorded each morning on the Brief Pain Inventory’s 0–10 numerical scale and summarized into weekly means; responder thresholds were reductions from baseline (A, p557; S, p9). No evidence indicates an unsuitable instrument.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 asks whether measurement is inappropriate, such as poor validity or inability to detect plausible effects; subjectivity alone is not inappropriateness.

evidence: Both groups used the same diaries, weekly averaging, baseline comparison, thresholds, and 24-week assessment (A, p557; S, p9). No differential ascertainment procedure is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses “the same measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times.

evidence: Participants—the assessors of their own pain—were masked with indistinguishable injections. Correct guesses were based on improvement, while many active participants guessed placebo; no identifying skin changes were reported (A, pp557, 562, 564).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: for participant-reported outcomes, “the outcome assessor is the study participant.” §5.1.3 cautions against interpreting efficacy-based guesses as demonstrated unblinding; §7.3 considers whether masking was successfully implemented.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. Pain could be influenced by treatment knowledge, but credible masking prevents this branch from being reached.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached; 4.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: No dated protocol or SAP is supplied. The article describes both responder thresholds, but cannot establish when these analysis intentions were finalized (A, pp557–559). R lists a 2016 update after January 2014 completion; the supplied record does not provide historical versions establishing prespecification.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” confirming intentions preceded unblinded data. §8.3.2 and Box 11, 5.1 require sufficient detail to verify the plan, rather than inferring its timing from published methods.

evidence: Both thresholds listed in the article’s methods are reported, including the nonsignificant ≥50% result (A, pp557, 560; S, p9), which weighs against selective measurement reporting. However, R’s “pain relief scale” at 24 weeks does not specify these diary-derived definitions, and the complete prospective set of eligible measurements cannot be verified.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: NI when analysis intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible. §8.3.2 permits comparison of methods and results, but their consistency does not establish the missing prospective detail.

evidence: Both responder proportions are presented, and the appendix labels additional 70% relief/worsening analyses post hoc (S, p9). Nevertheless, no prospective plan establishes all intended responder analyses or missing-data strategies. The additional imputation analyses address continuous pain, not these proportions (S, pp12–13).
guidance: Box 11, 5.3: NI when intentions are insufficiently detailed and multiple analyses are possible; examples include different cut-points and missing-data strategies. Multiplicity alone does not establish results-based selection.

evidence: An independent pharmacist prepared a schedule that “randomly assigned the treatments in blocks of four” (A, p557). This describes randomized ordering, although the particular random-number generator is unspecified.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 requires “a random component”; §4.3.1 accepts random allocation within blocks.

evidence: Centralized allocation was controlled by an independent pharmacist; the allocation code remained sealed until study end, and site pharmacists supplied indistinguishable preparations (A, pp556–557). The envelope held the code; it was not described as the participant-enrolment allocation mechanism.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 accepts centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel. §4.3.2 identifies predictability from fixed blocks when preceding allocations are known; masking protected those allocations here.

evidence: Table 1 describes 34 active and 32 placebo participants, whereas 34 per group were randomized. Their measured characteristics are broadly comparable, but baseline data for the two excluded placebo participants are absent (A, pp558–559, Figure 1 and Table 1).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 specifies NI for studies reporting “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis.” §4.3.3 says assessment should use all randomized participants; chance-compatible differences do not establish a problem.

evidence: Solutions were “transparent and indistinguishable.” Participants’ treatment guesses reflected perceived improvement; none identified active treatment from skin changes or injection pain (A, pp557, 562).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness. §5.1.3 states that successful guessing can occur “even when the blinding has been preserved.”

evidence: Syringes were prepared so injecting physicians “would not recognise the treatment”; investigators were masked. Pharmacists had no other study role, and assessors reported no identifying skin changes (A, pp557, 562).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among carers and intervention providers, including awareness through distinctive adverse effects. Such distinguishing effects were not reported.

evidence: Not reached because both awareness questions are PN. Missed administrations are documented, but do not independently establish trial-context deviations (A, p558, Figure 1).
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.3 is NA; no separate assessment of the documented missed administrations is required here.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: The responder analysis retained participants missing the second administration in their assigned groups. The two initial placebo exclusions followed immediate withdrawal and failure to provide any pain diaries (A, pp558–559; S, p9). Missing outcome data are the most plausible explanation; no exclusion of available responder outcomes because of nonadherence is reported. This remains an inference, hence PY.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 accept mITT analyses excluding missing outcomes. §6.1 places missing outcomes and their imputation in D3. An ITT label alone does not establish appropriateness (§1.3.1).

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is PY.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.7 only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Only 52/68 randomized participants completed the study: 29 active and 23 placebo (A, pp558–559). LOCF supported the 34/32 analysis denominators. Exact observed week-24 responder-data counts are not separately reported, but S, p14 confirms missingness concentrated late in follow-up. Completion counts support substantial missingness; they are not themselves an exact pain-data inventory.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.” For binary outcomes, judge missingness against event frequency; these losses are not negligible relative to the responder counts.

evidence: The strongest evidence against bias is agreement across imputation methods, but those analyses concern the continuous primary outcome, not either responder proportion (S, pp12–13). evidence: R lists 36-month and five-year outcome horizons; B, p.651, calls time to death prespecified and describes ITT, Kaplan–Meier and Cox methods, consistent with A, p.4530. However, the available registry snapshot does not establish the historical timing of these specifications. S, dated 4 January 2021, only addresses pandemic-related surgical delays and promises “appropriate statistical procedures”; it is not a detailed plan for the target long-term mortality analysis. A sufficiently detailed plan demonstrably finalized before unblinded outcomes is absent.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” confirming finalization before unblinded data were available. Box 11, 5.1 requires accordance with that plan; §1.1 supports NI when available detail cannot establish either probable answer.

evidence: B, p.651 specifies time to death; R, Registered outcomes, includes five-year follow-up. A, p.4533, Table 4 reports all-cause mortality at extended follow-up, with the same outcome also reported in the earlier publication, including its then non-significant finding (B, p.656). Thus mortality was not introduced only after becoming significant. Exact prospective specification of the extended reporting cutoff is not established, but the available evidence does not suggest selection of a favourable mortality definition or time point.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results” from eligible measurements. §8.3.2 permits inference by comparing reports and requires explaining inferences from incomplete intentions.

evidence: A, p.4530 reports ITT Cox analysis of time-to-event secondary outcomes, consistent with B, p.651. This consistency argues against obvious analysis switching. Nevertheless, R and S do not sufficiently specify the intended long-term mortality analyses, adjustment choices or censoring strategy to establish whether all eligible intended analyses were reported. No direct evidence establishes result-driven selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 explicitly directs NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and “there is more than one way” to analyse the outcome. Multiple possible analyses alone do not establish selective reporting.

evidence: ER, p.650: allocation was “computer-generated,” stratified by centre, using a “permuted-block sequence with variable block size.” This directly establishes a random component.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: Yes when sequence generation uses a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: ER, p.650: eligibility assessment preceded assignment through a “web-based interactive response system.” Concealment is probable, although operator independence and access safeguards are not explicitly described. Variable block sizes reduce predictability.
guidance: §4.3.2/Table 2 identify central allocation as adequate; Box 4, 1.2 includes internet-based randomization services. §1.1 permits probable answers based on justified inference.

evidence: LT, p.4530, Table 2: 78 versus 79 participants; modest age imbalance (P=.02), haemoglobin imbalance (P=.01), and diabetes difference (P=.07), among numerous baseline comparisons. These do not establish differences clearly beyond chance. Time to surgery is post-randomization despite its placement in this table.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: a small number of conventionally significant differences should usually be considered “compatible with chance.”

evidence: REG, Design/Masking: “Masking: NONE”; LT, p.4527 describes an open-label trial. Participants knew whether they were assigned early surgery or watchful waiting.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants knew their assigned intervention.

evidence: REG, Design/Masking, and LT, p.4527: no masking in a surgical versus conservative treatment trial. Intervention providers knew assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among carers and intervention providers.

evidence: ER, p.650, Figure 1 records infections, refusal, death and lost contact among six patients not initially receiving surgery. ER, p.651 and LT, p.4531, Table 3 establish that later conservative-group surgery followed clinical indications. LT, p.4534 acknowledges pandemic-related surveillance changes and delays; AM, p.2 documents anticipated COVID-related delays. These are substantive care changes, but their reported circumstances support ordinary clinical/pandemic causes, without evidence that trial engagement or personnel undermining the protocol caused them.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Yes/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” deviations arose because of trial context; No/PN applies to changes consistent with the protocol or “what could occur outside the trial context.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN. Potential clinical consequences of the changes described in LT, p.4534 do not independently activate this question.

guidance: Box 6, 2.5: “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

guidance: Box 6, 2.6 considers ITT appropriate; §5.3.1 assigns missing-outcome bias separately to D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y; LT, p.4530 and Figure 3 support analysis by randomized assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

Table 4, p.4533 records 40 deaths: 13 versus 27. One unresolved participant among 157, relative to these event counts, supports “nearly all”; the missingness reason remains unknown. The separate assertion of complete three-year follow-up does not establish complete long-term follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by potential impact and notes that bias is necessarily small when observed events greatly exceed missing participants. §6.1.5 counts loss-related censoring as missing data.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=Y. No missing-data sensitivity analysis is claimed as justification; the decision rests on the limited missingness reported in LT, p.4531.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: “If N/PN/NI to 3.1”; §6.3(1) allows stopping when all/nearly all outcomes are available.

guidance: Box 8, 3.3: “If N/PN to 3.2.”

guidance: Box 8, 3.4: “If Y/PY/NI to 3.3.”

evidence: LT, p.4528: visits or telephone contact identified events, medical records were requested and reviewed, and events were adjudicated. These methods are suitable for determining all-cause death.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome they are intended to evaluate.”

evidence: LT, p.4528 describes common follow-up and event-review procedures. No differential death-ascertainment method is reported. Surgical patients had additional encounters, but death was actively followed in both groups; pandemic-related difficulties detecting symptoms do not establish differential detection of death.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 considers comparable methods/timing and whether extra encounters create additional opportunities to identify the assessed outcome.

evidence: LT, p.4528: DSMB members “were not blinded to the treatment allocation during events review.” Their independence does not establish blinding.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 asks whether outcome assessors were aware of the intervention received.

evidence: The target is all-cause death, reported in LT, Figure 3 and Table 4, pp.4532–4533. Knowing allocation could affect cause-of-death attribution, but does not plausibly change determination that death occurred here.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 and §7.1, outcome type 2: knowledge is unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes without judgement, “for example all-cause mortality.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.4=N.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5: “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: ER, p.651 calls time to death prespecified and describes ITT/Kaplan–Meier/Cox methods consistent with LT, p.4530. REG includes five-year outcomes. However, ER is already a results report, and the supplied registry snapshot lacks historical versions establishing when the relevant specifications were entered. AM, dated 4 January 2021, addresses surgical delays and promises “appropriate statistical procedures”; it does not specify the target mortality analysis. A sufficiently detailed plan demonstrably finalized before unblinded outcome access is unavailable.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires confirmation that analysis intentions preceded unblinded outcome data; Box 11, 5.1 requires analysis according to such a plan. §1.1 supports NI when neither probable answer is adequately supported.

evidence: ER, p.651 identifies time to death, and p.656 reports the earlier non-significant mortality finding. REG includes five-year follow-up; LT, Table 4 reports extended all-cause mortality. These support continuity of the outcome and argue against selecting mortality only after significance emerged. The exact prospective cutoff remains insufficiently documented, so this is a probable inference, not proof of complete prespecification.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results” from eligible measurements. §8.3.2 permits comparisons across reports and requires explaining inferences from incomplete intentions.

evidence: ER, p.651 and LT, p.4530 describe consistent ITT survival methods, which argues against obvious switching. Nevertheless, REG and AM do not establish sufficiently detailed intended analyses for this long-term mortality result to verify selection among adjustment, censoring or other analytical alternatives. No evidence demonstrates result-driven selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 explicitly specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and more than one analysis is possible; High requires evidence of likely result-based selection.

evidence: Article p.2 reports random assignment using “permuted blocks of three,” stratified by baseline proteinuria; Supplement p.8 confirms permuted-block randomization. This explicitly describes a random allocation method.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when “a random component was used”; §4.1.1 describes random ordering within blocks.

evidence: Treatment assignments were maintained by the Interactive Response System (Supplement p.8). Investigators contacted the IRS after confirming eligibility (Protocol p.48, §3.5). Central assignment and subsequent masking protected concealment; fixed blocks alone do not establish predictability.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: centrally administered allocation supports Yes. §4.3.2 identifies prediction concerns when recruiters know block boundaries and previous allocations are revealed.

evidence: Article p.4, Table 1 shows differences: baseline UPCR 1.55 versus 1.97 g/g, median eGFR 68 versus 47, and male participants 59% versus 33% (cemdisiran versus placebo). Blood pressure also differed. These merit consideration, but the small sample and 22:9 allocation provide no convincing evidence of differences beyond chance or manipulated assignment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias”; small trials can have substantial chance imbalances.

evidence: “All site personnel and patients were blinded” through week 36; packaging was identical and syringes masked (Supplement p.8). Home self-administration could omit syringe masking, but its actual use or resulting unblinding is not reported. Injection-site reactions occurred in both groups, 41% versus 22% (Article p.6), without evidence participants recognized treatment-specific reactions.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 and §5.1.3: assess actual awareness and potentially recognizable treatment-specific effects; attempted blinding alone is not conclusive. §1.1 permits a qualified judgement using PY/PN.

evidence: Supplement p.8 reports blinded site personnel and masked syringes for administration. Protocol p.48 explicitly leaves sponsor personnel unblinded, but does not identify those personnel as treating carers or intervention deliverers. The home-administration exception creates uncertainty, without evidence of actual awareness among carers.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns “carers and people delivering the interventions.” Sponsor awareness is not automatically awareness among these groups.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are both PN. Treatment interruptions for adverse events are described in Article p.6, but do not themselves establish deviations caused by trial participation.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. Protocol-consistent treatment changes are not qualifying deviations.

evidence: Not reached; 2.3 is NA.

evidence: Not reached; 2.4 is NA.

evidence: Article p.3 defines the mITT population and states: “Patients were grouped by their assigned treatment at randomization.” Figure 2A, p.5, shows all 31 participants had post-baseline UPCR observations. Safety denominators also include all 31 treated participants (Table 2, p.8), so the dose requirement did not exclude randomized participants. Supplement p.9 states that data collected after discontinuation were included.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT and mITT analyses excluding only missing outcomes are appropriate for this domain; missing-outcome bias belongs in D3.

evidence: Article p.5, Figure 2A, visually checked, reports week-32 counts of 22/22 cemdisiran and 8/9 placebo, or 30/31 (96.8%). Supplement p.9 says missing values were not routinely imputed. One missing observation is 11.1% of the small placebo group, warranting caution, but the near-complete continuous outcome supports a qualified “nearly all” judgement. Counts for spot UPCR or eGFR are not substituted for this result.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: for continuous outcomes, “availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient”; imputed outcomes count as missing. §6.1.3.2 cautions that this is not a universal threshold.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1 is PY. Supplement pp.11–12 describes sensitivity methods but does not provide numerical sensitivity results establishing robustness to missingness. This judgement does not assume that MMRM removes missing-data bias.
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.2 only if 3.1 is N/PN/NI. §6.1.6 does not treat repeated-measures methods as automatic protection against informative missingness.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1 is PY. The report does not explicitly link the one missing week-32 24-hour UPCR observation to a specific reason.
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.3 only if 3.2 is N/PN.

evidence: Not reached under the preceding answers.
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.4 only if 3.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Twenty-four-hour samples were analyzed centrally (Article p.2). Baseline and week-32 UPCR averaged two valid collections; collection duration was 22–26 hours with no missed voids (Supplement p.10). The removed creatinine criterion had incorrectly rejected valid samples; the protocol explains why UPCR protects against collection variability (Protocol p.171). These changes do not demonstrate an inappropriate measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1: concerns require an unsuitable measurement method, such as poor validity or inadequate sensitivity. §7.3 distinguishes measurement suitability from whether the outcome is a suitable surrogate.

evidence: Both groups followed the same scheduled collection, validity and central-laboratory procedures (Article p.2; Supplement pp.8–10). The sample-validity amendment applied generally (Protocol pp.171, 183). No systematic difference in collection or ascertainment between groups is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses “the same measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times.

evidence: Site personnel and participants were blinded (Supplement p.8), but the supplied documents do not explicitly establish the central laboratory assessors’ masking status. Sponsor personnel were unblinded (Protocol p.48); neither fact establishes laboratory awareness.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 requires assessment of outcome-assessor awareness. §1.1 reserves NI for details insufficient to support a reasonable PY/PN judgement.

evidence: UPCR is a quantitative central-laboratory result, with standardized collection-validity criteria (Article p.2; Supplement p.10). Laboratory knowledge of assignment would be unlikely to alter this measurement materially; the participants and site personnel involved in collecting specimens were reportedly blinded.
guidance: §7.1, outcome type 2, and Box 10, 4.4: observer-reported outcomes without substantive judgement are unlikely to be influenced by treatment knowledge.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is PN.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The reported log-scale MMRM matches SAP §7.1 (pp.19–20). However, SAP amendment 1, dated 29 April 2021 (p.36), changed the covariance structure to unstructured (p.62); amendment 2 is dated 31 March 2022 (p.3). Sponsor personnel were unblinded, and informal sponsor data looks were planned (pp.10, 16). The documents do not establish that the final relevant analysis choices preceded access to unblinded outcomes. Matching the final SAP therefore does not establish prospective finalization.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1: finalization “must precede availability of unblinded outcome data”; dated amendments and their timing must be considered. §1.1 supports NI where that timing cannot be determined.

evidence: Protocol amendment 3 exchanged total urine protein and UPCR as primary/secondary outcomes. It explicitly explains that UPCR “protects against variability from collection factors” after removal of inappropriate creatinine-validity criteria (Protocol p.171). The article reports both 24-hour and spot UPCR, and total protein is reported in Supplement Table 2, p.19. The specified week-32 24-hour UPCR result is therefore unlikely to represent selection of a favorable measurement.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 permits N/PN when an inconsistency has an explanation unrelated to the results; assessment is restricted to eligible measurements. §8.3.2 recognizes legitimate protocol changes.

evidence: Article p.3 and Supplement p.10 report the primary MMRM specified in SAP pp.19–20. The covariance change has an explicit methodological rationale: only two post-baseline assessments (SAP p.62). Rank and missing-data sensitivity analyses were planned, but their numerical results are absent; the latter was conditional on missingness (Supplement pp.11–12). This limits verification, but there is no evidence the primary estimate was chosen because alternative analyses were less favorable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely selection “on the basis of the results,” rather than merely multiple possible analyses. §8.3.2 allows legitimate explained changes; §1.1 permits PN based on the available evidence.

evidence: Article p.2 specifies random assignment using “permuted blocks of three”; Supplement p.8 confirms permuted-block randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: Yes when “a random component was used”; §4.1.1 describes random ordering within blocks.

evidence: Assignments were maintained by the IRS (Supplement p.8). Investigators contacted it after confirming eligibility (Protocol p.48, §3.5). Small fixed blocks create a theoretical predictability concern, but previous allocations were masked and no foreknowledge is reported.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 accepts central allocation. §4.3.2 identifies predictability when recruiters know block boundaries and allocations are revealed after assignment.

evidence: Article p.4, Table 1 shows differences in UPCR, eGFR, sex and blood pressure: for example, mean UPCR 1.55 versus 1.97 g/g and median eGFR 68 versus 47, cemdisiran versus placebo. These are meaningful prognostic differences, but do not convincingly exceed chance expectations in 31 participants or indicate manipulated allocation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias”; small trials can have substantial chance imbalances.

evidence: Supplement p.8 reports blinded participants, identical packaging and masked syringes. Protocol p.48 acknowledges visual differences and permits unmasked home self-administration; actual use or resulting awareness is not reported. Injection-site reactions occurred in both groups (Article p.6). These qualifications support PN rather than definite N.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 considers actual awareness and recognizable treatment-specific effects. §5.1.3 states that attempted blinding does not ensure successful blinding; §1.1 permits qualified inference.

evidence: Site personnel were reportedly blinded and administration syringes masked (Supplement p.8). Sponsor personnel were unblinded (Protocol p.48), but are not identified as the treating carers or intervention deliverers. The home-administration exception remains a limitation, without documented awareness among carers.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns “carers and people delivering the interventions”; sponsor awareness alone does not establish awareness in those groups.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. Adverse-event treatment interruptions are reported (Article p.6), but their occurrence does not establish trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. Protocol-consistent changes, including toxicity-related cessation, are not qualifying deviations.

evidence: Not reached; no qualifying deviations were established through 2.3. See Supplement p.8 and Article p.6.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA; the reported interruptions do not activate this branch (Article p.6).
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Article p.3 states participants were grouped by assigned treatment. Although mITT required dosing and a post-baseline assessment, the treatment denominators and Figure 2A establish that all 31 randomized participants received treatment and contributed post-baseline UPCR data (Article pp.5, 8). Post-discontinuation observations were included (Supplement p.9).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 accept ITT and mITT analyses excluding only missing outcomes. The dose requirement would matter if it actually excluded eligible randomized participants.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is Y; no exclusion or regrouping requiring this assessment was identified (Article pp.3, 5, 8).
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.6 is N/PN/NI.

evidence: Figure 2A reports week-32 24-hour UPCR data for 22/22 cemdisiran and 8/9 placebo, totaling 30/31, 96.8% (Article p.5). Routine imputation was not used (Supplement p.9). The single missing placebo observation represents 11.1% of that arm, so the pooled percentage is not conclusive; nevertheless, near-complete ascertainment of this continuous outcome supports PY.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “availability of data from 95% … will often be sufficient” for continuous outcomes. §6.1.3.2 warns that there is no universal threshold.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1 is PY. Supplement pp.11–12 describes sensitivity methods without numerical results demonstrating robustness to informative missingness; these are not being used to justify Low.
guidance: Box 8: ask only if 3.1 is N/PN/NI. §§6.1.6–6.1.7 do not treat MMRM or a planned sensitivity analysis as automatic evidence against bias.

evidence: Not reached. Article pp.3 and 5 do not explicitly link the single missing week-32 UPCR observation to a particular reason; later deaths cannot automatically be assigned as its cause.
guidance: Box 8: ask only if 3.2 is N/PN.

evidence: Not reached under the preceding answers; the arm-specific counts are reported in Article p.5, Figure 2A.
guidance: Box 8: ask only if 3.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Central-laboratory measurement used the average of two valid baseline and week-32 collections, with duration and missed-void criteria (Article p.2; Supplement p.10). Removing creatinine-based validity criteria was justified because they rejected valid samples; UPCR addressed collection variability (Protocol p.171). This does not demonstrate an unsuitable measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 requires evidence of inappropriate measurement, such as poor validity or inadequate sensitivity. §7.3 distinguishes measurement validity from the choice of surrogate outcome.

evidence: Both groups followed the same collection schedule, validity rules and central analysis (Article p.2; Supplement pp.8–10). The amendment applied generally (Protocol pp.171, 183); no treatment-dependent measurement change is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable methods use the same methods and thresholds at comparable times.

evidence: Participants and site personnel were blinded, but central-laboratory assessor masking is not explicitly documented (Article p.2; Supplement p.8). Unblinded sponsor personnel do not establish laboratory awareness (Protocol p.48).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 concerns the outcome assessors specifically. §1.1 supports NI when the evidence cannot reasonably establish awareness or unawareness.

evidence: This is a quantitative central-laboratory result with standardized collection rules; collection participants and site staff were reportedly blinded (Article p.2; Supplement pp.8–10). Material influence from laboratory knowledge of treatment is unlikely.
guidance: §7.1, outcome type 2, and Box 10, 4.4: observer-reported outcomes without substantive judgement are unlikely to be influenced by treatment knowledge.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is PN; the relevant measurement procedures are in Article p.2 and Supplement p.10.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The reported analysis matches SAP pp.52–53, dated 29 April 2021. However, the pre-enrolment protocol specified a baseline-adjusted linear primary analysis, with MMRM as sensitivity analysis (Protocol p.253, dated 20 September 2019). Subsequent plans changed the analysis and covariance structure. Sponsor personnel were unblinded and informal sponsor data looks were planned (SAP pp.10, 16). The supplied record does not establish that all relevant final choices preceded access to unblinded outcomes. The late 2022 SAP date alone is not the reason: its listed changes mainly concern presentation and additional summaries (pp.30–31).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require finalization before unblinded outcomes were available. Changes “clearly unrelated to the results” are acceptable, but the available explanations do not establish that condition for the entire evolution of this analysis.

evidence: Week-32 24-hour UPCR was already a specified secondary measurement before enrolment (Protocol p.253). Its promotion to primary had an explicit collection-validity rationale (p.171). The publication reports 24-hour UPCR, spot UPCR and total urine protein (Article p.5; Supplement p.19). These facts argue against selecting a favorable measurement.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 allows N/PN for explained inconsistencies unrelated to results and restricts attention to eligible measurements. §8.3.2 recognizes legitimate changes.

evidence: The published MMRM corresponds to the detailed SAP primary analysis (Article p.3; SAP pp.52–53). The covariance change was explained by there being only two post-baseline assessments (SAP p.62). Numerical sensitivity results are absent, and the earlier primary model differed (Protocol p.253), but there is no evidence that competing estimates were calculated and the favorable one selected.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely selection “on the basis of the results.” §8.3.2 distinguishes discrepancies from established result-driven selection; §1.1 permits PN where a reasonable inference is possible.

evidence: A, p. 1801, “Randomization and masking”: “computer-generated randomization schedule,” stratified by neoadjuvant treatment, using “random permuted blocks of 4 and 6.”
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when “a random component was used,” including computer-generated random numbers.

evidence: A, p. 1801: allocations were “sequentially numbered and placed in opaque, sealed envelopes” opened “at the time of randomization.” This supports concealment; tamper-proof sealing and irreversible enrolment before opening are not explicitly documented.
guidance: §4.3.2, Table 2: sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes meet minimal concealment criteria. Box 4, 1.2 permits “Probably yes” when procedural detail is incomplete.

evidence: A, Fig. 1, p. 1802 shows equal randomized groups, 64/64. Table 1, p. 1803 shows broadly comparable characteristics, but only for 61/61 analysed participants; S, Table S2 includes 59/59. Baseline characteristics for all randomized participants are unavailable.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer NI when studies report “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis”; §4.3.3 requires consideration of all randomized participants. This does not establish problematic imbalance.
