evidence: A common IVF protocol and pregnancy-test schedule are described, with diet as the assigned difference (p. 98, Setting, Diet and Figure 1). No different pregnancy-testing opportunities or thresholds are reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 concerns systematic differences in methods or timing; §7.3 notes that methods are likely comparable in most randomized trials.

evidence: The pregnancy assessor’s identity and blinding are unspecified (pp. 98–100). Participants being unaware of pregnancy status during the earlier anxiety assessment does not establish assessor blinding to diet (p. 99).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 asks about assessors’ knowledge of intervention status; §1.1 supports NI when that knowledge cannot be established.

evidence: The scheduled pregnancy test supports an assessment involving little subjective judgement (p. 98, Figure 1). Knowledge of diet would therefore probably not change classification. This does not establish a particular pregnancy subtype.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 and §7.1 distinguish judgement-dependent assessments from objective observations unlikely to be influenced by intervention knowledge.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 = PN.
guidance: Box 10: 4.5 applies only when 4.4 = Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The supplied source is the main article; no prospective protocol or SAP is available. Its statistical methods predominantly describe anxiety analyses and do not establish a pregnancy-analysis plan finalized before unblinded data (p. 99).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require sufficiently detailed analysis intentions finalized before unblinded outcome data.

evidence: “Became pregnant” is reported without a precise definition (p. 100). Figure 1 gives a test time, but the complete intended set of pregnancy definitions or measurements is unavailable. There is no affirmative evidence of results-based selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple measurements are possible; Y/PY requires evidence supporting selection based on results.

evidence: The 69-woman analysis is explicit (pp. 99–100), but alternative pregnancy analyses and prospective intentions are unknown. Its inappropriate restriction does not establish that the analysis was selected because of the findings.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible; §8.1 requires selection based on direction, magnitude or significance.

evidence: Patients were assigned “according to the minimization principle,” balancing several prognostic characteristics (p.63, Methods). The implementation and random component are not described.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random.” PY reflects the inference rather than documented random-number generation.

evidence: Methods describe minimization after examination but give no concealment mechanism or allocation responsibilities (p.63). Physician blinding during follow-up (p.65) does not establish allocation concealment.
guidance: §4.1.2 distinguishes concealment from subsequent blinding; §1.1 permits NI when details cannot support PY or PN.

evidence: Table 1 explicitly describes patients “who eventually returned for follow-up” (p.63): 45 and 49, rather than all 55 and 51 randomized. These available characteristics show no striking imbalance, but cannot establish balance in the randomized population.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: NI when studies report “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis”; §4.3.3 requires consideration of all randomized participants.

evidence: Participants received an intensive, 39-hour-per-week program or no treatment from the investigators (p.65, Treatment and The control group). Only the examining physician was described as blinded.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns participants’ awareness of their assigned intervention. These visibly different interventions establish awareness.

evidence: Staff delivered physical training, occupational therapy and psychological treatment to the intervention group; controls were “not treated by us” (p.65).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness among “carers and people delivering the interventions,” separately from outcome-assessor blinding.

evidence: Withdrawal reasons included illness, increased pain, difficulty tolerating the program and smoking restrictions (pp.64–65). These could occur outside a trial. Controls explicitly “could go anywhere else for treatment” (p.65), so outside care was permitted. No trial-induced departure is identified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: answer N/PN for non-adherence “consistent with what could occur outside the trial context,” and for changes consistent with the protocol. Awareness alone does not establish a deviation.

evidence: No qualifying trial-context deviation identified at 2.3 (pp.64–65).
guidance: Box 6: 2.4 is reached only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Question 2.4 was not reached.
guidance: Box 6: 2.5 is reached only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: The analysis excluded all nine treatment non-starters/withdrawals, although “two could be contacted after 4 months” (p.67, Dropouts). This suggests some exclusion beyond simple loss to follow-up, although outcome availability for those two is not explicit. No reassignment between groups is reported.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6: exclusion solely for missing outcomes is acceptable here, but naïve per-protocol analyses and exclusions of eligible participants are inappropriate. PN acknowledges uncertainty about the contacted patients’ data.

evidence: The identifiable concern beyond unavailable follow-up concerns two contacted but excluded patients (p.67). Adding both as unable to work changes 29/45 to 29/47, reducing the between-group difference from approximately 35.9 to 33.1 percentage points. A substantial effect from these exclusions is unlikely; genuinely missing outcomes are assessed in D3.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact,” considering outcome frequency and prognosis rather than a fixed percentage threshold. §6.1 separates available-but-excluded data from missing data.

evidence: Only 45/55 intervention participants and 49/51 controls contribute (p.64, Figure 1; p.66). Seven of the nine intervention non-starters/withdrawals could not be contacted, alongside one graduate and two controls (pp.64,67). Thus at least ten participants lacked follow-up; outcome availability for two contacted exclusions is unclear. This amount could materially alter the estimate.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires that missing outcomes “could have made no important difference”; the denominator is all randomized participants.

evidence: The reported analysis uses the 45 and 49 participants; no missing-data correction or sensitivity analysis is reported (p.66, Statistical methods and Results; p.67, Dropouts).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from methods correcting bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions. Merely reporting a statistically significant result does not supply that evidence.

evidence: Withdrawal reasons include increased back pain, inability to tolerate the program, disk herniation and neurological disease; all program dropouts were initially on sick leave (pp.64–65). These circumstances could relate to subsequent work ability.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: when withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Unavailable follow-up was more common in the intervention arm: at least 8/55 versus 2/51 (Figure 1 and p.67). Health-related treatment withdrawals were concentrated in that arm. Although dropouts reportedly resembled graduates on measured baseline characteristics (p.65), this does not exclude worse subsequent work ability. Individual missingness reasons are incompletely linked to patients.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 identifies unequal missingness proportions and outcome-related reasons as evidence supporting likely dependence. §§6.1.4.1–6.1.4.2 explain these mechanisms.

evidence: “Workability” was defined as “having a job, being in school, or seeking work”; component counts are reported (p.66, Return to work). No evidence shows that the method was unsuitable for this defined endpoint. It is broader than employment alone.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement, not whether the “choice of outcome being evaluated was sensible.” A broad endpoint definition is not itself inappropriate measurement.

evidence: The same physician examined both groups (p.65). Controls were matched at randomization so the baseline-to-follow-up interval was “identical”; the same workability definition applies to both groups (p.66).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable ascertainment as the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. The reported procedures meet this requirement.

evidence: Physician blinding was broken in “about 10%” of cases, equally between groups (p.65). Participants knew their treatment and probably supplied work-status information during follow-up, although the exact information source is not specified (p.66).
guidance: §7.3 says assessments involving an unblinded participant and blinded collector should generally be treated as aware. Box 10, 4.3 also addresses assessor awareness directly.

evidence: The endpoint classifies concrete activities—employment, schooling or job-seeking—rather than asking patients to rate perceived capacity (p.66). Most positive classifications were employment or schooling: 22/29 and 11/14. Job-seeking leaves some reporting uncertainty, but the largely blinded physician and factual categories make material differential classification unlikely. Actual changes in job-seeking are part of the intended outcome.
guidance: §7.1 distinguishes outcomes by the “degree of judgement involved”; §7.3 and Box 10, 4.4 recognize that knowledge need not influence factual outcome assessment. §1.2.1 specifies “risk of material bias.”

evidence: Assessment was judged unlikely to be susceptible to material influence at 4.4.
guidance: Box 10: 4.5 is reached only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: The article describes statistical tests and four-month assessment (p.66), but no dated protocol or analysis plan establishes that these decisions preceded access to unblinded data. The supplied source inventory contains only the main article.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available; §8.3.1 requires attention to the plan’s date. Publication methods alone cannot establish this.

evidence: The stated workability definition, component counts and four-month result are reported consistently (pp.62,66). However, without prospective intentions, alternative eligible definitions or measurements cannot be ruled out. Being first in the abstract does not establish primary-outcome status or selective reporting.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficient and more than one measurement is possible. §8.1 distinguishes selection within an outcome from non-reporting of other outcomes.

evidence: Both the follow-up comparison and an additional baseline-related Fisher–Irwin analysis are reported (p.66), which argues against obvious suppression of that alternative. Nevertheless, intended analyses and missing-data strategies are not prospectively documented, so completeness cannot be established.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when analysis intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible. High requires evidence that selection was likely based on the results, not merely that alternatives existed.

evidence: Assignment used “the minimization principle,” balancing several prognostic characteristics (p.63, Methods). The implementation’s random component is not specified.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random.” PY acknowledges inferred rather than explicitly documented randomness.

evidence: No concealment mechanism or allocation responsibilities are reported (p.63, Methods). Follow-up physician blinding (p.65) does not establish concealment during recruitment.
guidance: §4.1 distinguishes allocation concealment from subsequent blinding; §1.1 permits NI when neither PY nor PN is supportable.

evidence: Table 1 is restricted to patients “who eventually returned for follow-up” (p.63). Its apparently reasonable balance concerns only 45 and 49 participants, not all randomized participants.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly permits NI for studies reporting “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis”; §4.3.3 requires assessment of the randomized population.

evidence: Participants received an intensive rehabilitation program or no treatment from investigators (p.65). Only the examining physician was described as blinded.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants knew their assigned intervention; these visibly different interventions establish awareness.

evidence: Staff delivered physical, occupational and psychological treatment, while controls were “not treated by us” (p.65).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness among those delivering interventions, separately from outcome-assessor blinding.

evidence: Reported non-adherence involved illness, pain, program difficulty and smoking restrictions (pp.64–65), consistent with ordinary treatment circumstances. Controls “could go anywhere else for treatment” (p.65), making outside treatment permitted care. No trial-induced departure is identified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: N/PN applies to non-adherence “consistent with what could occur outside the trial context” and changes consistent with the protocol.

evidence: No qualifying trial-context deviation was identified at 2.3 (pp.64–65).
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Question 2.4 was not reached.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: All nine intervention non-starters/withdrawals were omitted, although two “could be contacted” (p.67, Dropouts). The article does not establish whether those two supplied workability outcomes. My earlier PN inferred inappropriate exclusion more confidently than the evidence permits. Other omissions involved unavailable follow-up; no analysis-group switching is reported (p.64, Figure 1).
guidance: §5.3.1 accepts analyses excluding missing outcomes. §6.1 assigns exclusions of participants “for whom outcome data are available” to D2. Contact alone cannot establish that distinction; §1.1 therefore supports NI.

evidence: The unresolved available-data exclusion concerns two contacted participants (p.67). Even adding both as unable to work changes the risk difference from approximately 35.9 to 33.1 percentage points. The outcome is common, and this potential analysis exclusion is unlikely to have substantial impact. Genuinely unavailable outcomes remain in D3.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 requires assessment of “potential for a substantial impact,” considering number excluded, outcome frequency and prognosis; §6.1 separates missing outcomes from available-data exclusions.

evidence: Analysis includes 45/55 intervention participants and 49/51 controls (pp.64,66). Seven intervention non-starters/withdrawals could not be contacted, plus one graduate and two controls (Figure 1; p.67). Thus at least ten lacked follow-up; outcomes for the two contacted exclusions are uncertain.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” These omissions are not negligible relative to the reported outcome counts.

evidence: No correction for missing outcomes or sensitivity analysis is reported (p.66, Statistical methods; p.67, Dropouts).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses showing little change across plausible missingness assumptions. Statistical significance alone is insufficient.

evidence: Reasons for stopping treatment include increased back pain, difficulty tolerating the program, disk herniation and neurological disease (pp.64–65). These could relate to subsequent ability to work.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal potentially related to “participants’ health status” supports possible dependence on the true outcome.

evidence: Unavailable follow-up affected at least 8/55 intervention participants versus 2/51 controls. Most intervention non-starters/withdrawals were uncontactable, and several withdrawal reasons were health-related (pp.64–65,67). Reported baseline similarity between dropouts and graduates is reassuring but does not establish similar subsequent outcomes. Individual withdrawal reasons are not linked to contact status.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 identifies unequal missingness proportions and outcome-related reasons as evidence of likely dependence; §§6.1.4.1–6.1.4.2 explain their relevance. PY accommodates incomplete individual linkage.

evidence: Workability meant “having a job, being in school, or seeking work,” with component counts reported (p.66). No evidence establishes an unsuitable measurement method for this defined endpoint.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 assesses measurement suitability, not whether the “choice of outcome being evaluated was sensible.” Its breadth alone does not establish bias.

evidence: The same physician assessed both groups (p.65); controls were matched so baseline-to-follow-up intervals were “identical” (p.66). Both groups used the same workability categories.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable ascertainment by the same methods and thresholds at comparable times.

evidence: Physician blinding was broken in approximately 10% of cases, equally between groups (p.65). Participants knew their treatment and probably supplied status information during follow-up; independent verification is not described (p.66).
guidance: §7.3 treats an interaction involving an unblinded participant and blinded collector as aware unless convincing contrary evidence exists; Box 10, 4.3 addresses assessor awareness.

evidence: Job-seeking contributed seven intervention and three control successes (p.66). Although employment and schooling are concrete, the report does not describe independent verification or operational criteria for “seeking work.” My earlier answer gave excessive reassurance from the endpoint’s factual components and physician blinding. Differential reporting could affect classification.
guidance: §7.1, participant-reported outcomes: a blinded interviewer does not eliminate participant awareness. Its composite-outcome guidance requires attention to component contributions; Box 10, 4.4 asks whether influence could occur.

evidence: Most positive classifications were employment or schooling—22/29 and 11/14—and the examining physician was blinded in approximately 90% of cases (pp.65–66). These features argue against likely systematic distortion, despite possible influence on reported job-seeking. The article does not document differential prompting or classification.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from influence that is likely. §7.3 directs consideration of assessor independence and circumstances; unblinded reporting does not automatically establish High risk.

evidence: Statistical methods are described (p.66), but no supplied dated protocol or analysis plan establishes decisions before access to unblinded outcomes. The source inventory contains only the main article.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require analysis intentions finalized before unblinded data were available, with attention to document dates.

evidence: The four-month definition and counts are reported consistently (pp.62,66), arguing against an obvious discrepancy. However, prospective intentions sufficient to exclude alternative eligible measurements or definitions are unavailable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficient and multiple measurements are possible. Being first in the abstract does not establish either prespecification or selective reporting.

evidence: Both the follow-up comparison and an additional baseline-related Fisher–Irwin analysis are reported (p.66), arguing against obvious suppression of that alternative. Intended analyses and missing-data strategies remain undocumented prospectively.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI for insufficient analysis intentions when multiple analyses are possible. High requires evidence of likely results-based selection, not merely analytical flexibility.

evidence: Allocation used “stratification by minimization” to balance age, gender, sick leave, rating-scale score, and smoking. Its random component is not explicitly described (p.2495, Materials).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random.” PY reflects the inference rather than explicit documentation of randomness.

evidence: Randomization followed informed consent, but no central allocation service, concealed envelopes, or other concealment mechanism is described (p.2495, Materials). Consent before allocation does not establish concealment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 requires concealment until enrolment and assignment; §1.1 permits NI when details cannot support PY or PN.

evidence: Table 1 shows broadly comparable starting groups: back pain 5.1 versus 6.0, P=0.19; work capability 53% versus 40%, P=0.10. Allocation counts were 64 versus 74 (Figure 1). No compelling imbalance suggests failed randomization, although baseline characteristics cover 127 starters rather than all 138 randomized participants (pp.2495–2496).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance” do not indicate bias. §4.3.3 requires caution when baseline data describe a subset.

evidence: Participants received distinguishable programs: full-day multidisciplinary FR versus 1.5-hour exercise sessions three times weekly. Awareness is inferred from these arrangements and the explanation of allocation to participants (pp.2495–2497).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 assesses awareness of assigned intervention; §1.1 uses “Probably” for an inferred answer.

evidence: Staff delivered the distinct programs; OIT exercise sessions were “led by the same staff” as FR. Provider masking is not described and is implausible for these treatment schedules (pp.2496–2497).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness among carers and intervention providers.

evidence: No trial-induced crossover or additional treatment is reported. Nonstarting commonly followed a job offer; other reasons included nonattendance and disc herniation. However, reasons for discontinuing treatment and information about non-protocol care are insufficient to determine whether trial-context deviations occurred (p.2495; Figure 1; p.2498).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” deviations arose through the trial context; NI may apply when this is unreported. Ordinary non-adherence alone does not establish such deviations.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=NI.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 is asked only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4=NA.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 is asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Table 3 is explicitly restricted to “Those Graduating.” Table 4 separately reports available one-year back-pain outcomes for 5 FR and 11 OIT discontinuers, demonstrating exclusion based on treatment completion rather than solely missing outcomes (p.2498, Tables 3–4).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: naïve per-protocol analyses “excluding trial participants who did not receive their assigned intervention” are inappropriate for assignment effects.

evidence: Sixteen participants with measured pain were excluded from the target comparison—11.6% of those randomized. Their median pain was 6 in FR and 7.5 in OIT, compared with 5.1 and 5.7 among graduates. These exclusions could materially alter the comparison (p.2498, Tables 3–4).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 assesses potential substantial impact from exclusions; impact can occur even below 5% when exclusions relate to prognosis.

evidence: Available pain outcomes total 114/138: 48+50 graduates and 5+11 discontinuers. Thus 24/138 (17.4%) are genuinely missing: 11/64 FR and 13/74 OIT. The 16 measured but excluded discontinuers are assessed under D2 (Figure 1; Tables 3–4).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 uses “all randomized participants”; “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make no important difference. §6.1 assigns exclusions of available outcomes to D2.

evidence: The authors compared baseline characteristics and state that a further comparison gave no indication of bias, but “The data are not presented.” No adequately described correction or sensitivity analysis establishes robustness to plausible missing pain values (pp.2498–2499, “Intention to Treat”).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires correction for bias or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions”; §6.1.7 requires addressing dependence on the missing outcome’s true value.

evidence: Missingness could relate to health: two nonstarters developed disc herniations, and job opportunities explained other nonstarts. Reasons for subsequent missed assessments and the missing pain item are not supplied (p.2495; Figure 1; Table 3).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: loss or withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” supports possible dependence on the true outcome.

evidence: Missing proportions are very similar—17.2% FR and 17.6% OIT—which argues against differential attrition. Nevertheless, reasons are incomplete, some reported circumstances involve clinical change, and the undocumented comparison cannot establish whether missingness actually depended on pain. Neither PY nor PN is sufficiently supported (p.2495; Figure 1; pp.2498–2499).
guidance: §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient evidence to support a probable answer. Box 8, 3.4 considers proportions, reasons, and circumstances; Table 10 maps NI at this branch to High.

evidence: Back pain used an 11-point box scale, 0=no pain to 10=worst possible pain, averaging the preceding two weeks. Nothing reported indicates an unsuitable instrument (p.2496).
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 targets methods unsuitable for the outcome, such as poor validity or inadequate sensitivity; subjectivity alone is not inappropriate measurement.

evidence: Both groups used the same pain scale and one-year questionnaire procedure; questionnaires were completed before the follow-up meeting (pp.2496–2497, Outcome Evaluation).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable assessment as the same methods used at comparable time points.

evidence: Participants supplied their own pain ratings and probably knew their treatment. The physician’s approximately 80% successful blinding does not blind the participant reporting pain (p.2497, Outcome Evaluation).
guidance: §7.1 and Box 10, 4.3: for participant-reported outcomes, “the outcome assessor is the study participant,” even with a blinded interviewer.

evidence: Pain ratings involve participants’ subjective assessment and could therefore be influenced by treatment knowledge (p.2496, pain measurement; p.2497, questionnaire procedure).
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 explicitly identifies participant-reported “level of pain” as susceptible to knowledge of intervention.

evidence: Differential expectations remain possible because FR was more intensive. Against likely influence, both arms received active treatment, participants were told “We don’t know whether FR is more effective,” assessment occurred at one year, and questionnaires were completed beforehand, with a mostly blinded physician resolving queries (pp.2495, 2497). These circumstances support possible rather than likely influence.
guidance: §7.3 identifies active comparators, interviewer independence, and delayed assessment as mitigating factors. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes “could have influenced” from “likely to influence.”

evidence: The article describes nonparametric analyses, but no dated analysis plan establishes that intentions were finalized before unblinded outcomes became available (p.2497, Statistical Methods; supplied document set).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data; §8.3.1 requires evidence of timing. Published methods alone do not establish this.

evidence: The described two-week-average pain scale and one-year assessment match Table 3. This consistency argues against an obvious discrepancy, but no prospective documentation establishes the complete set of intended eligible measurements (pp.2496–2498).
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when analysis intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible. Absence of a plan does not itself establish results-based selection.

evidence: Between-group tests, within-group changes, and dropout analyses are described, but no prospective plan establishes which analyses were intended. The graduate restriction establishes a D2 problem, not evidence that this result was chosen because of its direction or significance (pp.2497–2499; Tables 3–5).
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple analyses are possible; §8.1 requires selection based on “direction, magnitude or statistical significance.”

evidence: “Stratification by minimization” balanced several prognostic characteristics; an explicit random component is not described (p.2495, Materials).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random.” §1.1 supports PY for an inference.

evidence: Allocation occurred after informed consent, but the report gives no mechanism preventing recruiters from knowing forthcoming assignments (p.2495).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 requires concealment until enrolment and assignment. Under §1.1, neither adequate nor inadequate concealment can reasonably be inferred here.

evidence: Table 1 describes 127 starters, not all 138 randomized participants. Available differences—including back pain 5.1 versus 6.0, P=0.19, and work capability 53% versus 40%, P=0.10—do not suggest failed randomization. Randomized counts were 64 versus 74 (p.2496, Table 1 and Figure 1).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance” do not indicate a problem. §4.3.3 requires caution with subset baseline data; the substantial starter sample remains informative.

evidence: Full-day multidisciplinary FR and shorter outpatient exercise sessions were readily distinguishable; participants were informed about the comparison and allocation (pp.2495–2497).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness of assignment; §1.1 supports PY when awareness is inferred.

evidence: Staff delivered the visibly different schedules and components; OIT exercise was “led by the same staff” (pp.2496–2497).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness among intervention providers, independently of outcome-assessor masking.

evidence: No trial-induced crossover is documented. Reported nonstarting reasons include job offers and disc herniation, which can occur outside trials. However, reasons for treatment discontinuation and information about non-protocol interventions are insufficient (p.2495; Figure 1; p.2498).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence or strong reason for trial-context deviations, and explicitly allows NI when their origin is unreported. Ordinary non-adherence alone does not justify Y.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=NI.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 applies only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4=NA.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Table 3 includes only “Those Graduating.” Table 4 separately supplies measured pain outcomes for 5 FR and 11 OIT discontinuers, so their exclusion was not simply an available-case analysis (p.2498).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 calls naïve per-protocol analyses inappropriate. §5.3.1 accepts exclusion solely for missing outcomes, which does not explain these 16 exclusions.

evidence: Sixteen measured outcomes were excluded—11.6% of all randomized participants. Their pain medians were 6 and 7.5, versus 5.1 and 5.7 among graduates, providing concrete potential for a material change in the comparison (p.2498, Tables 3–4).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks about potential substantial impact; it does not require proof that including excluded participants changes statistical significance.

evidence: Tables 3–4 document 114 pain measurements: 48+50 graduates and 5+11 discontinuers. Against 138 randomized, 24 are missing: 11/64 FR and 13/74 OIT. The 16 available but excluded outcomes are not counted as missing (Figure 1; Tables 3–4).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 uses all randomized participants and defines “nearly all” by negligible potential impact. §6.1 places exclusion of available outcomes in D2.

evidence: Baseline comparisons and an unspecified comparison involving nonattenders are reported as reassuring, but “The data are not presented.” No described analysis establishes robustness to plausible missing pain outcomes (pp.2498–2499, “Intention to Treat”).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires correction for bias or sensitivity analyses across plausible assumptions. §6.1.7 requires addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Two nonstarters developed disc herniations; other nonstarts followed job offers or unexplained nonattendance. Reasons for later missed assessments and the missing pain item are not given (p.2495; Figure 1; Table 3).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” permits dependence on the true outcome.

evidence: Almost equal missing proportions—17.2% versus 17.6%—are reassuring. Nevertheless, incomplete reasons, some clinical changes, and an undocumented comparison do not establish either likely dependence or probable independence from pain. Worse outcomes among observed discontinuers cannot simply be attributed to those genuinely missing (pp.2495, 2498–2499; Figure 1; Tables 3–5).
guidance: §1.1 requires NI when neither probable answer is justified. §6.1.3 explains that outcome-dependent missingness can bias a continuous outcome even without unequal missing proportions. Table 10 explicitly maps this NI branch to High.

evidence: The reported 0–10 box scale measures average pain over the preceding two weeks; no evidence indicates inadequate validity or sensitivity (p.2496).
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 targets unsuitable measurement methods. Subjectivity does not itself make a pain scale inappropriate.

evidence: Both groups used the same scale and one-year questionnaire procedure, with questionnaires completed before the follow-up meeting (pp.2496–2497).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods and time points; no systematic measurement difference is described.

evidence: Participants reported their own pain and probably knew their treatment. The physician’s approximately 80% successful masking does not mask participants (p.2497, Outcome Evaluation).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 and §7.1: “the outcome assessor is the study participant,” including when a blinded interviewer assists.

evidence: Participants’ subjective pain ratings could reflect treatment expectations (p.2496, pain scale; p.2497, questionnaire procedure).
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 explicitly identifies participant-reported pain as potentially influenced by treatment knowledge.

evidence: FR’s greater intensity could create different expectations. Countervailing evidence is an active exercise comparator, the statement “We don’t know whether FR is more effective,” one-year assessment, and questionnaires completed before physician discussion. Strong differential beliefs affecting reporting are not documented (pp.2495, 2497).
guidance: §7.3 identifies active comparators and delayed assessment as mitigating circumstances. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from likely influence; PN is a contextual judgement, not a claim that reporting was unaffected.

evidence: Published statistical methods describe the analysis but do not establish prospective finalization. No protocol, dated analysis plan, or registry record is supplied (p.2497, Statistical Methods; supplied document set).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require analysis intentions finalized before unblinded outcomes were available.

evidence: The described pain scale and one-year assessment correspond to Table 3, with no evident discrepancy. However, the complete prospectively intended set of measurements cannot be verified (pp.2496–2498).
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible; missing documentation does not establish results-based selection.

evidence: Between-group, within-group, and dropout analyses are described, but prospective intentions are unavailable. The graduate-only analysis is problematic for D2 without demonstrating that its reporting was selected because of its results (pp.2497–2499, Tables 3–5).

guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only if Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. §5.1.2.1: ordinary treatment cessation does not itself bias the assignment effect.

evidence: Not reached; 2.3 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only if Y/PY to 2.3.

evidence: Not reached; 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only if Y/PY/NI to 2.4.

evidence: A p. 3 specifies “all available follow-up data from all participants who underwent randomization” with an ITT approach. S Fig. S2 includes the eight untreated participants in the ITT population. One duplicate randomization identifier was removed, retaining that person’s first assignment (A Table 1 footnote; S Fig. S2). P pp. 641, 646 confirms analysis by randomized assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT analysis is appropriate; missing outcome data are assessed separately in D3. Removing a duplicate identifier does not exclude a distinct randomized participant.
