guidance: Box 6: ask 2.7 only if N/PN/NI to 2.6.

evidence: A p. 4 reports 96.0% trial completion but 99.6% known vital status. S Fig. S2 shows 224/5795 canagliflozin and 184/4347 placebo participants did not complete follow-up. Knowing survival does not establish complete ascertainment of nonfatal MI or stroke. The documents do not demonstrate that the unobserved follow-up could make no important difference to this composite estimate.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference,” not simply exceeding a percentage threshold. §6.1.5 counts early-censored follow-up as missing outcome data.

evidence: Evidence against bias: imputation produced HR 0.85 (0.75–0.97), close to the main result (A p. 6). P pp. 647–648 describes a substantive Weibull model using treatment discontinuers, retrieved follow-up, trial/CV-history strata and prognostic covariates. However, the reported result does not demonstrate robustness to residual outcome-dependent missingness, and the documents do not establish that these variables explain the missingness–outcome relationship sufficiently. This is reassurance, but insufficient evidence to dismiss bias.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 permits correction methods or informative sensitivity analyses. §6.1.6 says multiple imputation does not remove MNAR bias unless it is explained by measured variables; §6.1.7 requires sensitivity analyses to address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: S Fig. S2 includes loss to follow-up and consent withdrawal. Their underlying reasons are not reported sufficiently to exclude a relationship with cardiovascular health. Site closures also occurred, providing a clearly less concerning explanation for some missingness. P p. 647 explicitly recognizes potentially informative dropout among treatment discontinuers.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness could depend on the outcome if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status”; low risk requires documented unrelated reasons for all missing outcomes.

evidence: S Fig. S2 shows broadly similar noncompletion proportions, 3.9% versus 4.2%, and similar reason categories: lost to follow-up 104 versus 102, withdrawal 85 versus 60, site closure 35 versus 22. Specific health-related withdrawal reasons are unavailable. Follow-up continued after drug discontinuation (A p. 3), and imputation was reassuring (A p. 6). Taken together, dependence is possible but not shown to be likely.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence; relevant evidence includes materially different missingness patterns, outcome-related reasons, and censoring at treatment cessation. §1.1 permits a reasoned PN instead of NI.

evidence: A p. 3 reports endpoint-committee adjudication. S pp. 8–17 specifies cardiovascular-death, MI and stroke criteria; MI assessment combines biomarkers with clinical, ECG or imaging evidence. These are appropriate methods for each composite component.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1, composite outcomes: consider the influential components; all three components have defined adjudication procedures here.

evidence: A p. 3: scheduled follow-up included inquiry about primary events at every contact, using the same procedures across randomized groups. S pp. 8–17 supplies common definitions. There is no evidence of treatment-dependent surveillance or diagnostic thresholds.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable ascertainment uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable times; assess systematic differences in opportunities to detect events.

evidence: P p. 646, §4.1: adjudication of the primary cardiovascular outcomes “has been done in a blinded fashion”; this also appears in the September 2016 SAP (P p. 588).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is N. MI, stroke and cardiovascular-cause classification can involve judgement, but the adjudicators were blinded.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only if Y/PY/NI to 4.3; §7.3 recognizes successful assessor blinding as protection against differential measurement error.

evidence: Not reached; 4.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if Y/PY/NI to 4.4.

evidence: The reported analysis matches the integrated SAP, but the supplied versions are dated 20 September 2016 and 20 March 2017 (P pp. 574, 631), after interim CANVAS results were disclosed for regulatory review. P pp. 579–580 confirms that the integrated analysis retains pre-November-2012 data and that analysis plans were subsequently revised. Against concern, later outcome data remained blinded and the main MACE definition and planned full-data analysis were retained. Nevertheless, the required pre-unblinding finalization condition is not met.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1: “finalization of the analysis intentions must precede availability of unblinded outcome data.” §8.3.1 exempts confidential monitoring-committee access, but the disclosure here extended to the sponsor/regulatory process.

evidence: The reported three-component MACE outcome and full follow-up correspond to the SAP (P pp. 588, 646), A p. 3 and S Fig. S1. P p. 580 explicitly states that the primary MACE endpoint “was not changed.” Although component classifications and other endpoints were available, there is no evidence that this measurement was selected for its favorable result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 asks whether selection was based on results, not merely whether alternative measurements existed; correspondence between intended and reported measurement supports N/PN.

evidence: P pp. 588 and 646 prespecify the reported first-event ITT Cox analysis, pooled canagliflozin doses, and stratification by trial and prior cardiovascular disease. Both noninferiority and conditional superiority were specified. A pp. 3–4 reports that approach and p. 6 also reports the imputed estimate. Additional analyses and SAP amendments existed (P p. 634), but there is no clear evidence that the reported primary estimate was selected from alternatives because it was favorable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence of likely result-based selection for Y/PY. §8.3.2 cautions that differences in analysis intentions can have legitimate explanations; timing concerns alone do not establish selective choice of an estimate.

evidence: Article pp. 2–3 specifies a “computer-generated randomization schedule with randomly permuted blocks.”
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when sequence generation contains a random component, including computer-generated random numbers.

evidence: Article p. 2: randomization was “performed centrally through an interactive Web-based response system.” Sponsor preparation of the schedule does not establish that enrolling personnel could access forthcoming allocations.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel supports Yes.

evidence: Article Table 1, p. 5: age 63.2 versus 63.4 years, HbA1c 8.2% in both groups, cardiovascular history 64.8% versus 66.7%. These differences do not indicate randomization failure. Pooled group-size inequality follows the planned CANVAS 1:1:1 and CANVAS-R 1:1 allocations (Article pp. 2–3).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance” do not raise bias concerns. §4.3.3.2 assesses group sizes against the intended allocation ratio.

evidence: Article p. 3 reports matching placebo and states that participants remained unaware of individual assignments. Recognizable adverse effects are a possible challenge, but the documents do not establish participants’ knowledge of allocation through those effects.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: blinding protects against awareness; side effects warrant Y/PY when participants knew they were specific to an intervention.

evidence: Article p. 3: “Participants and all trial staff were unaware of the individual treatment assignments until completion.” Interim sponsor access to outcome results is documented separately (Protocol pp. 579–580); it does not establish allocation awareness among carers or intervention-delivery personnel.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness among “carers and people delivering the interventions.” Sponsor analytical access alone does not answer this question affirmatively.

evidence: Not reached. Article pp. 3–4 nevertheless documents guideline-directed background treatment and similar drug discontinuation, 29.2% versus 29.9%, without evidence that these represented trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. §5.1.2.1 excludes ordinary treatment cessation from bias in the assignment effect.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3 is NA; the documented discontinuation rates do not activate this branch.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if Y/PY to 2.3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if Y/PY/NI to 2.4.

evidence: Article p. 3 specifies all randomized participants and all available follow-up under ITT. Appendix Fig. S2, p. 24, retains eight untreated participants. The duplicate enrolment was represented by its first randomization rather than counted twice (Article Table 1 footnote). Protocol p. 646 specifies the primary ITT analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: ITT is appropriate. §5.3.1 separates missing outcomes from exclusions based on adherence. Removing a duplicate identifier does not exclude a distinct participant.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is Y. The target is the full ITT analysis, not the additional dosed-only analysis described in Protocol p. 648.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if N/PN/NI to 2.6.

evidence: Article p. 4 reports 96.0% study completion and 99.6% known vital status. Appendix Fig. S2 shows 224/5795 versus 184/4347 noncompleters. Vital-status recovery does not establish complete nonfatal MI/stroke ascertainment; the documents do not demonstrate negligible possible impact from all unobserved follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires missing outcomes to make “no important difference.” §6.1.5 treats early-censored follow-up as missing even when earlier observations enter the analysis.

evidence: Article p. 6 reports an imputed HR of 0.85 (0.75–0.97), essentially unchanged. Protocol pp. 647–648 explicitly models potentially informative dropout using treatment discontinuers, retrieved post-discontinuation follow-up, trial/CV-history strata, treatment, completion status and prognostic covariates. On reconsideration, this supplies a reasonable basis for judging material bias unlikely. Uncertainty about residual unmeasured differences remains, so PY is preferable to Y.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 permits evidence from “analysis methods that correct for bias” or sensitivity analyses. §6.1.6 requires justification for the imputation assumptions and variables. The retrieved follow-up and targeted covariates provide that justification sufficiently for PY; a range of sensitivity scenarios is not mandatory when the correction-method route is supported.

evidence: Not reached after revised 3.2=PY. Loss to follow-up and consent withdrawal remain documented in Appendix Fig. S2; the change is conditional branching, not a claim that health-related missingness was impossible.
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.3 only if N/PN to 3.2.

evidence: Not reached after revised 3.2=PY. The similar noncompletion proportions in Appendix Fig. S2 remain supporting context, rather than an independent guarantee against bias.
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.4 only if Y/PY/NI to 3.3; Figure 4 stops at Low after 3.2=Y/PY.

evidence: Article p. 3 documents endpoint adjudication; Appendix pp. 8–17 provides cardiovascular-death, MI and stroke criteria. MI assessment incorporates biomarkers and clinical, ECG or imaging evidence. No unsuitable measurement method is apparent.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for inappropriate measurement. §7.1 requires consideration of the influential components of a composite; each component here has defined assessment procedures.

evidence: Article p. 3 describes common scheduled visits and telephone contacts, with primary-outcome inquiry at every follow-up. Appendix pp. 8–17 supplies common definitions. There is no evidence of treatment-dependent surveillance or diagnostic thresholds.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 asks about systematic differences in methods, thresholds or opportunities for ascertainment. Comparable scheduled procedures support PN.

evidence: Protocol p. 646, §4.1: primary-outcome adjudication “has been done in a blinded fashion”; the earlier SAP says the same (p. 588).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is N. The adjudication criteria permit clinical judgement, but documented blinding protects those judgements (Protocol pp. 588, 646).
guidance: Box 10: ask only if Y/PY/NI to 4.3. Blinded adjudication, rather than an assumption that MACE is entirely objective, determines this branch.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if Y/PY/NI to 4.4.

evidence: The supplied integrated SAPs are dated September 2016 and March 2017 (Protocol pp. 574, 631). Protocol pp. 579–580 documents earlier disclosure of interim CANVAS outcomes, an October 2013 integrated plan, and retention of the previously disclosed follow-up in the target analysis. The strongest contrary evidence is that the MACE endpoint and full-data approach were retained and later outcomes stayed blinded. Nevertheless, finalization of this integrated plan preceded neither all contributing outcome disclosure nor the resulting program redesign.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available. §8.3.1 excludes confidential monitoring-committee access from this concern, but the documented disclosure extended beyond that setting.

evidence: The reported three-component MACE measurement matches Protocol pp. 588 and 646 and Article p. 3. Protocol p. 580 states that the primary MACE endpoint “was not changed.” Alternative component classifications do not establish favorable-result selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 requires likely selection on the basis of results. Correspondence between the intended and reported measurement supports PN.

evidence: Protocol pp. 588 and 646 specifies first-event ITT Cox analysis, pooled doses, trial/CV-history stratification, and noninferiority followed by conditional superiority. Article pp. 3–4 reports that approach and p. 6 reports the imputed result too. Additional analyses were added (Protocol p. 634), but there is no clear evidence that the target estimate was chosen for a favorable result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely result-based selection among eligible analyses for Y/PY. §8.3.2 recognizes legitimate changes; multiplicity or amendments alone do not demonstrate selection.

evidence: The Independent Statistical Centre provided “computer-generated balanced blocks of four treatments with random allocation,” stratified by centre and disease subgroup (article p.1332, Assignment).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when “a random component was used,” including computer-generated random numbers.

evidence: Drugs were allocated sequentially from supplies “packaged in a predetermined order”; blister packs were “indistinguishable.” Code access was restricted to independent statistical/monitoring personnel and drug-preparation companies; treatment labels could not be opened and resealed undetectably (p.1332, Assignment and Blinding). These safeguards support concealment despite fixed blocks of four.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2: appropriately used sequential drug containers support concealment. §4.3.2 identifies small fixed blocks as problematic when previous allocations are revealed; routine allocations here remained masked.

evidence: Table 4 reports all randomized participants: 9599 versus 9586, mean age 62.5 years in both groups, 72% male in both, diabetes 20% in both, and hypertension 52% versus 51% (p.1332). Small differences in other vascular histories do not suggest failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No if “any observed imbalances are compatible with chance.” §4.3.3 requires differences clearly beyond chance before identifying a problem.

evidence: Participants received indistinguishable active/placebo blister packs (p.1332, Blinding). There were 21 code breaks, but the article does not say participants were informed. Participant awareness is therefore probably absent, rather than definitively excluded. Different adverse-event frequencies are reported, without evidence that participants identified their assignment (p.1335, Table 9).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: participant blinding may prevent awareness; intervention-specific effects warrant Y/PY when participants knew they identified treatment. §1.1 permits a “Probably” response when judgement is required.

evidence: Although personnel were generally masked, “21 (0·11%) code breaks” occurred at clinical centres: 11 clopidogrel and ten aspirin (p.1332, Blinding). Thus some personnel became aware of assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among carers and intervention providers. Under §5.3.1, awareness leads to assessment of whether trial-context deviations occurred; it does not itself establish bias.

evidence: Drug discontinuation was similar: 21.3% versus 21.1%, with similar reasons—adverse events, withdrawn consent, contraindicated medication, non-compliance, and other reasons (p.1333, Participants and follow-up). Toxicity stopping rules were specified (p.1330). No trial-context-driven departures are reported; the reported changes support ordinary clinical stopping/non-adherence. Detailed management after the rare code breaks is absent.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused protocol departures. Answer N/PN for non-adherence consistent with what occurs outside trials and for protocol-consistent toxicity cessation.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; no qualifying trial-context deviations identified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: answer only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached. Similar discontinuation rates support 2.3 but do not require answering this conditional question.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: The primary analysis used first events “among all patients randomised” (p.1333). The planned ITT analysis retained patients irrespective of compliance (p.1331); Figure 2 includes all randomized patients, including 46 versus 40 who never took study drug (p.1332). All 16 subsequently found ineligible were also followed and analysed (p.1333).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT analyses are appropriate; missing outcome data are assessed separately in D3. The separately reported on-treatment analysis is not the target result.

evidence: Not reached because the target analysis appropriately retained randomized groups and participants.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: answer only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Only 42/19,185 participants (0.22%) were lost: 22 versus 20. Their follow-up was censored at last contact; missing follow-up represented 49 patient-years (0.13%) (p.1333). Against 1960 primary first events, this constitutes nearly complete ascertainment. Treatment discontinuation was not loss to outcome follow-up in the ITT analysis (pp.1331–1333).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” depends on potential impact, not a fixed percentage; when observed events greatly exceed missing participants, bias is necessarily small. §6.1.5 requires counting lost follow-up as missing despite partial observation.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=Y. No missing-data sensitivity analysis is reported, but one is not required on this branch.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: answer only “If N/PN/NI to 3.1”; §6.3(1) permits stopping when outcome data are available for nearly all.

evidence: Not reached. Individual reasons for the 42 losses are not supplied; this does not negate the near-complete-data assessment.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: answer only “If N/PN to 3.2.”

evidence: Not reached. The target ITT analysis did not censor follow-up at treatment cessation; that rule belonged to the separate on-treatment analysis (p.1331).
guidance: Box 8, 3.4: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 3.3.” Its treatment-cessation censoring concern applies to analyses using that rule.

evidence: Stroke had specified neurological-duration and imaging criteria; MI used clinical, enzyme, and ECG criteria (pp.1330–1331, Tables 1 and 3). Death classification was defined, and reported events underwent independent review by two Central Validation Committee members, with disagreements resolved centrally (pp.1330–1331). Table 7 shows substantial contributions from stroke and MI, so this is not treated as a judgement-free mortality outcome.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1(5) requires considering the contribution and assessment of influential composite components. These defined, centrally validated methods are appropriate.

evidence: Both groups followed the same scheduled visits, event definitions, and central validation procedures (pp.1330–1331). No systematic difference in ascertainment is reported. The follow-up schedule changed during the trial after blinded safety review, rather than differing by assigned treatment (p.1330).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable ascertainment uses the same methods and thresholds “at comparable time points.” §7.3 seeks systematic differences in opportunities to identify outcomes.

evidence: The Central Validation Committee adjudicated events, while code access was restricted to other specified personnel; the Coordinating and Methods Centre received the randomization code only after supplying the final database (pp.1331–1332). This supports masked adjudication. An explicit statement that every adjudicator remained blind is absent, and rare local code breaks occurred, so PN is preferable to N.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: answer No when assessors were blinded. §1.1 permits a probable answer supported by trial circumstances; §7.3 requires identifying the actual outcome assessors.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=PN. Stroke, MI, and vascular-cause classification can involve judgement, but that alone does not establish bias with masked adjudication.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3”; §7.1 distinguishes judgement-dependent events from all-cause mortality.

evidence: Not reached.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: The article says the primary analysis “was to be the unadjusted intention-to-treat comparison” of this composite (p.1331), and reports that result (p.1333, Table 6). It also describes protected interim analyses and delayed code release (pp.1331–1332). However, no dated protocol/SAP or dated finalization of the complete analysis intentions is supplied, so prospective specification cannot be verified.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require finalization before unblinded outcome data were available, with a confirming “date-stamp.” §1.1 supports NI where available details do not justify a probable answer to that timing question.

evidence: The Methods identify first occurrence of this exact composite and describe its components (pp.1330–1331); Table 6 reports the same definition across follow-up. No competing eligible measurement or selectively chosen follow-up time is evident. This is an inference from the article, not confirmation against a prospective protocol.
guidance: §8.3.2 permits comparing Methods with Results when prospective intentions are unavailable and requires explaining inferences. Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection based on results, rather than the mere possibility of alternative measurements.

evidence: Multiple analyses existed, but the article explicitly designated the unadjusted ITT analysis as primary (p.1331), reported all five stated outcome clusters including nonsignificant results (p.1333, Table 6), disclosed that adjusted effects were virtually unchanged, and reported the more favourable on-treatment estimate of 9.4% (p.1335). The additional post hoc subgroup analysis was identified separately (p.1335, Table 8). These observations argue against selecting this whole-cohort result for favourability, although a complete prospective plan is unavailable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3: multiplicity becomes bias when an estimate is selected “on the basis of the results”; composite alternatives are considered here. §8.3.2 permits inference from reported intentions and results. §8.1 restricts the assessment to selection of the specific reported result.

evidence: “Computer-generated balanced blocks of four treatments with random allocation,” stratified by centre and disease subgroup (p.1332, Assignment). Fixed block size does not remove the random component.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when “a random component was used,” including computer-generated random numbers.

evidence: Sequential allocation from supplies packaged in a predetermined order; indistinguishable blister packs; restricted code access; treatment-code labels could not be opened and resealed undetectably (p.1332, Assignment and Blinding). These safeguards counter the potential predictability of blocks of four.
guidance: Table 2 and Box 4, 1.2 support appropriately used sequential drug supplies. §4.3.2 identifies block predictability particularly when previous allocations are revealed; that was not routine here.

evidence: Table 4 includes 9599 versus 9586 randomized participants. Age, sex, diabetes, and other major vascular characteristics were closely balanced; small differences in hypertension and vascular histories are compatible with chance (p.1332).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when observed imbalances are “compatible with chance.” §4.3.3 requires differences clearly beyond chance to suggest failed randomization.

evidence: Double-dummy supplies were indistinguishable (p.1332). Although 21 codes were broken, whether participants were informed is unreported. Differing adverse-event frequencies do not establish participant recognition of assignment (p.1335, Table 9).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 considers participant awareness; intervention-specific effects warrant Y/PY when participants knew they identified treatment. §1.1 permits probable answers based on the available circumstances.

evidence: There were “21 (0·11%) code breaks,” 11 versus ten, at clinical centres (p.1332, Blinding). Thus some personnel knew assignments despite generally maintained masking.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among intervention providers. §5.3.1 requires examining resulting trial-context deviations rather than equating awareness with bias.

evidence: Discontinuation was 21.3% versus 21.1%, with similar reasons: adverse events, withdrawn consent, contraindicated medications, non-compliance, and other reasons (p.1333). Toxicity-related stopping was specified (p.1330). No reported departure was attributed to trial engagement or personnel undermining the comparison. Specific management after code breaks is absent.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused departures for Y/PY. N/PN applies to ordinary non-adherence and protocol-consistent toxicity cessation. Similar frequencies alone are not the deciding criterion.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; no qualifying trial-context deviations were identified from the reported discontinuation information (p.1333).
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: applicable only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached. The similar discontinuation frequencies on p.1333 do not independently activate this question.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: applicable only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Primary efficacy analysis included “all patients randomised” (p.1333). Follow-up was intended irrespective of compliance (p.1331). Figure 2 retains patients who never started treatment; all 16 subsequently found ineligible were also followed and analysed (pp.1332–1333).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 accept ITT analyses. Missing outcomes belong in D3. The separately reported on-treatment analysis is not the assessed result.

evidence: Not reached because the target analysis appropriately retained randomized participants and assignments (pp.1331–1333).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: applicable only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Only 42/19,185 participants were lost: 22 versus 20. Their follow-up was censored at last contact, losing 49 patient-years, or 0.13% of total follow-up (p.1333). There were 1960 primary first events. Drug discontinuation did not itself terminate ITT outcome follow-up (pp.1331–1333).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by potential impact and states that when observed events greatly exceed missing participants, bias is necessarily small. §6.1.5 requires recognizing censored losses as missing despite partial follow-up.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=Y. The article reports no missing-data sensitivity analysis; near-complete ascertainment, rather than such an analysis, supports this route (p.1333).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 applies only after N/PN/NI to 3.1. §6.3(1): no further questions are needed when outcome data are available for nearly all.

evidence: Not reached. Individual reasons for the 42 losses are absent from the follow-up report (p.1333), but the negligible extent of missing follow-up determines the preceding branch.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3 applies only “If N/PN to 3.2.”

evidence: Not reached. Censoring 28 days after drug cessation was specified for the separate on-treatment analysis, not the target ITT analysis (p.1331).
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 3.3.” Its treatment-cessation censoring concern applies when that censoring rule is actually used.

evidence: Stroke and MI had specified clinical, imaging, enzyme, and ECG criteria (pp.1330–1331, Tables 1 and 3). Death categories were defined; two committee members independently reviewed each reported event, with central resolution of disagreements (pp.1330–1331).
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1(5) requires considering influential composite components; appropriate assessment of stroke and MI matters here, not merely death ascertainment.

evidence: Common follow-up visits, event definitions, and central validation applied to both groups (pp.1330–1331). Early changes to visit frequency followed blinded safety reviews and were not treatment-specific. No systematic difference in event ascertainment is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods and thresholds “at comparable time points.” §7.3 focuses on systematic differences in opportunities to detect outcomes.

evidence: Events were centrally adjudicated; code access was restricted to specified statistical, monitoring, and drug-preparation personnel. The coordinating centre received the code after supplying the final database (pp.1331–1332). Adjudicator masking is supported indirectly, not expressly guaranteed for every event; local code breaks do not establish central adjudicator awareness.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: No when assessors were blinded. §1.1 permits PN where evidence supports an inference; §7.3 requires identifying who assessed the outcome.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=PN. Stroke, MI, and vascular-cause classification involve judgement, but the assessment process was probably masked (pp.1330–1332).
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 applies only after Y/PY/NI to 4.3. §7.1 distinguishes these events from judgement-free all-cause mortality.

evidence: Not reached under the preceding branch; the documented central review process supports 4.3=PN (pp.1331–1332).
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: Strong supporting evidence exists: the primary analysis “was to be the unadjusted intention-to-treat comparison”; interim analyses used the primary cluster; code release was restricted (pp.1331–1332). Nevertheless, the supplied article does not establish when the complete final analysis intentions were finalized relative to unblinded access. No dated protocol/SAP is supplied.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded data availability. §8.3.1 calls for a confirming “date-stamp”; §8.3.2 recognizes limitations from incomplete documentation. The problem is unresolved timing, not a rule that a separate SAP must always exist.

evidence: Methods identify the exact first-event composite and planned follow-up; Table 6 reports that outcome (pp.1331, 1333). No evidence indicates selection of a favourable measurement or time point. This inference is supported by detailed reported intentions, although prospective documentation is unavailable.
guidance: §8.3.2 permits comparing Methods and Results when prospective intentions are unavailable and requires explaining inferences. Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: The article designates the unadjusted ITT analysis as primary and reports all five stated outcome clusters, including nonsignificant estimates (pp.1331, 1333, Table 6). It discloses similar adjusted effects, the more favourable on-treatment result, and a separate post hoc subgroup analysis (pp.1333, 1335). These observations oppose selective choice of the target estimate, although all analytic decisions cannot be independently audited.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely result-based selection, not multiplicity alone; alternative composite definitions belong here. §8.3.2 permits inference from reported intentions and results. §8.1 makes this assessment specific to the reported result.

evidence: “Unblinded block randomization at inclusion” is reported, but the method generating the sequence and random ordering within blocks are absent (p. 2, Study Design).
guidance: §4.3.1.1: blocked allocation without confirmation of a random component should generally receive “‘No information’.”

evidence: No central allocation, envelopes, or other concealment procedure is described (p. 2). “Unblinded” does not establish whether forthcoming allocations were known before enrolment.
guidance: §4.1: “Allocation concealment should not be confused with blinding.” Box 4, 1.2 requires evidence about concealment until assignment; §1.1 permits NI when inference is insufficiently supported.

evidence: Baseline data cover all 121 randomized knees. Groups were 61 versus 60, with similar ages, sports participation and meniscal status; no implausible imbalance is apparent (p. 4, Table 2).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when “no imbalances are apparent or…observed imbalances are compatible with chance.”

evidence: The trial is described as “unblinded”; LET also required extension of the lateral incision. Participant masking is not described (pp. 2–3). Awareness is probable rather than explicitly confirmed for participants.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants were aware; §1.1 permits “Probably” responses when judgement is necessary.

evidence: Surgeons delivered the visibly different procedures: “For the BTB-LET group, an extra-articular tenodesis was added” (p. 3); the trial was unblinded (p. 2).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 includes “people delivering the interventions”; awareness of the procedure establishes Y.

evidence: Surgical techniques and clinically indicated meniscal treatment are described, but trial-induced departures, rehabilitation adherence and non-protocol co-interventions are not adequately reported (pp. 2–3). Later revision surgery does not itself establish a trial-context deviation (pp. 5–6).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” deviations arose because of trial context; “‘No information’ may be appropriate” when this is unreported. Treatment of intervention consequences is not itself a deviation.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3 = NI; trial-context deviations were not established from the treatment descriptions (pp. 2–3).
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 applies only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is not applicable. No established trial-context deviations require a balance assessment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: One originally eligible patient “underwent a total knee replacement… and was excluded from the analysis” (p. 4). Figure 2 places this exclusion in BTB. Otherwise, the original groups appear preserved, including participants with graft failure/revision (Tables 4 and 6).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: “Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should…be considered inappropriate.” §5.3.1 assigns exclusions solely for missing outcomes to D3 instead.

evidence: The identified treatment-related exclusion concerns one of 61 BTB knees; there is no reported reassignment in analysis. Although knee replacement is prognostically relevant, one exclusion is unlikely to substantially change this continuous-score comparison, whose stated clinically important difference is 10 points (p. 3; p. 4, Figure 2; Table 4).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 requires judging whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact”; “It is not possible to specify a precise rule.” §1.2.1 concerns material bias.

evidence: Questionnaires were available for 80/121 knees: 42 BTB and 38 BTB-LET. Figure 2 identifies 18 and 22 losses, respectively, plus the separate BTB knee-replacement exclusion (p. 4; Table 4). The narrative inconsistently labels patient/knee counts, but substantial loss is clear.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” as sufficiently few missing outcomes that they could make “no important difference”; these losses do not meet that criterion.

evidence: No missing-data correction or sensitivity analysis is reported (p. 3, Statistics). Baseline comparisons between retained and lost participants are provided (Table 3), but do not demonstrate robustness to missing IKDC values.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires methods correcting bias or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions” about missingness and true outcomes.

evidence: Reasons for loss are not reported. Participation in follow-up could plausibly depend on knee symptoms or function. The article demonstrates substantially lower IKDC among patients with unrevised graft failure (72 versus 84.5; p. 4), although it does not show that such patients were more often lost.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if loss “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Loss rates differed modestly: 18/61 BTB versus 22/60 BTB-LET (Figure 2). Conversely, measured baseline characteristics were not statistically different between retained and lost participants (Table 3). Without reasons for loss or subsequent health information, whether missingness *likely* depended on IKDC cannot be established.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely” and considers differences in loss proportions and reasons. §1.1 supports NI when neither probable answer is adequately supported; Table 10 maps NI here to High.

evidence: Subjective IKDC was the stated primary measure and was collected through patient questionnaires; no unsuitable modification or measurement limitation is reported (p. 3, Outcome Evaluation; Table 4).
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for “methods…unsuitable for the outcome”; subjectivity alone does not make a method inappropriate.

evidence: Both groups completed subjective IKDC at the same long-term follow-up. Some participants attended examination and others completed questionnaires alone, but no systematic difference in questionnaire ascertainment by assignment is reported (pp. 1, 3–4; Figure 2).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 considers “the same measurement methods…used at comparable time points”; §7.3 focuses on systematic between-group differences.

evidence: Participants were probably aware in this unblinded surgical trial (pp. 2–3). The examiner was “independent from the original surgeon,” but examiner independence does not establish participant blinding (p. 3).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “For participant-reported outcomes, the outcome assessor is the study participant.” §7.1 applies this even with a blinded interviewer.

evidence: IKDC is explicitly a patient-reported, subjective assessment (p. 3; Table 4), allowing knowledge and expectations about surgery to influence responses.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: knowledge “could influence participant-reported outcomes.”

evidence: The assessment occurred approximately 19 years after two active surgical interventions and was recorded by an examiner independent of the original surgeon (pp. 3–4). Investigators expressed belief in LET (p. 2), but strong participant expectations or surgeon-led elicitation of favourable answers are not documented. Material influence is possible but judged unlikely.
guidance: §7.3 identifies active comparators, independent interviewers and distant assessment timing as factors reducing likely influence. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from influence likely to have occurred.

evidence: The article specifies primary IKDC and statistical testing, but provides no dated analysis plan demonstrating finalization before unblinded outcomes were available (p. 3). No separate plan was supplied.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1: “finalization of the analysis intentions must precede availability of unblinded outcome data.” §8.3.1 requires attention to document dates.

evidence: The target fixes subjective IKDC at approximately 19 years, and that measurement is reported in Table 4. Other named functional scales are also reported. Earlier follow-up nonpublication is attributed to extensive loss (p. 3); those earlier time points are outside this target.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: “Attention should be restricted to outcome measurements that are eligible” for this assessment. §8.3.2 permits comparison of article methods and reported results when prospective intentions are unavailable.

evidence: The report specifies t tests or Mann–Whitney tests according to normality and presents final-score comparisons (p. 3; Table 4). Without prospective intentions, selection among eligible analytical approaches cannot be verified; there is no affirmative evidence of results-based selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and “there is more than one way” the measurement could have been analysed.

evidence: “Unblinded block randomization at inclusion” provides no sequence-generation method or confirmation of random ordering within blocks (p. 2, Study Design).
guidance: §4.3.1.1: blocked allocation without an explicit random component should generally receive “‘No information’.”

evidence: Table 2 covers all 121 randomized knees: allocation numbers were 61 versus 60, with no conspicuous differences in baseline age, sports participation or meniscal status (p. 4).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: N when no imbalances are apparent or observed differences are “compatible with chance.” §4.3.3 requires consideration of all randomized participants.

guidance: Box 6, 2.2 includes “people delivering the interventions.”

guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires sufficiently few missing outcomes that they could make “no important difference.”

guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions” relating missingness to true outcomes.

evidence: The article specifies primary IKDC and statistical methods, but supplies no dated plan establishing that these intentions preceded access to unblinded outcomes (p. 3).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcomes became available; §8.3.1 requires attention to a confirming “date-stamp.”

evidence: The requested subjective IKDC measurement at approximately 19 years is reported, alongside the other named functional scales (Table 4). Earlier nonpublication is explained by extensive loss (p. 3), and earlier time points are outside this target.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: restrict attention to outcome measurements “eligible for consideration” by the assessor. §8.3.2 permits comparison of article methods and results without prospective intentions.

evidence: A, p. 2: allocation involved “selecting and opening a sealed envelope.” Neither A nor R describes sequence generation, shuffling, or explicitly random selection of envelopes. R, Design, states “RANDOMIZED.”
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer NI when the information establishes only that the study was randomized. §4.3.1 requires evidence of a “random component.”

evidence: A, p. 2: envelopes were opened after arthroscopic confirmation of the tear, supporting concealment until eligibility was established. guidance: Box 4, 1.2, and Table 2: appropriate envelopes should be “opaque, sequentially numbered” and sealed. §1.1 permits NI when there is insufficient basis for PY or PN.

evidence: A, Table 1, p. 4, footnote: “Patient data … are analyzed for 18 patients.” Thus characteristics concern the analysed subset, rather than all 20 enrolled participants. Reported differences do not clearly exceed chance, but the complete randomized baseline comparison is unavailable.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: NI applies where studies report “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis.” §4.3.3 requires assessment based on all randomized participants.

evidence: R, Design → Masking info: “Masking: NONE.” A reports no participant-blinding procedure.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 addresses whether participants knew their assignment; §5.1.3 distinguishes awareness from deviations actually causing bias.

evidence: R identifies no masking. A, pp. 2–3: surgeons assigned and performed ACLR with or without the additional LET operation.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether “people delivering the interventions” were aware; the operating surgeons necessarily knew which procedure they delivered.

evidence: A, p. 3: “All patients followed the standardized post-ACLR physical therapy protocol according to meniscal condition.” Surgical delivery is described without crossovers or context-driven co-interventions. Rehabilitation effects were not assessed (p. 8). R’s hamstring/Marcacci description differs from A’s quadriceps-or-BTB/modified-Lemaire procedures, but R’s eligibility criteria also specify quadriceps or BTB grafts. These inconsistencies do not establish deviations caused by trial participation or knowledge of assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that the trial context caused departures from intended treatment. §5.1.2.1 requires deviations to arise from trial context, conflict with the protocol, and influence outcomes.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3 = PN.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: A, pp. 2–3: participants were assigned to the two surgical groups; comparisons retain those groups. evidence: R, Enrollment: actual enrollment 20; Description specifies 20 surgical patients randomly assigned. A, p. 3: 18 completed 6-month testing and 16 completed 12-month testing. guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference”; 95% availability will often suffice for continuous outcomes. §6.1.3.2 cautions against a universal threshold.

evidence: 6 months: A, p. 3: “Two patients withdrew from participation at 6 months”; reasons are absent, so withdrawal could relate to knee function or ability to run. 12 months: two additional patients “reinjured their ACL graft,” directly implicating knee stability and the ability to complete kinematic testing.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness may depend on the outcome. Low risk requires documented reasons unrelated to the outcome.

guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness may depend on the outcome. Low risk requires documented reasons unrelated to the outcome.

evidence: A, p. 3 and Figure 2, p. 4: both groups underwent the same laboratory protocol at 6 and 12 months, with three trials averaged per knee, identical coordinate conventions, and the same SSD calculation.

evidence: A, p. 3: validated image registration, automatically determined anatomical coordinate systems, standard mathematical conventions, and averaging of three trials substantially constrain subjective assessment. guidance: §7.1, outcome type 2: observer-reported outcomes involving little judgement are usually unlikely to be influenced by assignment knowledge. Box 10, 4.4 focuses on whether knowledge could influence assessment.

evidence: A, p. 3, specifies SSD comparisons at 10% gait-cycle increments using Mann–Whitney tests, but does not establish prospective finalization. guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” establishing finalization before unblinded data. §8.3.2 and Box 11, 5.1 require sufficiently detailed intentions to verify correspondence.

evidence: A, Figures 5–6, pp. 7–8, displays ATT and TR at all five specified gait instants at both visits, including nonsignificant findings. guidance: Box 11, 5.2: NI when intentions are “not reported in sufficient detail” and multiple measurements are possible. Y/PY requires evidence of selection “on the basis of the results.” §8.1.2 restricts assessment to eligible measurements.

evidence: A, p. 3, describes final postoperative SSD comparisons and separate longitudinal tests; R does not specify the exact analysis, gait-phase contrast, covariate handling, or missing-data strategy. guidance: Box 11, 5.3: NI applies when analysis intentions lack sufficient detail and multiple analyses are possible. High risk requires evidence that the reported analysis was selected based on its results.

evidence: Art, p. 2: “selecting and opening a sealed envelope.” Neither envelope shuffling/random drawing nor the sequence-generation method is described. Reg, Design, says “RANDOMIZED,” without additional detail. Selecting an envelope does not itself establish a random component.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 and §4.3.1: random generation requires a “random component”; a statement that allocation was randomized is insufficient.

evidence: Groups contained 35 and 37 infants. Gestational age, birth weight and respiratory measures were similar. Maternal diabetes differed, 23% versus 5%, P=.032, but this isolated difference among numerous comparisons is compatible with chance (A, Table I, p.3; Table II, p.7).

evidence: The exclusion involved 30 of 17,190 randomized participants, approximately 0.17%, against 1,559 MACE events and 913 cardiovascular-death/heart-failure events (A Fig.2; S Fig.S1). evidence: S Fig.S1, p.43: consent withdrawal was 97 versus 127 and loss to follow-up 12 versus 18—up to 254 participants with incomplete follow-up.
