Against 1,559 and 913 events, an immaterial impact cannot confidently be assumed.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §§6.1.3.2 and 6.1.5 reject a universal percentage cutoff and count prematurely censored follow-up as missing.

evidence: SAP §§4.4.1.3, pp.40–42 plans multiple-imputation and tipping-point analyses, but their results are absent from the supplied reports. S Table S2, p.50 reports competing-risk and per-protocol analyses; these do not test plausible outcome-dependent loss to follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7: evidence must correct missing-data bias or demonstrate robustness under assumptions about the relationship between missingness and the true outcome. A planned analysis is not a demonstrated result.

evidence: SAP p.40 states that follow-up between last clinical contact and planned closure is missing for relevant withdrawals. P §5.9, p.48 provides for collecting withdrawal reasons, but outcome-specific reasons are not reported. Health-related withdrawal therefore remains possible.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on its true value.

evidence: Missing follow-up was modest and fairly similar: 109/8,582 versus 145/8,578. No reported reasons establish outcome-dependent withdrawal. Importantly, treatment discontinuation did not itself censor the primary analysis: SAP §2.1.1, p.19 includes events after discontinuation; P p.48 separates discontinuation from withdrawal. The modest imbalance warrants consideration but does not establish likely informative censoring.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely,” considering differential missingness, reasons and treatment-related censoring. §1.1 allows PN where evidence supports a reasoned inference despite incomplete reporting.

evidence: A journal p.349 reports adjudication of all primary-outcome components. S §D specifies cardiovascular death, MI and stroke criteria; pp.35–36 require HF admission, duration, symptoms, objective evidence and treatment intensification. These are suitable methods for the stated composites.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1 requires considering influential components of composite outcomes, rather than treating them as all-cause mortality.

evidence: A journal p.349 specifies the same six-month visits and intervening telephone contacts. P §12.4.1, p.85 requires reporting suspected events and at least monthly database searches. No differential ascertainment procedure is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable methods use the same measurement methods, thresholds and comparable time points; consider unequal opportunities for detection.

evidence: P §12.4.1, p.85 specifies an “independent, blinded CEC”; A p.349 confirms adjudication. Clinical personnel were also blinded (P p.42), relevant because hospitalization involves provider decisions. Actual unblinding frequency is unavailable.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: blinded assessors support No/Probably no. §7.1 identifies care providers as assessors for hospitalization decisions and requires considering composite components.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. MI, stroke classification and HF hospitalization involve judgement, but assessor awareness was not established.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI; subjective judgement alone does not bypass this branch.

evidence: Question 4.4 was not reached.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: P pp.76–77 and SAP pp.38–39 specify the reported composites, first-event analysis, full analysis population and stratified Cox model. A journal p.348 says the endpoint amendment preceded comparative MACE access; S p.20 dates the decision to December 2015 and first DMC MACE review to February 2016. The exact final investigator-unblinding date is absent, so PY is appropriate.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1: changes before unblinded data availability “do not raise concerns.” §8.3.1 requires checking dates and distinguishes confidential DMC access from investigator access.

evidence: Both specified primary composites are reported, including nonsignificant MACE (A Figs.1–2; S Table S2). The addition of cardiovascular death/HF followed external findings, with its timing and rationale documented (A p.348; S p.20). No evidence identifies selection of a favourable definition or time point using DECLARE results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: justified differences unrelated to the trial’s results support No/Probably no; §8.3.2 recognizes legitimate protocol amendments.

evidence: Reported estimates match the designated primary Cox analyses (P p.77; SAP p.38; A pp.349–350). Alternative competing-risk and per-protocol results are also shown (S Table S2). Some planned sensitivity results are absent, and SAP p.9 removed an optional analysis including site 5709; neither establishes that the reported primary estimate was chosen because of its result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely selection “on the basis of the results.” §8.1 distinguishes selection of an available estimate from non-reporting; multiple possible analyses alone do not establish selective choice.

evidence: P §5.2.1, pp.40–41: allocation codes were “computer generated” using GRAND, with balanced blocks and stratification. This directly establishes a random sequence.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: computer-generated random numbers satisfy the requirement for a “random component.”

evidence: P pp.40–42: IVRS/IWRS assigned eligible participants a randomization number and kit identifiers; site personnel could not access the allocation scheme. Fixed blocks do not establish predictability when assignments remain concealed.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 accepts centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel. §4.3.2 identifies prediction concerns when previous assignments and block boundaries are known.

evidence: A Table 1, p.351: similar age, cardiovascular disease, heart failure, renal function and medications; group sizes 8,582 versus 8,578. The 30 excluded participants are absent from this table, but the remaining near-complete baseline information gives no indication of compromised randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No for differences “compatible with chance.” §4.3.3 requires considering exclusions when interpreting baseline information.

evidence: P p.42 specifies tablets identical in “size, color, smell, and taste”; A p.349 confirms double-blind treatment. Genital infections were more frequent with dapagliflozin (A Table 2), but actual recognition of assignment or unblinding frequency is not reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 considers blinding and adverse effects known to identify treatment. §5.1.3 cautions that blinding procedures do not guarantee successful blinding; §1.1 permits a supported probable answer.

evidence: P §5.4, p.42 excludes study delivery teams and site staff from the allocation scheme; emergency code-breaking was restricted. Actual code-breaking counts are absent. The double-blind report supports probable lack of awareness, without proving universal concealment throughout follow-up.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 assesses awareness among carers/deliverers, including recognizable toxicities. §1.1 permits inference rather than automatically assigning NI.

evidence: Both awareness questions remain PN. Discontinuation and open-label SGLT2 use occurred (A p.350), but these do not themselves establish awareness-driven, trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. §5.1.2.1 distinguishes ordinary nonadherence from deviations arising because of the trial context.

evidence: Not reached through 2.3; the treatment changes reported on A p.350 do not bypass that branch.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached through 2.4. Differences in discontinuation reported in S Fig.S1 do not independently activate this question.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: A pp.349–350 and SAP §2.1, p.19: participants were analysed by assignment regardless of adherence, except 30 randomized participants intentionally excluded because of concerns about site 5709. They were not documented as ineligible. P p.76 and S Table S2 confirm that MACE noninferiority used the full analysis set, rather than the treated-only safety set.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: excluding eligible participants after randomization is inappropriate; the explicit eligibility exception does not cover this site exclusion. §5.3.1 assesses the actual analysis, not its ITT label.

evidence: Thirty exclusions represent approximately 0.17% of 17,190 randomized participants. There were 1,559 MACE and 913 cardiovascular-death/HF events (A Fig.2; S Fig.S1). Site integrity was the stated reason, not treatment response. Excluded outcomes and their arm distribution are unavailable, but substantial impact appears unlikely.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 requires judging potential “substantial impact,” considering event frequency and prognosis rather than a universal percentage threshold.

evidence: S Fig.S1, p.43: 97 versus 127 withdrew consent; 12 versus 18 were lost. These 254 participants are an upper bound on affected first-event outcomes: some may already have experienced an endpoint. That breakdown and missing follow-up duration are unreported. Vital-status recovery does not establish complete MI, stroke or HF follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by whether missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §6.1.3.2 rejects a fixed percentage cutoff; §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing follow-up.

evidence: SAP pp.40–42 plans imputation and tipping-point analyses, but their results are not supplied. S Table S2, p.50 reports competing-risk and per-protocol analyses; neither directly evaluates outcome-dependent withdrawal.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence of correction or robustness. §6.1.7 says sensitivity analyses are helpful only if they address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: SAP p.40 explicitly treats the interval after last clinical contact as missing for event-free participants with incomplete follow-up. Withdrawal reasons sufficient to exclude a relationship with health status are unavailable, although P p.48 required their collection.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: health-related withdrawal makes dependence on the true outcome possible; documented outcome-unrelated reasons could instead support No.

evidence: Combined withdrawal/loss was approximately 1.27% versus 1.69% (S Fig.S1). This modest difference warrants scrutiny but, without outcome-related reasons or another mechanism, does not establish likely informative censoring. SAP p.19 includes events after drug discontinuation; P p.48 distinguishes discontinuation from study withdrawal.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely,” examining differential missingness, reasons and censoring at treatment cessation. §1.1 permits PN when contextual evidence supports it.

evidence: A p.349 reports adjudication of all primary components. S §D provides clinical definitions; pp.35–36 require HF admission, specified duration, symptoms, objective evidence and treatment intensification. Clinical judgement is involved, but these are appropriate measurement methods.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 addresses unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1 requires examining influential components of composites, rather than assuming every component is fully objective.

evidence: A p.349 describes common six-month visits and intervening telephone contacts. P p.85 requires event reporting and at least monthly database searches for potential events. No systematically different surveillance is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 considers common methods, thresholds and timing, including unequal opportunities to detect events.

evidence: P p.85 specifies an “independent, blinded CEC”; A p.349 confirms adjudication. P p.42 also supports blinding of clinical personnel, important for hospitalization decisions. Actual unblinding frequency is absent.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 supports N/PN for blinded assessors. §7.1 identifies providers as assessors for hospitalization decisions; committee blinding alone would not settle that component.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. Judgement in MI, stroke and HF assessment does not establish assessor awareness (S §D; P pp.42,85).
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached through 4.4; no additional document finding changes that branch.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: P pp.76–77 and SAP p.38 specify the reported composites, first-event approach and stratified Cox model. A p.348 describes amendment without comparative MACE knowledge; S p.20 places the decision in December 2015, before the February 2016 DMC MACE review. Exact final investigator-unblinding timing is absent, supporting PY rather than Y.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 permits changes before unblinded data availability. §8.3.1 requires checking dated intentions and distinguishes confidential monitoring access from investigator access.

evidence: Both primary composites, including nonsignificant MACE, are reported (A Figs.1–2; S Table S2). The added HF composite has a documented external rationale and amendment chronology (A p.348; S p.20). No evidence demonstrates selection of a definition or time point using DECLARE results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 permits N/PN when discrepancies have explanations unrelated to the results; §8.3.2 recognizes legitimate amendments.

evidence: The primary estimates match the planned analyses (P p.77; SAP p.38; A pp.349–350). S Table S2 reports alternatives. Some planned sensitivity results are absent, and SAP p.9 removed an optional site-inclusive analysis, but no evidence shows that the reported primary analysis replaced another because its result was preferable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely selection “on the basis of the results.” The availability of multiple analyses and incomplete reporting warrant examination but do not alone establish such selection.

evidence: Protocol §6.3, p.36: “randomisation codes will be computer generated,” with balanced blocks and central IxRS allocation. Appendix p.21 confirms use of this allocation procedure.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when sequence generation uses a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: Protocol §6.3, p.36: patients “centrally assigned” through an interactive voice/web response system; investigators received kit identification numbers. Appendix p.21 confirms allocation after consent and eligibility assessment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: remote or centrally administered allocation supports Yes; §4.3.2 and Table 2 identify central randomization as adequate concealment.

evidence: Article Table 1, p.4, and Appendix Table S4, pp.34–35: groups numbered 3131/3132 and were similar in age, ejection fraction, renal function, diabetes and prior HF hospitalization. NYHA III differed somewhat (25.8%/23.1%), but the pattern does not suggest failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: “differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.”

evidence: Article p.2 describes a double-blind trial with “matching placebo”; Protocol §6.3, p.36 describes controlled emergency code breaking. Actual participant awareness or the frequency of unblinding is not reported; the safeguards support probable unawareness.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding may prevent awareness. §1.1 permits a probable response when supported by circumstances; §5.1.3 cautions that attempted blinding does not guarantee success.

evidence: Protocol §6.3, p.36: investigators dispensed IxRS-designated kits; codes should not be broken except for medical emergencies. Article p.2 confirms double blinding. Actual emergency unblinding is not enumerated, but no evidence establishes material awareness among treating personnel.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding can prevent personnel awareness. §1.1 supports an inferential PN rather than NI where the evidence permits a judgement.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. Article p.3 reports discontinuation in 444/442 patients; Protocol §§7.1–7.1.2, pp.39–40 permits clinically necessary discontinuation and continued follow-up. Discontinuation alone does not establish a trial-context deviation.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 is conditional on “Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2.” §5.1.2.1: deviations not arising because of the trial context do not bias the assignment effect.

evidence: Not reached: 2.3 is NA. The discontinuation information in Article p.3 does not activate this branch.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: answer only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached: 2.4 is NA. Similar discontinuation counts in Article p.3 are not treated as evidence about the balance of trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Appendix p.22: “all patients who underwent randomization” were included according to ITT. SAP §2.1.1, p.22 specifies analysis by randomized assignment irrespective of treatment received or adherence. Article Table 2, p.5 uses all 3131/3132 patients; the five untreated patients per group were excluded only from safety analyses.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT analyses are appropriate; missing-outcome bias is assessed separately in D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is Y. The primary efficacy population includes all randomized patients (Appendix p.22; Article Table 2).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: answer only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Appendix Figure S2, p.27 reports incomplete primary-endpoint follow-up in 29/3131 (0.93%) versus 23/3132 (0.73%). These 52 participants are few relative to 1122 observed primary events (Article Table 2). Reasons for every incomplete assessment are not detailed, but material bias is unlikely at this extent. This uses composite-endpoint completeness, not merely the four unknown vital statuses. Protocol p.40 requires continued endpoint collection after stopping treatment.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” depends on whether missing outcomes could importantly change the estimate; when observed events greatly exceed missing participants, bias is necessarily small. §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing follow-up.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1 is PY. SAP §4.2.3.2, p.34 describes optional imputation/tipping-point analyses; their results were not located in the supplied reports and are not assumed to demonstrate robustness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2: answer only “If N/PN/NI to 3.1.” §6.1.7 requires sensitivity analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and true outcome.

evidence: Not reached after 3.1=PY. Figure S2, Appendix p.27 establishes the small amount of incomplete composite follow-up; it does not fully explain its causes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: answer only “If N/PN to 3.2”; §6.3(1) allows stopping when data are available for nearly all participants.

evidence: Not reached after 3.1=PY. Treatment discontinuation is not equated with loss of endpoint follow-up: Protocol §7.1.2, p.40 requires continued data collection.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 3.3.” §6.1.5 specifically distinguishes censoring at treatment cessation from continued observation.

evidence: Appendix p.22 defines unplanned HF hospitalization or urgent HF visit requiring intravenous therapy, or cardiovascular death. Article p.3 reports adjudication of potential HF events and deaths using prespecified criteria. SAP p.23 specifies standardized event definitions and adjudication.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods, not whether the outcome choice is desirable. Prespecified clinical criteria and adjudication provide an appropriate method.

evidence: Appendix p.21 specifies the same follow-up schedule—approximately days 30 and 120, then every 120 days—and common pandemic adaptations. Appendix p.22 describes common adjudication criteria. No differential surveillance or thresholds are reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable ascertainment uses “the same measurement methods and thresholds, used at comparable time points.”

evidence: Article p.3: the independent clinical-events committee was “unaware of the trial-group assignments.” Treating personnel were also probably blinded (Protocol p.36). This matters because HF hospitalization/urgent visits were influential components: 368/455 patients, compared with 231/261 cardiovascular deaths (Article Table 2). Actual treating-personnel unblinding is not enumerated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 supports No for blinded assessors. §7.1 identifies care providers as assessors of hospitalization decisions and requires consideration of the composite’s “most influential components.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. HF admission decisions and cause-of-death adjudication involve judgement, but probable assessor blinding determines this branch (Article p.3; Protocol p.36).
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA; no separate inference of influence is required from the outcome’s subjectivity. Supporting blinding evidence: Article p.3 and Protocol p.36.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: SAP pp.1, 22–23 and 32 specifies the dated plan, full randomized population, first-event composite and diabetes-stratified Cox analysis, matching Article p.3/Table 2. Protocol §9.4, p.60 requires final amendments before database lock and analysts to remain blinded until lock. Appendix p.22 confirms sponsor/academic leadership did not receive unblinded interim results. An explicit actual database-lock/unblinding date was not located, so timing is judged probable rather than certain.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded data availability. §8.3.1 excludes confidential monitoring-committee analysts from this restriction and requires scrutiny of dated amendments.

evidence: The first-event composite was already defined in the original SAP dated 27 August 2018 (Protocol bundle p.204), and remains defined in final SAP p.23 and reported in Article Table 2. The November 2020 amendment added concurrent LVEF <60% testing (Appendix p.22); both population results are reported (Article p.3; Appendix Table S5). There is no indication that a favorable definition or time point replaced the intended full-population outcome.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N when reported eligible measurements correspond to intended measurements; selection must be “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: SAP §4.2.3, p.32 prespecifies the reported ITT Cox model with diabetes stratification. Additional analyses existed, but the designated primary estimate was retained. Appendix p.25 transparently reports violation of proportional hazards and an alternative estimate of 0.80 (95% CI 0.71–0.89). Not every planned sensitivity result is displayed, but there is no evidence that this primary estimate was chosen because it was more favorable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns results-based selection among eligible analyses; multiplicity alone does not establish it. §8.1 distinguishes selection of this estimate from non-reporting of other results.

evidence: Protocol §6.3, p.36: “randomisation codes will be computer generated,” using balanced blocks. Appendix p.21 confirms implementation of the randomization procedure.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers,” supports Y.

evidence: Protocol p.36 specifies central IxRS assignment and dispensing by kit identification number; Appendix p.21 confirms allocation after consent and eligibility assessment. Emergency access to an individual’s assigned treatment does not demonstrate advance knowledge of forthcoming assignments.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2: centrally administered allocation supports concealment. §4.1 distinguishes allocation concealment from subsequent blinding.

evidence: Article Table 1, p.4: 3131/3132 participants; similar age, ejection fraction, diabetes and renal function. NYHA III was 25.8%/23.1%, but this isolated difference does not establish a defective allocation process. Appendix Table S4, pp.34–35 supplies additional balanced prognostic characteristics.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences compatible with chance do not imply bias; a small number of conventional statistically significant differences can occur by chance.

evidence: Article p.2 describes double blinding and matching placebo. Protocol p.36 restricts code breaking to medical emergencies. Actual unblinding frequency and participant recognition of treatment are not reported; the described safeguards support probable unawareness, not certainty.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 addresses actual awareness, including recognized treatment-specific effects. §1.1 permits probable answers where circumstances support inference; §5.1.3 cautions that attempted blinding may fail.

evidence: Protocol p.36 specifies coded kits and restricted emergency unblinding. No report establishes systematic awareness among treating personnel. The availability of emergency code breaking alone does not demonstrate that it occurred.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding may prevent personnel awareness. §1.1 supports PN rather than NI when sufficient contextual evidence permits judgement.

evidence: Not reached because both awareness answers are PN. Article p.3 reports 444/442 treatment discontinuations; Protocol pp.39–40 allows clinically necessary discontinuation and requires continued study participation. These counts alone do not establish trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 applies only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. §5.1.2.1 excludes ordinary non-adherence unrelated to trial context from bias in the assignment effect.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3 is NA; the discontinuations reported in Article p.3 do not independently activate this question.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA. Similar discontinuation numbers in Article p.3 are not substituted for evidence about the balance of trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Appendix p.22 explicitly includes “all patients who underwent randomization” according to ITT. SAP p.22 specifies analysis by randomized assignment regardless of adherence or treatment received. Article Table 2, p.5 retains 3131/3132 patients; the five untreated patients per group were excluded only from safety analyses.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT analysis is appropriate; missing-outcome concerns belong in D3, not in this analysis question.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 is Y. Appendix p.22 and Article Table 2 support inclusion of the randomized efficacy population.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Appendix Figure S2, p.27 reports incomplete primary-endpoint follow-up in 29/3131 and 23/3132 participants, approximately 0.93%/0.73%. These 52 participants are few relative to 1122 observed primary events (Article Table 2). Reasons and timing for all incomplete assessments are not supplied, so this remains a judgement of probable negligible material impact. It does not rely on the smaller count of unknown vital statuses.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” depends on the possible effect of missing outcomes; observed events greatly exceeding missing participants supports low risk. §§6.1.3.2 and 6.1.5 prohibit a universal percentage threshold and count premature censoring as missing data.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1 is PY. SAP p.34 proposes optional imputation/tipping-point analyses, but their results were not located; planning them is not evidence that they demonstrated robustness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 applies only after N/PN/NI to 3.1. §6.1.7 requires actual sensitivity evidence addressing outcome-dependent missingness.

evidence: Not reached after 3.1=PY. Appendix Figure S2 does not fully explain missingness, and no assumption that missingness was unrelated to health is needed for this route.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3 applies only after N/PN to 3.2; §6.3(1) allows stopping when nearly all outcome data are available.

evidence: Not reached. Protocol §7.1.2, p.40 requires endpoint collection after treatment discontinuation, so the much larger discontinuation counts cannot be treated as equivalent losses to follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 applies only after Y/PY/NI to 3.3. §6.1.5 specifically identifies censoring at treatment cessation as a concern when it occurs.

evidence: Appendix pp.18–20 defines hospitalization and urgent HF events using symptoms, objective findings and treatment requirements; p.22 reports blinded adjudication against prespecified criteria. Clinical judgement remains involved, but the method is not unsuitable.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for inappropriate measurement methods, rather than whether the outcome itself is desirable or entirely objective.

evidence: Appendix p.21 describes common scheduled follow-up and pandemic adaptations; p.22 describes common adjudication. No differential assessment thresholds, schedules or additional surveillance by allocation are reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable ascertainment uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable times; differential opportunities for detection would raise concern.

evidence: Article p.3 explicitly describes an independent committee unaware of assignment; Protocol p.36 supports probable blinding of treating personnel. The latter matters because hospitalizations and urgent visits involve provider decisions and were frequent components (Article Table 2). Actual provider unblinding is not enumerated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 supports N/PN for blinded assessors. §7.1 identifies care providers as assessors of decision outcomes and requires attention to a composite’s most influential components.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. HF admission decisions could be influenced if providers knew allocation, but Article p.3 and Protocol p.36 support the preceding blinding judgement.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.” Subjectivity alone does not activate the branch.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA; the supporting assessor-blinding evidence remains Article p.3 and Protocol p.36.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5: “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: SAP dated 8 December 2021, pp.1, 22–23 and 32, specifies the reported population, endpoint and diabetes-stratified Cox analysis. Protocol p.60 requires final amendments before database lock and continued analyst blinding. Appendix p.22 states sponsor/academic leadership did not receive unblinded interim results. An explicit actual lock/unblinding date was not located; timing therefore remains probable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded data availability. §8.3.1 permits confidential monitoring-committee analysis and requires consideration of dated amendments.

evidence: The original SAP defines the same first-event composite (Bundle p.204); final SAP p.23 and Article Table 2 retain it. The added LVEF <60% analysis is disclosed (Appendix p.22), and both population results are reported (Article p.3; Appendix Table S5). No favorable replacement definition or time point is evident.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N when eligible reported measurements correspond to intended measurements; the concern is selection “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: SAP p.32 specifies the reported ITT Cox model. Appendix p.25 discloses a proportional-hazards violation and an alternative estimate of 0.80 (95% CI 0.71–0.89). Some planned sensitivity results, including the undetermined-death analysis in SAP p.34, are not displayed in the supplied reports. Nevertheless, the designated primary estimate was retained, with no evidence that it was selected for greater favorability.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence of results-based selection among analyses. §§8.1–8.3 distinguish selection of the assessed estimate from multiplicity or incomplete reporting alone.

evidence: A p.9: “Randomization occurred in variable block sizes and was stratified by BMRC grade.” A p.11 acknowledges a “random list holder,” but neither source describes how the sequence was generated or explicitly establishes a random component within blocks.
guidance: §4.3.1.1: when blocked allocation is reported without confirmation of random ordering, “‘No information’ should generally be provided.”

evidence: A pp.9–11 describes matching placebo, blinding and a list holder, but does not describe centralized allocation, concealed envelopes/containers, or recruiters’ access before assignment. These safeguards are supportive but do not establish concealment.
guidance: §4.1: allocation concealment “should not be confused with blinding.” Box 4, 1.2 requires concealment until enrollment and assignment; §1.1 permits NI when an inference is insufficiently supported.

evidence: A p.4, Table 1: 20 participants per arm; similar age, consciousness and TBM severity. Differences in sex, HIV status and CSF protein are compatible with chance in this small trial; no convincing pattern suggests allocation manipulation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when “any observed imbalances are compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 excludes chance imbalance from systematic bias.

evidence: A pp.9–10 describes equal tablet counts and “matching placebo tablets”; R, “Masking info,” lists participants as masked. One patient’s dose was unblinded after grade IV hepatotoxicity (A pp.3–4), but the report does not establish that the participant learned the assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 addresses participants’ awareness. §1.1 allows “Probably” responses when judgement is needed; §5.1.3 distinguishes actual awareness from merely experiencing adverse effects.

evidence: Personnel were ordinarily masked (R, “Masking info”), but A p.4 explicitly reports that “the blinding to the dose of rifampin was removed” when treating one patient’s grade IV hepatotoxicity.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether carers or intervention providers were aware during the trial; this documented exception establishes some awareness.

evidence: The unblinded patient’s drugs were interrupted and rifampin reduced after grade IV toxicity (A pp.3–4); A p.10 specifies stopping treatment for grade IV events. Other withdrawals followed clinical deterioration or detected resistance (A pp.4–5). No evidence indicates deviations caused by allocation preferences or trial engagement.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: answer No/Probably no for protocol-consistent changes, including “cessation of a drug intervention because of acute toxicity.” Yes requires evidence that the trial context caused non-protocol changes.

evidence: No qualifying trial-context deviation identified in 2.3; reported treatment changes were clinical responses (A pp.3–5, 10).
guidance: Box 6: 2.4 is reached only if 2.3=Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached following 2.3=PN.
guidance: Box 6: 2.5 is reached only if 2.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: A p.10: “The data for safety/tolerability and survival were analyzed by the intention-to-treat principle.” Table 3 retains all 20 randomized participants in each assigned arm; no safety-analysis exclusion or regrouping is reported. evidence: FAS inclusion required starting follitropin stimulation or achieving spontaneous pregnancy, alongside a follow-up variable (Article, p. 1623, Statistical analysis). Consequently, 8/160 intervention and 4/157 comparator participants were excluded (Fig. 1). Retained women were analysed as randomized regardless of diet completion, which supports the analysis, but does not remedy treatment-dependent exclusions. One pregnancy contraindication might qualify as an appropriate eligibility exclusion; the remaining exclusions cannot all do so.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6: excluding eligible randomized participants is inappropriate; the acceptable mITT exception concerns missing outcomes, not failure to receive treatment. Independently established baseline ineligibility can justify exclusion.

evidence: The exclusions warrant concern, particularly because reasons relate to receiving fertility treatment and include one comparator pregnancy after other treatment. However, only 12/317 participants were excluded, compared with 87 observed live births, and retained participants were not regrouped (Article, Fig. 1; Table II). A substantial distortion is judged unlikely, although a modest change remains possible. For scale only, retaining the reported events with all randomized denominators gives a difference of approximately 1.4 rather than 2.2 percentage points; this does not establish the excluded women’s outcomes.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: judge whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact”; there is “no … precise rule,” and fewer than 5% can matter with rare outcomes or strong prognostic selection. This PN judgement considers outcome frequency and exclusion reasons, rather than applying a percentage threshold alone.

evidence: “No patients were lost to follow up,” with zero losses in both arms in Fig. 1; pregnancy follow-up was completed in February 2017 (Article, pp. 1623–1624). The 12 FAS omissions are described as treatment/eligibility exclusions, not lost outcome ascertainment. Their individual live-birth outcomes are not tabulated, preventing an unequivocal Y.
guidance: §6.1 distinguishes genuinely missing outcomes from “data deliberately excluded”; the latter belong in D2. Box 8, 3.1 concerns outcome availability for all randomized participants, not simply inclusion in the reported denominator.

evidence: Live birth was defined as “at least one child born alive regardless of gestational age” (Article, p. 1623, Outcomes); pregnancy follow-up was completed (p. 1623). No unsuitable measurement method is identified.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for methods “unsuitable for the outcome”; an explicitly defined, objective birth event does not indicate such a problem.

evidence: The same definition was applied to both groups, including births after spontaneous pregnancies (Article, p. 1623; Table II, p. 1626). Registry follow-up was approximately 10–16 months “depending on study group.” The extra pre-IVF time was an intended intervention difference; there is no indication of different birth-detection methods or thresholds. Detailed ascertainment procedures are not supplied.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 assesses comparable methods, thresholds and time points. §7.1 concerns differential ascertainment; additional opportunities to conceive under the assigned strategy do not themselves establish differential detection of births.

evidence: Registry, Design/Masking, specifies “OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR” masking. The article identifies embryologists and statisticians as masked, while physicians were unblinded (p. 1623). Neither source identifies who specifically ascertained live births or establishes that person’s masking status.
guidance: §7.1 requires identifying the outcome assessor; §5.1.3 cautions that broad masking descriptions may not identify who was blinded. Under §1.1, NI is appropriate when the available details do not support either probable answer for this particular assessor.

evidence: Whether at least one child was born alive, regardless of gestational age, entails essentially no discretionary assessment (Article, p. 1623, Outcomes). Knowledge of assignment would not plausibly change classification of this event.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 and §7.1, outcome type 2: knowledge is unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes “not involving judgement.”

guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if 4.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The article describes FAS, PP, unadjusted and adjusted analyses (p. 1623), but supplies no dated analysis plan. Registration was submitted in March 2012 after recruitment began in October 2010; the supplied registry reflects later updates (Registry, Status and dates). These documents cannot establish when the particular analysis intentions were finalized relative to available unblinded outcomes.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” establishing prior finalization; Box 11, 5.1 requires an adequately specified plan finalized before unblinded outcome data. Late registration alone does not prove result-driven selection.

evidence: Registry, Registered outcomes, identifies primary “Live birth per participating woman,” approximately 10–16 months after randomization. The article reports that endpoint for one treatment cycle, including spontaneous pregnancies (pp. 1622–1623; Table II). The registry separately describes a two-year follow-up aim. There is no indication that the specified index-treatment result was selected from competing measurements because of its findings.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection based on results among eligible measurements. Concordance between the registered primary endpoint and the reported measurement supports PN, while the absence of registry history limits certainty.

evidence: Multiple analyses were possible and performed: FAS, PP, adjusted and subgroup analyses (Article, p. 1623; SI–SIII). PP live births are reported, and the article states that adjustment for previous pregnancy termination “did not alter the results” (p. 1628), which argues against obvious favourable selection. Nevertheless, the supplied material does not specify all prospective analytical choices or fully report the adjusted estimate.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficiently detailed and more than one analysis was possible. Multiple analyses alone do not establish selection; Y/PY requires evidence that reporting was selected on the basis of results.

evidence: Computerized allocation used “Pocock’s minimization technique for sequential randomization” (Article, pp. 1622–1623). An explicit random-component specification is absent, but minimization is documented.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random.” Its incompletely described random component does not require NI under this specific rule.

evidence: “Computerized randomization programme with concealed allocation” supplied by the coordinating centre (Article, p. 1622). Local physicians/nurses performed randomization (p. 1623), but nothing indicates access to forthcoming allocations. Technical safeguards are unspecified.
guidance: §4.3.2 and Box 4, 1.2: assess concealment until assignment; incomplete operational detail can justify “Probably yes.” Local execution does not itself demonstrate foreknowledge.

evidence: Baseline characteristics are reported only for the FAS (Article, Tables I and III, pp. 1625, 1628). Previous pregnancy termination differed: 7.9% versus 20.3%, P=0.0029; most other characteristics were similar. The excluded participants’ baseline data are unavailable.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly gives baseline reporting limited to the final analysis population as an example supporting NI. §4.3.3 requires assessment using all randomized participants.

evidence: “Blinding was not possible for patients” (Article, p. 1623).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: participants aware of assignment → Y.

evidence: Physicians were also unblinded; only embryologists and statisticians were explicitly described as unaware of allocation (Article, p. 1623).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns carers and those delivering intervention, rather than whether some other personnel were masked.

evidence: Documented departures included divorce, spouse illness, personal/medical reasons, delays, and another fertility treatment in one woman per arm (Article, Fig. 1, p. 1624). Their occurrence is clear, but trial-induced causes are not reported. Individual counselling after inability to complete the diet and the intervention-arm IVF delay were intended (Article, p. 1623; Registry, Description).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused departures for Y/PY. Departures consistent with ordinary care circumstances support PN; §5.1 excludes protocol-consistent changes.

evidence: FAS inclusion required starting IVF stimulation or achieving spontaneous pregnancy, plus a follow-up variable (Article, p. 1623). Thus 8/160 versus 4/157 randomized women were omitted (Fig. 1). Analysing retained women as randomized and retaining diet noncompleters are strengths, but do not remove these eligibility-for-analysis restrictions. One baseline pregnancy contraindication might justify exclusion; the other exclusions cannot all be explained as baseline ineligibility.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6: “Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization” are inappropriate. The acceptable mITT exception concerns missing outcomes, not failure to start treatment.

evidence: Twelve participants were excluded, compared with 87 observed births; retained participants stayed in their assigned groups (Article, Fig. 1; Table II). Exclusions related to treatment access and pregnancy make bias plausible, including asymmetric treatment of pregnancies following other fertility treatment. Nevertheless, the limited numbers and predominantly non-initiation reasons support a likely modest impact rather than substantial distortion. This is a judgement, not demonstrated robustness.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 requires assessing “potential for a substantial impact,” with “no … precise rule.” Neither fewer than 5% excluded nor a nonsignificant result proves safety; outcome frequency and exclusion reasons must also be considered.

evidence: “No patients were lost to follow up”; Fig. 1 records zero losses in both arms (Article, p. 1624). Pregnancy follow-up was completed in February 2017 (p. 1623). Individual outcomes for the excluded women are not tabulated, so availability is probable rather than certain; their documented exclusion mechanism is treatment/eligibility based.
guidance: §6.1 distinguishes genuinely missing outcomes from deliberately excluded data, assigning the latter concern to D2. Box 8, 3.1 concerns availability, not whether every participant appears in the analysis denominator.

guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for measurement methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” rather than whether another outcome might have been preferable.

evidence: Both arms used the same live-birth definition and included spontaneous pregnancies (Article, p. 1623; Table II). evidence: Registry, Design/Masking, states “OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR” masking. The article specifically confirms masking only for embryologists and statisticians and reports unblinded physicians (p. 1623). It does not identify the live-birth assessor. Neither definite awareness nor definite masking for this endpoint is established.
guidance: §7.1 requires identification of the relevant assessor; §5.1.3 cautions that broad masking descriptions may not identify who was blinded. §1.1 permits NI when neither probable answer is adequately supported.

evidence: Classification of whether a child was born alive under the reported definition involves essentially no discretionary judgement (Article, p. 1623, Outcomes).
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 and §7.1, outcome type 2: knowledge is unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes “not involving judgement.”

evidence: Statistical methods are described retrospectively in the article (p. 1623), but no dated analysis plan is supplied. Registration followed recruitment commencement, and the supplied registry contains later updates (Registry, Status and dates). Neither the timing nor sufficient prospective detail of these analytical intentions can be established.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” confirming finalization before unblinded outcome availability; Box 11, 5.1 requires analysis in accordance with that plan. Registration of an outcome alone does not meet this requirement.

evidence: Registry, Registered outcomes, specifies primary “Live birth per participating woman.” The article reports this endpoint after the index treatment strategy, including spontaneous pregnancies (pp. 1622–1623; Table II). The separately described two-year follow-up is a distinct aim. No result-based choice among competing measurements is evident.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 addresses selection “on the basis of the results.” Agreement between the stated primary measurement and reported endpoint supports PN, although unavailable historical versions limit certainty.

evidence: FAS, PP, adjusted and subgroup analyses were undertaken (Article, p. 1623; SI–SIII). PP results are reported; adjustment for prior pregnancy termination reportedly “did not alter the results” (p. 1628). These facts oppose obvious favourable selection, but prospective analytical details and the numerical adjusted estimate are unavailable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficiently detailed and multiple analyses are possible. Y/PY requires evidence of result-based selection; multiplicity or incomplete reporting alone does not establish it.

guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes if “a random component was used”; computer-generated random numbers qualify.

evidence: An otherwise uninvolved statistician supplied the sequence to pharmacy; access was restricted, encrypted and password protected. The pharmacist prepared treatment “Following randomization” (p. 8).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: centrally administered allocation controlled independently of enrolment personnel qualifies; §4.3.2 and Box 3 recognize pharmacy-controlled allocation.

evidence: Groups contained 30 infants each. Birthweight differed (830 versus 970 g; P=.02); Table 1 also shows differences in growth restriction and some perinatal characteristics. Gestation and PDA severity were similar. These differences in a small trial do not establish a pattern clearly beyond chance (pp. 10, 18, Table 1).
guidance: §4.3.3.1: “Chance imbalances are not a source of systematic bias.” Box 4, 1.3: answer No when observed imbalances are compatible with chance; a small number of conventional statistically significant differences usually qualify.

evidence: Participants were newborn infants; the report explicitly states that participants and families remained blinded throughout (p. 8).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 and §5.1.3: assess awareness of assigned intervention; participant blinding prevents assignment-related behavioural differences.

evidence: “Health care providers” remained blinded; ibuprofen and saline preparations were “indistinguishable” (p. 8). The designated pharmacist knew allocation to prepare syringes, but clinical providers did not. Rescue treatment was open label, without reported disclosure of original allocation (pp. 9–10).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness of the assigned intervention among carers and intervention providers. §5.1.3 distinguishes explicit blinding evidence from merely describing a study as double blind.

guidance: §4.3.3.1: “Chance imbalances are not a source of systematic bias.” Box 4, 1.3: No when differences are compatible with chance; isolated conventional significance is insufficient.

evidence: P pp. 41–42, §§8.4–8.5: kit numbers were computer-generated; the study biostatistician supplied the randomization scheme, and the central system generated the patient randomization list. The precise random-number generation method is not stated, but this supports a genuinely random sequence.

guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation controlled independently of enrolment personnel.

evidence: M Table 1, pp. 2250–2251; A Table S1: 3034 participants per group. Four of 35 baseline comparisons were nominally significant, including age, eGFR, HbA1c and prior stroke. The differences are modest and compatible with chance; they do not indicate failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: “differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias”; a small number of conventional statistical differences ordinarily remains compatible with chance.

evidence: M p. 2249 describes double-blind allocation with volume-matched placebo; P p. 41, §8.4 says products were “indistinguishable.” Gastrointestinal events caused more treatment discontinuations with lixisenatide (A Table S4), so some guessing is possible, but actual participant awareness is not documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding can prevent awareness; answer Y/PY for side effects participants “knew to be specific” to an intervention. That knowledge is not established here, supporting PN rather than an absolute N.

evidence: M p. 2249 and P p. 41 describe blinded treatment and inaccessible allocation codes. P §8.8 permits emergency unblinding, but the supplied reports do not quantify its occurrence. Differential adverse effects provide a possible clue, without evidence that treating personnel generally knew assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding may prevent awareness; intervention-specific toxicities known to carers can establish awareness. §1.1 permits a supported probabilistic answer despite incomplete reporting.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. Treatment discontinuation was 27.5% versus 24.0% (M p. 2251); P p. 41 explicitly allowed dose reduction or cessation for intolerance and adjustment of background diabetes treatment. These observations do not independently establish trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 is asked only if either preceding answer is Y/PY/NI. Its elaboration also excludes protocol-consistent changes, including “cessation of a drug intervention because of acute toxicity.”

evidence: No qualifying deviations were identified through the applicable branch; see M p. 2251 and P p. 41.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: applicable only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA; the differing treatment-discontinuation percentages do not themselves activate this question. M p. 2251.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: applicable only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: M p. 2249 identifies the primary ITT analysis; Table 2 includes all 3034 randomized participants per group. SAP §2.3.1.1, P p. 308: “all randomized patients analyzed according to the treatment group allocated by randomization,” irrespective of discontinuation or treatment received. The five never-treated participants were not excluded from this efficacy result.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT analyses are appropriate for assignment effects; missing outcome data are assessed separately in D3.

evidence: The target uses the appropriate randomized-group analysis, rather than the separate on-treatment analysis in A Table S2.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: asked only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: M p. 2251: among survivors, 96.3% versus 96.1% completed the study; vital status was unavailable for 29 versus 42 patients. Vital-status ascertainment does not establish complete nonfatal-event ascertainment. Exact composite-outcome completeness is not reported, and the roughly 4% incomplete survivor follow-up cannot confidently be considered immaterial relative to 805 first events.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires missing outcomes to make “no important difference,” rather than meeting a fixed percentage. §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing data even when partial follow-up enters the analysis.

evidence: A Table S2 reports on-treatment and baseline-adjusted sensitivity analyses, not analyses varying assumptions about unobserved events. SAP §2.4.4.1, P p. 312, censors at the last available cardiovascular-outcome information. No reported analysis establishes robustness to informative missingness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7 require correction for missing-data bias or sensitivity analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome. Ordinary censoring and the reported sensitivity analyses do not demonstrate this.

evidence: Reasons for incomplete composite follow-up are not reported in M p. 2251. P p. 207, §11.3 recognizes withdrawal/non-return and requests attempts to recover health status. Such loss could relate to cardiovascular health; the records do not establish exclusively outcome-independent reasons.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if loss or withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Incomplete follow-up was modest and closely balanced: survivor completion 96.3% versus 96.1%, with median follow-up 25 months in both groups (M p. 2251). SAP §2.4.4, P p. 312 explicitly includes events after treatment discontinuation. Reasons and timing of remaining losses are insufficiently reported, but the available evidence does not make outcome-dependent missingness likely.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence and considers differing loss rates, reasons, and censoring at treatment cessation. §1.1 allows PN when a reasoned inference is possible; balanced losses support, but do not prove, absence of informative censoring.

evidence: P pp. 47–48, §9.1.3.1 specifies component definitions, including biomarkers/ECG/clinical criteria for MI and definitions of stroke and unstable-angina hospitalization. M p. 2249 confirms independent adjudication. These methods are appropriate for the specified composite.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” not whether the chosen outcome is desirable; prespecified outcomes ordinarily warrant N/PN.

evidence: SAP §2.1.3, P pp. 299–300 applies common reporting and adjudication procedures, including adverse-event searches and medical review to identify overlooked cardiovascular events. M p. 2249 describes matched placebo and blinded treatment. No systematic difference in cardiovascular ascertainment is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods, thresholds and timing and considers unequal opportunities for detection. The common surveillance procedures support PN.

evidence: M p. 2249: adjudication committees were “unaware of the study-group assignments.” SAP §2.1.3, P p. 300 confirms blinded cardiovascular adjudication. MI accounted for 502/805 first events; unstable angina accounted for only 19/805 (M Table 2), and care delivery was also blinded.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded.” §7.1, composite-outcome guidance requires considering component frequency and the most influential components.

evidence: Not reached because adjudicators were blinded (M p. 2249). MI and hospitalization can involve judgement, but that does not establish assessor awareness.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: applicable only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA; blinded adjudication is documented in M p. 2249.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5: applicable only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: SAP title, P p. 284, dates versions to 19 July 2012 and 20 November 2014. SAP §§2.3.1.1 and 2.4.4.1, P pp. 308, 312, specify the reported ITT, treatment-and-region Cox HR and 95% CI. P p. 239 requires revisions based on “blinded review”; M pp. 2249, 2251 documents protected interim access and final follow-up ending February 2015. The exact final unblinding date is absent, so PY is appropriate.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires prespecification before unblinded outcome availability. §8.3.1 accepts blinded refinements and excepts staff supplying confidential monitoring analyses. Dated plans and documented access protections support the inference.

evidence: The original protocol §9.1.1, P p. 46, and SAP §2.1.3.1, P p. 300, specify this exact four-component first-event endpoint. M Table 2 reports it and its components. M p. 2251 explains that closeout was projected without assignment knowledge; 805 rather than the anticipated 844 events does not indicate selection of a favourable observation period.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results.” Correspondence with the planned measurement supports N/PN; the existence of alternative measurements alone does not establish selective reporting.

evidence: The target matches the primary Cox analysis in SAP §2.4.4.1, P p. 312. The change from country to region adjustment was dated 19 July 2012, before the first interim analysis (P pp. 294–295). A Table S2 also reports post-hoc adjusted and on-treatment estimates. Some additional planned sensitivity analyses (P p. 314) lack reported results, but there is no indication that the prespecified primary HR was selected because of its findings.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence that the reported estimate was selected from eligible analyses “on the basis of the results.” §8.1 distinguishes selection of this result from non-reporting of other results; multiplicity alone is insufficient.

evidence: P pp. 41–42, §§8.4–8.5 describes computer-generated kit numbers, a biostatistician-supplied randomization scheme and a centrally generated patient allocation list. guidance: Box 4, 1.1 and §4.3.1.1 permit PY when specific details are absent in a large trial run by experienced trial personnel. §1.1 permits inference rather than automatically using NI.

evidence: P p. 42: IVRS/IWRS assigned treatment after screening review and baseline assessments. P p. 41: investigators “will not have access to the randomization (treatment) code.” M p. 2249 confirms centralized assignment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation independent of enrolment personnel.

evidence: M Table 1, pp. 2250–2251, and A Table S1 show equal groups of 3034. Four of 35 comparisons were nominally significant; age, eGFR, HbA1c and prior stroke differences deserve scrutiny but do not constitute persuasive evidence of failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias”; a small number of conventional statistically significant differences ordinarily remains compatible with chance.

evidence: M p. 2249 describes double-blind treatment with volume-matched placebo; P p. 41 calls the products “indistinguishable.” More gastrointestinal discontinuations occurred with lixisenatide (A Table S4), but participant recognition of assignment is not documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 requires Y/PY when participants experienced effects they “knew to be specific” to an intervention. Differential adverse effects alone do not establish that knowledge; §1.1 supports PN with incomplete evidence.

guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness, including knowledge of intervention-specific toxicity. §1.1 allows a probabilistic judgement where NI would be unnecessarily uninformative.

evidence: Both awareness answers are PN. The 27.5% versus 24.0% discontinuation rates (M p. 2251) do not themselves establish trial-context deviations; P p. 41 permits stopping or reducing treatment for intolerance and adjusting background therapy.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 is reached only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. Its elaboration excludes protocol-consistent changes such as “cessation of a drug intervention because of acute toxicity.”

evidence: No applicable trial-context deviation branch was reached; see P p. 41 and M p. 2251.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: asked only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Question 2.4 is NA. Differences in ordinary treatment discontinuation do not activate this branch (M p. 2251).
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: M p. 2249 identifies the primary ITT analysis; Table 2 includes 3034 per group. The five never-treated patients were included in this efficacy population.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 accept ITT analyses for assignment effects and assess missing outcomes separately in D3.

guidance: Box 6, 2.7: asked only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”
