P p. 207 explicitly distinguishes obtaining vital status from preferably also obtaining cardiovascular endpoint status.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by whether missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §6.1.3.2 states there is “no sensible threshold” based solely on the missing percentage; §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing follow-up.

evidence: A Table S2 tests on-treatment restriction and baseline adjustment, not assumptions about unobserved cardiovascular events. SAP §2.4.4.1, P p. 312 uses last available cardiovascular information for censoring. No reported analysis demonstrates robustness to informative missingness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7 require correction for missing-data bias or sensitivity analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and its true value. Ordinary censoring and these sensitivity analyses do not establish that protection.

evidence: M p. 2251 does not report reasons for incomplete composite follow-up. P p. 207, §11.3 anticipates withdrawal and failure to return. These could relate to health status; exclusively outcome-independent reasons are not established.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Evidence against likely informative loss includes closely balanced completion and identical median follow-up (M p. 2251), plus inclusion of events after treatment cessation (SAP §2.4.4, P p. 312). Reasons and timing of losses remain incompletely reported. This supports a cautious PN, not certainty that censoring was non-informative.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence and considers differential loss, reasons and censoring at treatment cessation. §1.1 allows PN where the circumstances support inference; balanced losses alone do not establish absence of bias.

evidence: P pp. 47–48, §9.1.3.1 gives clinical definitions for death, MI, stroke and unstable-angina hospitalization. M p. 2249 confirms independent event adjudication. No unsuitable measurement method is identified.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” rather than the desirability of the selected endpoint.

evidence: SAP §2.1.3, P pp. 299–300 specifies common event reporting, adverse-event searches, queries and medical review for overlooked events. Blinded, matched-placebo treatment is described in M p. 2249. Central adjudication alone would not exclude differential referral, but these additional surveillance procedures support comparable ascertainment.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 considers comparable methods and opportunities for detection, including “diagnostic detection bias.” The documented common surveillance supports PN.

evidence: M p. 2249 says committee members were “unaware of the study-group assignments”; P p. 300 confirms blinded cardiovascular adjudication. M Table 2 shows MI contributed 502/805 first events and unstable angina 19/805. Treating investigators were also blinded.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded.” §7.1 requires weighting composite components by their frequency or contribution; it does not treat this whole composite as judgement-free.

evidence: Adjudicator awareness was answered N (M p. 2249). Clinical judgement in classifying events does not activate this branch without awareness or uncertainty about it.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Question 4.4 is NA; blinded adjudication is documented in M p. 2249 and P p. 300.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5: asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: P p. 284 dates the original and amended SAPs to 19 July 2012 and 20 November 2014. P pp. 308, 312 specifies the reported ITT, treatment-and-region Cox HR and 95% CI. P p. 239 requires revisions based on “blinded review.” M pp. 2249, 2251 describes protected interim access and follow-up ending February 2015. The actual final unblinding date is absent, so the timing inference remains PY.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome availability. §8.3.1 accepts blinded refinements and distinguishes confidential monitoring access from investigator access. A dated SAP alone would not suffice; the blinding protections provide additional support.

evidence: The exact four-component first-event endpoint appears in the original protocol (P p. 46) and SAP (P p. 300), and is reported in M Table 2. Additional composites existed, including a later three-component analysis (P p. 296), but the reported target was already designated primary. M p. 2251 says closeout projections were made without allocation knowledge.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 asks whether selection was “on the basis of the results.” The existence of other definitions or observation periods does not itself show such selection.

evidence: The target follows SAP §2.4.4.1, P p. 312. Region replaced country adjustment in July 2012, before the first interim analysis (P pp. 294–295). A Table S2 reports adjusted and on-treatment alternatives. Some planned sensitivity analyses lack reported results (P p. 314), creating a challenge to completeness, but there is no persuasive indication that the designated primary HR was chosen for its findings.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires that an analysis be “likely to have been selected on the basis of the results.” Unreported alternatives warrant scrutiny but do not, by themselves, establish that the reported primary analysis was selected this way.

evidence: Article p.3: “computer-generated random-sequence.” Protocol p.72, §7.5 specifies a validated system with a “pseudorandom number generator” producing non-predictable allocations.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when sequence generation uses a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: Article p.3 describes an “interactive voice- and Web-response system.” Protocol p.72 specifies centrally arranged randomization, packaging and labelling through IVRS/IWRS.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: remote or centrally administered allocation, including “telephone or internet-based randomization service providers,” supports Yes.

evidence: Appendix Table S2, pp.36–39, shows comparable prognostic characteristics: pooled empagliflozin/placebo age 63.1/63.2 years, previous MI 46.7%/46.4%, previous stroke 23.1%/23.7%, HbA1c 8.07%/8.08%. The table covers 7020 treated participants, excluding eight randomized participants; their baseline data are unavailable. This almost complete cohort provides useful evidence against problematic imbalance.
guidance: §4.3.3 requires consideration of the “proportion of and reasons for missing data” when baseline tables cover a subset. Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance” do not indicate bias; §1.1 permits a qualified judgement when evidence supports it.

evidence: Protocol pp.39–40: patients remain blinded after randomization; matching active/placebo tablets were supplied. Article p.2 describes the conducted trial as double-blind. Genital infections were more frequent with empagliflozin (Article p.1), but the documents do not establish that participants recognized their assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding can prevent awareness; side effects warrant Yes/PY when participants “knew [them] to be specific” to an intervention. §1.1 supports Probably no where some inference remains necessary.

evidence: Protocol pp.39–40 explicitly includes investigators and trial personnel in blinding. Emergency code breaks were permitted, but the supplied reports do not document awareness sufficient to establish compromised blinding.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding may prevent awareness; intervention-specific side effects must be known as such to carers/personnel. Permission for emergency unblinding alone does not establish that it occurred.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. Contextually, background treatment adjustment was permitted by protocol (Article p.3); medication discontinuation alone does not establish a trial-context deviation.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 is conditional on Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. §5.1: changes “consistent with the trial protocol” are not deviations.

evidence: No qualifying deviations question is reached.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 applies only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: No assessment of outcome-affecting trial-context deviations is reached.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Article p.4: primary analysis included only patients who “received at least one dose”; 7020/7028 randomized patients were included. Appendix Figure S1, p.34 identifies eight untreated exclusions. Retained participants were assigned analytically according to randomization (SAP p.209), but the exclusion criterion was treatment receipt.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: “Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.” §5.3.1 distinguishes exclusion for nonreceipt from an acceptable mITT exclusion solely for missing outcomes.

evidence: Only eight of 7028 randomized participants—0.11%—were excluded, versus 772 observed primary events (Article pp.1, 4; Appendix Figure S1). Their allocations and detailed non-treatment reasons are unreported. A substantial effect on the estimated HR is unlikely given these numbers, although the analysis was not full ITT.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks whether exclusions were “sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact”; there is “no precise rule,” and event frequency matters.

evidence: Appendix Figure S1, p.34: 144/4687 pooled empagliflozin and 67/2333 placebo participants did not complete the study. These 211 participants potentially have incomplete composite-outcome follow-up; exact numbers still event-free at withdrawal are not given. Article p.4 reports 99.2% vital-status ascertainment, which does not establish complete nonfatal MI/stroke ascertainment. Given 772 events and a modest estimated effect, negligible impact under every missing-outcome scenario cannot be assumed.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §6.1.5: participants censored during follow-up may have missing outcomes despite contributing some follow-up.

evidence: Appendix §F, p.33 and Table S9, p.52 report on-treatment and per-protocol sensitivity analyses. These do not vary assumptions about outcomes after loss of follow-up. Article p.4 describes last-event-free censoring; no reported analysis establishes robustness to informative missingness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses across plausible missing-outcome assumptions. §6.1.7: sensitivity analyses are helpful only if they address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Appendix Figure S1: withdrawal of consent occurred in 71 pooled empagliflozin and 31 placebo participants; loss to follow-up for the primary endpoint occurred in 17 and 11, respectively. Health-related withdrawal is possible; reasons underlying consent withdrawal are absent. Site closures explain other incomplete follow-up but not all of it.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” dependence on the true outcome is possible; documented outcome-independent reasons must explain all missingness to exclude this concern.

evidence: Noncompletion was similar: 3.1% pooled empagliflozin versus 2.9% placebo. Figure S1 shows comparable reason patterns: consent withdrawal 71/31, site closure 56/25, primary-endpoint loss 17/11. Primary-analysis censoring was “independent from study drug intake” (SAP p.232). Thus unequal medication discontinuation—23.4%/29.3% in Table S1—does not establish unequal outcome loss. There is no affirmative evidence that missingness likely depended on cardiovascular outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely”; relevant evidence includes unequal missingness, outcome-related reasons, differing reasons, or censoring when treatment stops. These indicators do not establish likely informative missingness here.

evidence: Article p.2 reports prospective clinical-event adjudication. Protocol p.29 specifies review of ECGs, laboratory results, imaging and clinical records against prespecified criteria; Appendix §E supplies event definitions. These are suitable methods for the specified composite.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome.” §7.1 requires considering the components of composites; both death classification and nonfatal events received adjudication.

evidence: Article p.3 specifies scheduled visits and cardiovascular follow-up after premature drug discontinuation. Protocol p.29 describes a common central adjudication process. No systematic difference in measurement methods, thresholds or opportunities is documented.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable ascertainment uses the “same measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times; §7.3 focuses on systematic between-group differences.

evidence: Protocol p.29: an independent external committee would adjudicate “centrally and in a blinded fashion.” Article p.2 confirms prospective adjudication by cardiac and neurological committees. No contrary evidence of assessor unblinding is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.”

evidence: Not reached because outcome assessors were blinded.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is not applicable.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: The dated 15 October 2013 protocol, pp.67–71, specifies pooled doses, the treated population, the adjusted Cox model, hierarchical superiority testing and final alpha 0.0249, matching Article pp.3–4. SAP p.263 records versions dated 24 August 2012 and 21 May 2015; pp.185–186 explain primary-analysis clarifications. Protocol p.71 separates interim analysts from the blinded trial team. The exact final unblinding date is not supplied, so PY reflects corroborated prespecification rather than complete verification of timing.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires analysis intentions before unblinded data. §8.3.1 accepts protocol-based intentions and confidential independent monitoring; §8.3.2 requires explaining inferences made from incomplete information.

evidence: Article p.3 identifies the specified three-component primary outcome; the protocol’s primary-analysis specification, pp.67–70, and SAP §7.4, pp.237–238, agree. The alternative four-component key secondary outcome is also reported despite nonsignificant superiority (Article p.4). There is no indication that the target measurement was chosen because its result was favourable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 assesses result-based selection among “eligible” measurements. §8.1.2: multiplicity creates bias when selection depends on direction, magnitude or significance.

evidence: The reported adjusted pooled-dose Cox result matches the designated primary analysis (Protocol pp.67–71; SAP p.237). Alternative on-treatment/per-protocol estimates are reported in Appendix Table S9, including nonsignificant results. Some additional planned analyses are not displayed in these reports, but this does not indicate that the explicitly designated primary estimate was selected from them based on results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence that a reported estimate was selected “on the basis of the results.” §8.1 distinguishes selection of this result from nonreporting of other results.

evidence: Article p.3 reports a “computer-generated random-sequence.” Protocol p.72, §7.5 specifies a validated pseudorandom-number generator and non-predictable allocation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: “computer-generated random numbers” establish a random component.

evidence: Article p.3 and Protocol p.72 describe IVRS/IWRS randomization, with centrally arranged medication allocation, packaging and labelling. No evidence indicates recruiter access to forthcoming assignments.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: remote or central allocation through “telephone or internet-based randomization service providers” supports Yes.

evidence: Appendix Table S2, pp.36–39: pooled empagliflozin/placebo age 63.1/63.2 years, previous MI 46.7%/46.4%, previous stroke 23.1%/23.7%, HbA1c 8.07%/8.08%. These data cover 7020/7028 randomized participants; baseline information for eight is absent. This limitation does not eliminate the useful evidence from virtually the entire randomized cohort.
guidance: §4.3.3 requires considering the “proportion of and reasons for missing data” when baseline information covers a subset. Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance” do not indicate a randomization problem.

evidence: Protocol pp.39–40 specifies matching placebo and participant blinding after randomization; Article p.2 reports a double-blind trial. Increased genital infections could have suggested treatment, but actual recognition of assignment is not established.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: intervention-specific adverse effects support awareness when participants “knew [them] to be specific.” §1.1 permits a probabilistic answer supported by circumstances.

evidence: Protocol pp.39–40 explicitly includes investigators and trial personnel in blinding. Emergency unblinding was available, but its availability is not evidence of actual widespread awareness.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses actual awareness, including recognition of intervention-specific adverse effects; blinding supports PN where implementation is reported but not exhaustively documented.

evidence: Both awareness questions are PN. Article p.3 also shows that background-treatment adjustments were permitted; unequal treatment changes alone would not establish trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 is reached only following Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. §5.1 excludes changes “consistent with the trial protocol.”

evidence: No qualifying trial-context deviation is reached through 2.3.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 applies only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: The preceding conditional assessment is not reached.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Article p.4 and Appendix Figure S1, p.34: eight randomized participants were excluded because they were not treated. SAP p.209 assigns retained participants according to randomization. Thus allocation was preserved among those included, but inclusion depended on receiving treatment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: “Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.” §5.3.1 distinguishes nonreceipt exclusions from exclusions solely for missing outcomes.

evidence: Eight exclusions represent 0.11% of 7028 randomized participants, compared with 772 observed composite events (Article pp.1, 4). Their allocations and detailed reasons for non-treatment are unreported. A substantial effect on the estimated treatment effect is unlikely.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks whether exclusions could have a “substantial impact”; there is no fixed percentage rule, and event frequency and prognosis matter.

evidence: Appendix Figure S1, p.34 reports 144/4687 pooled empagliflozin and 67/2333 placebo participants who did not complete the study. These 211 are not necessarily 211 missing first events: some could already have experienced the endpoint. However, their event status and remaining unobserved follow-up are not provided. The 99.2% vital-status ascertainment in Article p.4 does not establish complete MI/stroke follow-up; SAP pp.232–233 explicitly distinguishes composite-event from mortality censoring.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires missing outcomes to be sufficiently few that they could make “no important difference.” §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal missing-percentage threshold; §6.1.5 includes incomplete follow-up despite partial observed data.

evidence: Appendix Table S9, p.52 gives similar on-treatment/per-protocol HRs, but these analyses change treatment exposure windows or populations. They do not test plausible outcomes after withdrawal or loss. Last-event-free censoring in Article p.4 does not itself establish non-informative censoring.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires correction for missingness or appropriate sensitivity evidence. §6.1.7: sensitivity analyses are helpful only when they address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Figure S1: consent withdrawal occurred in 71 pooled empagliflozin and 31 placebo participants; primary-endpoint loss to follow-up in 17 and 11. The underlying withdrawal reasons are absent. Site closure accounts for other losses, but cannot explain all potentially incomplete follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” permits dependence on the true outcome; all missingness must have documented unrelated causes to exclude it on that basis.

evidence: Figure S1 shows similar noncompletion rates, 3.1%/2.9%, and similar reason patterns: withdrawal 71/31, closure 56/25, loss 17/11 for pooled empagliflozin/placebo. SAP p.232 states censoring is independent of drug intake. Differential medication discontinuation in Table S1 therefore does not demonstrate differential outcome loss. No documented pattern makes outcome-dependent missingness likely.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely”; evidence includes unequal missingness, differing/outcome-related reasons, or censoring at treatment discontinuation. Balanced losses alone do not prove absence of bias.

evidence: Protocol p.29 specifies adjudication using ECGs, laboratory results, imaging and clinical records against prespecified criteria. Article p.2 confirms prospective adjudication; Appendix §E defines events. These methods appropriately assess all three components.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for measurement methods “unsuitable for the outcome.” §7.1 requires considering the influential components of composite outcomes.

evidence: Article p.3 describes scheduled visits and cardiovascular follow-up after medication discontinuation. Protocol p.29 provides a common adjudication process. No systematic arm-specific measurement schedule, threshold or diagnostic opportunity is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods, thresholds and time points; §7.3 targets systematic differences in ascertainment. Incomplete follow-up is assessed separately under D3.

evidence: Protocol p.29 specifies an independent committee adjudicating “centrally and in a blinded fashion”; Article p.2 confirms cardiac and neurological adjudication committees. No contrary evidence of assessor awareness is supplied.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is N. MI, stroke and cardiovascular death classification can involve judgement, but assessor blinding resolves this branch.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached through 4.4.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: Protocol pp.67–71, dated 15 October 2013, specifies pooled doses, the treated population, adjusted Cox model, hierarchical testing and final alpha 0.0249. These match Article pp.3–4 and SAP p.237. SAP p.263 dates versions to August 2012 and May 2015; p.185 explains primary-analysis clarifications. Protocol p.71 separates interim analysts from the blinded trial team. The exact final unblinding date remains unreported, preventing an unqualified Y.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires intentions preceding unblinded analysis; §8.3.1 recognizes dated protocols and independent confidential monitoring. §8.3.2 permits explained inferences from incomplete information.

evidence: Article p.3 and Protocol/SAP primary-endpoint specifications agree on the target composite. The alternative four-component endpoint is also reported despite nonsignificant superiority (Article p.4). Multiple definitions exist, but no evidence indicates favourable-result selection of this prespecified measurement.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 asks about selection “on the basis of the results,” restricted to eligible measurements; multiplicity by itself does not establish selection.

evidence: The target is the designated pooled-dose adjusted Cox analysis (Protocol pp.67–71; SAP p.237). Appendix Table S9 reports alternative estimates, including nonsignificant results. Some additional planned analyses are not displayed, so complete reporting of every analysis cannot be claimed; nevertheless, the target’s prior designation and matching implementation support PN.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely result-based selection among eligible analyses. §8.3.1 calls for comparing planned and reported analyses; §1.1 permits a supported probabilistic judgement.

evidence: Protocol §4.1.3, p.40: “computer generated random sequence.” Section 7.6, p.75 specifies a validated “pseudo-random number generator”; Article p.1452 describes permuted blocks and stratification.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when a random component is used, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: Protocol §4.1.3, p.40: assignment occurred “in a blinded fashion via Interactive Response Technology.” Section 4.1.5.1, p.41 states that Clinical Trial Support kept the randomization code secret until database lock. This supports central allocation concealed from enrolling personnel.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel supports Yes; §4.3.2 includes telephone/internet systems.

evidence: Article Table 1, p.1455: groups numbered 2997/2991; age 71.8/71.9 years, diabetes 48.9%/49.2%, mean EF 54.3%/54.3%, and prior HF hospitalization 23.3%/22.4%. Differences are compatible with chance, without a concerning pattern.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when “any observed imbalances are compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 states that chance imbalances are not systematic bias.

evidence: Protocol §§4.1.1–4.1.5, pp.39–41 specifies matching placebo and blinded patients; Article p.1452 confirms double-blind assignment. Infections and hypotension were more frequent with empagliflozin (Article p.1451), but actual participant recognition or the frequency of emergency unblinding is not reported. Probably no reflects that limitation.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding prevents awareness; answer Y/PY for side effects participants knew were intervention-specific. Section 5.1.3 cautions that attempted blinding does not guarantee success; §1.1 permits reasoned “Probably” responses.

evidence: Protocol §4.1.5.1, p.41: “Patients, Investigators and everyone involved in trial conduct or analysis” remain blinded until database lock; emergency code breaking was restricted. evidence: A, Figure 1 and pp.1602–1604: the main imputed analysis retained 52/66 PREHAB and 43/58 REHAB participants in their assigned groups. Exclusions for benign diagnosis or metastatic cancer could represent permissible recognition of ineligibility. However, another 2 versus 6 participants were excluded because they “did not have surgery”; the documents do not establish that these were assignment-independent eligibility corrections. The concern is this exclusion rule, not subsequent missing measurements or the separately reported per-protocol analysis.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6: excluding eligible participants after randomization is inappropriate; later recognition of ineligibility can be appropriate only when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment. Missing-outcome exclusions alone belong in D3.

evidence: A, Figure 1: the potentially inappropriate no-surgery exclusions alone affected 8/124 participants, unevenly distributed between arms (2/66 versus 6/58). Their unexplained relationship to clinical course could materially affect these small between-group differences. The other diagnostic exclusions are not automatically counted as inappropriate.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks about potential substantial impact and states that there is no precise threshold; even fewer than 5% can matter when exclusions relate strongly to prognosis.

evidence: A, pp.1602 and 1604 reports missing data at the preoperative, 4-week and 8-week visits of 35%, 43% and 48%, respectively. Table 2’s denominators of 52 and 43 include imputed values. The complete-case/per-protocol comparison included only 28 and 19 participants.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.” “Nearly all” means missing outcomes could make no important difference; these losses do not meet that condition.

evidence: A, p.1602 describes ten fully conditional multiple imputations using other observed data; p.1604 reports similar complete-case and imputed conclusions. These are reassuring checks, but the imputation variables and assumptions are insufficiently described, and no sensitivity analysis examines plausible outcome-dependent missingness.
guidance: §§6.1.6–6.1.7: multiple imputation requires justification that measured variables explain outcome-dependent missingness; sensitivity analyses are helpful only if they address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: A, p.1607 acknowledges “loss to follow-up.” Neither Figure 1 nor the results explains missed follow-up assessments. Attendance and ability to complete a walking test could depend on functional health; exclusively administrative causes are not documented.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal or loss to follow-up “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on its true value.

evidence: A provides neither reasons for missing follow-up measurements nor arm-specific missingness rates at each visit. Table 4 reports two PREHAB deaths, but does not establish their timing or contribution to the missing walking tests. Thus outcome dependence is possible, but its likelihood cannot be resolved. Similar complete-case conclusions do not resolve this uncertainty.
guidance: §1.1 supports NI when neither PY nor PN is defensible. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence using reasons, differential rates and trial circumstances. Table 10 explicitly routes NI here to High when preceding answers are N/PN/NI, N/PN, Y/PY/NI.

evidence: A, p.1601 describes the 6MWT as a validated measure of exercise tolerance, administered with a “standardized protocol and script” according to ATS guidelines. No evidence establishes an unsuitable measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for methods unsuitable for the outcome, such as demonstrated poor validity or insensitivity; it does not assess whether the chosen outcome is the ideal clinical endpoint.

evidence: A, p.1601 specifies the same test, script and assessment schedule for both groups; Table 2 applies common change thresholds. Missing visits are assessed in D3.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable measurement as the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points.

evidence: A, p.1601 explicitly states that the test assessor was blinded; this specific statement is more informative about the observer than R’s broad “Masking: NONE.” Nevertheless, participants knew their intervention and actively performed the test with encouragement and feedback (R, Primary outcome description). The assessment therefore involved an unblinded participant interacting with a blinded observer.
guidance: §7.3: for assessment involving interaction between participant and data collector, assessors should be considered aware if either is unblinded, “unless convincing evidence is available to the contrary.”

evidence: The test requires participants to sustain walking effort, with encouragement and feedback (R, Primary outcome description). Knowledge of receiving prehabilitation could influence effort during measurement, even though distance itself is recorded objectively.
guidance: §7.3 and Box 10, 4.4 ask whether knowledge could influence assessment. Objective recording does not necessarily eliminate influence on an interactive performance assessment.

evidence: A, p.1601 documents a blinded observer and standardized script; both groups received active multimodal programs. No differential encouragement, testing behavior or strong participant expectations are documented. These safeguards support possible rather than likely differential influence.
guidance: §7.3 identifies an active comparator and independent assessment as mitigating considerations. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence.

evidence: R, Status and dates: first submitted February 2016, first posted October 2016, with the supplied record updated in March 2018. A, p.1600 reports enrollment beginning November 2014. R names the 8-week 6MWT but provides no detailed SAP; neither source establishes that the reported analysis choices were finalized before unblinded outcomes became available.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” confirming analysis intentions preceded unblinded data. §8.3.2 and §1.1 support NI where available detail cannot establish this; absence does not prove post hoc selection.

evidence: R, Primary outcome identifies the 8-week 6MWT, which is reported. A, p.1601 lists baseline, preoperative, 4-week and 8-week assessments; Tables 1–2 and Figure 2 report those measurements. evidence: A, pp.1602–1604 reports repeated-measures analysis, changes from baseline, recovery categories and supplementary complete-case/compliance analyses. guidance: Box 8, 3.1: imputed values remain missing outcomes; “nearly all” requires that missing outcomes could make no important difference.

evidence: A, p.1602 describes fully conditional multiple imputation using other observed data. The supplementary complete-case/per-protocol comparisons produced similar conclusions (p.1604). These support robustness to those particular analyses, but neither the imputation model nor sensitivity analyses establish robustness to outcome-dependent missingness.
guidance: §§6.1.6–6.1.7: multiple imputation needs justified assumptions and predictors; useful sensitivity analyses address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome. Box 8, 3.2 does not equate imputation with correction of bias.

evidence: A, p.1607 acknowledges loss to follow-up without explaining missed walking assessments. Functional health could affect attendance or ability to complete the test; exclusively outcome-unrelated reasons are not documented.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: possible association between loss to follow-up and health status supports possible dependence on the true outcome.

evidence: A gives no visit-specific reasons or arm-specific missingness rates. Table 4 reports two PREHAB deaths, but does not establish their timing or contribution to the missing tests. High missingness alone does not prove dependence on functional status, and there is insufficient evidence to answer PN.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence using reasons, differential rates and circumstances. §1.1 permits NI; Table 10 routes NI here to High after the preceding responses.

evidence: A, p.1601 describes a validated walking test, standardized protocol and ATS-based script. There is no evidence of an unsuitable instrument.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns demonstrated inadequacy, such as poor validity or insensitivity—not whether another outcome might be preferable.

evidence: A, p.1601 specifies common testing methods and assessment times; Table 2 uses common change thresholds. Missing visits do not establish different measurement procedures.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparability through common methods, thresholds and time points. Missing measurements are addressed separately in D3.

evidence: A, p.1601 explicitly states that the observer was blinded, outweighing R’s nonspecific “Masking: NONE” for that observer. However, participants were unblinded and performed an interactive test with encouragement and feedback (R, Primary outcome).
guidance: §7.3 says that, for assessments involving participant–data-collector interaction, either party’s awareness counts unless convincing contrary evidence is available. The blinded observer is a safeguard, but does not blind the participant.

evidence: R, Primary outcome instructs participants to walk at a pace making them tired by the end, with encouragement and feedback. Distance is objectively recorded, but effort during this assessment could respond to treatment expectations.
guidance: §7.3 and Box 10, 4.4 concern whether knowledge could influence the assessment, not solely whether the final number requires subjective interpretation.

evidence: A, p.1601 documents a blinded observer and standardized script, and both groups received active programs. No differential encouragement or strong participant expectations are documented. These safeguards argue against likely differential influence.
guidance: §7.3 identifies active comparators and independent assessment as mitigating considerations. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from likely influence.

evidence: R names the 8-week 6MWT, but supplies no detailed analysis plan. Its first submission occurred in February 2016 and the supplied record was updated in March 2018; A, p.1600 reports enrollment beginning November 2014. These dates do not establish when detailed analysis intentions were finalized relative to unblinded data.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a date-stamp establishing that analysis intentions preceded unblinded data. §8.3.2 permits NI where detail is insufficient; this does not prove retrospective selection.

evidence: The registered 8-week 6MWT is reported. A, p.1601 lists baseline, preoperative, 4-week and 8-week assessments; Tables 1–2 and Figure 2 report those measurements. This internal concordance weighs against selection of favorable measurement times, despite incomplete prospective documentation.
guidance: §8.3.2 permits comparing article methods and results when prospective intentions are unavailable. Box 11, 5.2 requires selection based on results, rather than the mere existence of multiple measurements.

evidence: A, pp.1602–1604 reports repeated-measures, change-score, categorical recovery and supplementary analyses. Their reporting argues against obvious cherry-picking, but neither R nor a supplied SAP establishes all intended models, thresholds and missing-data strategies.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when analysis intentions are insufficiently detailed and multiple analyses are possible. Multiplicity alone does not establish selective reporting.

evidence: Paper p.3 describes stratified random allocation through an “interactive web response system”; Protocol §7.2, p.33, specifies equal allocation across six arms. The exact sequence-generation procedure is absent, but this centrally implemented, multicentre randomization supports a probable random component.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1, and §4.3.1.1 allow “Probably yes” from the trial’s circumstances when the precise generation method is unreported.

evidence: Participants meeting eligibility criteria were assigned at Visit 3 through IWRS (Protocol §7.2, p.33). The randomization code was stored in IWRS and inaccessible to the blinded study team (SAP §7.1, p.42).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation, including internet-based randomization.

evidence: Randomized arm sizes were 51–55 (Paper Figure 1, p.5). Table 1, p.6, shows broadly comparable age, BMI, HbA1c and diabetes duration. Sex proportions differ, but without an implausible pattern. Baseline data exclude two untreated participants, limiting certainty slightly.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias”; §4.3.3 requires consideration of the population represented in baseline tables.

evidence: Protocol §7.3, p.34: participants knew the nominal dose cohort but “will not know whether” they received tirzepatide, dulaglutide or placebo. Double-dummy administration matched the injections (SAP §5.1, p.12). GI symptoms could suggest active treatment, but actual unmasking is not documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 addresses awareness of the assigned intervention; §5.1.3 distinguishes possible deductions from established failures of blinding.

evidence: Investigators were masked to drug identity by the same double-dummy scheme (Protocol §7.3, p.34; SAP p.12). SAP §7, p.42, withheld assignments from investigators and site personnel until final database lock. Restricted sponsor interim access does not establish awareness among those delivering care.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns “carers and people delivering the interventions,” rather than every individual involved in analyses.

evidence: Both 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. For context, toxicity-related stopping and rescue treatment were protocol provisions (Protocol §§7.8.1 and 8.1); no trial-context deviation is established.
guidance: Box 6 branching: answer 2.3 only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. Its elaboration excludes protocol-consistent cessation for toxicity.

evidence: No qualifying deviation was identified through the applicable branch.
guidance: Box 6: 2.4 applies only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Question 2.4 is not reached.
guidance: Box 6: 2.5 applies only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Safety analyses required receipt of at least one dose. One randomized participant in each of the 1-mg and 10-mg groups was excluded because they were “not treated” (Paper p.5, Figure 1). SAP Table 6.1, p.16, also specifies classification by actual treatment. No treatment-group reassignment is demonstrated, but the two treatment-based exclusions occurred.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: analyses “excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization” are inappropriate. §5.3.1 distinguishes exclusion for nonreceipt from exclusion solely for missing outcomes.

evidence: Only two of 267 pooled active-arm participants were excluded, which argues against a large denominator effect. However, each paper endpoint has only two affected participants, and registry serious pancreatitis has one. Outcomes and reasons for nonreceipt in the excluded participants are not supplied; exclusions therefore have potential to materially change these sparse numerators (Paper Figure 1/Table 3; Registry p.1).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 explicitly warns that substantial impact can occur with “fewer than 5%” excluded “if the outcome is rare.” This assesses potential impact, not proof that excluded participants experienced events.

evidence: Only 283 participants completed the study: 238/267 randomized to pooled active treatment and 45/51 to placebo (Paper p.5, Figure 1). Treatment stopping did not necessarily end observation, but complete endpoint ascertainment after study withdrawal is not demonstrated. Protocol §9.2.1, p.43, says investigators were “not obligated to actively seek AEs or SAEs” after study discontinuation. Safety denominators alone do not establish complete observation.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make no important difference; for dichotomous outcomes this depends on event frequency. §6.1.1 cautions against equating analysis inclusion with observed outcomes.

evidence: No missing-data sensitivity analysis or correction is reported for these event counts. The imputation and sensitivity analyses in Paper pp.4–5 concern efficacy outcomes; SAP §6.10 specifies descriptive safety summaries.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires correction for missing-data bias or sensitivity analyses addressing plausible relationships between missingness and the outcome.

evidence: Figure 1 includes study withdrawals for adverse events, participant decisions and loss to follow-up. These do not exclude health-related missingness. Active collection could cease after study withdrawal (Protocol p.43).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: when withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Evidence for *likely* dependence on these specific diagnoses is limited. Pooled study completion was similar to placebo (238/267 versus 45/51). Protocol p.39 encouraged continued observation after treatment stopping; pancreatitis required treatment cessation but continued study participation (pp.45–46). Hurricane-related missed visits are also documented (amendment summary, pp.82–83). Although some withdrawals involved AEs, their reported reasons do not establish unobserved cholecystitis or pancreatitis.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence and directs attention to proportions and reasons. §§6.1.4.1–6.1.4.2 require outcome-specific interpretation, rather than treating every AE-related treatment withdrawal as missing outcome data.

evidence: Pancreatitis had defined clinical, enzyme and imaging criteria and independent adjudication (Protocol §9.2.1.2.5, pp.45–46; Supplement printed p.7). Cholecystitis was clinically identified and MedDRA-coded, with calculous and acalculous cases described (Paper p.10; Registry p.1). A separate cholecystitis adjudication procedure is not supplied, but no unsuitable measurement method is demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” not whether every outcome received independent adjudication.

evidence: Safety visits and AE recording applied across arms (Protocol §§2 and 9.2). Pancreatic enzymes were measured in every patient at scheduled visits, with common thresholds for additional investigation (p.46). The asymptomatic cholecystitis case warrants consideration of incidental detection (Paper p.10), but the documents do not establish arm-specific diagnostic thresholds or systematic differences in ascertainment.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparability through the same methods, thresholds and comparable timing; §7.1 also requires consideration of diagnostic detection bias. Shared surveillance supports PN despite that possibility.

evidence: Site investigators remained masked to drug identity (Protocol p.34; SAP §7, p.42). Pancreatitis was independently adjudicated (Paper p.4). The adjudicators’ masking is not explicitly stated, so PN rather than N reflects inference from the masked study arrangements; independence alone is not treated as proof of masking.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 and §7.3 concern the actual assessors’ awareness. §1.1 permits a probable answer when contextual evidence supports it despite incomplete reporting.

evidence: Assessors were judged probably unaware for both clinical cholecystitis assessment and pancreatitis assessment.
guidance: Box 10: 4.4 is reached only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Question 4.4 is not reached.
guidance: Box 10: 4.5 is reached only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Detailed safety intentions exist: Protocol §10.3.4, p.59, specifies patient incidence by preferred term and reported/adjudicated pancreatic events; SAP §§6.10.3, 6.10.4.5 and 6.15 specify safety counts, pancreatitis sources and registry reporting. SAP revision history, p.8, places version 1 before first production transfer, version 2 before the first interim analysis, and version 3 before primary database lock. Listed revisions concern efficacy methods, not these event-count analyses. Earlier SAP versions are absent and unblinded interim reviews occurred, so prespecification is probable rather than certain.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require sufficiently detailed intentions established before relevant unblinded results; amendments and dates must be examined. §1.1 permits PY based on supporting evidence without definitive documentation.

evidence: Adjudicated and investigator-reported pancreatic events were explicitly planned as separate outputs (SAP §6.10.4.5, pp.29–30); registry serious events were separately specified (§6.15, p.41). Thus the paper’s two adjudicated cases and registry’s one serious-event participant are not interchangeable measurements. Their patient-level reconciliation is unavailable, but different stated definitions do not demonstrate results-based selection. Both cholecystitis terms are available in the Registry, p.1.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 and §8.1.2 restrict assessment to eligible measurements and require selection “on the basis of the results.” Multiple planned definitions alone do not establish such selection.

evidence: SAP §6.10.3 specifies patient frequencies and percentages; §6.15 explicitly separates participants affected from numbers of events. Paper Table 3 and registry reporting follow those forms. No evidence shows selection of a favourable adjusted model or analysis population from competing analyses for these results. Pooling the five active arms is the requested synthesis choice.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 assesses results-based selection among eligible analyses. The suitability of the safety population for ITT is assessed in D2, not automatically carried into D5.

evidence: Paper p.3 describes stratified random allocation through an “interactive web response system.” Protocol §7.2, p.33, specifies equal randomization. The exact sequence-generation method is absent, but centrally implemented randomization in this multicentre trial supports a probable random component.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1; §4.3.1.1 permit PY where contextual evidence supports random sequence generation despite incomplete methodological reporting.

evidence: Eligible participants were assigned through IWRS at Visit 3 (Protocol §7.2, p.33). Allocation codes were stored in IWRS and restricted from the blinded team (SAP §7.1, p.42).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation, including internet-based services.

evidence: Randomized groups contained 51–55 participants (Paper Figure 1, p.5). Table 1, p.6, shows broadly comparable clinical characteristics. Sex proportions vary, but without compelling evidence of non-chance imbalance. The baseline table excludes two untreated participants, so it is not a complete randomized-cohort comparison.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.” §4.3.3 requires attention to the population represented by baseline data.

evidence: Participants knew their nominal dose cohort, but not whether injections contained tirzepatide, dulaglutide or placebo (Protocol §7.3, p.34). Double-dummy administration protected this distinction (SAP p.12). GI symptoms might suggest active treatment; documented identification of treatment is absent.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness of assigned intervention. §5.1.3 explains why side effects and successful guesses do not necessarily demonstrate failed masking.

evidence: Investigators were masked to drug identity (Protocol p.34). SAP §7, p.42, restricted site personnel’s access to assignments until final database lock. Selected sponsor personnel’s interim access does not establish awareness among carers or treatment providers.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 specifically concerns “carers and people delivering the interventions.”

evidence: Both preceding answers are PN. Toxicity-related cessation, rescue treatment and hurricane-related interruptions are documented, but do not establish trial-context deviations (Protocol §§7.8.1, 8.1; amendment summary pp.82–83).
guidance: Box 6 branching reaches 2.3 only after Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. Its elaboration excludes protocol-consistent cessation for toxicity.

evidence: Question 2.3 is not reached.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.4 only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Question 2.4 is not reached.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.5 only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The safety population required at least one dose. One randomized participant in each of the 1-mg and 10-mg arms was excluded as “not treated” (Paper p.5, Figure 1). SAP Table 6.1, p.16, also specifies actual-treatment classification, although actual cross-group reassignment is not demonstrated. The explicit treatment-based exclusions prevent calling this a fully appropriate assignment-effect analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: analyses “excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization” are inappropriate. §5.3.1 distinguishes nonreceipt exclusions from exclusions solely because outcomes are missing.

evidence: The two exclusions comprise 2/267 pooled active assignments; neither participant received study treatment. There is no documented exclusion after developing a treatment-associated event, and no demonstrated reassignment across the pooled active/placebo boundary (Paper Figure 1; SAP Table 6.1). The outcomes are rare, so a small percentage alone is insufficient reassurance. Nevertheless, the earlier PY rested too heavily on hypothetical additional events in these two untreated people. On balance, substantial impact from this particular analysis exclusion is probably absent; reasons for nonreceipt and subsequent outcomes remain unreported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 says substantial impact may occur below 5% when outcomes are rare, not that rarity automatically establishes it. §1.2.1 requires assessment of “risk of material bias.” This is a revised factual judgement, not an algorithm override.

evidence: Paper Figure 1 reports 283 study completers: 238/267 active assignments and 45/51 placebo assignments. Continued safety observation after treatment cessation was possible, but complete observation after study withdrawal is not established. Protocol §9.2.1, p.43, states investigators were “not obligated to actively seek AEs or SAEs” after study discontinuation. The safety denominator cannot establish complete observation of every participant.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by whether missing outcomes could materially affect the estimate, explicitly considering event rarity. §§6.1.1 and 6.3 distinguish analysis inclusion from outcome availability.

evidence: No correction or sensitivity analysis for missing cholecystitis or pancreatitis outcomes is supplied. Paper pp.4–5 and SAP §6.9.2.3 describe efficacy imputation; SAP §6.10 describes safety summaries without a corresponding missing-event sensitivity analysis.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses addressing plausible relationships between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Study withdrawals included adverse events, participant decisions and loss to follow-up (Paper Figure 1). Those reasons do not establish that all unobserved follow-up was unrelated to health. Active AE ascertainment could cease after withdrawal (Protocol p.43).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” permits missingness to depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Pooled study completion was similar to placebo. Treatment discontinuation did not necessarily terminate safety observation; participants with pancreatitis were to stop treatment but continue the study (Protocol pp.39, 45–46). Hurricane-related missed visits also occurred (pp.82–83). Some withdrawals were AE-related, but their reported reasons do not establish likely missingness specifically related to unobserved cholecystitis or pancreatitis.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence using proportions, reasons and circumstances. Similar attrition alone does not eliminate bias (§6.1.3), but it is relevant alongside these other facts.

evidence: Pancreatitis assessment used clinical, enzyme and imaging criteria, with independent adjudication (Protocol §9.2.1.2.5, pp.45–46; Paper p.4). Cholecystitis was clinically identified and MedDRA-coded; Paper p.10 describes calculous and asymptomatic acalculous cases. A separate cholecystitis adjudication procedure is absent, but no unsuitable assessment method is demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for measurement methods “unsuitable for the outcome”; independent adjudication is not mandatory for every clinical endpoint.

evidence: Scheduled safety procedures and AE recording applied across groups (Protocol §§2, 9.2). Every patient had scheduled pancreatic-enzyme measurements, with common investigation thresholds (p.46). The asymptomatic cholecystitis case raises an incidental-detection possibility, but the documents do not demonstrate different diagnostic thresholds or systematic ascertainment practices between groups.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires consideration of comparable methods, thresholds and timing; §7.1 specifically describes diagnostic detection bias. Here the common surveillance arrangements support PN.

evidence: Investigators were masked to drug identity (Protocol p.34; SAP §7, p.42); pancreatitis had independent adjudication (Paper p.4). The adjudicators’ masking is not explicitly documented. PN therefore rests on the masked trial arrangements, not on treating independence as proof of blinding.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 and §7.3 concern assessors’ actual awareness. §1.1 permits a probable answer supported by context despite incomplete reporting.

evidence: Outcome assessors are judged probably unaware.
guidance: Box 10: reach 4.4 only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Question 4.4 is not reached.
guidance: Box 10: reach 4.5 only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Protocol §10.3.4, p.59, specifies AE patient incidence and reported/adjudicated pancreatic events. SAP §§6.10.3, 6.10.4.5 and 6.15 specify the safety and registry outputs. Its revision history, p.8, places version 1 before first production transfer and version 2 before the first interim; the later listed changes do not identify revisions to these event-count analyses. Earlier SAP versions are unavailable, and unblinded interim reviews occurred (§6.14), preventing certainty but not a supported PY inference.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require examining detailed intentions, dates and amendments before relevant unblinded results. §1.1 supports PY rather than NI when the available evidence permits a reasonable inference.

evidence: Investigator-reported and adjudicated pancreatic events were separately planned (SAP §6.10.4.5, pp.29–30), as were registry serious events (§6.15, p.41). Paper Table 3 reports adjudicated cases; Registry p.1 reports serious-event participants and event counts. Patient-level reconciliation is absent, but these different definitions do not themselves show results-based selection. Both relevant cholecystitis preferred terms are available.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 and §8.1.2 require selection “on the basis of the results” among eligible measurements. Prespecified, distinct reporting definitions are not sufficient evidence of such selection.

evidence: Patient frequencies and percentages were planned (Protocol p.59; SAP §6.10.3). Registry reporting separately specifies participants affected and event counts (SAP §6.15). No evidence identifies a selectively chosen model or competing analysis for these counts. Pooling the five active arms is the requested synthesis decision.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns results-based selection among eligible analyses. The safety population’s ITT limitation belongs to D2 and does not independently establish selective reporting.

evidence: A p3: “computer-generated in permuted blocks of four participants (unknown to investigators)”, stratified by centre and baseline oxygenation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when a random component was used, including “computer-generated random numbers”.

evidence: A p3: allocation used a “centralised web-based management system” after validation of inclusion criteria; block size was unknown to investigators.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: remote or centrally administered allocation supports Yes. Section 4.3.2 identifies predictable, known blocks as a concern; that circumstance is not reported here.

evidence: A Table 1, p4, and S Table S1, p10, describe only the 313 analysed participants, not all 322 randomized. Available characteristics are broadly similar. The oxygenation-stratum imbalance is acknowledged and attributed to incomplete blocks across centres (A p8), rather than demonstrated manipulation. Full randomized-cohort baseline information is absent.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly permits NI when only baseline characteristics of the final analysis sample are reported. Section 4.3.3 requires assessment using all randomized participants; §4.3.3.1 says chance imbalances are not systematic bias.

evidence: A pp2–3 describes an open-label trial in which “individual patient assignments could not be masked”. Patients probably recognized the mask versus nasal cannula during preoxygenation, although subsequent induction limited awareness.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness “during the trial”. Section 1.1 permits PY where the answer requires inference.

evidence: A p3 explicitly states that individual assignments could not be masked; personnel administered visibly different devices (A p4).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether carers or intervention personnel knew the assignment.

evidence: Preoxygenation stopped in three NIV and six high-flow patients, mainly because of severe hypoxaemia (A p7; S Table S2, p11). The protocol explicitly allowed switching or immediate intubation for inefficacy or intolerance (S pp48,116). Protocol monitoring and reported delivery settings support implementation (A pp3,6); no trial-context-driven departure is identified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: answer N/PN for changes “consistent with the trial protocol”; Y/PY requires evidence or strong reason that the trial context caused prohibited departures. Section 5.1 likewise excludes planned rescue changes.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; the reported rescue changes were permitted (S p116; A p7).
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only if 2.3=Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached; no qualifying deviations were identified in 2.3.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only if 2.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The analysis retained patients who stopped preoxygenation and was labelled ITT (A pp5–7). However, Figure 1 excludes one NIV patient “not intubated” and one high-flow patient who “did not receive treatment”; the text describes the latter exclusion as cardiac arrest (A pp3,6). A blinded board reviewed eligibility, and cardiac arrest/legal protection were exclusion criteria (A p3; S p111), but the documents do not establish whether both procedural exclusions reflected pre-existing ineligibility unaffected by assignment. Missing recordings are considered separately in D3.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: available-case ITT is appropriate; exclusions of eligible participants are inappropriate; exclusions for ineligibility are acceptable only when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment. Section 1.1 supports NI when the distinction cannot reasonably be resolved.

evidence: The uncertain procedural exclusions concern one patient per group, against 80 observed events (A Figure 1 and Table 2). Even allowing either outcome for these two patients would change the absolute difference by less than one percentage point. Cardiac arrest is prognostically concerning, but the number involved makes substantial impact unlikely.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 requires assessment of whether the number excluded could have a “substantial impact”, considering event frequency and prognostic selection rather than applying a fixed percentage rule.

evidence: Outcome data are reported for 313/322 randomized participants (97.2%). Figure 1 identifies five without recorded data, one consent withdrawal, and three other exclusions: five participants absent from NIV analysis and four from high-flow analysis (A pp3,6). Even conservatively treating all nine as unavailable, they are few relative to 80 observed events. Reasons for the five recording losses are not explained, but material missing-data bias is unlikely at this extent.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: assess “all, or nearly all” randomized participants; for binary outcomes, consider missing participants relative to observed events. Section 6.1.3.2 rejects a universal percentage threshold.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=PY. The reported sensitivity analysis adjusts baseline oxygenation, rather than evaluating missing-outcome assumptions (A pp5–6).
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.2 only if 3.1=N/PN/NI.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=PY; recording-loss reasons remain incompletely documented (A Figure 1).
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.3 only if 3.2=N/PN.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=PY.
guidance: Box 8: ask 3.4 only if 3.3=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Severe hypoxaemia was defined as SpO₂ <80% for at least five seconds. Dedicated monitors recorded values every second for subsequent analysis (A pp4–5). No evidence indicates an unsuitable measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 addresses unsuitable methods, such as instruments unable to detect relevant values or demonstrated to have poor validity.

evidence: A pp4–5: dedicated monitors and sensors were supplied to all centres “to ensure that all centres monitored pulse oximetry equivalently”; the same threshold and induction-to-five-minutes-after-intubation window applied to both groups.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable ascertainment uses “the same measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times.

evidence: A p3: the adjudication committee was “unaware of the study groups”; an independent biostatistician unaware of allocation extracted stored oximetry curves. S p7 identifies this committee’s role in determining primary-outcome episodes. Unblinded bedside personnel collected secondary outcomes, which does not establish unblinded assessment of this primary result.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: answer No if outcome assessors were blinded. Section 7.1 requires identifying the actual assessor for the outcome concerned.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=N; primary-outcome adjudication was blinded (A p3).
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only if 4.3=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=N.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if 4.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Protocol versions dated July 2014 and May 2016 specify SpO₂ <80% and a between-group χ² comparison (S pp42,63,109,121); the later protocol specifies the relevant observation window (S p117). These support prespecification, and investigators reportedly remained unaware of group outcomes until database lock on October 11, 2017 (A p3). However, the published minimum five-second duration (A p4) is absent from the supplied protocol definitions and amendment summaries (S pp86,133–136). Its adoption before unblinded analysis cannot be verified.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires sufficiently detailed intentions finalized before unblinded outcomes were available. Sections 8.3.1–8.3.2 require checking dates and acknowledging insufficient detail.

evidence: The <80% threshold and procedural window are supported by the protocol, but the minimum episode duration is unspecified there (S pp42,109,117 versus A p4). Continuous recordings permit alternative duration definitions. There is no evidence that alternatives were actually compared and selected for favourable results, but insufficient detail to exclude that possibility confidently.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: NI applies when intentions are “not reported in sufficient detail” and multiple measurements are possible. Y/PY requires evidence of likely results-based selection, not merely an undocumented refinement.

evidence: The target is the unadjusted full-sample comparison specified in both protocol versions (S pp63,121) and reported in Table 2 (A p5). Adjusted full-sample estimates are also reported (A p6), alongside subgroup results. Thus the available analyses do not suggest replacement of the planned target analysis by a more favourable one.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns selection on the basis of results among eligible analyses. The protocol-specified comparison and reporting of additional estimates support PN; multiplicity alone does not establish selective reporting (§8.1.2).

evidence: “Computer-generated in permuted blocks of four participants,” stratified by centre and oxygenation (Article p3). Fixed block size does not negate the random component.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: computer-generated random numbers qualify as random sequence generation.

evidence: Allocation followed validation of inclusion criteria through a “centralised web-based management system”; block size was “unknown to investigators” (Article p3). No evidence of foreknowledge is reported.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 supports Yes for central allocation; §4.3.2 warns about small fixed blocks when recruiters can predict assignments.

evidence: Table 1 describes the 313 analysed participants, not all 322 randomized (Article pp3–4). Available baseline characteristics are broadly similar; the mild-hypoxaemia stratum differs in size. The authors attribute this to incomplete blocks across centres (Article p8), but complete randomized-cohort baseline data are absent.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly identifies reporting only the final analysis sample as a reason for NI. Section 4.3.3 requires consideration of all randomized participants; chance differences do not establish a randomization problem.

evidence: Individual assignments “could not be masked” (Article p3). Patients probably recognized mask versus nasal-cannula treatment during preoxygenation, although awareness subsequently decreased with induction (Article p4).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness during the trial; §1.1 permits PY for an evidence-based inference.

evidence: The trial was open-label, and clinicians administered visibly different devices (Article pp3–4).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether carers or intervention personnel knew the assigned intervention.

evidence: Three NIV and six high-flow patients stopped preoxygenation, mainly because of severe hypoxaemia (Article p7; Supplement Table S2, p11). Protocol monitoring and delivery data support implementation (Article pp3,6); no trial-context-driven prohibited departure is identified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: answer N/PN for changes “consistent with the trial protocol”; Y/PY requires evidence or strong reason that trial context caused prohibited departures.

evidence: Evidence supporting Low includes the planned blinded eligibility review and retention of patients whose preoxygenation stopped (Supplement pp63,121; Article p7). Nevertheless, Figure 1 excludes one patient “not intubated” and another who “did not receive treatment”; the Results describe a cardiac-arrest exclusion (Article pp3,6). Cardiac arrest and legal protection were eligibility exclusions (Supplement p111), but the timing and circumstances needed to establish that both procedural exclusions reflected baseline ineligibility are absent. This does not prove inappropriate exclusion, but prevents a confident PY.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 permit exclusions for ineligibility only when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment. Missing-outcome exclusions alone are appropriate for D2. Section 1.1 supports NI when neither probable answer is sufficiently justified.

evidence: The unresolved procedural exclusions involve one participant per group, compared with 80 observed events (Article Figure 1 and Table 2). Hypothetically adding either event status for those two participants would change the absolute difference by less than one percentage point. Cardiac arrest raises prognostic concern, but substantial impact remains unlikely.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 evaluates the number excluded, outcome frequency and prognostic selection; it specifies that there is no universal numerical rule.

evidence: Data are reported for 313/322 randomized participants. Figure 1 accounts for five unavailable recordings, one consent withdrawal and three other exclusions: five participants absent from NIV analysis and four from high-flow analysis (Article pp3,6). Even treating all nine conservatively as unavailable, their number is small relative to 80 events. Reasons for recording loss are unspecified; the judgement therefore remains PY rather than Y.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires “all, or nearly all” and relates completeness for binary outcomes to event frequency. Section 6.1.3.2 rejects an automatic percentage cutoff.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=PY. The reported baseline-oxygenation sensitivity analysis does not establish robustness to missing outcomes (Article pp5–6).
guidance: Box 8: 3.2 is asked only after 3.1=N/PN/NI; §6.1.7 requires sensitivity analyses addressing the missingness mechanism.

evidence: Not reached because 3.2=NA. The unspecified causes of recording loss are acknowledged in 3.1 (Article Figure 1).

guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns unsuitable measurement methods, including inability to detect relevant values or demonstrated poor validity.

evidence: Dedicated monitors and sensors were supplied to all centres to ensure equivalent monitoring. Both groups used the same threshold and induction-to-five-minutes-after-intubation window (Article pp4–5).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable ascertainment through the same methods, thresholds and comparable measurement times.

guidance: Box 10, 4.3: answer No when outcome assessors were blinded. Section 7.1 requires identifying the assessor for the particular outcome.

evidence: The dated protocols specify the <80% primary outcome and χ² comparison (Supplement pp42,63,109,121); the later protocol specifies the relevant observation window (p117). Investigators reportedly remained unaware of group outcomes until October 11, 2017 (Article p3). These strongly support prespecification. However, the published “at least 5 s” requirement (Article p4) is absent from the supplied protocol definitions and amendment summaries (Supplement pp86,133–136). Its timing cannot be verified.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires sufficiently detailed intentions finalized before unblinded outcomes were available. Sections 8.3.1–8.3.2 require checking dates and acknowledging insufficient detail; a potentially legitimate refinement does not establish when it occurred.

evidence: The threshold and procedural window agree with the protocol, but episode duration is incompletely specified (Supplement pp109,117 versus Article p4). Continuous recordings permit alternative duration definitions. No evidence shows results-driven selection, but the documents do not establish whether the five-second definition was fixed before comparative results were available.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 specifies NI when intentions are insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible. Y/PY requires evidence that selection was likely based on results; that evidence is absent.

evidence: The unadjusted full-sample comparison was planned and reported (Supplement pp63,121; Article Table 2, p5). Full-sample adjusted estimates were also reported (Article p6). The target result was not displaced by the more favourable subgroup findings.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 and §8.1.2 address selection based on results among eligible analyses. Multiple analyses alone do not demonstrate such selection.

evidence: A p3: sequence generated by the statistician using “block randomisation (R command blockrand).” This explicitly identifies a computer-generated random sequence.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when “a random component was used,” including computer-generated random numbers.

evidence: A p3: the code was held by the manufacturer and emergency unblinding service; packages arrived with “anonymous participant numbers”; only masked investigators enrolled and assigned participants. Sequential dispensing is not explicitly described, but concealment is strongly supported.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: appropriately coded drug containers support concealment; when operational detail is incomplete, “a judgement may be required” for Probably yes. Section 4.3.2: small fixed blocks threaten concealment when previous allocations are known; investigators remained masked here.

evidence: A Table 1 and S Figure S2 (appendix p5) show no persuasive problematic imbalance. S Table S5 baseline CWS means are 46.61, 57.75 and 45.65, with substantial uncertainty. These differences and arm sizes 23/24/23 are compatible with chance.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when “any observed imbalances are compatible with chance.” Section 4.3.3.1: chance imbalances are not systematic bias.

evidence: A p6 says the target summaries came from raw data. guidance: Box 8, 3.2: evidence requires correction for bias or sensitivity analyses under plausible missingness assumptions. Sections 6.1.6–6.1.7: imputation needs justified assumptions; sensitivity analyses must address the relationship between missingness and the outcome.

evidence: Week 16 required a site visit (A p3), and CWS measures withdrawal symptoms (A p4). Symptom severity could plausibly affect attendance. Figure 1 includes loss to follow-up and missed visits, without establishing outcome-independent reasons for all missing Week 16 scores.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: when follow-up loss “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on its true value.

Neither likely dependence nor likely independence can be supported.
guidance: §1.1: use NI when information cannot reasonably support PY or PN. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence using proportions, reasons and circumstances; Table 10 explicitly routes NI here to High.

guidance: Box 10, 4.1: the question identifies unsuitable measurement methods, such as demonstrated poor validity; established specified outcomes ordinarily warrant N/PN.

guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness could depend on its true value when follow-up loss “could be related to participants’ health status.”

guidance: §4.3.2 and Box 4, 1.2 require concealment until assignment; central allocation must be independent of enrolment personnel. §1.1 permits NI when insufficient details prevent a defensible probable answer.

evidence: A, Tables 1–2, pp.86–87, present baseline characteristics only for the 149 analysed participants, rather than all 184 randomized. guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly permits NI for studies reporting “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis.” §4.3.3 requires assessment using all randomized participants; chance differences are not bias.

evidence: A, pp.83–84: participants received exercise instructions, diaries, supervised sessions and psychological preparation, while controls received ERAS and nutritional care. R, Masking info, does not list participants as masked.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness of assigned intervention; the visibly different programmes establish awareness.

evidence: A, pp.83–84: physiotherapists supervised intervention-specific training and a psychologist delivered preparation. R separates these providers from masked assessors. Blinding surgeons does not blind intervention providers.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether “carers or people delivering the interventions” were aware.

evidence: A, pp.83–85, and R, Detailed description, describe the intended programmes. Figure 1 records cancellations, deaths, emergency interventions and inoperability, but provides no evidence of deviations caused by recruitment, disappointment with assignment or personnel undermining the protocol. Additional exercise and contact were intended treatment components.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: answer Y/PY “only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol changes. Ordinary non-adherence or clinical changes do not themselves establish this.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; see the programme and participant-flow evidence above.
