evidence: A, p.84: “After completion of the whole study,” 23 TAMIS patients were excluded because their primary and secondary outcomes differed. Figure 1 identifies 11 intervention and 12 control exclusions. This was an analysis exclusion after observing outcomes, not simply exclusion of missing measurements or confirmation of a previously specified eligibility restriction. The authors’ “intention to treat” label does not resolve this.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6: “Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.” The exception for independently established ineligibility is not demonstrated here.

evidence: The 23 TAMIS exclusions comprise 12.5% of randomized participants. A, p.84 states that “both the primary and secondary outcomes were dramatically different” in this subgroup. Although exclusions were numerically balanced, removal of a substantial prognostically distinct subgroup could materially alter the assignment effect.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 considers the number excluded and whether exclusions relate to prognostic factors; no fixed percentage establishes negligible impact.

evidence: A, Figure 1, p.85: 184 were randomized; nine did not receive treatment following cancellation, preoperative death or emergency intervention. The diagram also records 16 versus 18 non-attenders with lost functional data, without identifying affected assessment visits. Table 2 gives group headings of 77 and 72 but no visit-specific denominators. Near-complete surgery-time ascertainment therefore cannot be established. The 23 deliberate TAMIS exclusions are not counted as missing data, and the 34 non-attendances are not assumed to have occurred before surgery.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires data for all or “nearly all” randomized participants; §6.1 separates genuine missing data from deliberate analysis exclusions. Because some missing-data information exists, PN is more appropriate than the question’s NI option, reserved for no information about extent.

evidence: A, statistical methods, p.84, reports conventional comparisons but no correction for informative missingness or sensitivity analysis for missing surgery-time 6MWD. R supplies none.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from methods correcting bias or sensitivity analyses demonstrating robustness across plausible missingness assumptions.

evidence: A, Figure 1, includes deaths before surgery and emergency interventions, making health-related missingness plausible. Reasons for non-attendance are unspecified. Poor health could affect both attendance/testing and walking capacity.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal or loss “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: A, Figure 1 and Table 2 do not establish which participants lacked the preoperative measurement or their reasons by group. Deaths and emergencies support concern, but the larger non-attendance counts could concern postoperative visits only. The documents do not permit a reliable judgement that dependence on surgery-time walking capacity was either likely or unlikely.
guidance: §1.1 permits NI when neither probable answer is defensible. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence using outcome-specific missingness proportions and reasons; Table 10 maps NI here to High.

evidence: A, p.84: participants walked on a treadmill for six minutes and distance was recorded in metres. Nothing supplied demonstrates poor validity or insensitivity for measuring walking distance.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods, such as demonstrated poor validity—not whether the chosen outcome is ideal.

evidence: A, p.84 specifies the same treadmill measurement and assessment schedule in both groups; R, Detailed description, also schedules preoperative 6MWD in both arms. Weekly intervention-arm assessments were part of training, not evidence that a different method or selectively chosen visit supplied the surgery-time result.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable ascertainment as the same methods at comparable time points. Mere additional intervention contact does not establish differential ascertainment of this scheduled result.

evidence: R, Masking info, states that investigators and assessors were blinded and intervention providers would not assess outcomes. However, participants knew their assignment and actively determined treadmill performance: A, p.84 instructed walking at a speed “that would make them tired.” Thus the measurement interaction included an unblinded participant despite masked observers.
guidance: §7.3 states that for assessments involving participant–collector interaction, assessors should be considered aware when either party is unblinded, unless convincing contrary evidence exists.

evidence: A, p.84: the test depends on the participant’s chosen speed and effort. Knowledge of having completed prehabilitation could influence effort during testing, even though distance itself is recorded objectively.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 asks whether knowledge could influence assessment. §7.3 requires considering the actual assessment process rather than assuming all numerical outcomes are immune.

evidence: R’s explicit assessor masking and separation of intervention providers from assessment reduce concern. Neither source reports differential encouragement, altered testing instructions or another indication that expectations probably affected the recorded surgery-time distance. Possible effort effects remain, but likely influence is not established.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from influence judged likely; §7.3 directs consideration of assessor independence and involvement in care.

evidence: No dated SAP is supplied. R first submission was 27 November 2018, whereas A, p.84 reports recruitment beginning October 2017; the available registry record was updated in March 2020. R specifies preoperative 6MWD change but not the percentage-ratio analysis or analysis population in sufficient detail to verify a plan finalized before unblinded data.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” establishing that intentions preceded unblinded data. Box 11, 5.1 requires sufficiently detailed prospective analysis intentions; §1.1 supports NI here.

evidence: R, Primary outcome 7, explicitly names 6MWD change by operation, assessed before surgery and at admission. A, Table 2, reports this measurement plus postoperative measurements, including non-significant results. There is no indication that the specified surgery-time 6MWD was selected from competing eligible measurements because of its result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 restricts consideration to “eligible” measurements. §8.1 separates selection within an outcome from non-reporting of other outcome domains; spirometry, SF-36 and HADS do not automatically create selection bias for this specified result.

evidence: A, Table 2 reports both absolute distances and percentages of baseline, which argues against simply suppressing the less favourable metric. Nevertheless, no prospective analysis specification verifies the selected metric and population. The outcome-informed TAMIS exclusion (A, p.84) raises concern, but its stated clinical justification and absence of alternative comparative estimates do not establish that this result was selected for a favourable treatment effect or significance.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when analysis intentions lack sufficient detail and multiple analyses are possible. §8.3.2 permits examining discrepancies in analysed samples, while §8.1 requires selection based on the intervention result’s direction, magnitude or significance for this bias mechanism.

evidence: A, p.83: allocation used “computerised random numbers.” Neither source contradicts random sequence generation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 explicitly accepts “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: A, p.83 identifies a coordinator “not involved in the clinical management.” This supports separation of roles, but does not establish concealment from enrolling personnel. R, Detailed description and Masking info, does not describe protection against foreknowledge before assignment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 requires concealment until enrolment and assignment; independent central allocation means independence from enrolment personnel. Under §1.1, incomplete reporting warrants NI when neither probable answer is sufficiently supported.

evidence: A, Tables 1–2, pp.86–87, describe only 77 intervention and 72 control participants, rather than all 184 randomized. Baseline 6MWD was similar, but some comorbidities differed. These selected-group data cannot reliably diagnose the original allocation process.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 explicitly identifies reporting “only baseline characteristics of participants in the final analysis” as grounds for NI. §4.3.3 requires considering all randomized participants.

evidence: A, pp.83–84: intervention participants received exercise instructions, diaries, supervised training and psychological preparation. R’s masking list excludes participants.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns awareness of assigned intervention; the visibly different programmes establish awareness.

evidence: A, pp.83–84: physiotherapists and psychologists delivered intervention-specific activities. R separates these providers from masked outcome assessors. Masking surgeons does not establish masking of intervention providers.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks about “carers and people delivering the interventions.”

evidence: A, pp.83–85, describes the intended programmes and clinical interruptions, without evidence of compensatory treatment-seeking or personnel undermining assignment. Additional training and contact were intended components. R likewise describes these components.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 permits Y/PY “only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol changes. Ordinary clinical interruptions or non-adherence are insufficient.

evidence: The exclusions comprise 23/184 randomized participants, or 12.5%. A, p.84 states that “both the primary and secondary outcomes were dramatically different.” Similar exclusion counts and the clinical rationale argue against a simple differential exclusion mechanism, but do not remove potential material effects from excluding this distinct subgroup.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks about potential substantial impact, considering numbers excluded and prognostic factors; it does not require proof that the treatment estimate actually changed.

evidence: A, Figure 1, records nine preoperative non-receipt events and three patients found inoperable at surgery. The 16 versus 18 missed follow-up visits probably concern postoperative assessments: R, Detailed description, separates admission testing from “Postoperative follow up.” Nevertheless, Table 2 lacks visit-specific denominators, so near-complete preoperative ascertainment is not established. The 23 TAMIS exclusions are not treated as missing data.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires availability for all or nearly all randomized participants. §6.1 separates missing measurements from deliberate exclusions. The stated 95% example for continuous outcomes is not an automatic threshold.

evidence: A, statistical methods, p.84, provides no analysis correcting informative missingness and no missing-data sensitivity analysis. R supplies none.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses demonstrating robustness under plausible missingness assumptions.

evidence: A, Figure 1: preoperative deaths and emergency interventions make a relationship between health, test availability and walking capacity plausible. Reasons for cancellation and missed visits are insufficiently detailed.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness could depend on the true outcome when withdrawal or loss “could be related to participants’ health status.”

evidence: A, Figure 1 and Table 2 do not identify which preoperative measurements were unavailable or their reasons by group. Health-related events support dependence, while the likely postoperative timing of the larger non-attendance counts limits their relevance. Neither likely nor unlikely dependence across the actual missing preoperative measurements can be established confidently.
guidance: §1.1 permits NI when neither probable answer is defensible. Box 8, 3.4 requires considering reasons and proportions for the relevant outcome; Table 10 maps NI here to High. The final domain override, explained below, concerns materiality rather than changing this factual uncertainty.

evidence: A, p.84: distance walked on a treadmill in six minutes was recorded in metres. The supplied documents do not demonstrate an unsuitable or insensitive measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for inappropriate methods, including poor validity or inability to detect plausible effects; it does not assess whether the chosen outcome is ideal.

evidence: A, p.84 and R, Detailed description, specify the same preoperative assessment in both groups. Weekly intervention-arm measurements supported training; no evidence shows that these replaced the scheduled surgery-time measurement or that different testing methods supplied the compared results.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods and time points. Additional encounters matter when they create differential ascertainment of the outcome being assessed.

evidence: R, Masking info, explicitly describes masked assessors and separation from intervention providers. However, participants were unblinded and actively determined test performance: A, p.84 instructed walking at a speed “that would make them tired.”
guidance: §7.3 states that in participant–collector assessment interactions, awareness by either party means assessors should be considered aware unless convincing contrary evidence exists. This does not imply that the external assessors themselves were unblinded.

evidence: A, p.84: speed and exertion were participant-dependent. Knowledge of assignment could affect effort during the measurement, even though the resulting distance is numerical and externally recorded.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 asks whether assessment could be influenced. §7.3 requires considering the assessment process and susceptibility to knowledge of assignment.

evidence: R’s masked assessors and separation from treatment delivery reduce the likelihood of differential encouragement or interpretation. Neither source documents such differences. Possible expectancy effects on effort do not establish that influence was likely.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from likely influence; §7.3 identifies assessor independence and involvement in care as relevant considerations.

evidence: R first submission was 27 November 2018; A, p.84 reports recruitment beginning October 2017. The supplied registry was subsequently updated, and its recruitment dates differ from A. No dated SAP establishes prospective specification of the percentage analysis or final analysis population.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a date-stamp showing intentions preceded unblinded outcome data. Box 11, 5.1 requires sufficiently detailed prospective intentions; §1.1 supports NI when this cannot be verified.

evidence: R, Primary outcome 7, specifies preoperative 6MWD change by operation. A, Table 2, reports this assessment and postoperative assessments, including non-significant results. Spirometry and psychological outcomes are not alternative measurements of this narrowly specified 6MWD result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 restricts attention to eligible measurements. §8.1 distinguishes selection of a result within an outcome from non-reporting of other outcome domains.

evidence: A, Table 2, reports both absolute distances and percentages of baseline, arguing against suppression of the less favourable metric. However, prospective analysis intentions are unavailable. The outcome-informed TAMIS exclusion raises concern, but A, p.84 gives a clinical rationale and does not show competing comparative estimates selected for direction or significance.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions lack sufficient detail and multiple analyses are possible. §8.3.2 permits scrutiny of analysed samples; §8.1 requires selection based on intervention-result direction, magnitude or significance for this specific bias mechanism.

evidence: A p.2498, “Randomization and masking”: “centrally generated randomized treatment kit number list,” with stratification by HbA1c and TZD use. The precise sequence-generation method is absent, but the centralized randomized list in this multicentre phase III trial supports probably random allocation.
guidance: §4.3.1.1 and Box 4, 1.1 permit “Probably yes” from trial circumstances when the generation method is incompletely reported.

evidence: A p.2498: treatment numbers were allocated through a “centralized interactive voice response system”; investigators “did not have access to the randomization code.”
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Yes for a “remote or centrally administered method,” including telephone randomization services.

evidence: A p.2499, Table 1: 223 participants per group; similar age, sex, race, BMI and background treatment. Diabetes duration differed modestly, 8.7 versus 9.6 years, with SDs approximately six years. No pattern suggests failed randomization. Event-specific baseline histories are not tabulated.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when observed imbalances are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 excludes chance imbalance from bias.

evidence: M, Design → Masking info: “Who masked: PARTICIPANT; INVESTIGATOR.” R p.1 describes volume-matching placebo; A p.2498 reports matching dose-escalation schedules. More nausea/vomiting could have prompted guesses, but actual recognition of assignment is not documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding may prevent awareness; answer Y/PY for side effects participants knew were intervention-specific. §5.1.3 cautions that successful guessing can occur even when blinding is preserved.

evidence: Investigators were masked and lacked access to the allocation code (M, Masking info; A p.2498). Both groups followed the same glargine-titration and rescue-treatment rules. Separate masking details for every care-provider role are absent, supporting PN rather than definitive N.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding may prevent awareness; §1.1 allows a supported probable answer rather than NI when details are incomplete.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. A pp.2498–2499 describes permitted rescue therapy and discontinuations, mainly for adverse events; these do not independently establish deviations caused by trial participation.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask only if either 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. It also excludes protocol-consistent changes such as “cessation … because of acute toxicity.”

evidence: No qualifying deviations established through 2.3; see A pp.2498–2499.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.3 is Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached; no qualifying deviations requiring a balance assessment.
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: M, Results: participant flow, and S p.3, Fig.2: all 223 randomized participants in each group entered the safety analysis. Although eligibility for safety analysis required receiving a dose, this excluded nobody. No reassignment between analysis groups is reported. A p.2498 describes analysis by treatment group. guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 require analysis in randomized groups without inappropriate participant exclusions; missing-outcome bias belongs in D3.

guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.6 is N/PN/NI.

evidence: R p.1 limits events to “First dose … up to 3 days after the last dose”; A p.2498 similarly specifies the “on-treatment period.” S Fig.2 shows 29/223 lixisenatide versus 12/223 placebo premature treatment discontinuations. Full planned-period event ascertainment after discontinuation is not demonstrated. All-participant denominators and equal median exposure of 169 days do not establish complete follow-up. With one observed event per target, missing follow-up cannot be dismissed as immaterial.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference”; the required completeness depends on event frequency. §6.1.5 explains that partial follow-up and inclusion in analysis do not establish complete outcomes.

evidence: A p.2498 reports descriptive safety analyses; R p.1 supplies exposure-limited counts. No sensitivity analysis or correction addressing missing subsequent GI events is supplied. LOCF concerns efficacy measurements, not these event counts.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires methods correcting bias or sensitivity analyses showing robustness under “plausible assumptions”; imputation alone does not establish absence of bias.

evidence: M, participant flow: adverse events accounted for 19 lixisenatide and nine placebo discontinuations. A p.2499 identifies ten GI-related discontinuations with lixisenatide versus none with placebo. Ending event observation shortly after treatment cessation could therefore depend on health status relevant to GI outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: when withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness may depend on its true value.

evidence: Observation ended in relation to treatment cessation, and premature discontinuation was substantially more frequent with lixisenatide, particularly for GI adverse effects (R p.1; S Fig.2; A p.2499). Most GI discontinuations involved nausea/vomiting, not documented target diagnoses, and equal median exposure provides some reassurance. Nevertheless, unequal, health-related truncation makes informative missingness likely enough to threaten these very sparse results; no correcting analysis is available.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 identifies differing proportions and reasons for missingness as evidence supporting Yes. §6.1.5 highlights a “particular risk” when observation is censored after stopping treatment because of toxicity.

evidence: A p.2498 describes TEAE reporting and laboratory safety monitoring, including amylase/lipase. R p.1 identifies the three serious outcomes using MedDRA 14.0. guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” such as poor validity or inadequate sensitivity; §7.3 concerns absent identification systems, not merely missing reporting detail.

evidence: Both groups used the same blinded trial procedures and reported AE framework (A p.2498; R p.1; M, Design). More nausea/vomiting could theoretically prompt additional investigations, but differential diagnostic testing or surveillance for these target events is not documented. The specific serious clinical events are distinct from subjective nausea reporting.
guidance: §7.3 asks about “systematic differences between the groups”; Box 10, 4.2 considers comparable methods, thresholds and timing, including diagnostic detection bias. Available evidence supports probably comparable ascertainment.

evidence: M explicitly identifies participant and investigator masking; A p.2498 states investigators lacked the code. These are the relevant reporters/clinical assessors. Independent adjudication is documented for allergic and cardiovascular events only and is not assumed for GI events. No actual unblinding of GI assessors is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: answer No when assessors were blinded; §1.1 permits PN where a judgment is necessary. §7.1 identifies intervention providers as assessors of clinical events.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. The clinical diagnoses can involve judgment, but this does not negate the evidence supporting masking.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.3 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached under the masking branch.
guidance: Box 10: ask only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: No protocol or dated SAP is supplied. A p.2502 says the sponsor prepared statistical analysis plans but provides no finalization date or detailed GI-event plan. guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” establishing intentions before unblinded data; Box 11, 5.1 requires sufficiently detailed prespecified intentions. Their absence supports NI, not a claim that no plan existed.

evidence: R p.1 presents the requested serious event terms with a common window; A p.2500 reports pancreatitis as a TEAE without establishing seriousness. Pancreatitis’s absence from the registry lists is not by itself a contradiction: the serious designation is unknown and other AEs have a 5% reporting threshold.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 explicitly specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and the outcome could be measured in multiple ways. §8.1 separates selection of a reported result from non-reporting of an outcome.

evidence: A p.2498 and R p.1 consistently describe descriptive safety-population analyses, which argues against an obvious unexplained analysis switch. However, no prospective plan establishes whether alternative observation-period, population or missing-data analyses were intended or performed for these outcomes. Results-based selection is not demonstrated.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when analysis intentions are unavailable or insufficient and multiple analyses are possible; Y/PY requires evidence that selection was likely based on results.

evidence: A p.2498: “centrally generated randomized treatment kit number list,” stratified by HbA1c and TZD use. The actual generation procedure is absent, but centralized randomization in this multicentre phase III trial supports PY.
guidance: §4.3.1.1 and Box 4, 1.1 allow “Probably yes” where circumstances support random generation despite incomplete methodological detail.

evidence: A p.2498: allocation through a “centralized interactive voice response system”; investigators lacked access to the randomization code.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation independent of enrolment personnel.

evidence: A p.2499, Table 1: 223 per group; similar age, sex, race, BMI and background medication. Diabetes duration was 8.7 versus 9.6 years, with SDs approximately six years. No implausible imbalance pattern.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: No when differences are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 excludes chance imbalance from bias.

evidence: M, Design/Masking: “PARTICIPANT; INVESTIGATOR.” Volume-matching placebo and corresponding titration schedules are documented (R p.1; A p.2498). Nausea/vomiting could permit guesses, but recognition of assignment is not established.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 requires Y/PY when participants knew side effects were intervention-specific; §5.1.3 cautions that guessing can occur despite preserved blinding.

evidence: Investigators were masked and lacked the allocation code (M, Masking; A p.2498). Both groups had the same titration and rescue rules. Masking of every ancillary care-provider role is not separately described.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 considers personnel awareness; §1.1 permits a supported probable answer when reporting is incomplete.

evidence: Not reached after PN/PN. A pp.2498–2499 documents permitted rescue therapy and adverse-event discontinuations, without establishing trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6 branching requires Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. Its elaboration excludes protocol-consistent “cessation … because of acute toxicity.”

guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: M, Results: participant flow, and S p.3, Fig.2 show all 223 randomized participants per group in the safety analysis. The one-dose requirement excluded nobody. No analysis-group switching is reported; A p.2498 describes analysis by treatment group.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 require retention in randomized groups and no inappropriate participant exclusions. A “safety population” label alone does not establish an inappropriate analysis.

evidence: Not reached after 2.6 PY; all randomized participants entered the safety analysis (M, participant flow).
guidance: Box 6: ask only if 2.6 is N/PN/NI.

evidence: R p.1 defines the event window as first dose through three days after last dose and includes 223/223 per arm. M, participant flow, confirms that this is the entire randomized population. A p.2498 and S Table 1 describe on-treatment TEAEs, including events causing discontinuation. Although 29 versus 12 stopped treatment, this does not establish missing event status within the specified safety window. Individual completeness is not explicitly certified, hence PY.
guidance: §2.2 makes assessment specific to the outcome and measurement time. Box 8, 3.1 asks whether data for “this outcome” were available. §1.1 permits PY when the evidence supports an inference; analysis inclusion alone would not suffice, but the defined window and retained discontinuers provide additional support.

evidence: Not reached after 3.1 PY. No missing-data sensitivity analysis is supplied (A p.2498; R p.1), but the algorithm does not require one on this branch.

evidence: Not reached. A p.2499 documents adverse-event treatment cessation; that is not itself evidence that the specified TEAE outcome was unavailable.

evidence: Not reached. My previous answer inferred informative missingness from unequal discontinuation and mostly nausea/vomiting-related withdrawals (A p.2499), without first establishing missing target-event data.
guidance: Box 8: ask only if 3.3 is Y/PY/NI. Its reasons concern differences in missing outcome data, not automatically differences in treatment cessation.

evidence: A p.2498 describes TEAE reporting and laboratory monitoring, including amylase/lipase; R p.1 uses MedDRA 14.0 for the serious events. Diagnostic criteria and GI-specific adjudication are absent, but an unsuitable identification method is not demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for methods “unsuitable for the outcome”; §7.3 distinguishes an inappropriate identification system from incomplete reporting of methods.

evidence: Common blinded procedures and AE-reporting methods applied to both groups (A p.2498; R p.1). More nausea/vomiting creates a possible diagnostic-testing mechanism, but additional investigations or systematic differential ascertainment of these particular events are not documented.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 and §7.3 assess comparable methods and “systematic differences,” including diagnostic detection bias; passive collection alone does not establish such differences.

guidance: Box 10, 4.3: No when assessors are blinded; §1.1 supports PN where inference remains necessary.

evidence: Not reached after 4.3 PN. Clinical diagnoses involve judgment, but the masking evidence remains applicable.

guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” establishing finalization before unblinded data; Box 11, 5.1 requires sufficiently detailed prospective intentions.

evidence: R p.1 provides the specified serious-event terms and window; A p.2500 reports pancreatitis without its seriousness classification. Prospective intentions concerning eligible definitions/windows are unavailable. No results-based choice is demonstrated.

guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficient and multiple analyses are possible; Y/PY requires evidence of likely results-based selection.

evidence: M, p. 177: participants were “randomized in a 2:2:1:1 ratio,” stratified by HbA1c and BMI. The trial involved 75 centres, sponsor trial infrastructure and independent monitoring. The sequence-generation method is absent; randomness is inferred from this context, rather than established directly.
guidance: §4.3.1.1 and Box 4 permit PY despite missing technical details in an experienced, large-trial setting. This is an inference beyond the word “randomized.”

evidence: M, “Randomization and blinding,” p. 177, and C, “Design,” provide no central allocation procedure, allocation-list safeguards, or numbered-container procedure. Matching placebo and subsequent masking do not establish concealment before assignment.
guidance: §4.1.2: allocation concealment “should not be confused with blinding”; Box 4, 1.2, requires evidence concerning concealment until enrolment and assignment.

evidence: M, Table 1, p. 178: most characteristics are similar, although placebo participants were older—58.2 versus 55.4/54.6 years. Group sizes fit the intended ratio. Baseline data cover 482/484 randomized participants; the two omitted participants were untreated placebo recipients. No convincing pattern establishes failed randomization or material prognostic imbalance for these outcomes.
guidance: §4.3.3 requires considering the extent of exclusions when baseline data concern a subset. Box 4 and §4.3.3.2 require imbalance indicating a randomization problem, including sufficient prognostic importance to bias the effect; an isolated difference is insufficient by itself.

evidence: C, “Design—Masking info”: “PARTICIPANT; INVESTIGATOR.” M, p. 177: matching placebo and blinding to active/placebo, although injection volume was visible. The pooled comparison does not depend on concealing titration regimen. GI effects could have suggested assignment, but actual recognition or unblinding is not documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo can prevent awareness; answer Y/PY for side effects participants “knew to be specific” to an intervention. §5.1.3 cautions that recognizable effects or successful guesses do not themselves establish failed blinding.

evidence: Investigator masking is explicit in C, “Design—Masking info”; M, p. 177, confirms active/placebo blinding. Other carers’ masking is not individually described. Characteristic GI effects are a possible challenge, but there is no documented disclosure of treatment assignment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: assess awareness among carers and intervention providers, including effects they knew were intervention-specific. §1.1 permits PN when contextual evidence supports an inference.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. M, p. 180, reports toxicity-related discontinuation; C, “Secondary outcome 5,” specifies glucose thresholds for rescue therapy. Neither establishes trial-context deviations.
guidance: Box 6 branching. Its elaboration also excludes protocol-consistent changes, including “cessation … because of acute toxicity,” from problematic deviations.

evidence: No qualifying deviations identified through the applicable branch; see M, p. 180, and C, rescue-therapy specification.

evidence: The branch assessing outcome-affecting trial-context deviations was not reached.
guidance: Box 6: answer only if 2.4 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: M, p. 178: safety population comprised randomized participants exposed to at least one dose; two randomized placebo participants “did not receive any treatment and were excluded.” R, p. 1, confirms this safety-population rule. The safety analysis is therefore not fully assignment-based. No treatment-group switching is reported; subsequent missing follow-up is assessed separately in D3.
guidance: §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6: excluding eligible randomized participants because they did not receive treatment is inappropriate. An mITT analysis is acceptable here when exclusions concern missing outcomes, not merely failure to receive treatment.

evidence: Five participants were excluded in connection with nonreceipt/withdrawal before intervention, three versus two by group (Fig. 1, p. 940). In this small trial, exclusions involving surgery occurrence, emergency surgery, and treatment location could materially affect postoperative recovery estimates. Reported similarity of baseline characteristics is reassuring but does not establish that these exclusions were harmless.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks about potential substantial impact, not proven bias; there is “no precise rule,” and even fewer than 5% excluded can matter when exclusions relate strongly to prognosis.

evidence: Only 77/89 randomized participants have documented target-outcome data. Seven were explicitly lost to follow-up: 4/45 prehabilitation and 3/44 rehabilitation; another five were excluded before the analyzed cohort (Fig. 1, p. 940). “All patients completed the 6MWT” refers to the 77 analyzed participants, not all randomized participants.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: the population is “all randomized participants”; “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make no important difference. Even the seven explicit losses exceed the usual approximately 5% benchmark for continuous outcomes.

evidence: Multiple imputation and complete-case comparisons concerned secondary outcomes (pp. 940–941, 945). No analysis addresses the unobserved 8-week walking outcomes among those lost. Similar baseline characteristics among excluded participants do not demonstrate robustness to their missing outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires correction for missing-data bias or sensitivity analyses under plausible relationships between missingness and outcome. Section 6.1.7 says sensitivity analyses must address that relationship.

evidence: Reasons for the seven follow-up losses are not given (Fig. 1, p. 940). In a postoperative functional-capacity study, ability or willingness to attend walking assessments could depend on recovery and health status. The documents do not establish exclusively outcome-independent reasons.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if loss “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on its true value.

evidence: Losses were fairly similar between groups—4/45 versus 3/44—and excluded participants reportedly resembled those analyzed at baseline (p. 940). These argue against assuming marked differential loss. Nevertheless, reasons for loss and subsequent functional trajectories are absent, so whether dependence on walking capacity was likely, rather than merely possible, cannot be determined.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely,” using proportions, reasons, and trial circumstances. Section 1.1 permits NI when evidence cannot reasonably support either probable answer. Table 10 maps this NI response to High.

evidence: The article describes a validated 6MWT, measured distance in meters over six minutes, standardized instructions, and a baseline practice walk (p. 939). No evidence shows that the method was unsuitable or insensitive.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns unsuitable measurement, such as poor validity or inability to detect plausible effects; it does not question whether the chosen outcome is desirable.

evidence: Both groups underwent the same scheduled 6MWT assessments with standard motivational messages (p. 939). The registry describes a 20-m hallway, whereas the article describes 15 m, but neither source suggests different procedures between randomized groups.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable assessment as the same methods at comparable times. A between-document procedural discrepancy is not itself evidence of between-group measurement differences.

evidence: The external assessor was explicitly “blinded to group assignment” (p. 939; also registry masking). However, the test involved an unblinded participant choosing walking effort and rests while receiving minute-by-minute encouragement. I treat this as an interactive assessment in which a contributing participant knew allocation.
guidance: Section 7.3: for outcomes assessed through participant–collector interaction, assessors should be considered aware when either party is unblinded, “unless convincing evidence is available to the contrary.”

evidence: Instructions were to walk at a pace that would make participants tired; rests were permitted and motivational messages were given (p. 939). Knowledge of assignment could therefore influence effort during testing, even though distance recording was objective and the recorder was blinded.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 asks whether knowledge could influence assessment; section 7.3 requires consideration of the extent to which assessment can be influenced.

evidence: Both groups received an active program through eight postoperative weeks, and the assessor was blinded with standardized encouragement (pp. 938–939). These safeguards reduce the likelihood of differential testing effort or encouragement. The documents provide no specific evidence that knowledge actually influenced assessment.
guidance: Section 7.3 identifies an active comparator and an independent assessor as mitigating factors. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from influence judged likely.

Although first posted in May 2011, the supplied record was updated in September 2015; no historical version or dated SAP establishes when the exact analysis intentions were finalized.
guidance: Sections 8.3.1–8.3.2 and Box 11, 5.1 require sufficiently detailed intentions finalized before unblinded outcome data were available; a confirming “date-stamp” matters.

guidance: Section 8.3.2 permits comparison of methods, results, and different sources when prospective intentions are unavailable. Box 11, 5.2 restricts attention to measurements eligible for the specified assessment; multiplicity alone does not establish results-based selection.

guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires methods correcting missing-data bias or sensitivity analyses under plausible relationships between missingness and the outcome; §6.1.7 specifies that relationship must be addressed.

evidence: Reconsidering all available evidence, follow-up losses were similar—4/45 versus 3/44—and excluded participants reportedly had comparable baseline characteristics (p. 940). Other exclusions include changes in treatment location and withdrawal, alongside one emergency operation. This supports a cautious judgement that outcome-dependent loss was possible but not probably the predominant mechanism. The inference is limited: comparable proportions and baseline characteristics do not prove independence.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes missingness that could depend on the outcome from dependence judged likely. Section 1.1 reserves NI for circumstances where a reasonable probable answer cannot be made; here the reported proportions and characteristics support PN, although not N.

evidence: A validated 6MWT measured distance over six minutes, with standardized instructions and a baseline practice walk (p. 939). No unsuitable instrument or inability to detect plausible differences is identified.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns inappropriate measurement, such as poor validity or insufficient sensitivity.

evidence: Both groups underwent the same scheduled walking assessments and standard motivational messages (p. 939). The registry’s 20-m versus article’s 15-m hallway description is a discrepancy between documents, not evidence of different procedures between groups.

evidence: The test was conducted “by an assessor blinded to group assignment” (p. 939), corroborated by registry masking. guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded.” Section 7.1 distinguishes observer-measured outcomes from participant reports. The interaction caution in §7.3 was considered, but blinded recording of distance under standardized procedures supports N here.

evidence: R, Primary outcome 1: “Difference in waist circumference,” “Months 0-8.” A, p.3 specifies baseline-to-33-week WC change, and Table 2 reports it. evidence: A, p.5, Table 2 reports endpoint and change values, with age-group bootstrapping noted for endpoint values; p.4 describes bootstrapping more generally. guidance: Box 4, 1.2: concern applies where there is “reason to suspect” knowledge of the forthcoming allocation. §4.1.2 identifies “knowledge of the sequence of assignments” as a concealment failure. PN reflects an inference from the described procedure, not proof of deliberate manipulation.

evidence: Article, p.5, Table 1 includes only 145 intervention and 160 control completers; Figure 1, p.4 shows 272 and 276 randomized. Completers’ baseline WC was similar, and the isolated age difference does not establish randomization failure. Full-cohort baseline characteristics are unavailable.

evidence: Article, p.2: “non-blinded RCT”; Registry, Design → Masking: “NONE.” Counselling and app access were apparent to participants.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants were “aware of their assigned intervention.”

guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns awareness among “carers and people delivering the interventions.”

guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness can depend on true outcome when withdrawal relates to “participants’ health status.”

evidence: Registry states “Masking: NONE”; Article describes a non-blinded trial. Article p.3 separates measurement nurses from intervention nurses but does not establish measurement-nurse blinding. Authors’ code blinding is not assessor blinding.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 concerns the actual outcome assessors. §1.1 permits PY where a reasonable inference is available instead of requiring NI.

evidence: Article, p.3: nurses performed the physical measurements. WC is quantitative, but manual measurement allows some judgement in placement and application of the measuring instrument. Standardization reduces this discretion without eliminating it.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 includes “observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement.” §7.1 distinguishes these from outcomes such as automated test results that do not involve observer judgement.

guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes influence that “could have” occurred from influence that was “likely.” §7.3 identifies assessor independence and degree of judgement as relevant considerations.

evidence: Article, p.4 identifies an approved 2015 protocol, but its analysis specifications are not supplied. guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires prospective finalization of analysis intentions. §8.3.1 requires sufficient detail and a confirming “date-stamp”; a protocol citation alone cannot establish compliance.

evidence: Registry, Primary outcome 1: “Difference in waist circumference,” “Months 0-8.” Article p.3 specifies baseline-to-33-week change, reported in Table 2. guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N/PN when eligible reported measurements correspond to intended measurements and restricts consideration to measurements eligible for the assessment.

evidence: Article p. 5, Table 1: groups number 4731/4732; age 64.1/64.2 years, previous MI 47%/47%, heart failure 20%/20%, and eGFR 79.1/78.9. Smaller differences, including insulin use 60%/58%, do not show a pattern suggesting failed randomization.

guidance: Box 6, 2.4: applicable only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

guidance: Box 8, 3.2: evidence requires methods correcting bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions; §6.1.7 requires addressing the missingness–outcome relationship. A planned analysis is not a demonstrated result.

evidence: Article p. 4, Figure 1 reports consent withdrawals, loss to follow-up and physician-directed withdrawal. Protocol p. 53 censors lost participants at their last confirmed MACE status.

evidence: Evidence against reassurance includes greater incomplete assessment with placebo and more consent withdrawals (74 versus 43) and losses to follow-up (68 versus 51). However, the absolute incompleteness difference is about 0.9 percentage points, follow-up-time loss is small, and broad withdrawal categories occur in both groups (Article p. 4). No outcome-specific reason establishes likely dependence; importantly, the primary analysis does not censor at medication cessation (Protocol pp. 53, 55; Article p. 4). On balance, dependence is possible but not judged likely.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely…depended”; differing proportions/reasons are evidence to weigh. §§6.1.4–6.1.5 and §1.2.1 require contextual judgment about material bias, not automatic escalation for any numerical difference.

guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1, composite-outcome guidance requires considering influential components; their need for clinical judgment does not itself make measurement inappropriate.

guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable methods use the same methods/thresholds at comparable times; §7.3 targets systematic ascertainment differences. Incomplete follow-up itself is addressed in D3.

evidence: Article p. 3: independent clinical-events committee members “were unaware of the trial group assignments” and assessed all primary-outcome components. Site investigators were also masked.

guidance: Box 10, 4.5 applies only if 4.4 is Y/PY/NI.

guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires prespecification before unblinded outcome availability. §8.3.1 exempts confidential monitoring analyses and permits blinded refinements; Box 11 permits changes made before unblinded data. §1.1 supports PY for the timing inference.

SAP pp. 23–26 also plans supportive analyses whose results are not supplied, limiting verification of their reporting. Nevertheless, the target estimate was designated primary beforehand; there is no indication it was selected after comparing results. On-treatment/per-protocol analyses estimate a different effect from the requested assignment effect.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns selection “on the basis of the results” among eligible analyses. §8.1.2 restricts assessment to eligible analyses; the existence or non-reporting of supplementary analyses alone does not establish result-driven selection of this prespecified estimate.

evidence: Article p. 3 explicitly reports a “computer-generated randomisation code” using balanced permuted blocks. “Fixed” describes the sequestered schedule, not deterministic assignment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers,” warrants Y.

evidence: Article p. 3 reports a sequestered code and interactive voice/web allocation. Protocol p. 34, §5.2 specifies that personnel contact the IVRS after eligibility prerequisites are met; the system assigns treatment. SAP p. 14 identifies the PPD allocation system.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and §4.3.2, Table 2: independent remote/central allocation supports concealment. Block allocation is not itself evidence of foreknowledge.

evidence: Article p. 5, Table 1: nearly identical group sizes, age 64.1/64.2, previous MI 47%/47%, heart failure 20%/20%, and eGFR 79.1/78.9. Smaller differences, including insulin use 60%/58%, do not establish a problematic pattern.

guidance: Box 6, 2.4: ask only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

The relevant overlap is unreported. Extensive follow-up is reassuring, but does not establish that unobserved outcomes could make no important difference.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by potential impact, not a percentage threshold. §6.1.3.2 states there is “no sensible threshold.” §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing follow-up; §1.1 supports PN rather than NI because substantial information is available.

evidence: SAP p. 26 specifies a tipping-point analysis varying non-completer hazards, but its results are absent from the supplied reports. Article p. 4 reports ordinary Cox analysis. Neither the plan nor ordinary censoring establishes robustness to informative missingness.

evidence: Figure 1, Article p. 4 lists consent withdrawal, loss to follow-up and physician-directed withdrawal. These could relate to health status; the documents do not establish exclusively outcome-unrelated reasons. Protocol p. 53 censors lost participants at their last confirmed MACE status.

guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable methods. §7.1 requires considering influential composite components; clinical judgment does not itself make a measurement method inappropriate.

evidence: Article p. 3 describes common four-monthly visits, reporting events when they occurred, and common adjudication. Protocol p. 34 applies escalation procedures to both groups. No systematic difference in cardiovascular ascertainment is demonstrated.

evidence: M pp.126–127 describes participant blinding using matched placebos. evidence: P p.131: “all randomized patients” analysed “according to the randomized treatment arm.” M Table 3 and A Table S8 retain denominators 409 and 408. The per-protocol exclusions described in M concern the additional primary-outcome analysis, not these safety results.

evidence: Not reached because the target analyses preserve randomized groups.
