guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires missing outcomes to be incapable of importantly changing the effect. §6.1.3.2 relates materiality to event frequency; only six participants had reported events here.

evidence: Article pp. 3–4 provides available-data reporting without an adverse-event sensitivity analysis or correction for incomplete observation. Registry denominators do not establish robustness to unobserved events.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses showing robustness under plausible assumptions. Neither is reported for this result.

evidence: Article p. 3 attributes withdrawals to logistics and repeated missed visits; Figure 1 also includes “no longer interested” and “lost to follow-up.” These descriptions do not exclude health or tolerability influencing missing observations, even though no adverse-event discontinuations were reported (p. 4).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” permits dependence on the true outcome. The documented reasons do not establish that every missing observation was unrelated to adverse events.

evidence: Article p. 4 explicitly reports no other medication discontinuations due to adverse events. Figure 1 mainly identifies logistical or engagement reasons. The pregnant participant remained monitored (p. 3), leaving potentially incomplete follow-up in three nabilone versus two placebo participants, rather than equating all treatment discontinuations with missing outcomes. A connection to adverse events remains possible but is not probably present.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence and directs consideration of reasons and between-group differences. §6.1.4.2 supports evaluating actual reasons; §1.1 permits a reasoned PN.

evidence: Article p. 4 describes an “open-ended interview and a comprehensive review of clinical measurements” at each visit. Registry confirms repeated staff questioning and physician assessment. No evidence establishes poor validity or inability to detect relevant adverse events.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 targets unsuitable measurement, including poor validity or insensitivity. §7.3 particularly flags adverse-event outcomes without systems for identifying occurrence; an active system existed here.

evidence: Article pp. 2–4 describes a common visit schedule and safety assessment for both groups. Registry, Results: adverse events, also describes common ascertainment. No intervention-specific surveillance procedure is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 concerns systematic differences in methods, thresholds or opportunities for detection. Incomplete observations from withdrawal remain a D3 issue rather than independently proving differential measurement procedures.

evidence: Registry explicitly lists participants, care providers, investigators and outcome assessors as masked. Thus both participant symptom reporting and clinician evaluation described in Article p. 4 were probably masked. Neither source reports unblinding; common symptoms occurred in both arms.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 identifies the participant as assessor for participant-reported outcomes. §7.3 requires considering awareness of both participants and data collectors. The available evidence supports probable unawareness of both.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. Subjective symptoms in Article p. 4 would be susceptible to knowledge, but susceptibility alone does not establish awareness.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 is asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 is asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: Protocol p. 1 is dated April 14, 2017; p. 4 refers to the completed 2 mg pilot. Its analysis section concerns cannabis and mood outcomes (pp. 10–11). Article p. 3 names safety as the primary hypothesis, but does not establish prospective specification of this analysis. No earlier sufficiently detailed safety plan is supplied.
guidance: §8.3.1 requires a “date-stamp” demonstrating finalization before unblinded outcomes. Box 11, 5.1 requires sufficiently detailed intentions for comparison. A late document cannot establish prospective compliance, but does not prove noncompliance either.

evidence: Article p. 4 reports treatment-period event totals. Protocol p. 6 describes a checklist and side-effect burden questionnaire, but cannot establish the pilot’s intended eligible measurements. Registry reports a 14-week window and zero Phase 1 “other” affected participants, inconsistent with the article. The discrepancy is unresolved; results-based selection of the specified published result is not demonstrated.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 directs NI when intentions are insufficiently detailed and multiple measurements are possible. Y/PY requires likely selection “on the basis of the results.” §8.3.2 permits considering discrepancies without assuming their cause.

evidence: Article pp. 3–4 lacks a prospective safety-analysis specification covering aggregation, analysis population and missing observations. Protocol p. 10 mentions ITT and completer analyses but does not establish the earlier pilot’s safety-analysis intentions. Registry inconsistencies do not reveal which alternative analyses were performed or why this result was selected.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 directs NI when analysis intentions are unavailable or insufficient and multiple analyses are possible. Missing documentation alone does not establish results-based selection.

evidence: M, p.2489: patients were “randomly assigned by a web-based application” developed by MRCC, without blocking or stratification. The random-number generation method is not explicitly described, but an independently administered computerized random process is probable. S, p.53, planned centre stratification; this discrepancy does not establish non-random allocation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 and §4.3.1.1 permit PY in a “large trial run by an experienced clinical trials unit” despite incomplete sequence-generation details. §4.3.1: randomization may be valid whether stratified or unstratified.

evidence: S, p.53: allocation followed eligibility confirmation and written consent and was “independently conducted online via Interactive Web Response Service” by MRCC. M, p.2489, confirms use of that system.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Y for remote or central allocation controlled independently of enrolment personnel, including an “internet-based randomization service”.

evidence: M, Table 1, p.2490: randomized groups were 2710 versus 2728, with similar age, diabetes, previous MI, clinical presentation and procedural characteristics. Small laboratory and medication differences do not form a convincing pattern of compromised randomization; see also S, Table S1, p.19.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer N when observed imbalances are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 cautions against interpreting a few conventional statistically significant differences as failure.

evidence: M, p.2489: “Participants and study investigators were not masked to the assigned group.”
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants knew their assigned intervention.

evidence: M, p.2489, explicitly identifies investigators as unmasked; treating physicians managed study medication and additional visits.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among “carers or people delivering the interventions”.

evidence: M, p.2491: 35 patients used another antiplatelet regimen; temporary discontinuations were similar, 281 versus 272. S, pp.53–54, permitted short interruptions and specified treatment changes for new anticoagulation needs. Individual reasons for the 35 changes are absent, but the reported pattern gives no strong indication of trial-induced departures beyond ordinary clinical care or non-adherence.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused departures. N/PN applies to non-adherence consistent with what could occur outside the trial and protocol-consistent changes.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; no trial-context deviation was identified as probable.
guidance: Box 6: 2.4 applies only “If Y/PY to 2.3”.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is not applicable.
guidance: Box 6: 2.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4”.

evidence: M, p.2490: “All patients randomly assigned were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis.” Figure 1, p.2489, retains 2710 and 2728 in their assigned groups, including regimen changes. The 92 screening/randomization failures appear before the 5438 randomized participants. PP exclusions belong to the separately reported PP analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 accept ITT analyses; missing outcome data are assessed separately in D3. §1.3.1 prioritizes the full ITT result.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y.
guidance: Box 6: 2.7 applies only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6”.

evidence: M, Figure 1 and p.2491: composite ascertainment was complete for 5338/5438; 49 clopidogrel patients and 51 aspirin patients had incomplete follow-up. Although completeness was 98.2% and vital status was checked for everyone, 100 incomplete composite outcomes are not negligible against 359 observed events and a 55-event between-group difference.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires that missing outcomes could make “no important difference”. §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal percentage threshold; §6.1.5 counts early-censored follow-up as missing.

evidence: M, p.2490, censors incomplete event-free follow-up. S, pp.60–61, proposes comparisons of followed versus lost patients and multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis, but corresponding results are absent from the supplied reports. The reported PP analysis does not establish robustness to outcome-dependent missingness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses addressing plausible missingness mechanisms. §6.1.7: analyses must address the relationship between missingness and the outcome’s true value.

evidence: M, Figure 1: losses to follow-up were 41 versus 50, and consent withdrawals 8 versus 1. Reasons beyond these categories are absent, so health-related loss of nonfatal-event information remains possible despite complete vital-status checks.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: when withdrawal or loss “could be related to participants’ health status”, missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Total incomplete follow-up was almost identical: 49/2710 versus 51/2728. Withdrawal categories differ somewhat, but no reported reasons establish outcome-related withdrawal. Vital status was checked in everyone; the ITT plan continued follow-up after drug discontinuation (S, p.60). These features weigh against *likely* informative missingness, while leaving uncertainty about nonfatal events.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence, considering differences in proportions, reasons and censoring at treatment changes. §1.1 permits a reasoned PN rather than automatically using NI.

evidence: M, pp.2488–2489, describes standardized event definitions, source-record monitoring and independent adjudication. S, pp.13–16, defines MI, stroke, ACS readmission and BARC bleeding. These are suitable measurement methods for the specified composite.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable or invalid measurement methods; it does not assess whether the chosen outcome itself was sensible.

evidence: M, p.2489: both groups had scheduled 12- and 24-month visits with “active surveillance” at each visit. Definitions, monitoring and adjudication were shared. Additional visits were discretionary, but systematic differences in surveillance opportunities are not reported. The admission-decision issue is considered in 4.3–4.5.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 and §7.3 concern systematic differences in measurement methods, thresholds, timing or opportunities for detection. Open treatment assignment alone does not establish such differences.

evidence: M, p.2488: the adjudication committee was blinded and received records stripped of treatment references. However, M, p.2489, identifies investigators as unmasked. For ACS readmission, the clinicians making admission decisions are also relevant outcome assessors, even though subsequent adjudication was blinded.
guidance: §7.1, outcome type 4: for provider-decision outcomes, “the outcome assessor here is the care provider making the decision”. Type 5 requires assessment of influential composite components.

evidence: S, pp.14–15: ACS readmission could qualify through an episode of rest discomfort lasting at least five minutes, without mandatory biomarker or ECG confirmation. Knowledge of treatment could influence interpretation of symptoms and the decision to admit.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4: knowledge can influence “intervention provider decision outcomes” and outcomes involving judgement.

evidence: ACS readmission was the most frequent component: 66 versus 109 (M, Table 2); unstable angina accounted for 47 versus 79 (S, Table S4, p.23). Its symptom-based admission criterion and unblinded decision-makers make influence probable and potentially material. Blinded adjudication, two active comparators and objective components provide protection, but cannot undo an influenced admission decision. Component counts overlap, so they do not precisely partition the composite effect.
guidance: §7.1, type 4: provider-decision outcomes are “usually likely to be influenced” when providers are aware. Type 5 requires attention to component frequency and influence. Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible from likely influence; §7.3 identifies active comparators as mitigating evidence.

evidence: S, pp.57 and 60–62, specifies the composite, 24-month ITT analysis, unadjusted analysis and censoring. However, the supplied protocol/SAP has no verifiable finalization date or amendment history establishing precedence over unblinded data. It specifies Kaplan–Meier/log-rank analysis, whereas M, p.2490, reports Cox estimation. M, p.2489, says no interim analysis occurred, but that does not establish SAP timing.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available. §8.3.1 requires a confirming “date-stamp”; §8.3.2 expressly identifies undated plans as a limitation.

evidence: S, pp.44 and 57, identifies the same five-component primary endpoint at 24 months; S, pp.13–16, supplies its component definitions. M, pp.2489 and 2491, reports that endpoint and time point. Other composites are explicitly labelled post hoc and reported separately. There is no indication that the target replaced another intended measurement because of its results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N/PN when the reported outcome corresponds to intended measurements. §8.1.2 restricts the assessment to eligible measurements of the target outcome.

evidence: S, pp.60–62, specifies ITT and supportive PP analyses, Kaplan–Meier/log-rank methods and missing-data sensitivity analysis. M, p.2490, reports Cox analysis; PP results appear in S, Table S9, but the planned missing-data sensitivity results are absent. The available material does not establish the complete analysis choices underlying this HR or whether selection occurred. There is insufficient evidence for results-driven selection to answer Y/PY.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 allows NI when analysis intentions are insufficiently detailed to assess selection among eligible analyses. Y/PY requires evidence that reporting was likely selected “on the basis of the results”; discrepancies alone do not establish this (§8.3.2).

evidence: M, p.2489: patients were “randomly assigned by a web-based application” developed by MRCC. The underlying random-number generator is unspecified, but a random process is probable in this independently administered system.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1; §4.3.1.1 permits PY despite incomplete reporting in a “large trial run by an experienced clinical trials unit”.

evidence: S, p.53: after eligibility confirmation and consent, randomization was “independently conducted online via Interactive Web Response Service”. M, p.2489, confirms the MRCC system was used.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: independent central or remote allocation, including internet-based services, supports Y.

evidence: M, Table 1, p.2490: group sizes were 2710 versus 2728, with similar age, diabetes, previous MI, clinical presentation and procedural characteristics. The observed differences do not suggest manipulation or failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer N when differences are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 cautions against treating isolated baseline differences as evidence of failure.

evidence: M, p.2489: “Participants and study investigators were not masked to the assigned group.”
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants were aware of assignment.

evidence: M, p.2489, explicitly identifies investigators as unmasked; attending physicians managed treatment and additional visits.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among carers and intervention providers.

evidence: M, p.2491: 35 patients changed antiplatelet regimen; temporary discontinuations were similar, 281 versus 272. S, pp.53–54, permitted short interruptions and clinically necessary changes. Reasons for individual regimen changes are absent, but the reported pattern is consistent with ordinary clinical care or non-adherence, without evidence of trial-induced departures.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” trial context caused departures for Y/PY. Ordinary non-adherence and protocol-consistent changes support N/PN.

evidence: Not reached after 2.3=PN, based on the treatment-change evidence in M, p.2491, and S, pp.53–54.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3”.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is not applicable.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4”.

evidence: M, p.2490: “All patients randomly assigned were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis.” Figure 1 retains all 2710 and 2728 participants in their assigned groups; regimen changes were excluded only from the separate PP analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 accept ITT analysis; bias from missing outcome data belongs in D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y; the ITT denominators are confirmed in M, Figure 1.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.7 only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6”.

evidence: M, p.2491 and Figure 1: composite ascertainment was complete in 5338/5438; incomplete follow-up affected 49 clopidogrel and 51 aspirin participants. Although completeness was 98.2%, these 100 participants are not negligible relative to 152 versus 207 composite events. Complete vital-status checks do not recover nonfatal events.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference”. §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal percentage threshold; §6.1.5 treats early-censored follow-up as missing.

evidence: M, p.2490, uses censoring for incomplete follow-up. S, pp.60–61, plans missing-data sensitivity analyses, but their results are absent. Reporting an ITT analysis and censoring does not demonstrate robustness to informative loss.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires evidence from appropriate correction or sensitivity analyses. §6.1.7 requires analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: M, Figure 1: 41 versus 50 were lost to follow-up, and 8 versus 1 withdrew consent. The underlying reasons are not supplied, so health-related missingness of nonfatal outcomes remains possible.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness could depend on the outcome when withdrawal or loss “could be related to participants’ health status”.

evidence: Incomplete follow-up proportions were almost identical, 49/2710 versus 51/2728. Withdrawal categories differ somewhat, but no outcome-related reason is reported. Vital status was checked for everyone, and follow-up after treatment discontinuation was intended (S, p.60). Together these weigh against *likely* outcome-dependent missingness without excluding it.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence using proportions, reasons and censoring circumstances. §1.1 permits a supported PN, rather than requiring NI whenever details are incomplete.

evidence: M, pp.2488–2489, describes standardized definitions, source-record monitoring and independent adjudication. S, pp.13–16, provides definitions for the composite components. No unsuitable measurement instrument or method is identified.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for methods “unsuitable for the outcome”; it does not question whether the outcome choice was sensible.

evidence: M, p.2489: both groups had scheduled 12- and 24-month visits with “active surveillance”. Definitions and adjudication procedures were shared. Additional visits were discretionary, but systematic differences in surveillance are not demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 and §7.3 address differences in methods, thresholds, timing or opportunities for detection; open-label treatment alone does not establish such differences.

evidence: M, p.2488: adjudicators were blinded and received records stripped of treatment references. Nevertheless, the investigators were unmasked (p.2489), and clinicians making readmission decisions remain relevant assessors for that component.
guidance: §7.1, type 4: for provider-decision outcomes, the assessor is “the care provider making the decision”. Type 5 requires consideration of influential composite components.

evidence: S, pp.14–15: ACS readmission could qualify through rest discomfort lasting at least five minutes; biomarker or ECG confirmation was not mandatory for every qualifying event. Treatment knowledge could influence symptom interpretation and admission decisions.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 identifies judgement-based and “intervention provider decision outcomes” as susceptible to treatment knowledge.

evidence: Readmission was frequent—66 versus 109—and unstable angina accounted for 47 versus 79 (M, Table 2; S, Table S4). These counts establish potential importance, not biased decisions. Blinded independent adjudication, standardized qualifying criteria and comparison of two active treatments reduce the likelihood of material influence. My earlier PY gave insufficient weight to these protections and inferred likelihood too readily from susceptibility.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes “could have influenced” from “likely to influence”. Although §7.1, type 4 says unblinded decisions are “usually likely” to be influenced, §7.3 directs consideration of active comparators and independent assessment; §1.2.1 requires material bias.

evidence: S, pp.57 and 60–62, supplies detailed outcome and analysis intentions, but no verifiable finalization date or amendment history establishes that this version preceded unblinded outcome access. M, p.2489, reports no interim analysis; that does not establish when the supplied SAP was finalized.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available. §8.3.1 calls for a confirming “date-stamp”; §8.3.2 identifies undated SAPs as a limitation.

evidence: S, pp.44 and 57, specifies the same five-component primary endpoint at 24 months. M, pp.2489–2491, reports that endpoint; other composites are explicitly labelled post hoc and reported separately. No result-driven replacement of the target measurement is apparent.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N/PN when reported measurements correspond to intended measurements; §8.1.2 restricts attention to eligible measurements of the target.

evidence: S, pp.60–62, specifies an unadjusted ITT analysis using Kaplan–Meier/log-rank methods. Crucially, M, Figure 2A, p.2492, reports log-rank p=0.0033 alongside the target Cox HR and p=0.0035; PP results also appear in S, Table S9. Thus the planned primary analysis was not displaced by selective presentation of Cox results. The unreported missing-data sensitivity analysis leaves uncertainty, but does not make selection of this primary estimate probable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns selection “on the basis of the results”. §8.3.2 requires distinguishing unexplained analytical differences from results-driven selection; §1.1 permits a reasoned PN when information supports it.

evidence: Article p.981 and original protocol §VII.2 (Protocol bundle p.24) describe central web-based, stratified, blocked randomization, with block sizes varying from 4–8. They do not specify how the allocation order within blocks was generated. This leaves the random component insufficiently documented; it does not demonstrate a nonrandom sequence.
guidance: §4.3.1.1 specifically states that blocked allocation without an explicit random within-block order should “generally” receive NI.

evidence: Article p.981: “Randomization was coordinated centrally with the use of a Web-based system,” after consent. Original protocol §VII.2 explicitly specifies “concealed, stratified and blocked randomization” (bundle p.24). Variable block sizes provide additional protection against prediction.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2 accept “remote or centrally administered” allocation, including internet-based systems. Concealment concerns forthcoming allocation, not subsequent blinding (§4.1).

evidence: Article Table 1, p.985: allocation sizes were 136/137; gestational age 26.1/26.0 weeks; male sex 51.5%/51.1%; PDA diameter 2.1/2.1 mm. HELLP syndrome differed, 7/136 versus 1/137, but this isolated imbalance among numerous characteristics does not establish failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer N when differences are “compatible with chance.” §4.3.3.1 cautions that a small number of baseline differences should ordinarily be considered chance imbalances.

evidence: Participants were extremely premature newborn infants, enrolled at 24–72 hours after birth (Article p.981); they could not understand their assigned management. Parental awareness is considered under carers in 2.2.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns whether participants were aware, because awareness may change health-related behaviour. Open-label status does not establish awareness in newborns.

evidence: Article p.988: “Our trial was unblinded.” Protocol §VII.2 also explicitly states that a blinded study was not possible (bundle p.24). Clinicians and parents knew the assigned strategy.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether carers or intervention providers were “aware of the assigned intervention.”

evidence: Deviations occurred: one off-criteria rescue treatment, one unblinded echocardiogram with management consequences, and three omitted second ibuprofen courses; the latter reflected clinician requests in two cases and parental refusal in one (Supplement Table S9, p.16; Article Fig.1, p.983). Other interruptions followed clinical contraindications (Supplement Fig.S1, p.6). These changes are consistent with decisions that could occur outside a trial. Their motivations are not fully reported, but there is no strong evidence that trial participation itself prompted them. Protocol-permitted rescue treatment and treatment cessation for contraindications are not themselves problematic deviations.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that deviations arose because of the trial context; it permits PN for changes “consistent with what could occur outside the trial context.” §1.1 permits a reasoned probable response rather than automatic NI.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3 = PN; the documented deviations are described in Article Fig.1 and Supplement Table S9.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA. Differences in cointervention use reported in Article Table 3 do not independently activate this question.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4”; it concerns the qualifying trial-context deviations, not every treatment difference.

evidence: Article p.982 states that ITT included “all the patients who had undergone randomization.” Fig.1 and Table 2 retain all 136/137 infants in assigned groups. The eight exclusions applied to the separately reported per-protocol analysis, not this result.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 accepts ITT analyses; §5.3.1 requires analysis in randomized groups regardless of treatment received. The requested estimand is assignment, so noninferiority does not make this ITT analysis inappropriate.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 = Y. Article Fig.1 and Table 2 establish that the target ITT analysis retained the randomized groups.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.7 only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Article p.984: “data regarding the composite primary outcome were available for all 273 infants.” Six infants without indicated oxygen-reduction testing received clinical classification by the blinded committee (pp.982, 984). These are assessed outcomes, not statistically imputed outcomes. Death is a component of the composite; the smaller survivor denominators for BPD do not represent missing composite outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 asks whether outcome data were available for “all, or nearly all” randomized participants. §6.3(1) establishes low risk when complete outcome data are available.

evidence: Not reached: complete composite-outcome ascertainment is reported on Article p.984.
guidance: Box 8: answer 3.2 only “If N/PN/NI to 3.1.”

evidence: Not reached because 3.2 is NA; no missing composite outcomes are reported (Article p.984).
guidance: Box 8: answer 3.3 only “If N/PN to 3.2.”

evidence: Not reached because 3.3 is NA; no missing composite outcomes are reported (Article p.984).
guidance: Box 8: answer 3.4 only “If Y/PY/NI to 3.3.”

evidence: Article p.982 and Supplement Table S2, p.8 specify all-cause death, Bell stage ≥IIa NEC, and standard BPD criteria at 36 weeks. Supplement Methods, p.4 provide explicit oxygen-reduction procedures and saturation thresholds. There is no evidence that these methods were unsuitable for measuring the specified outcome.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns unsuitable measurement methods, not whether the outcome choice is sensible; for prespecified outcomes the answer will usually be “No” or “Probably no.”

evidence: The same component definitions, thresholds and 36-week assessment applied to both groups (Article p.982; Supplement Methods p.4 and Table S2 p.8). Six omitted oxygen tests were handled by blinded expert review. Their distribution between groups is not stated, but no systematic difference in composite-outcome ascertainment is reported. Different PDA echocardiography schedules concerned management and ductal closure, rather than different measurement schedules for this composite.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable measurement as the “same measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times; §7.3 distinguishes systematic ascertainment differences from assessor awareness.

evidence: The trial was unblinded, and general blinding of routine clinical outcome assessors is not reported (Article p.988). Blinding is explicitly documented only for the committee classifying the six infants without indicated oxygen testing (p.982). Thus awareness is probable for routine assessments, despite that protected subset.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 asks whether outcome assessors knew intervention status. §7.1 identifies the intervention provider as assessor when outcomes arise from clinical examinations or decisions.

evidence: NEC staging involves clinical interpretation, and BPD classification partly depends on respiratory-support status. BPD was the most frequent component—39 versus 57 infants—and largely drove the composite difference (Article Table 2 and discussion, p.986). Objective death ascertainment therefore does not remove the potential influence on the composite.
guidance: §7.1, outcome types 3–5: observer judgements and provider decisions can be influenced; composite assessments must consider the “frequency or contribution” of components and the “most influential components.”

evidence: Influence remains possible, but standardized physiological testing and explicit thresholds constrain discretion (Supplement Methods p.4). The six cases needing substitute clinical judgement were reviewed by experts “unaware of treatment assignments” (Article p.988). The documents do not show group-dependent application of diagnostic criteria or provide a strong reason to conclude that knowledge probably influenced classification.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes assessment that could be influenced from assessment likely to be influenced. Standardization and blinded adjudication support the former, yielding Some concerns rather than High.

evidence: SAP states it was “written and submitted without knowledge of the data” (bundle p.97); analyses would start after database checks/lock and SAP submission (p.102). It prespecifies ITT, crude absolute risk difference and a one-sided 95% CI (pp.102–104), matching Article Table 2. Although received on 13 April 2021, after recruitment ended, its explicit account establishes prospective analysis intentions. Original protocol and amendments are also supplied (bundle pp.3, 81).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require finalization before unblinded outcome data were available for analysis—not necessarily before recruitment ended. The stated timing and matching analysis satisfy this requirement.

evidence: The primary composite, Bell threshold and 36-week time point match the SAP (bundle pp.97–98). The alternative BPD classification was specified as a sensitivity analysis (p.104) and is also reported (Supplement Table S12, p.20). Thus the existence of another definition does not indicate result-based selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 permits N/PN when reported results correspond to intended measurements. Multiple measurements alone are insufficient: selection must be “on the basis of the results.”

evidence: The planned unadjusted ITT risk-difference analysis is reported alongside per-protocol results (Article Table 2). Supplement Table S12 also reports alternative-classification and adjusted analyses. Some adjustment implementation differs from the SAP—for example, logistic rather than planned Poisson adjustment for gestational age—but these analyses are disclosed and do not replace the prespecified target ITT result (SAP bundle p.98; Supplement Methods p.4 and Table S12).
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns selection among eligible analyses based on their results. §8.1.2 restricts assessment to the specific eligible result; disclosed supplementary analyses do not themselves establish selective reporting of the prespecified primary analysis.

evidence: Central web-based allocation, stratification and variable blocks of 4–8 are described, but the method generating the within-block allocation order is not specified (Article p.981; Protocol p.24, §VII.2). Central administration alone does not prove random sequence generation.
guidance: §4.3.1.1: blocked allocation without an explicit random component should “generally” receive NI. This reporting gap does not establish a nonrandom sequence.

evidence: Allocation was centrally coordinated through a web-based system after consent (Article p.981). Protocol p.24 explicitly specifies “concealed, stratified and blocked randomization.” No evidence shows recruiters could access forthcoming assignments.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2 accept central/internet-based allocation. §4.1 distinguishes allocation concealment from subsequent blinding.

evidence: Article Table 1, p.985 shows similar gestational ages, sex distributions, respiratory support and PDA diameters. HELLP syndrome was imbalanced, 7 versus 1, but this isolated difference among numerous characteristics does not demonstrate failed randomization. Group sizes were 136/137.

evidence: Reported tests match the statistical-methods description and table footnotes (p. 4; Tables 2–4). No prospective specification resolves choices among final values, changes, adjusted analyses or missing-data strategies. There is no affirmative evidence of results-based selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when intentions are unavailable and multiple analyses are possible; Y/PY requires evidence that selection depended on the results.

evidence: A, p.1879, Randomisation and masking: “computer-generated 1:1 randomisation,” generated by a statistician uninvolved in eligibility determination or outcome assessment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when a random component was used, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: A, p.1879: “opaque sealed envelopes.” This supports concealment, but sequential numbering, controlled opening after irrevocable enrolment, and custody are not described. The independent statistician generated the sequence; independent administration of allocation is not established. There is also no evidence of actual foreknowledge.
guidance: §4.3.2, Table 2: minimal envelope criteria are “sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes.” Box 4 permits judgement with incomplete reporting; §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient information to support either probable answer. The available description does not establish the missing safeguards.

evidence: A, Table 1, pp.1883–1884, and S, Table 1, p.6, show broadly comparable measured characteristics, including age and severity scores. However, these describe only 49 analysed participants; Fig.2, p.1882, shows 50 randomized. Baseline information for the excluded control participant is absent.
guidance: §4.3.3: assessment “should be based on data for all randomized participants.” Box 4, 1.3 specifically permits NI when only baseline characteristics of analysed participants are reported. Observed differences do not independently establish a randomization problem.

evidence: A, pp.1879–1880 and Fig.1: both groups had nasal cannulae, concealed equipment and matched equipment noise, but the stated blinding concerned the observer. Participant awareness was not reported; severe hypoxaemia and later anaesthesia do not establish unawareness throughout preoxygenation. R, Design, lists masking as “NONE.”
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns participants’ actual awareness. §1.1: NI applies when neither probable answer is sufficiently supported; §5.1.3 cautions that blinding descriptions do not necessarily identify who was blinded.

evidence: A, p.1885: “the operator could not be blinded, given the flow of the HFNC.”
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 asks whether carers or people delivering the intervention were aware; awareness of the intubating operator is sufficient.

evidence: S, p.3: “The unit protocols … were followed for each intubation procedure,” including induction, rescue ventilation, protective ventilation and vasopressors. A, p.1881, identifies two eligibility violations, retained in the target analysis, but does not link these to trial-induced departures. No crossover or preferential non-protocol care is described. These positive procedural details support probably no trial-context deviations, despite incomplete reporting of subsequent ICU care.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that the trial context caused non-protocol intervention changes. Protocol-consistent rescue treatment warrants N/PN. §5.1.2.1 restricts this assessment to deviations arising because of the trial context.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; the documented procedures are described in S, p.3.

evidence: Not reached; no qualifying trial-context deviation was identified in 2.3.

evidence: A, p.1881 and Fig.2: one randomized control patient was excluded because procedural SpO₂ could not be recorded owing to peripheral vasoconstriction. Table 2 consequently uses 25 versus 24 participants. Missing SpO₂ is not a valid reason to exclude an otherwise eligible participant from mortality analysis; mortality missingness is not stated. The two intervention-group eligibility violations remained in this target analysis and were removed only from the separate per-protocol analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: “Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.” The exception for excluding missing outcome data concerns the outcome being assessed (§5.3.1). An “ITT” label does not itself establish appropriate analysis (§1.3.1).

evidence: A, Fig.2 and Table 2: one control participant was excluded, against 17 observed deaths. Restoring that participant would produce control mortality of either 9/25 or 10/25. The mortality risk difference would therefore be −4 or −8 percentage points, compared with the reported −5.5 points. Although vasoconstriction could indicate poorer prognosis, this single exclusion probably lacks substantial impact on this result.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 assesses whether excluded numbers could have a “substantial impact”; there is “no precise rule,” and outcome frequency and prognostic selection matter. This judgement uses outcome-specific bounds, not a percentage threshold.

evidence: A, Table 2, provides day-28 status for 49/50 randomized patients, with no additional mortality-data loss or imputation reported. The excluded control patient’s mortality-data availability is unclear. Even treating that outcome as unavailable, only one status is uncertain against 17 observed deaths; the possible effect bounds are given under 2.7.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” depends on potential impact; for binary outcomes, when observed events greatly exceed missing participants, bias is necessarily small. §6.1 distinguishes missing outcomes from deliberate analytical exclusions.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=PY; no missing-mortality sensitivity analysis is reported in A or S.
guidance: Box 8: answer 3.2 only “If N/PN/NI to 3.1.”

guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1 identifies all-cause mortality as an observer-reported outcome “not involving judgement.”

evidence: A, Table 2, uses the same day-28 endpoint for both groups; S, p.4 and Fig.1, p.10, describes a common follow-up schedule. Detailed tracing procedures are absent, but nothing suggests different ascertainment methods or time points between groups.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable methods use the same methods and thresholds “at comparable time points.” §7.3 notes that methods are likely comparable in most randomized trials.

These specific descriptions support assessor blinding despite R’s generic “NONE” masking field and the acknowledged unblinded operator.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded.” §7.3 distinguishes assessor blinding from participant/personnel blinding.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=N. Independently, the target is day-28 vital status rather than a subjective clinical judgement.

evidence: A, pp.1880–1881, says a predefined analysis plan was published, but that document is not supplied. guidance: Box 11, 5.1: finalization must “precede availability of unblinded outcome data.” §8.3.1 requires attention to date stamps; §8.3.2 recognizes insufficient detail and uncertain timing. A later available record does not prove either prospective specification or a results-driven change.

evidence: R, Description—Data collection and Outcomes; A, p.1879; and S, p.4/Fig.1 consistently identify mortality at day 28. A, Table 2, reports its exact survival complement. guidance: Box 11, 5.2 allows N/PN where reported results correspond to intended measurements and restricts attention to measurements eligible for this assessment. §8.1.2 requires selection based on the results; survival/death coding at the same time point does not itself establish such selection.

evidence: R specifies chi-square/Fisher tests for categorical outcomes, consistent with A, p.1880. Both the designated ITT result (A, Table 2) and per-protocol result (S, Table 3, p.9) are reported, which argues against suppression of one of these analyses. Nevertheless, the available intentions do not sufficiently specify the mortality analysis population or handling of exclusions, and the full SAP is absent.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3: answer NI when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and multiple analyses are possible. Reporting both populations argues against Y/PY but does not establish that all intended eligible analyses were reported.

evidence: A, p.1879: “computer-generated 1:1 randomisation,” generated by a statistician uninvolved in eligibility determination or outcome assessment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers,” warrants Y.

evidence: A, p.1879 explicitly reports “opaque sealed envelopes” containing allocation cards, alongside independently generated randomization. Sequential numbering and opening safeguards remain undocumented. On reconsideration, these positive safeguards support probable concealment; my earlier answer treated incomplete reporting too much like absence of a usable concealment method. This does not establish every safeguard or independent administration.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 acknowledges that full envelope details are “rarely provided” and permits judgement to justify PY. §4.1.2 states that incomplete reporting does not necessarily indicate inappropriate methods. Table 2’s fuller criteria prevent an unequivocal Y here but do not preclude the explicitly permitted PY judgement.

evidence: A, Table 1, pp.1883–1884, shows broadly similar measured characteristics, but covers 49 analysed participants; Fig.2, p.1882, shows 50 randomized. Baseline data for the excluded control participant are unavailable. The observed differences do not establish a randomization failure.
guidance: §4.3.3 calls for baseline data on all randomized participants. Box 4, 1.3 gives baseline reporting restricted to analysed participants as an example supporting NI. This uncertainty does not imply problematic imbalance.

evidence: A, pp.1879–1880/Fig.1 describes sham cannula placement, hidden equipment and matched noise, but identifies the observer as blinded. Participant awareness is not established. Severe hypoxaemia and subsequent anaesthesia do not establish unawareness throughout preoxygenation. R, Design, lists masking as “NONE.”
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 concerns participant awareness specifically. §1.1 supports NI when neither probable answer is sufficiently justified; §5.1.3 warns against inferring who was blinded from general descriptions.

evidence: A, p.1885: “the operator could not be blinded, given the flow of the HFNC.”
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 includes “people delivering the interventions”; the operator’s awareness suffices even if other personnel were blinded.

evidence: S, p.3: “The unit protocols … were followed for each intubation procedure,” with specified induction, rescue ventilation, sedation and haemodynamic management. No trial-induced crossover or preferential non-protocol treatment is documented. The two eligibility violations described in A, p.1881, are not shown to have arisen because of the trial context.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that the trial context caused non-protocol changes before answering Y/PY. Protocol-consistent rescue treatment warrants N/PN. §5.1.2.1 limits this domain’s deviation component to trial-context departures.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; relevant procedural safeguards are in S, p.3.
guidance: Box 6: answer only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: A, p.1881/Fig.2: one randomized control patient was excluded because procedural SpO₂ could not be recorded owing to vasoconstriction. Table 2 therefore contains 25 versus 24 patients. guidance: Box 6, 2.6 considers post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate. §5.3.1 accepts exclusion for missing outcome data, but the documented missing measurement here is SpO₂, not the assessed mortality endpoint. The ITT label alone is insufficient (§1.3.1).

evidence: A, Fig.2/Table 2: only one control participant was excluded. Including that participant would yield control mortality of either 9/25 or 10/25. The intervention-minus-control risk difference would be −4 or −8 percentage points instead of −5.5. Vasoconstriction might indicate adverse prognosis, but even the two possible outcomes suggest limited rather than substantial impact.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 asks about “substantial impact,” considering numbers, outcome frequency and prognostic selection; there is no fixed percentage rule. This answer uses outcome-specific bounds.

evidence: A, Table 2 accounts for day-28 status in 49/50 randomized participants, without reported mortality imputation or further losses. The excluded control patient’s mortality-data availability is unclear. Even counting it as missing, there is one uncertain outcome against 17 observed deaths, with the limited bounds described above.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by potential impact, not a universal threshold; many more events than missing participants support small bias. §6.1 distinguishes missing outcome data from analytical exclusions.

evidence: Not reached because 3.1=PY. A, pp.1880–1881 and Table 2 do not report a mortality-specific missing-data sensitivity analysis.

guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1 identifies all-cause mortality as an observer-reported outcome not involving judgement.

evidence: A, p.1879 reports a blinded data-collecting observer; p.1885 describes an independent assessor unaware of allocation. S, p.3 states that case-report-form collectors were blinded. These specific descriptions outweigh R’s nonspecific “NONE” field for assessing outcome-collector blinding.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded.” §7.3 distinguishes assessor blinding from personnel blinding.

guidance: Box 10: answer only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.” Its elaboration states that knowledge is unlikely to influence all-cause mortality assessment.

evidence: A, pp.1880–1881 says a predefined analysis plan was published. However, R, reference 28, dates the cited protocol publication to 12 August 2016, after trial completion on 17 March 2016. R’s available record was updated in April 2017; no historical version or supplied full SAP establishes when the relevant analysis intentions were finalized. These dates do not prove that planning itself occurred late.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data became available. §8.3.1 requires attention to date stamps and amendments. A later publication neither verifies timely finalization nor establishes retrospective planning, supporting NI.

evidence: R, Description—Data collection/Outcomes; A, p.1879; and S, p.4/Fig.1 consistently identify day-28 mortality. Table 2 supplies its survival complement. “ICU mortality” in the abstract is less precise, but no competing eligible mortality time point or definition is shown to have displaced the requested result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 permits N/PN when reported measurements correspond to intended measurements and restricts assessment to eligible measurements. §8.1.2 requires selection based on results, not merely different wording or complementary event coding.

evidence: R specifies categorical-data tests consistent with A, p.1880. Both the designated ITT mortality result (A, Table 2) and per-protocol result (S, Table 3, p.9) are available, arguing against selective suppression of either. Nevertheless, the supplied intentions do not sufficiently specify the mortality analysis population or exclusion handling, and the full SAP is unavailable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 specifies NI when analysis intentions are insufficiently detailed and multiple analyses are possible. Reporting both analyses argues against Y/PY, but does not establish that every intended eligible analysis was reported.

evidence: “A randomisation schedule was created by an independent person”; allocation used “blocks of nine” (p. 833, Randomisation). Neither the generation method nor random ordering within blocks is described. Independent preparation supports credibility but does not establish a random component.
guidance: §4.3.1.1: blocked allocation without an “explicit statement” of random ordering should generally receive “No information.”

evidence: Centres received “sealed, serially numbered opaque envelopes” (p. 833, Randomisation). These support concealment. Sequential opening after irreversible enrolment and tamper-proof seals are not described. Fixed blocks of nine were used, but there is no evidence recruiters knew block boundaries or anticipated assignments.
guidance: Table 2 lists sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes as minimum criteria. Box 4, 1.2 permits “Probably yes” when operational details are incompletely reported; §4.3.2 identifies prediction when recruiters know block boundaries.

evidence: Table 2 (p. 835) includes all 100 participants per arm. Baseline ALT medians were 17.1, 19.1 and 17 IU/l; age, weight, sex and hepatitis status show no conspicuous imbalance suggesting failed randomization. Equal group sizes match the blocked allocation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when observed imbalances are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 excludes ordinary chance imbalance from bias.

evidence: “No attempt was made to conceal the treatment regimen after randomisation from patients” (p. 833, Randomisation).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 assesses whether participants were “aware of their assigned intervention.”

evidence: The same statement explicitly includes “researchers or health care staff” (p. 833). Laboratory and independent clinical assessor blinding does not establish blinding of treatment providers.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 concerns “carers and people delivering the interventions,” separately from outcome assessors.

evidence: Treatment ingestion was supervised (pp. 833–834). One R15 patient interrupted treatment for jaundice/hypersensitivity and subsequently restarted standard treatment; other adverse events generally did not interrupt treatment (p. 835). These are clinically motivated changes. No evidence identifies non-protocol treatment changes caused by trial participation or knowledge of allocation.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol deviations. It specifies N/PN for cessation because of “acute toxicity.” Open-label status alone is insufficient.

evidence: Although the methods define safety analysis as patients receiving “at least one dose” (p. 834), the CONSORT figure shows 100 randomized and 100 in the toxicity population in each arm (p. 835). The target result retains those denominators and allocated groups (p. 834). Thus, the stated restriction produced no demonstrated exclusion. Efficacy exclusions concern another outcome.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 requires analysis in randomized groups without inappropriate exclusions. §5.3.1 assigns missing outcome observations separately to D3.

evidence: Question not reached because the actual safety analysis includes all randomized participants in their allocated groups (pp. 834–835).

evidence: Only 1719/1800 scheduled ALT results were available (p. 834). Table 3 (p. 836) reports 15/600, 38/600 and 28/600 missing tests in R10, R15 and R20. These are test counts, not participant counts. Despite 95.5% test availability and complete analysis denominators, complete ascertainment of this rare, potentially transient event cannot be assumed: only seven events were observed, and six normalized by the next visit (p. 835).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by whether missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §6.1.3.2 states there is “no sensible threshold”; the binary event frequency matters.

evidence: The Analysis and Safety sections and Table 3 provide no missing-data correction or sensitivity analysis demonstrating robustness of the ALT result (pp. 834–836). Checking case-report forms for missing entries (p. 834) did not eliminate the reported missing tests.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires analysis correcting bias or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions.” Inclusion in the denominator is not such evidence.

evidence: Reasons and timing for the missing ALT tests are not supplied (Table 3, p. 836). Health-related interruption of observation is plausible: an R15 participant withdrew with cancer and an R20 participant died at week 12 (p. 835). These events do not prove ALT-dependent missingness, but an exclusively outcome-independent explanation cannot be established.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Missing-test frequencies differ across arms (Table 3), supporting concern. However, the number of affected participants, visit-specific distribution and reasons are absent. The known serious events do not establish that missing ALT values were likely abnormal. The statement that centres did not differ in losses to follow-up (p. 837) does not resolve missing ALT observations by randomized arm.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence and considers differing missingness and reasons. §1.1 permits NI when insufficient information supports neither PY nor PN; Table 10 routes NI here to High.

evidence: ALT was measured serially and graded using DAIDS criteria and each laboratory’s normal range (p. 834). Table 3 defines grade 3 as >5–10×ULN and grade 4 as >10×ULN (p. 836). No evidence indicates an unsuitable assay or grading method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” not whether the chosen outcome adequately represents a broader outcome domain.

evidence: All groups had scheduled ALT measurements at weeks 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16 (p. 833), using the same grading framework. Extra visits for side effects were allowed, but differential testing by allocation is not documented. Missing scheduled observations are assessed in D3.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable ascertainment as the same methods and thresholds at “comparable time points”; §7.3 targets systematic group differences.

evidence: “The laboratory staff” were “blinded to the regimen” (p. 833, Randomisation). They are the relevant assessors for this laboratory ALT result; the independent clinical assessor was also blinded.

guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization to “precede availability of unblinded outcome data”; §8.3.1 requires sufficient detail and a confirming date-stamp.
