guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” deviations arose because of trial context; protocol-consistent toxicity management and deviations compatible with usual circumstances support N/PN.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN. The reported changes and implementation failures are considered in the preceding row.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: applicable only if 2.3=Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is not applicable.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: applicable only if 2.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: All 669 patients in the specified endocrine-pretreated randomization strata were analyzed as assigned, including five who received no allocated intervention (A Fig.1, p.2876; S §6.1.1, p.11). The 44 endocrine-naïve patients belonged to a separate baseline stratum, excluded from this primary population by amendment (b); this preserved the randomized comparison within the target population (B §5.2, pp.21–22). The result is not a treatment-adherent subset analysis.
guidance: §1.1 of the introduction makes assessment result-specific; §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 require analysis in randomized groups regardless of treatment receipt. Missing outcome data are assessed separately in D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: applicable only if 2.6=N/PN/NI.

evidence: Fig.1 reports only 6/446 and 4/223 lost to follow-up, supporting good retention. However, arm-specific counts for missing baseline/postbaseline scans, consent withdrawal and censoring after missed assessments are absent. These are explicit censoring categories (S Table JPBL.6.1, p.15). The 379 events and inclusion of all 669 patients do not establish nearly complete PFS observation (A pp.2876, 2879).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make no important difference. §6.1.5: censored participants may have missing outcomes despite inclusion in analyses. Administrative censoring itself is not treated as missingness.

evidence: Reported sensitivity analyses used central review and the later starting-dose cohort (A pp.2879–2880). Neither tests plausible outcome-dependent missingness. Additional analyses were planned (S §6.7.5, pp.20–21), but the supplied documents do not report a missing-data robustness analysis that establishes absence of bias.
guidance: §6.1.7 and Box 8, 3.2: sensitivity analyses must address “the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value”; planning an analysis is insufficient.

evidence: Withdrawal, loss to follow-up and missed imaging could relate to health or progression. The primary rules censor progression/death following at least two missed scheduled assessments at the last adequate assessment (S Table JPBL.6.1, p.15).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal or loss could relate to health status, missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: On balance, outcome-dependent missingness is possible but not shown likely: reported loss was small and similar, 1.3% versus 1.8% (A Fig.1); imaging was to continue after treatment cessation, including in untreated randomized patients (P §10.1.2, p.45); primary PFS rules did not automatically censor treatment cessation or subsequent therapy (S pp.15, 20). Reasons and counts for other premature censoring remain unavailable. PN is an inference from these safeguards and observed retention, not proof that censoring was non-informative.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence. §6.1.5 specifically identifies stopping-treatment censoring as a concern; that mechanism was not built into this primary analysis. §1.1 permits a supported PN rather than automatic NI.

evidence: PFS used investigator-assessed RECIST 1.1 progression or death, with CT/MRI and explicit criteria for nonmeasurable bone-only disease (A pp.2877–2878; P §10.1.3, p.45). These are suitable measurement methods for the specified outcome.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods, not whether the chosen outcome is a desirable surrogate.

evidence: Both groups had the same imaging schedule—every eight weeks in year one, every twelve weeks thereafter—and the same progression criteria (A p.2877). Follow-up imaging continued after cessation (P §10.1.2). Actual scan-timing comparisons are not reported, but there is no evidence of systematic arm-specific ascertainment.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds “at comparable time points”; §1.1 permits a reasoned PN.

evidence: The assessors were investigators, formally blinded, but probably aware for some patients through recognizable toxicities (A Table 3; P §§8.2, 9.5.3). The protocol expressly acknowledges potential unblinding of “site personnel performing assessments.” The extent of actual awareness is not reported.
guidance: §7.3 requires assessment of whether blinding was successfully implemented. Box 10, 4.3 concerns the actual outcome assessor; §1.1 permits inference using PY.

evidence: Investigator interpretation of imaging, new lesions and “unequivocal progression” involves judgement (P §10.1.3, p.45). Knowledge of allocation could therefore influence the progression component, even though death is objective.
guidance: §7.1, outcome types 3 and 5: observer-reported outcomes involving judgement can be influenced; composites require consideration of their influential components. Box 10, 4.4 applies that rule.

evidence: RECIST criteria and scheduled imaging limit discretion. The blinded central assessment also favored abemaciclib, HR 0.460 (95% CI 0.363–0.584), compared with investigator HR 0.553 (A pp.2879–2880, Fig.2). This supports—but does not prove—the absence of important influence on investigator assessment. No documented pattern of treatment-aware adjudication is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from likely influence; “could have influenced … but there is no reason to believe that it did” supports Some concerns rather than High.

evidence: S was approved July 8, 2016 and explicitly states finalization before sponsor unblinding and the first efficacy interim analysis (§3, p.7). It specifies investigator RECIST PFS, the endocrine-pretreated population, stratified log-rank/Cox analyses, Kaplan–Meier medians and final analysis near 378 events (§§6.1.1, 6.7.2, pp.11, 15–16). The reported result used 379 events at the planned final analysis (A pp.2878–2879).
guidance: §8.3.1 and Box 11, 5.1: analysis intentions must precede unblinded outcome availability; changes made before that availability do not themselves raise concerns.

evidence: Investigator-assessed PFS was explicitly primary before unblinding; central-review PFS was planned as supportive and was also reported (S pp.15, 21; A Fig.2). The amended final event target was documented prospectively (P §5.4, pp.22–23). There is no indication the investigator measurement or cutoff was chosen because its result was more favorable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results,” not merely the existence of multiple measurements. §§8.3.1–8.3.2 require consideration of amendment timing and explanations.

evidence: The reported primary analysis matches the specified population, stratification and effect-estimation methods (S pp.11, 14–16; A pp.2878–2879). Several planned sensitivity analyses are not reported, so complete reporting cannot be confirmed. Nevertheless, the target primary analysis was explicitly identified in advance; no evidence indicates substitution of a more favorable analysis. Reporting two-sided P values at .05 rather than one-sided values at .025 does not establish selection of a different HR.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence that a result was selected because of its findings. §8.3.2 allows reasoned assessment of discrepancies; §1.1 permits PN where sufficient evidence supports it despite incomplete reporting.

evidence: Assignment used a “computer-generated random sequence using the IWRS” (P §9.3, p.35; S §7, p.30). No contrary sequence-generation evidence was identified.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 explicitly accepts “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: Eligible participants were assigned centrally through IWRS; sites confirmed assigned medication packages through the system. Treatment codes were protected in the database (P §9.3, p.35; S §7, p.30).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2 accept remote, centrally administered allocation that prevents recruiting personnel knowing forthcoming assignments.

evidence: The 446:223 allocation matches 2:1. Primary endocrine resistance, visceral disease and ECOG status were similar. Differences such as median age 59 versus 62 do not establish failed randomization (A Table 1, p.2877).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.”

evidence: Participants were explicitly blinded (P §8.2, p.33). Diarrhea differed substantially between arms (A Table 3), but the documents do not establish that participants recognized their allocation. The protocol says unblinding “may occur,” describing a possibility rather than an observed breach (P §9.5.3, p.41). My previous PY overstated that evidence.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 requires toxicities participants “knew to be specific” for the toxicity-based Y/PY response. §5.1.3 cautions that treatment guesses can reflect adverse effects without demonstrating failed blinding.

evidence: Investigational sites were explicitly blinded, access to assignments restricted, and unblinded analyses separated from routine conduct (P §§8.2, 9.5; S §7, p.30). Toxicities could provide clues, but no actual pattern of personnel awareness is reported. A general protocol warning does not establish probable awareness.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 applies the recognizable, intervention-specific toxicity condition to personnel. §1.1 permits PN when the reported safeguards support an inference despite incomplete information.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are both PN. Relevant underlying evidence remains that toxicity-related adjustments were permitted and switching prohibited (A p.2877).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 is reached only if either 2.1 or 2.2=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached: 2.3 is NA under the revised blinding responses.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 applies only if 2.3=Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached: 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 applies only if 2.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: All 669 participants in the target endocrine-pretreated randomization strata were analyzed as assigned, including five untreated participants (A Fig.1; S §6.1.1, p.11). The 44 endocrine-naïve participants were a separate baseline randomization stratum removed from the primary population prospectively; the target comparison preserved randomization (B §5.2, pp.21–22).
guidance: §§1 and 2.1 make assessment specific to the result and its population. §5.3.1 and Box 6, 2.6 require analysis by assignment regardless of receipt/adherence; missing outcomes are assessed separately.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y; the analysis retained the target population in assigned groups (S p.11; A Fig.1).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 applies only if 2.6=N/PN/NI.

evidence: Only 6/446 and 4/223 were reported lost to follow-up (A Fig.1), strongly supporting retention. However, counts for absent scans, consent withdrawal and censoring after missed assessments are not supplied, although these are explicit PFS censoring categories (S Table JPBL.6.1, p.15). The 36 versus 9 response-unevaluable patients (A Table 2) cannot be equated with missing PFS, but also do not resolve PFS completeness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires missing outcomes to be sufficiently few that they could make no important difference. §6.1.5 warns that analyzed participants may still have missing follow-up. Administrative censoring is not itself missing outcome data.

evidence: Reported central-review and starting-dose sensitivity analyses support efficacy consistency (A pp.2879–2880), but do not examine plausible outcome-dependent missingness. Planned additional analyses in S §6.7.5, pp.20–21 do not provide reported evidence resolving that issue.
guidance: §6.1.7 and Box 8, 3.2 require sensitivity analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome; general consistency is insufficient.

evidence: Withdrawal and missed imaging could relate to deteriorating health. Progression or death after at least two missed scheduled assessments was censored at the last adequate assessment (S Table JPBL.6.1, p.15).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: health-related loss or withdrawal makes dependence on the true outcome possible.

evidence: Evidence against likely informative missingness includes small, similar reported losses, continued imaging after treatment cessation or non-initiation, and no automatic primary-analysis censoring at treatment cessation or subsequent therapy (A Fig.1; P §10.1.2, p.45; S pp.15, 20). Other censoring reasons/counts remain absent. PN is a qualified inference from these safeguards and observed retention, not proof of independent censoring.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence. §6.1.5 identifies stopping-treatment censoring as a particular risk; it was not the primary rule here. §1.1 allows a reasoned PN despite incomplete detail.

evidence: Investigator-assessed RECIST 1.1 progression or death, CT/MRI, and explicit bone-only progression criteria are appropriate for the specified PFS outcome (A pp.2877–2878; P §10.1.3, p.45).
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods, not whether the endpoint is a desirable surrogate.

evidence: Both groups used the same criteria and imaging schedule: every eight weeks initially, then every twelve weeks (A p.2877). Imaging continued after treatment cessation (P §10.1.2). Actual arm-specific scan adherence is unreported, but no systematic ascertainment difference is demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparable methods, thresholds and time points. §1.1 supports PN where the protocol and reported conduct permit that inference.

evidence: Investigators and assessment personnel were covered by explicit blinding and assignment-access restrictions (P §§8.2, 9.5; S §7). The toxicity imbalance and warning about possible unblinding (A Table 3; P §9.5.3) challenge blinding but do not establish probable awareness. My earlier answer treated potential unblinding too strongly.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 directs N when assessors were blinded; §7.3 requires examining implementation. With safeguards documented and actual compromise unreported, §1.1 supports the qualified PN response.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=PN. Progression assessment still involves judgement (P §10.1.3); that characteristic does not independently establish bias when assessors are probably unaware.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 applies only if 4.3=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA. Central-review results remain supportive (A Fig.2), but are not being used to replace assessment of investigator blinding.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 applies only if 4.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: S was approved July 8, 2016 and states finalization before sponsor unblinding and the first efficacy interim analysis (§3, p.7). It specifies the target population, investigator RECIST PFS, stratified log-rank/Cox analysis, Kaplan–Meier medians and approximately 378 final events (pp.11, 15–16). The reported analysis used 379 events (A p.2879).
guidance: §8.3.1 and Box 11, 5.1 require sufficiently detailed intentions finalized before unblinded outcome availability. Pre-unblinding amendments do not themselves imply bias.

evidence: Investigator PFS was prospectively primary; central-review PFS was supportive and also reported (S pp.15, 21; A Fig.2). The revised event target was documented before the efficacy analysis (P §5.4, pp.22–23). No result-driven choice of measurement or cutoff is evident.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results,” not the mere availability of multiple measurements.

evidence: The reported primary population and analysis match S pp.11, 14–16. Some planned sensitivity analyses are unreported, preventing confirmation of exhaustive reporting, but no favorable substitute for the prespecified primary analysis is evident. Two-sided P-value reporting does not show selection of a different HR (A p.2878).
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence supporting result-based selection. §8.3.2 calls for evaluating discrepancies and their implications; §1.1 permits PN when intentions and the reported primary result support that judgement.

evidence: P §9.3, p.36: assignment used a “computer-generated random sequence using the IWRS,” stratified by disease site and prior endocrine therapy.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when sequence generation includes a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: P §9.3, p.36: sites obtained consent, established eligibility, and used the IWRS for assignment and medication-package confirmation. A p.3639 confirms actual use of interactive web randomization and matching placebo. This supports centrally controlled allocation unavailable to recruiters beforehand.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2: remote or centrally administered allocation, including internet-based randomization, provides adequate concealment.

evidence: A Table 1, p.3641: 328 versus 165 participants matches the intended 2:1 ratio; median age was 63 in both groups and visceral disease occurred in 52.4% versus 53.9%. The treatment-free interval imbalance—<36 months in 28% versus 40% of previously treated participants—is compatible with chance alongside the other baseline differences.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3; §4.3.3.1: “differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.” No pattern clearly beyond chance is evident.

evidence: Although matching placebo was used (A p.3639), conspicuous toxicities could probably reveal assignment to some participants: diarrhea occurred in 81.3% of abemaciclib recipients, with substantially less diarrhea on placebo (A abstract and Table 3, p.3645). P §9.6.5 specifically instructed participants about diarrhea management. This is an inference; actual recognition of assignment was not measured.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: answer Y/PY when participants experience toxicities they know to be specific to an intervention. §5.1.3 acknowledges that side effects can permit detection despite attempted blinding; §1.1 permits probability judgements.

evidence: Investigational sites were formally blinded, but marked diarrhea and hematologic toxicity differences probably allowed some treating personnel to infer assignment: grade 3/4 neutropenia was 21.1% versus 1.2% (A abstract; Table 3). No systematic record of inferred assignment is supplied.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: intervention-specific toxicities known to carers or intervention providers warrant Y/PY; attempted blinding alone does not establish successful blinding (§5.1.3).

evidence: Reported dose reductions, interruptions and toxicity-related cessation followed prespecified management rules (A pp.3639–3640; P §9.4.1.1). Crossover was prohibited. One placebo-assigned participant received abemaciclib during cycle 1 (A Fig.1 footnote), but no evidence connects this isolated error to awareness or trial-context behaviour. Trial-context deviations are therefore probably absent.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused nonprotocol changes. Answer N/PN for protocol-consistent toxicity management; §5.1.3 states that deducing treatment does not itself establish bias.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.4 only if 2.3=Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is not applicable.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.5 only if 2.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: A p.3639 specifies the ITT primary analysis; Fig.1 includes all 328 and 165 randomized participants in efficacy analyses. S §6.1.1, p.12 specifies analysis “by assigned treatment arm.” The participant receiving the wrong drug was reassigned only for safety analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6; §5.3.1: ITT analysis is appropriate. Missing-outcome issues belong in D3, rather than being counted again here.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.7 only if 2.6=N/PN/NI.

evidence: Complete or materially near-complete PFS follow-up is not established. A Fig.2A, p.3642 shows early censoring; Fig.1 reports only 3 versus 1 lost to follow-up, without a complete breakdown of PFS censoring reasons. S Table JPBM.6.1, p.17 permits censoring for absent assessments, withdrawal, and progression/death after ≥2 missed assessments. Inclusion of everyone in the analysis does not resolve this uncertainty.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make no important difference. §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing outcome data. NI is reserved for no information about extent; some information is available here.

evidence: No reported analysis demonstrates robustness to plausible informative missingness. The blinded central-review result was similar (A p.3640; Fig.2B), but it does not recover unobserved follow-up. S §6.7.5.1, p.24 lists sensitivity analyses, without supplying results addressing the full missingness concern for this interim estimate.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2; §6.1.7: sensitivity analyses must address “the potential relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value.” Agreement between assessors is insufficient for that purpose.

evidence: Withdrawal and missed tumour assessments could relate to deteriorating health or impending progression. These are explicit censoring situations in S Table JPBM.6.1, p.17; the report does not establish exclusively outcome-independent reasons for premature censoring.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal or loss to follow-up could relate to health status, missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Dependence is possible but probably not established as likely. Reported loss was small and similar—3/328 versus 1/165 (A Fig.1). P §10.1.2, p.47 required continued tumour assessment after treatment cessation or noninitiation. The primary censoring rules do not automatically censor treatment discontinuation or subsequent therapy; censoring at subsequent therapy is a separate sensitivity analysis (S pp.17,24). Reasons for all early censoring remain unavailable, limiting confidence in this inference.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible dependence from likely dependence. Its reason 5 concerns censoring when treatment stops or changes, which is not the primary rule here. §6.1.5 distinguishes administrative censoring from informative loss; toxicity-related treatment cessation alone does not establish missing PFS.

evidence: PFS was time from randomization to objective progression or death, assessed with CT/MRI using RECIST 1.1 (A p.3639; S §6.7.2.1, p.16). This is an appropriate measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable or invalid measurement methods; it does not judge whether the selected outcome is a suitable surrogate.

evidence: A p.3639 specifies the same imaging schedule and RECIST criteria for both arms. P §§10.1.1–10.1.2, pp.46–47 requires consistent methods and continued imaging after treatment cessation. Although toxicity could increase clinical contacts, no evidence shows systematically different tumour ascertainment.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable times. §7.3 concerns systematic differences in ascertainment, rather than merely additional clinical contact.

evidence: Investigators were intended to be blinded, but the conspicuous treatment-associated toxicity pattern probably disclosed assignment for some patients (A Table 3; P §§9.4–9.6). Actual assessor awareness was not documented, so this is a probabilistic inference rather than confirmed unblinding.
guidance: §7.3 requires assessment of whether blinding was successfully implemented; Box 10, 4.3 concerns actual assessor awareness. §1.1 supports PY where judgement rather than firm evidence is necessary.

evidence: Investigator interpretation of serial imaging and progression involves judgement despite RECIST criteria (A p.3639). Knowledge of treatment could influence borderline progression assessments.
guidance: §7.1, outcome type 3, and Box 10, 4.4: observer-reported outcomes involving judgement can be influenced by treatment knowledge.

evidence: Material influence is probably unlikely: assessment was standardized and blinded independent central review gave a similar HR, 0.51 (95% CI 0.36–0.72), versus investigator HR 0.54 (A p.3640; Fig.2). This supports the investigator result without proving that every assessment was unbiased. No actual treatment-aware manipulation or systematic assessment discrepancy is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes knowledge that “could have influenced” assessment from influence that was likely. The independent-review agreement supports PN, while possible unblinding prevents the fully blinded route to Low.

evidence: S pp.1,8 dates version 5 to 14 April 2017 and explicitly states approval “prior to unblinding of the sponsor and prior to the first interim analysis for efficacy.” S §§6.7.1–6.7.2, pp.16–18 specifies ITT investigator RECIST PFS, stratified log-rank testing, Cox HR estimation and an interim analysis at approximately 189 events. A pp.3639–3640 reports these methods at 194 events.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require sufficiently detailed intentions finalized before unblinded outcomes became available. Pre-unblinding amendments are acceptable; confidential DMC access does not itself violate this requirement.

evidence: Investigator-assessed PFS was explicitly primary in S §6.7.2.1. The interim timing was prespecified, and the additional blinded central assessment was also reported (A Fig.2A–B). No evidence indicates selection of a favourable assessor, definition or time point after seeing results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: assess whether selection from eligible measurements was based on results. Prespecified measurement and timing, with corroborating assessment reported, support PN.

evidence: The reported ITT stratified analysis matches S §§6.1.1 and 6.7.2. Multiple sensitivity analyses were planned, and not all their outputs appear in A, but the reported estimate is the prospectively designated primary analysis. There is no evidence that a favourable alternative replaced it.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence of result-based selection, not merely multiple possible analyses. §8.1.2 focuses on selection according to direction, magnitude or significance; the primary-analysis designation supports PN.

evidence: P §9.3, p.36 explicitly specifies a “computer-generated random sequence using the IWRS,” with stratification. No evidence contradicts that method.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: “computer-generated random numbers” constitute an adequate random component.

evidence: P §9.3, p.36 describes consent and eligibility preceding assignment through IWRS, which also assigned medication packages. A p.3639 confirms actual web-based randomization and matching placebo.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2: remote, centrally administered allocation—including internet-based randomization—supports concealment.

evidence: A Table 1, p.3641: 328 versus 165 matches 2:1 allocation; age and major disease characteristics are similar. The treatment-free interval difference, 28% versus 40% below 36 months among previously treated patients, does not establish a randomization failure.
guidance: §4.3.3.1 and Box 4, 1.3: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.” A prognostically relevant difference alone is insufficient.

evidence: Matching placebo and double blinding are documented (A p.3639). Toxicity differences are substantial (A Table 3), but the documents do not establish that participants recognized their assignments. P §9.5.3, p.42 describes the potential for symptom-related unblinding, rather than reporting that it occurred. My earlier answer treated that possibility as probability too readily.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 refers to toxicities participants “knew to be specific” to an intervention. §5.1.3 distinguishes possible detection from demonstrated failure of blinding; §1.1 permits PN based on contextual evidence.

evidence: Investigational sites were blinded, with restricted treatment-code access and controlled emergency unblinding (P §§8.2, 9.5; S §7, p.33). Toxicities could prompt suspicion, but no actual pattern of treatment awareness is reported. The evidence supports probable continued masking rather than probable awareness.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 requires awareness, including recognition of intervention-specific toxicity. §5.1.3 warns that attempted blinding is imperfect but does not require assuming it failed.

evidence: Not reached because both 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. For the domain-level challenge, A pp.3639–3640 describes protocol-permitted toxicity management; Fig.1 reports one wrong-drug exposure without evidence of trial-context motivation.
guidance: Box 6 branching: ask 2.3 only if either 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only if 2.3=Y/PY.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only if 2.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: A p.3639 and Fig.1 specify ITT efficacy analysis of all 328 versus 165 randomized participants. S §6.1.1, p.12 specifies analysis by assigned arm. The participant who received the wrong drug changed groups only for safety analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT analyses are appropriate; missing-outcome concerns are assessed separately in D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.7 only if 2.6=N/PN/NI.

evidence: A Fig.1 reports only 3 versus 1 lost to follow-up, favouring completeness, but Fig.2A also shows early censoring whose reasons and counts are not tabulated. S Table JPBM.6.1, p.17 includes censoring for absent assessments, withdrawal and events after ≥2 missed assessments. The four reported losses cannot confidently be treated as the complete inventory of unavailable PFS follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires missing outcomes too few to materially change the estimate. §6.1.5: prematurely censored participants may have missing outcomes despite inclusion in analysis. NI is reserved for no information about extent; some information exists here.

evidence: The similar central-review HR (A p.3640; Fig.2B) does not resolve missing follow-up. S §6.7.5.1, p.24 prespecifies sensitivity analyses, but the supplied report does not demonstrate robustness of this estimate across plausible informative-missingness assumptions.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7: sensitivity analyses must address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome. Reassessment of available scans does not establish robustness to unavailable observations.

evidence: Withdrawal and missed scans could follow deteriorating health or impending progression. These are censoring situations in S Table JPBM.6.1, p.17; outcome-independent reasons are not documented for all premature censoring.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal or loss related to health status makes dependence on the true outcome possible.

evidence: Evidence against likely dependence includes small, similar reported losses (A Fig.1), mandatory continued imaging after treatment cessation/noninitiation (P §10.1.2, p.47), and no automatic primary-analysis censoring at treatment changes (S pp.17,24). These safeguards support PN, although incomplete censoring details prevent certainty. Toxicity-related cessation alone is not evidence that PFS became unobserved.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 separates possible from likely dependence. Reason 5 applies when follow-up is actually censored at stopping/changing therapy. §1.1 permits a reasoned PN; it must not merely substitute for absent evidence.

evidence: Investigator PFS used objective progression or death, with CT/MRI assessed by RECIST 1.1 (A p.3639; S §6.7.2.1, p.16). No evidence identifies an unsuitable measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods that are insensitive or invalid for the outcome, not whether PFS is the preferred clinical endpoint.

evidence: The same imaging schedule and progression criteria applied to both groups (A p.3639; P §§10.1.1–10.1.2, pp.46–47). More toxicity-related contacts could occur, but systematic differences in tumour ascertainment are not reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable methods use the same thresholds at comparable times; §7.3 concerns systematic differences in ascertainment.

evidence: Investigators were blinded, and treatment-code access was restricted (P §9.5; S §7, p.33). The toxicity imbalance and protocol acknowledgment of possible unblinding do not establish probable assessor awareness. My earlier inference exceeded the evidence. Similar blinded central-review results provide additional reassurance (A Fig.2), although they do not independently prove successful masking.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 directs N when assessors were blinded; §7.3 requires considering whether blinding was successfully implemented. PN reflects the documented safeguards with residual uncertainty (§1.1).

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=PN. Investigator interpretation could involve judgement, but that does not activate this question when awareness is probably absent.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only if 4.3=Y/PY/NI. §7.1, outcome type 3, concerns influence when the observer is aware.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA. A Fig.2’s central-review agreement remains supporting evidence, not a substitute for the branching rules.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only if 4.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: S pp.1,8 dates approval to 14 April 2017 and states it preceded sponsor unblinding and the first efficacy interim analysis. S pp.16–18 specifies ITT investigator PFS, stratified log-rank/Cox analyses and approximately 189 events. A pp.3639–3640 reports that analysis at 194 events.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require a sufficiently detailed, dated plan preceding unblinded outcome availability. Pre-unblinding amendments and confidential DMC access are permissible.

evidence: Investigator RECIST PFS and interim timing were prespecified (S §§6.7.2.1–6.7.2.2). Both investigator and central-review results appear in A Fig.2. No evidence indicates selection of an assessor, definition or time point because its result was preferable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results”; multiple measurements alone do not establish it.

evidence: The reported ITT stratified primary result matches S pp.12,16–18. Although not all planned sensitivity outputs are presented, no evidence shows that a favourable alternative displaced the designated primary analysis.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 and §8.1.2 require result-based selection among eligible analyses. The existence or incomplete reporting of ancillary analyses alone does not establish selection of this estimate.

evidence: Article p.4: treatment was determined by a “computer-generated random sequence”; cohort A used stratification and blocks of six.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when sequence generation includes “computer-generated random numbers.”

evidence: Article p.4 and SAP §5.3, pp.10–11: allocation used an interactive web response system, which assigned treatment and verified medication packages. Sites enrolled eligible patients before assignment. Masking prevented previous allocations from revealing the fixed-block sequence.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: remote or centrally administered allocation supports Yes. §4.3.2 identifies predictable blocks as problematic when previous assignments are known.

evidence: Article Table 1, p.3: median age was 54 in both arms; visceral disease was 60.9% versus 59.6%; measurable disease 85.0% versus 83.8%. The ≥65-year category differed (24.2% versus 16.2%), but does not indicate failed randomization. Allocation of 207 versus 99 is compatible with the intended 2:1 ratio.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when differences “are compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 states that chance imbalances are not systematic bias.

evidence: Article p.4: “Patients, physicians, and investigators were masked,” with matching placebo. Diarrhea was more frequent with abemaciclib (80.0% versus 16.2%; Table 4, p.10), making recognition possible, but actual participant awareness or recognition of assignment-specific effects is not reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 requires Y/PY when participants experienced effects they “knew to be specific” to an intervention. §5.1.3 distinguishes possible detection from established loss of blinding; §1.1 permits a reasoned Probably response.

evidence: Article p.4 explicitly reports physician and investigator masking. Toxicity differences could provide clues (Table 4), and Protocol §9.5.3, p.45 acknowledges this possibility; no actual unblinding of treatment personnel before the target assessment is reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness, including effects personnel “knew to be specific” to treatment. §5.1.3: an attempt to blind does not guarantee success, so PN reflects uncertainty rather than assuming perfect masking.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. Article pp.4–5 describes permitted dose modifications; Supplement Figure 1 identifies two treatment discontinuations for protocol deviations but does not establish trial-context-induced departures.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 is conditional on Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. Its elaboration excludes changes “consistent with the trial protocol,” including toxicity management.

evidence: No qualifying deviations established through the applicable branch; see Article pp.4–5 and Supplement Figure 1.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 is asked only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached; treatment modification frequencies in Article p.5 do not independently trigger this question.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 is asked only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Article p.5: efficacy analyses included “all randomly assigned patients.” Supplement Figure 1, p.8 confirms 207 versus 99 in the ITT analysis, including the two abemaciclib-assigned patients never treated. SAP §6.1.1, p.12 specifies grouping according to randomized treatment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: ITT analyses are appropriate. §5.3.1 assigns missing-outcome bias separately to D3 rather than treating it as an allocation-group analysis failure.

evidence: All randomized patients were retained in their assigned groups for this analysis; Supplement Figure 1 and SAP §6.1.1.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 is conditional on N/PN/NI to 2.6.

evidence: Complete or nearly complete PFS ascertainment cannot be established. Supplement Figure 1 reports withdrawal by patient in 7/207 versus 8/99 and loss to follow-up in 0 versus 2; it describes treatment disposition, without subsequent PFS completeness. Article p.5 reports 66 versus 53 events, but does not partition remaining observations into administrative and premature censoring. Protocol §10.1.2, p.50 required continued scans after treatment cessation, which argues against equating all discontinuations with missing outcomes.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing data, while censoring at a specified closing date may be non-informative. Some extent information exists, so NI is not used here.

evidence: No reported sensitivity analysis establishes robustness to informative missingness. SAP Table JPBQ.6.1, p.17 specifies censoring for loss/withdrawal and progression or death after ≥2 missed assessments; Article pp.5–7 reports conventional survival analyses without missing-data sensitivity results.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires correction for bias or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions.” §6.1.7 requires analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Loss, withdrawal, and missed scans could relate to clinical deterioration and unobserved progression. These are recognized censoring situations in SAP Table JPBQ.6.1, p.17. Reasons demonstrating that all premature losses were unrelated to health are absent.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on its true value; censored follow-up can constitute missing outcome data.

evidence: The documents do not report actual premature PFS censoring by reason and arm, or health status at loss. Against likely informative censoring, Protocol §10.1.2 required continued assessments after stopping treatment, and SAP Table JPBQ.6.1 does not automatically censor at treatment cessation or a change of therapy. However, these provisions do not establish actual follow-up completeness. Treatment-discontinuation differences cannot reliably substitute for missing-outcome differences.
guidance: §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient information without a defensible Probably response. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes possible from likely dependence using actual missingness proportions, reasons, and censoring practices; Table 10 maps NI at this branch to High.

evidence: Article p.4: investigator-assessed progression used CT/MRI and RECIST 1.1; PFS ran from randomization to objective progression or death. These are suitable methods for the specified outcome.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns measurement methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” not whether the endpoint is an ideal surrogate.

evidence: Article p.4 specifies the same scheduled CT/MRI assessments for both arms: baseline, every second cycle through cycle 18, then every third cycle, with additional assessment after clinical progression. No systematic difference in assessment methods or timing is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparability as the same “measurement methods and thresholds, used at comparable time points.” §1.1 supports PN where implementation is inferred from the reported common procedures.

evidence: The target assessors were investigators, explicitly masked according to Article p.4. Toxicity differences and Protocol §9.5.3 acknowledge possible inadvertent unblinding, but actual assessor awareness is not documented. No independent-review result is substituted for the requested investigator result.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: blinded outcome assessors support N; §1.1 permits PN for a judgement rather than certainty. §7.3 requires assessing actual assessor blinding.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. RECIST progression involves investigator judgement (Article p.4), but this does not independently trigger the conditional question.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 is conditional on Y/PY/NI to 4.3; §7.1 identifies radiographic assessments as observer outcomes involving judgement.

evidence: Not reached under the assessor-awareness branch; Article p.4 supplies the masking evidence.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 is conditional on Y/PY/NI to 4.4.

evidence: SAP revision history, p.6: “SAP Version 2 was approved prior to the first unblinded interim efficacy analysis by the DMC.” Its approval was 25 April 2019; version 1 was approved 8 March 2019 (p.1). Although version 2 followed the data cutoff, the relevant milestone is unblinding. SAP §§6.7.1 and 6.13 specifies investigator PFS, the 119-event interim analysis, stratified log-rank testing, Cox HR and Kaplan–Meier estimates, matching Article p.5.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1: finalization must precede “availability of unblinded outcome data.” §8.3.1 allows analysis refinements while data remain blinded and requires attention to amendments and dates.

evidence: SAP §6.7.1.1, p.16 identifies investigator-assessed RECIST PFS in cohort A; §6.7.1.2, p.17 specifies the approximately 119-event interim analysis. Article p.5 reports precisely that endpoint and event count. Serial scans and a planned later analysis do not show result-driven choice of the reported measurement.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results” among eligible measurements. Correspondence between intended and reported measurements supports N/PN.

evidence: The reported stratified Cox HR and medians match SAP §6.7.1.3.1, p.18, with the ITT population specified in §6.1.1. Additional analyses were planned, including restricted mean PFS (§6.7.1.3.2), which is not reported in the article; this limits confirmation of complete reporting but does not demonstrate selection of this prespecified HR because of its result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence that the numerical result was selected “on the basis of the results”; multiplicity alone is insufficient. Its eligibility rule restricts attention to analyses relevant to the specified result.

evidence: Article p.4 reports a “computer-generated random sequence,” stratified allocation and blocks of six. Fixed blocks do not make the sequence non-random.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: a random component, including “computer-generated random numbers,” supports Y.

evidence: Article p.4 and SAP §5.3, pp.10–11 describe allocation through IWRS after eligibility assessment, with medication-package verification. SAP §7, p.28 describes protection of treatment codes. Fixed-block predictability would require knowledge not shown to have been available to recruiters.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 accepts remote/central allocation. §4.3.2 identifies fixed blocks as problematic when previous assignments and block boundaries are known.

evidence: Article Table 1, p.3: visceral disease 60.9% versus 59.6%, measurable disease 85.0% versus 83.8%, median age 54 in both arms. The difference in participants aged ≥65 years—24.2% versus 16.2%—is compatible with chance. The 207:99 allocation is compatible with the intended 2:1 ratio.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer N for imbalances “compatible with chance.” §4.3.3.1 excludes chance imbalance from systematic bias.

evidence: Article p.4 explicitly reports participant masking and matching placebo. Diarrhea differed substantially—80.0% versus 16.2% (Table 4, p.10)—but actual awareness or recognition of effects as assignment-specific is not documented. This possibility warrants PN rather than certainty.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 requires Y/PY when participants experienced effects they “knew to be specific” to an intervention. §5.1.3 discusses possible detection without assuming that masking necessarily failed.

evidence: Article p.4 explicitly reports physician and investigator masking. Protocol §9.5.3, p.45 acknowledges possible inadvertent unblinding through treatment-related signs; it does not report that this occurred. Toxicity differences challenge, but do not overturn, the reported masking.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses personnel awareness, including recognized intervention-specific effects. §1.1 permits a reasoned Probably response when certainty is unavailable.

evidence: Not reached. Article pp.4–5 reports protocol-permitted dose interruptions/reductions. The two protocol-deviation treatment discontinuations in Supplement Figure 1 do not establish deviations caused by trial context.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 applies only after Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. It excludes changes “consistent with the trial protocol,” including toxicity management.

evidence: No qualifying deviation branch was reached; Article pp.4–5 and Supplement Figure 1 provide the relevant treatment-change information.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 applies only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached. The different dose-modification frequencies in Article p.5 do not independently trigger this question.
guidance: Box 6, 2.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Article p.5 defines efficacy analyses as including “all randomly assigned patients.” Supplement Figure 1, p.8 confirms 207 versus 99 in ITT, including two untreated abemaciclib-assigned participants. SAP §6.1.1, p.12 specifies analysis according to randomized treatment.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 accepts ITT analysis. §5.3.1 assigns missing-outcome concerns separately to D3.

evidence: Supplement Figure 1 and SAP §6.1.1 support inclusion in the randomized groups; 2.6 is Y.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 applies only after N/PN/NI to 2.6.

evidence: Supplement Figure 1 reports patient withdrawal in 7/207 versus 8/99 and loss to follow-up in 0 versus 2, but describes treatment disposition rather than complete PFS follow-up. Protocol §10.1.2, p.50 requires continued scans after stopping treatment, supporting completeness but not documenting its achievement. Moreover, §7.3.4, p.29 permits removal of the lost-to-follow-up designation once vital status is found; this does not establish progression status. Thus two recorded losses cannot safely be treated as the full missing-PFS count.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by whether missing outcomes could make “no important difference.” §6.1.5 distinguishes premature censoring from administrative censoring. Some extent information exists, so NI is not used here.

evidence: No reported analysis demonstrates robustness to informative missingness. SAP Table JPBQ.6.1, p.17 specifies censoring for withdrawal/loss and progression or death after ≥2 missed assessments. Article pp.5–7 supplies conventional survival results, without sensitivity results addressing these mechanisms.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or sensitivity analyses under “a range of plausible assumptions.” §6.1.7 requires examination of the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Withdrawals, loss and missed assessments could relate to deterioration or unobserved progression; SAP Table JPBQ.6.1 expressly accommodates these censoring situations. No documentation establishes that all premature censoring was unrelated to health.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness could depend on outcome when loss or withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status.”

evidence: Evidence against likely informative censoring includes continued-scan requirements, approximately 16-month median follow-up in both arms (Article p.5), and no automatic censoring at treatment cessation/change in SAP Table JPBQ.6.1. Nevertheless, actual premature PFS censoring counts, reasons and health status are absent. Treatment-withdrawal counts cannot establish their relationship to PFS. These facts support neither likely dependence nor a sufficiently grounded “probably not.”
guidance: §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient information where PY/PN would be unreasonable. Box 8, 3.4 requires distinguishing possible from likely dependence through missingness proportions, reasons or circumstances. Table 10 explicitly maps NI at this branch to High.

evidence: Article p.4 specifies CT/MRI, RECIST 1.1 progression and death from any cause. Investigator judgement does not make this method unsuitable.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” rather than whether judgement is involved or the endpoint is a surrogate.

evidence: Article p.4 gives common assessment methods and scheduled intervals for both arms, including additional imaging after clinical progression. No systematic arm-specific ascertainment procedure is reported. Actual schedule adherence is not fully tabulated, hence PN.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable ascertainment as the same methods and thresholds “at comparable time points.”

evidence: Article p.4 explicitly identifies investigators as masked. Toxicity differences and Protocol §9.5.3 make inadvertent awareness possible, but actual assessor awareness is not established. Independent central review is not assumed for this investigator-assessed result.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 supports N when assessors are blinded; §1.1 permits PN when this remains a judgement. §7.3 requires examining the masking of the actual assessors.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. Article p.4’s radiographic progression assessment involves judgement, but that alone does not activate this branch.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 applies only after Y/PY/NI to 4.3. §7.1 distinguishes observer outcomes involving judgement from assessor awareness.

evidence: Not reached; the relevant masking evidence is Article p.4.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 applies only after Y/PY/NI to 4.4.

evidence: SAP p.6 states that version 2 “was approved prior to the first unblinded interim efficacy analysis by the DMC.” Although approved on 25 April 2019, after the data cutoff, it preceded the relevant unblinded analysis. SAP §§6.7.1 and 6.13 specifies the investigator endpoint, 119-event interim analysis and statistical methods reported in Article p.5.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before “unblinded outcome data were available.” §8.3.1 allows refinement while data remain blinded and requires checking amendments and timing.

evidence: SAP §6.7.1.1–2, pp.16–17 specifies investigator-assessed RECIST PFS and the approximately 119-event interim analysis. Article p.5 reports that measurement and exactly 119 events. Neither serial scanning nor the planned later analysis establishes result-driven measurement selection.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 requires selection “on the basis of the results.” Correspondence between intended and reported measurements supports N/PN.

evidence: Article p.5’s stratified Cox HR and median estimates correspond to SAP §6.7.1.3.1, p.18, in the specified ITT population. Restricted mean PFS was also planned (§6.7.1.3.2) but not reported. That omission challenges complete reporting, without establishing that this prespecified HR was selected because it was favourable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely result-based selection among eligible analyses; multiple possible analyses alone do not establish it. Its eligibility rule focuses assessment on the specified result.

evidence: The allocation list was generated by a separate contract research organisation team using an interactive response system, with stratification and “permuted blocks of four” (A p3, Randomisation and masking).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: answer Yes when “a random component was used”; §4.3.1 recognises random permuted blocks.

evidence: Allocation used the interactive response system after eligibility confirmation; a separate unmasked team generated the list (A p3; P §5.3, p35). Recruiting personnel were masked.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: centrally administered allocation controlled independently of enrolment personnel warrants Yes.

evidence: Groups contained 182 participants each. Baseline median eGFR was 56.14 versus 55.11 and mean UPCR was 1.48 in both groups. Diabetes and pre-diabetes were more frequent with Nefecon, but these isolated differences do not establish failed randomisation (A p5, Table 1; p7). Baseline data omit the two incorrectly randomised patients.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: “differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.”

evidence: Capsules matched in taste, smell and appearance, but “unmasking occurred for three patients” (A p3). Excess acne and facial oedema could also reveal treatment to some participants (S p15, Table S8). Whether the three patients themselves were informed is unspecified.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: treatment-specific side effects can justify Yes/Probably yes; §5.1.3 cautions that attempted blinding does not ensure successful blinding.

evidence: Although investigators and site staff were generally masked, treatment assignments were explicitly unmasked “at local sites” for three patients in potential medical emergencies (A p3).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among carers and intervention providers; §5.3.1 considers whether “some of these groups were not blinded.”

evidence: Rescue treatment was permitted when clinically necessary, with continued follow-up (P §5.6.2, p39). Treatment discontinuation and adverse events occurred, but 94% in each group took ≥80% of capsules (A p6). No evidence identifies departures caused by trial-related awareness or engagement.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Yes/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused prohibited departures; protocol-consistent treatment changes warrant N/PN.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; the documented clinical treatment changes do not establish trial-context deviations (P p39).
guidance: Box 6: 2.4 applies only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is not applicable.
guidance: Box 6: 2.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: The target analysis excluded observed measurements after rescue medication (S p10, Table S3, footnote). Its stated aim was efficacy “free from the effects of rescue medication,” rather than the full assignment effect (A p4). Keeping participants in their assigned groups and imputing values does not restore deliberately excluded observations. Five untreated participants were retained; the later China cohort was excluded according to the defined recruitment boundary (A pp4–5; P p59).
guidance: §5.3.1 requires analysis regardless of adherence. §6.1 explicitly assigns exclusions of eligible participants with available outcomes to D2; Box 6, 2.6 rejects inappropriate post-randomisation exclusions.

evidence: Twenty Nefecon and 27 placebo participants had some/all data excluded following rescue, prohibited immunosuppression or dialysis (S p6). These are clinically selected, prognostically relevant exclusions. Including post-rescue data changed the time-averaged endpoint little—5.05 to 4.79—but an equivalent check for the target slope is not reported (S pp9–10, Tables S2–S3). Substantial impact on this result remains possible.
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: substantial impact can occur even below 5% when exclusions are “strongly related to prognostic factors.” The question concerns potential impact, not proof of bias.

evidence: A valid 24-month eGFR was available for 161/182 (88%) versus 165/182 (91%) participants (A p7; S p18, Figure S2). Thus genuine missingness was appreciable even before deliberate analytical exclusions. Figure 1’s smaller analysis counts also reflect exclusions and are not treated as pure loss to follow-up.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make no important difference; “imputed data should be regarded as missing data.”

evidence: Imputation used previous eGFR measurements (A p4; S pp3–4), which is reassuring. Alternative missingness assumptions produced similar results for the time-averaged endpoint (S p9, Table S2), but target-specific robustness under plausible outcome-dependent missingness is not demonstrated. The slope models in Table S3 do not supply that test.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §§6.1.6–6.1.7: imputation is not automatically corrective; sensitivity analyses must address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Actual study withdrawals included dialysis, deaths, loss to follow-up and withdrawal of consent (S p18, Figure S2). These reasons cannot all be classified as unrelated to health or kidney function.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on its true value.

evidence: Dialysis explicitly caused study withdrawal in one versus two participants; two deaths occurred with Nefecon. Other withdrawals included loss to follow-up (5 vs 2) and consent withdrawal (10 vs 10), whose underlying reasons are insufficiently described (S p18, Figure S2). Similar retention and previous-eGFR imputation mitigate concern, but do not establish that subsequent missing trajectories were explained. The clinical withdrawals support likely outcome-dependent missingness. Deliberately excluded post-rescue observations are assessed separately in D2.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4, reasons 2–3: reported reasons and differences in reasons can indicate outcome-dependent missingness. §6.1.6 requires considering trajectories “after the last recorded measurement,” even with repeated-measurement prediction.

evidence: eGFR was calculated centrally using the CKD-EPI equation, with duplicate measurements at baseline and 24 months (A pp3–4; S p10, Table S3). No evidence identifies an unsuitable measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns unsuitable data collection, not whether the outcome is an appropriate surrogate; prespecified measures generally warrant N/PN.

evidence: Both groups had the same scheduled visits, central laboratory assessment and eGFR calculation (A pp3–4). No differential measurement procedure is reported.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses “the same measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times.

evidence: “Key efficacy endpoints were calculated at a central laboratory by personnel masked to treatment assignment” (A p3). Local emergency unmasking does not establish laboratory unmasking.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.”

evidence: Not reached because the central laboratory assessors were masked, 4.3=N (A p3).
guidance: Box 10: 4.4 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is not applicable.
guidance: Box 10: 4.5 applies only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: The dated protocol specifies a random-coefficients slope model, with a different conditional sensitivity analysis (P §9.2.1.2, p61). The supplement explains replacing that approach with annualised robust-regression change because of an acute effect; it explicitly dates the spline model before full-study unblinding, but does not establish equivalent timing for the exact 2.95 analysis (S p4). Part A results were available to the sponsor (P p35). No supplied dated amendment resolves this; the registry snapshot was updated after completion (R, Status and dates).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require finalisation before unblinded outcome data were available. §8.3.2 permits NI where documentation cannot establish the analysis intentions; an unexplained date is not proof of selective reporting.

evidence: Two-year eGFR slope was planned (P p61), and the article reports the scheduled eGFR trajectory through 24 months (A p6, Figure 1). There is no indication that a favourable timepoint or measurement method was selectively substituted for the specified two-year target.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection based on results among eligible measurements; reporting the intended measurements supports N/PN.

evidence: The analysis change and larger selected estimate raise concern, but all three slope analyses are fully reported: random coefficients 1.82, robust regression 2.95, and spline 2.78, each with CI and p value (S p10, Table S3). The authors provide a methodological explanation concerning the acute effect (S p4). These facts argue against selective suppression of eligible analyses; uncertainty about prospective specification remains under 5.1.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely results-based selection from multiple analyses, particularly when only a subset is fully reported. §§8.1 and 8.3.2 distinguish selective reporting from legitimate methodological changes; multiplicity alone does not establish selection.

evidence: A separate contract research organisation team generated the allocation list using an interactive response system and “permuted blocks of four” (Article p3).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: Yes when “a random component was used”; §4.3.1 recognises random permuted blocks.

evidence: Central interactive allocation followed eligibility confirmation, independently of masked recruiting personnel (Article p3; Protocol §5.3, p35). Fixed block size does not itself demonstrate predictability under these arrangements.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2 accepts independently controlled central allocation. §4.3.2 identifies predictability when recruiters can know previous assignments and block positions.

evidence: The groups had 182 participants each and similar baseline eGFR, proteinuria and UPCR. Diabetes/pre-diabetes differed, but no pattern establishes failed randomisation (Article p5, Table 1). The table excludes two incorrectly randomised participants, a limitation insufficient to invalidate the remaining baseline comparison.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.”

evidence: Participants received capsules matched in taste, smell and appearance. Three assignments were disclosed at local sites, without stating that participants were informed (Article p3). My earlier answer inferred participant awareness too readily from this and the adverse-event differences (Supplement p15, Table S8).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 refers to actual/probable awareness, including side effects participants knew were treatment-specific. §1.1 permits a reasoned probability judgement; possible awareness alone does not establish PY.

evidence: Despite general masking, local-site emergency unmasking occurred for three patients (Article p3). Thus at least some personnel knew assignments.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among carers/providers; §5.3.1 considers situations where “some of these groups were not blinded.”

evidence: Clinically necessary rescue and treatment changes were permitted, with continued follow-up (Protocol §5.6.2, p39). No evidence links departures to trial-related disappointment, preferences or personnel interference. Adherence was high and similar (Article p6).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused departures; protocol-consistent clinical changes warrant N/PN.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; documented clinical treatment changes do not establish trial-context deviations (Protocol p39).
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.4 only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Table S3 explicitly excludes “data observed after receiving rescue medication” (Supplement p10). The analysis estimates efficacy free of rescue effects (Article p4), not the full assignment effect. Inclusion of all 364 participants through imputation does not restore these observed outcomes. The prospectively defined later China cohort exclusion is a separate issue (Protocol p59).
guidance: §5.3.1 requires inclusion regardless of adherence. §6.1 assigns deliberate exclusions where outcome data are available to D2; Box 6, 2.6 rejects inappropriate post-randomisation exclusions.

evidence: Some/all measurements were excluded for 20 versus 27 participants following rescue, prohibited immunosuppression or dialysis (Supplement p6). These counts are not equivalent to complete participant exclusions, but indicate appreciable clinical selection. Including post-rescue observations changed the time-averaged effect only modestly, 5.05 to 4.79; the equivalent target-specific estimate is absent (Supplement pp9–10, Tables S2–S3).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7 assesses potential substantial impact, including when exclusions are “strongly related to prognostic factors.” §1.2.1 requires materiality; the related-endpoint sensitivity analysis mitigates concern but does not exclude material impact here.

evidence: Valid 24-month eGFR was available for 161/182 versus 165/182 participants—88% and 91% (Article p7; Supplement p18, Figure S2). This concerns actual availability before additional analytical exclusions.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires that missing outcomes could make no important difference; imputed values remain missing for this question.

evidence: Imputation conditioned on previous eGFR; alternative assumptions incorporating treatment duration and recent UPCR gave similar time-averaged results (Article p4; Supplement p9, Table S2). This is relevant reassurance, but it does not demonstrate robustness of the exact 24-month/annualised result.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §§6.1.6–6.1.7: imputation is not automatically corrective, and sensitivity analyses must address the relationship between missingness and the true outcome.

evidence: Withdrawals included dialysis, deaths, consent withdrawal and loss to follow-up (Supplement p18, Figure S2). Health-related missingness is possible.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal that “could be related to participants’ health status” supports Y/PY.

evidence: My earlier answer over-weighted a few clinical withdrawals. Dialysis withdrawals were 1 versus 2, consent withdrawals 10 versus 10, and retention was similar. Serial eGFR informed imputation, with reassuring related-endpoint sensitivity results (Article p4; Supplement pp9,18). The flowchart does not map every withdrawal reason to the missing 24-month measurements. On balance, material residual dependence on unobserved eGFR is possible but probably not likely after accounting for recorded trajectories. This is a judgement, not demonstrated absence of bias.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes could from likely, and recognises adjustment for characteristics explaining missingness. §6.1.6 recognises repeated measurements can reduce bias; §1.2.1 requires “risk of material bias.” Unexplained withdrawals alone do not establish likely material dependence.

evidence: Central laboratory eGFR used CKD-EPI, with replicate baseline and 24-month measurements (Article pp3–4; Supplement p10). No unsuitable measurement instrument is identified.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 assesses inappropriate data collection, not whether a surrogate outcome was the best clinical choice.

evidence: Both groups used the same scheduled visits, laboratory methods and eGFR calculation (Article pp3–4). Missing or deliberately excluded measurements do not establish different measurement procedures.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 requires comparison of measurement methods, thresholds and timing; §6.1 places missingness and analytical exclusions elsewhere.

evidence: Central laboratory personnel calculating key efficacy endpoints were explicitly masked (Article p3). Local-site unmasking does not establish laboratory unmasking.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.3=N (Article p3).
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.4 only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 10: ask 4.5 only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

evidence: The dated protocol specifies a random-coefficients slope model, not this annualised robust-regression estimate (Protocol §9.2.1.2, p61). The supplement explains the change and explicitly states pre-full-unblinding specification for the spline model, but does not establish the timing for the exact target analysis (Supplement p4). No supplied dated amendment resolves this.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require finalisation before unblinded outcome data were available. §8.3.2 recognises insufficient documentation; missing timing information neither establishes prospective specification nor proves selective reporting.

evidence: Two-year slope was planned, and the scheduled eGFR trajectory through 24 months is reported (Protocol p61; Article p6, Figure 1). No evidence identifies results-based selection of an eligible measurement/timepoint.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection on the basis of results among eligible outcome measurements; reporting intended measurements supports N/PN.

evidence: The larger estimate and changed method warrant scrutiny. However, random-coefficients, robust-regression and spline estimates—1.82, 2.95 and 2.78—are all fully reported with uncertainty (Supplement p10, Table S3). The acute-effect rationale is disclosed (Supplement p4). Reporting all alternatives is evidence against selective suppression, although it does not establish prospective specification.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely results-based selection among eligible analyses; §§8.1 and 8.3.2 distinguish selective reporting from methodological changes. Multiple analyses or a larger highlighted estimate alone do not establish High risk.

evidence: Protocol §4.3 describes “interactive randomization technology” and a “central computerized system”; §5.1 specifies stratified 2:1 random assignment (P, pp.166–167). The actual sequence-generation procedure is not described. A random component is nevertheless probable in this centrally administered, multinational trial.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 and §4.3.1.1 permit “Probably yes” when detailed sequence generation is absent but the trial context supports that inference.

evidence: Eligible patients were enrolled through a “centralized internet/telephone registration system” after consent, baseline assessments and eligibility approval; IRT assigned medication (P, pp.167–168, §§5.1–5.2).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation independent of enrolment personnel.

evidence: Allocation was exactly 444:222. Most baseline characteristics were similar, including visceral disease, disease-free interval and prior hormonal therapy. ECOG 0 was more frequent with palbociclib, 57.9% versus 45.9%, but this isolated imbalance does not establish failed randomization (A, Table 1, pp.1928–1929).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: “differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias”; isolated imbalances should not automatically be treated as randomization failure.

evidence: Placebo was “indistinguishable” (P, p.169), and double blinding was maintained (A, p.1933). Nevertheless, some participants probably inferred treatment from characteristic toxicity and dose changes: grade 3–4 neutropenia was 66.4% versus 1.4%; dose reductions were 36.0% versus 1.4% (A, pp.1925, 1931). Actual participant awareness was not measured or reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: treatment-specific “side effects or toxicities” can justify Y/PY despite intended blinding. This is an inference, not documented code-breaking.

evidence: Clinicians reviewed blood counts and adjusted doses (P, pp.170, 190). The pronounced neutropenia and dose-reduction differences probably revealed assignment for some patients, despite matching placebo and restrictions on breaking the blind (P, pp.168–169; A, Table 2 and p.1931).
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: answer Y/PY when carers recognize toxicities “specific to one of the interventions.”

evidence: Reported dose reductions occurred “according to protocol”; toxicity-related discontinuation was permitted, and crossover was prohibited (A, pp.1927, 1931; S, Tables S1 and S3). Figure S1 records some protocol violations but does not establish outcome-relevant deviations caused by the trial context. Such deviations are probably absent.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol changes; protocol-consistent toxicity management warrants N/PN.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN; the documented treatment modifications were primarily protocol-directed (A, p.1931; S, Table S1).
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: applicable only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 is NA. Unequal dose-reduction rates do not independently activate this question (S, Table S3).
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: applicable only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: Figure S1 includes all 444 and 222 randomized participants in their assigned groups; Figure 1A explicitly identifies the ITT primary analysis (S, p.11; A, p.1933). SAP §5.1 specifies assignment according to initial randomization regardless of treatment received (P, p.472).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6: “Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses” are appropriate here; missing-outcome bias is assessed separately (§5.3.1).

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y; no exclusion or reassignment is evident in the primary-analysis populations (S, Figure S1; A, Figure 1A).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: applicable only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: Complete inclusion in the analysis does not establish complete PFS observation. SAP §6.1.1 censors withdrawal, new anticancer therapy and progression/death after prolonged assessment gaps (P, pp.544–545). Figure S1 records consent withdrawal and loss to follow-up but describes treatment disposition, not a complete accounting of premature PFS censoring (S, p.11). Nearly complete outcome ascertainment cannot be established.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” requires missing outcomes to make “no important difference.” §6.1.5 counts premature censoring as missing data even when follow-up contributes to analysis.

evidence: SAP §8.2.2 planned analyses following patients beyond new therapy and counting censored adverse-event/deterioration withdrawals as events (P, p.564). Their results are absent from the supplied results reports. The independent imaging analysis is reported, but it does not test assumptions about unobserved outcomes (A, pp.1932–1933).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7 require analyses demonstrating robustness under “plausible assumptions” about missingness and the true outcome; merely planning them is insufficient.

evidence: Censoring at new anticancer therapy can depend on prognosis (P, p.544). For bone-only disease, censoring also applied to fracture, palliation and “clinical worsening not objectively confirmed” (P, p.189). These mechanisms can relate to underlying progression.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: missingness can depend on the outcome when withdrawal relates to “participants’ health status.” §6.1.5 specifically identifies switching to second-line therapy.

evidence: The rules permit prognosis-related censoring, but actual PFS censoring counts and reasons by arm are not reported. Conversely, stopping treatment alone did not require stopping tumour assessments: follow-up was prescribed until progression, new therapy or study withdrawal (P, pp.183, 544). Treatment discontinuations for toxicity/deterioration in Figure S1 therefore cannot be equated with missing PFS. The available evidence cannot distinguish possible from likely informative censoring.
guidance: §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient evidence to infer PY/PN. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence using actual proportions, reasons and circumstances; Table 10 explicitly maps NI here to High.

evidence: The outcome used radiologically confirmed RECIST 1.1 progression or death, with CT/MRI and bone imaging (A, p.1927). No evidence indicates an invalid measurement method.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome”, not whether PFS is the preferred clinical outcome.

evidence: Both groups had imaging every 11–13 weeks and bone scans every 23–25 weeks (A, p.1927). Protocol assessments followed the calendar “regardless of treatment delays resulting from toxicity” (P, p.186). Actual scan adherence by arm is not reported, but systematic differential ascertainment is not indicated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparable ascertainment as the same methods and thresholds at “comparable time points.” §1.1 permits PN when contextual evidence supports it.

evidence: The target was assessed by local investigators, who also had access to toxicity information. Recognizable neutropenia and dose modifications probably revealed some assignments despite intended blinding (A, pp.1930–1933; P, pp.168–169, 190, 209). Actual assessor awareness is unreported.
guidance: §7.3 requires consideration of whether blinding was “successfully implemented”; Box 10, 4.3 concerns the assessors of the specified result. The separate blinded central review does not replace them.

evidence: Investigator interpretation of scans and progression involves judgement; bone-only progression required interpreting and confirming lesions (A, p.1927; P, p.189). Knowledge of assignment could affect these assessments.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 identifies “observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement” as susceptible; §7.1 includes radiograph interpretation.

evidence: RECIST criteria, common assessment schedules and maintained formal blinding constrain influence. Independent blinded review also supported benefit, HR 0.65 (95% CI 0.51–0.84), versus investigator HR 0.58 (A, pp.1932–1933).
