This does not prove freedom from bias, but provides evidence against likely material influence; the numerical difference alone does not demonstrate it.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from influence “likely” to occur. §1.2.1 specifies “risk of material bias.”

evidence: Original SAP v1.0, dated February 18, 2013, specifies investigator PFS, ITT, Kaplan–Meier medians, HR/CI and disease-site-stratified log-rank testing (P, pp.461, 474, 489); these match A, pp.1927–1929 and Figure 1A. SAP v3.0 is dated March 15, 2016, after cutoff, and the exact unblinded-analysis date is absent; however, the target’s core methods were already specified in 2013. Amendments document external pharmacology and regulatory rationales (P, pp.528, 533–535).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires intentions finalized before unblinded analysis; §8.3.1 permits inference from dated plans and accepts changes “clearly unrelated to the results.” PY reflects the remaining timing uncertainty.

evidence: Investigator RECIST PFS was the planned primary measurement; central review was supportive (original SAP, P, pp.474, 489). Both assessments were reported (A, Figure 1). The specified investigator result therefore appears unlikely to have been chosen because it was more favourable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 concerns selection “on the basis of the results” among eligible measurements; multiplicity alone is insufficient.

evidence: The reported ITT primary analysis matches original SAP §8.2.1 (P, p.489). Additional populations and sensitivity analyses were planned, but their incomplete reporting does not establish selection of this prespecified primary estimate. The final analysis had 331 events versus approximately 347 planned; no results-driven choice of cutoff is demonstrated (A, p.1930; P, p.539).
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires evidence that the reported analysis was “selected on the basis of the results.” §8.1 distinguishes selection of a reported estimate from non-reporting of other results.

evidence: Protocol §§4.3–5.1 describes central computerized IRT and stratified random assignment (P, pp.166–167). The sequence-generation method remains unspecified, but genuine randomization is probable in this centrally administered multinational trial.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1; §4.3.1.1 allow “Probably yes” when trial circumstances support random generation despite incomplete methodological detail.

evidence: A “centralized internet/telephone registration system” allocated eligible patients after consent and baseline assessment; IRT assigned medication (P, pp.167–168).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: “remote or centrally administered” allocation supports Yes.

evidence: The strongest challenge is ECOG imbalance: ECOG 0, 57.9% versus 45.9%, P=0.004. However, allocation was exactly 444:222 and other reported baseline characteristics were generally comparable (M, Table 1, pp.1928–1929). This isolated difference does not convincingly establish randomization failure.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3; §§4.3.3.1–4.3.3.2 distinguish chance differences from imbalances “clearly beyond what is expected due to chance.” Statistical significance alone is insufficient.

evidence: Placebo was “indistinguishable,” and the article states double blinding was maintained (P, p.169; M, p.1933). My previous answer inferred participant knowledge from toxicity and dose changes. The documents do not establish that participants recognized these as identifying palbociclib. Intended masking therefore supports probable unawareness.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 requires toxicities participants “knew to be specific” to an intervention; §5.1.3 distinguishes possible detection from established awareness. §1.1 permits a contextual PN rather than automatically using NI.

evidence: Unlike participants, clinicians reviewed local blood counts and managed doses (P, p.190). Neutropenia was already recognized as characteristic in the trial rationale (P, p.535); grade 3–4 neutropenia occurred in 66.4% versus 1.4%, and dose reductions in 36.0% versus 1.4% (M, pp.1925, 1931). Some clinician inference remains probable despite formal masking.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 explicitly allows Y/PY for recognizable intervention-specific “side effects or toxicities.” PY denotes inference, not documented code-breaking.

evidence: Dose reductions were “according to protocol”; toxicity-related cessation was permitted, and crossover prohibited (M, pp.1927, 1931; S, Table S1). Figure S1 lists some protocol violations but does not establish deviations caused by trial context.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” that trial context caused non-protocol changes. Protocol-consistent toxicity management warrants N/PN.

evidence: Not reached because 2.3=PN. Unequal protocol-directed dose modification does not activate this branch (M, p.1931; S, Table S1).
guidance: Box 6, 2.4: applicable only “If Y/PY to 2.3.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4=NA; the unequal dose-reduction rates are documented but are not established trial-context deviations (S, Table S3).
guidance: Box 6, 2.5: applicable only “If Y/PY/NI to 2.4.”

evidence: All 444 and 222 randomized participants were included in their assigned groups in the primary ITT analysis (S, Figure S1; M, Figure 1A). SAP §5.1 specifies initial randomized assignment regardless of treatment received (P, p.472).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 accepts ITT analysis; §5.3.1 places bias from missing outcomes in the separate missing-data domain.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y; no primary-analysis exclusions or regrouping are evident (S, Figure S1; M, Figure 1A).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: applicable only “If N/PN/NI to 2.6.”

evidence: All participants entered the analysis, but PFS was censored for withdrawal, new anticancer therapy and prolonged assessment gaps (P, pp.544–545). Figure S1 reports nine consent withdrawals in each arm and one loss to follow-up, but describes treatment disposition rather than all premature PFS censoring. Nearly complete observation cannot be established (S, p.11).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires missing outcomes to make “no important difference.” §6.1.5 states that prematurely censored participants can have missing outcomes despite inclusion in analysis.

evidence: Planned sensitivity analyses addressed new therapy and censored withdrawals for adverse events or deterioration (P, p.564). Their results are absent from the supplied results reports. Blinded central imaging review is reported, but does not resolve unobserved follow-up (M, Figure 1).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2; §6.1.7 require demonstrated robustness under “plausible assumptions” about missing outcomes. Planned analyses are not evidence of their results.

evidence: New anticancer therapy triggered censoring (P, p.544). Bone-only disease rules also censored fracture, palliation and “clinical worsening not objectively confirmed” (P, p.189). Such mechanisms can depend on underlying disease status.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3 identifies missingness related to “participants’ health status.” §6.1.5 specifically identifies treatment switching as a potential source of informative censoring.

evidence: The strongest argument against my earlier High judgement is that tumour follow-up continued after treatment cessation (P, p.544), and recorded loss to follow-up was rare (S, Figure S1). Thus toxicity discontinuations cannot simply be counted as missing PFS. Nevertheless, actual premature censoring counts/reasons and subsequent outcomes are not reported sufficiently to distinguish possible from likely outcome-dependent missingness.
guidance: §1.1 reserves NI for insufficient evidence to infer PY/PN. Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence using proportions, reasons and circumstances; Table 10 explicitly includes NI.

evidence: RECIST 1.1 progression or death was assessed with CT/MRI and bone imaging (M, p.1927). No evidence indicates that the measurement method was invalid.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns methods “unsuitable for the outcome,” not whether PFS is the preferred endpoint.

evidence: Imaging schedules were common to both groups: every 11–13 weeks, with bone scans every 23–25 weeks (M, p.1927). Assessments were required on the calendar schedule “regardless of treatment delays resulting from toxicity” (P, p.186). Actual adherence by arm is unreported, but systematic differences are not indicated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 defines comparability through common methods, thresholds and “comparable time points.” §1.1 permits PN supported by context.

evidence: The strongest counterevidence is maintained double blinding and indistinguishable placebo (M, p.1933; P, p.169). However, the target assessors were local investigators, with access to characteristic neutropenia and dose-management information (P, pp.190, 209, 535; M, Table 2). Some inferred awareness remains probable; formal code-breaking is not required for that inference.
guidance: §7.3 asks whether blinding was “successfully implemented.” Box 10, 4.3 concerns the actual assessors of this result; §5.1.3 explains possible identification through characteristic toxicity.

evidence: Local interpretation of radiographic progression involves judgement, including confirmation of bone lesions and clinical worsening (M, p.1927; P, p.189). RECIST standardization reduces discretion but does not eliminate it.
guidance: Box 10, 4.4 and §7.1 identify “observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement,” including radiograph assessment, as susceptible to knowledge of assignment.

evidence: Common schedules, RECIST criteria and formal masking constrain influence. Independent blinded review also supported benefit, HR 0.65 versus investigator HR 0.58 (M, pp.1932–1933). This supports probable absence of material influence, but neither proves investigator blinding nor makes the two results interchangeable.
guidance: Box 10, 4.5 distinguishes possible influence from influence “likely” to occur; §1.2.1 requires consideration of “material bias.”

evidence: Original SAP v1.0, February 18, 2013, specifies investigator PFS, ITT, Kaplan–Meier medians, HR/CI and disease-site-stratified log-rank testing (P, pp.461, 474, 489), matching the report (M, pp.1927–1929). The final SAP postdates cutoff, and the exact unblinded-analysis date is absent, but the target’s principal methods were already specified. Amendment rationales describe pharmacology/regulatory developments (P, pp.528, 533–535).
guidance: Box 11, 5.1; §8.3.1 require pre-unblinding intentions and comparison of dated versions. Changes “clearly unrelated to the results” do not themselves raise concerns.

evidence: Investigator PFS was designated primary and central review supportive in the original SAP (P, p.489); both were reported (M, Figure 1). Reporting the more favourable investigator HR therefore does not demonstrate selection after seeing results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 requires selection “on the basis of the results.” Multiple measurements alone do not establish it.

evidence: The primary ITT analysis matches original SAP §8.2.1 (P, p.489). The strongest challenges are unreported sensitivity results and 331 observed events versus approximately 347 planned (M, p.1930; P, p.539). Neither establishes selection of this primary estimate from competing analyses because of its findings.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires likely results-based selection; §8.3.2 cautions that discrepancies may have legitimate explanations. Prespecification of the reported primary analysis weighs against selection.

evidence: P p159, §11: “IV/WRS will ensure random assignment” in a 1:1 ratio within strata. The underlying random-number generation method is not described. The centralized system and large multicentre trial support probably random allocation.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1 and §4.3.1.1 permit “Probably yes” when the trial context supports random generation despite incomplete methodological detail.

evidence: P pp158–159, §§10–11: investigators used the interactive voice/web response system for allocation and dispensed only system-assigned numbered units. Treatment codes required a separate documented emergency code break. This supports concealment through assignment.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation; Table 2 identifies central randomization as adequate concealment.

evidence: M p844, Table 1: groups numbered 1591/1592; mean age 66/66 years, HbA1c 8.2/8.2%, eGFR 74/74, and established cardiovascular/chronic kidney disease 84.9%/84.5%. Differences in smoking and other characteristics are compatible with chance.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when “any observed imbalances are compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 excludes chance imbalances from systematic bias.

evidence: The target ITT stratified Cox methods match those specified in S pp 94–96. The documents do not support confidently classifying dependence as either likely or unlikely.

guidance: Box 10: reached only “If Y/PY/NI to 4.4.”

The requirement to finish the SAP before the first interim analysis (p.140) does not establish that final intentions preceded availability of unblinded outcomes.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 and §8.3.1 require finalization before unblinded outcome data were available, rather than simply before publication or formal interim analysis. §8.3.2 recognizes uncertainty from incomplete timing information.

evidence: The end-of-study absolute change was specified in the original protocol, and CKD-EPI in the amended protocol/SAP (protocol bundle pp.48–49, 86, 174). Table 2 reports the specified endpoint; Appendix Figure S1 also reports the eGFR trajectory. The measurement amendment merits scrutiny, but the documents do not indicate that this reported measurement was selected because of its results.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 assesses likely results-based selection among eligible measurements. Correspondence with documented intentions supports PN; §8.3.2 cautions that amendments can have legitimate explanations.

Article p.2228 describes available-case multivariable analyses with those factors and directs readers to the SAP. No results-based choice among competing analyses is identified.

evidence: Randomization used a “stochastic minimization algorithm” balancing assignments within centres (M, p. 2415).
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random”; here the random component is explicit.

guidance: Box 4, 1.2 and Table 2: centrally administered randomization meets the allocation-concealment criterion. Open-label treatment after assignment does not negate concealment (§4.1).

evidence: Randomized numbers were balanced, 1523 versus 1522. However, Table 1 describes only the 3009 analysed patients, excluding 36 withdrawals. It shows broadly similar risk profiles alongside differences in smoking, age and prior CABG; baseline data for the excluded patients are absent (M, Figure 1, p. 2418; Table 1, pp. 2419–2420).
guidance: §4.3.3: assessment “should be based on data for all randomized participants.” Box 4, 1.3 gives baseline characteristics restricted to the final analysis as an example warranting NI. These incomplete baseline comparisons do not establish failed randomization.

evidence: The trial was explicitly “open-label”; patients followed visibly different medication schedules (M, pp. 2415–2416).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 asks whether participants knew their assigned intervention.

guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses awareness among carers and intervention providers, separately from blinded outcome adjudication.

evidence: Adherence was imperfect: 95.2% of the short-DAPT group stopped DAPT by day 60; 88.2% of controls maintained it through day 335. However, the protocol allowed clinically necessary dose reductions, switches and additional antithrombotics. No reported evidence attributes departures to recruitment effects or personnel undermining the comparison (M, p. 2418; S2, pp. 12–13, §4.1). Reasons for individual departures are incompletely reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3: Y/PY requires “evidence, or strong reason to believe” deviations arose because of trial context. Protocol-consistent changes and ordinary non-adherence support N/PN. §1.1 permits a reasoned PN despite incomplete reporting.

evidence: Patients retained in the analysis were analysed as randomized, including non-adherers. However, 23 versus 13 consent withdrawals were excluded entirely. The SAP states that their data “are excluded from the analysis totally,” contrasting this with retaining available observations for patients lost to follow-up. Thus, this appears to exclude eligible participants beyond simply omitting unavailable outcomes; the amount of previously observed outcome information removed is unspecified (M, pp. 2416, 2418; S2, pp. 106, 123, “Withdrawal/follow-up”).
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: analyses “excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization” are inappropriate; mITT excluding only missing outcomes is acceptable. PN reflects uncertainty about precisely which available observations were removed.

evidence: The 36 complete exclusions are substantial relative to 90 observed primary events and the 20-event difference between groups. Exclusions were also unequal, 23 versus 13. Their outcomes are not reported, so a substantial effect cannot reasonably be ruled out merely because they represent 1.2% of randomized patients (M, Figure 1, p. 2418; Table 2, p. 2422).
guidance: Box 6, 2.7: substantial impact is possible “even if fewer than 5%” were excluded “if the outcome is rare.” This assesses potential impact, not proof that exclusions changed the result.

evidence: Complete follow-up was documented for 2974/3045 randomized patients. Besides the 36 consent withdrawals, 22 versus 13 patients were lost to follow-up. Some incompletely followed patients already had events, but the sensitivity analysis still adds 20 experimental-group events—material relative to the observed 35 versus 55 (M, Figure 1, p. 2418; S1, p. 37, eFigure 4).
guidance: Box 8, 3.1: “nearly all” means missing outcomes could make “no important difference”; for event outcomes, completeness must be assessed relative to event frequency. §6.1.5 treats prematurely censored follow-up as missing outcome information.

evidence: The sensitivity analysis changes HR 0.64 to 1.00 (95% CI 0.69–1.46), retaining noninferiority but losing superiority (P=.98). Its denominators remain 1500/1509, so it does not restore the 36 excluded withdrawals. It therefore does not establish robustness of the specified estimate and combined claim (S1, p. 37, eFigure 4; M, p. 2416).
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 requires bias-correcting methods or results “little changed under a range of plausible assumptions.” §6.1.7 cautions that extreme scenarios alone may not describe plausible missingness. Persistence of noninferiority alone does not demonstrate an unbiased HR.

evidence: Loss to follow-up and consent withdrawal could relate to cardiovascular or bleeding illness. Although the SAP required recording withdrawal details, the supplied results do not report reasons sufficient to establish independence from health status (M, Figure 1; S2, pp. 106, 123).
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if loss or withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” missingness could depend on the true outcome.

evidence: Loss was more frequent with 1-month DAPT: 22/1500 versus 13/1509; consent withdrawals were also more frequent, 23 versus 13. This asymmetry raises concern, but reasons and outcome histories are unavailable. Conversely, follow-up was highly complete and the main analysis did not censor merely for changing treatment. The evidence does not adequately establish whether outcome-dependent missingness was likely or unlikely (M, pp. 2416, 2418; S2, p. 123).
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely” and identifies differing missingness proportions as evidence to consider. §1.1 supports NI when neither PY nor PN is reasonably supported. Table 10 explicitly maps this unresolved branch to High.

evidence: Components used defined clinical criteria: ARC MI/stent-thrombosis definitions and TIMI bleeding thresholds, with source-document adjudication (M, p. 2416).
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods; it does not judge whether selecting a particular composite was clinically sensible.

evidence: Both groups had the same scheduled assessments and event definitions. The protocol required questioning about interim hospitalizations and bleeding, cardiac biomarker testing for suspected MI, and haemoglobin/haematocrit testing for suspected bleeding. Open-label clinicians could influence detection, but no systematic difference in surveillance or thresholds is documented (S2, pp. 13–14, 104; M, p. 2416).
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable methods use the same methods and thresholds at comparable times. §7.3 targets systematic ascertainment differences; lack of blinding alone does not establish them.

evidence: “All clinical events comprising the primary end points” were adjudicated from source documents by an independent committee “blinded to randomized treatment group” (M, p. 2416). This covers bleeding, which contributed importantly to the difference: 6 versus 23 TIMI major/minor bleeds (Table 2, p. 2422).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: answer N when outcome assessors were blinded. §7.1, composite outcomes, requires attention to influential components; those components were included in blinded adjudication.

evidence: The January 19, 2018 SAP specifies the 12-month composite, unadjusted Cox analysis, HR margin 1.5, and superiority following noninferiority. No interim analysis was planned. Exact unblinding dates are absent, and the article and protocol history date the margin amendment differently, but the combined evidence supports prospective specification before unblinded analysis (S2, pp. 44, 99, 103–110, 114, 120, 126; M, pp. 2415–2416).

evidence: The original protocol already specifies the same component combination at 12 months. The report presents that outcome, its components and alternative bleeding definitions; there is no unexplained substitution of the target measurement or time point (S2, p. 21, §7.1; M, Table 2, p. 2422).

evidence: The target follows the planned unadjusted Cox analysis and sequential noninferiority/superiority testing. Alternative analyses are also disclosed, including per-protocol and as-treated estimates that do not show superiority. guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns selection based on results, not merely conducting multiple analyses. §8.3.2 requires considering legitimate amendments; §8.1.2 restricts assessment to eligible analyses of the target result.

evidence: Allocation used a “stochastic minimization algorithm” balancing treatment within centres (M, p. 2415).

evidence: Randomization was “performed centrally through the electronic data capture system,” after consent and eligibility confirmation (M, p. 2415; S2, p. 56, §3.3).

Individual reasons are incompletely reported.

Although the SAP says their data were “excluded … totally,” it does not establish that usable outcome data remained available for analysis after withdrawal. My previous answer inferred inappropriate removal of available outcomes too strongly. I now treat this as withdrawal-related unavailable data in D3 (M, p. 2416 and Figure 1; S2, pp. 106, 123).

evidence: Complete follow-up was documented for 2974/3045 randomized patients, approximately 97.7%; the reported 98.8% uses the denominator after consent withdrawals. There were 23 versus 13 withdrawals and another 22 versus 13 losses. With only 35 versus 55 primary events, incomplete outcome information cannot be dismissed using a percentage threshold (M, Figure 1, p. 2418; Table 2, p. 2422).

guidance: Box 10, 4.2 identifies comparable methods as the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points.

evidence: P pp.10–12 specifies the composite, per-protocol analysis, χ² comparison, risk-difference CI and −20% margin, broadly matching M pp.757–758. However, version 7.0 has no finalization date or amendment history establishing that these intentions preceded unblinded data. guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires finalization before unblinded outcome data were available. §8.3.1 calls for a “date-stamp”; §8.3.2 specifically identifies undated analysis plans as limiting assessment. §1.1 supports NI when neither PY nor PN is adequately justified.

guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N/PN when intended and reported measurements correspond. §8.3.2 permits explicitly explained inferences from incomplete information.

guidance: Box 11, 5.3 asks whether selection occurred “on the basis of the results.” §8.3.2 cautions that discrepancies need interpretation. An inappropriate assignment-effect analysis belongs in D2 and does not independently establish selective reporting.

evidence: Randomization was stratified, in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, through an interactive voice/web response system (P p188, §11). The sequence-generation method is not specified. Genuine random generation is probable given the centralized system and large multicentre trial, but not directly documented.
guidance: §4.3.1.1 and Box 4 permit “Probably yes” in a large, professionally conducted trial despite absent sequence-generation details; §1.1 reserves NI for circumstances where inference is unreasonable.

evidence: “A randomisation session will be carried out by using the IV/WRS”; treatment codes were accessed through controlled code-breaking procedures (P p188, §§11–11.1).
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Yes for “remote or centrally administered” allocation, including telephone/internet services.

evidence: Allocation totals were 1648 versus 1649. Baseline age, HbA1c, blood pressure, cardiovascular history and other characteristics show no pattern suggesting failed randomization (M p4, Table 1).
guidance: Box 4, 1.3: answer No when differences are “compatible with chance”; §4.3.3.1 says chance imbalances are not systematic bias.

evidence: Although volume-matched placebo maintained blinding within dose (M p2), treatment discontinuation attributed to “Suspicion of placebo” occurred in 6 semaglutide and 25 placebo participants; gastrointestinal intolerance also differed substantially (A pp79–80, Table S5). Some participants probably inferred assignment, although suspicion does not prove accurate knowledge.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 addresses awareness, including recognizable adverse effects. §5.1.3 cautions that successful guessing can reflect treatment effects and does not itself establish bias.

evidence: The trial was double-blind, with active drug and placebo “identical with regard to appearance, taste and smell” (P p184; M p2). Table S5 records participants’ reasons for stopping but does not establish carers’ knowledge; no material breakdown of personnel blinding is documented.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2: blinding can prevent differences in implementation. Under §1.1, PN reflects a supported inference rather than treating absent confirmation as NI.

evidence: Stopping because of “Suspicion of placebo” or “Trial fatigue” is specifically attributable to trial participation: respectively 6 versus 25 and 10 versus 26 participants (A pp79–80, Table S5). These differ from ordinary intolerance-related discontinuation. Protocol-directed safety stopping and additional standard-care treatment were allowed (P pp162–163; M p3).
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence of departures arising because of the “trial context”; protocol-consistent toxicity management does not count. §5.1.2.1 distinguishes trial-induced behaviour from ordinary non-adherence.

evidence: The identified contextual discontinuations involved 16/1648 semaglutide and 51/1649 placebo participants (A Table S5). Most therefore stopped placebo; fewer than 1% stopped active treatment for these reasons. A material effect on the cardiovascular composite is unlikely. Follow-up continued after treatment stopping (M p2; P p162). Timing and subsequent treatment for these particular participants are not reported.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 asks whether contextual deviations affected the outcome; §1.2.1 defines risk of bias as risk of “material bias.” This is an inference about likely impact, not proof of no effect.

evidence: Not reached because 2.4 = PN. The numerical imbalance is nevertheless considered in evaluating 2.4.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.5 only if 2.4 = Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The primary analysis used the full analysis set, “all patients who underwent randomization according to the planned treatment” (M p3); A pp27–29 specifies analysis “as randomized” using the in-trial period. All 3297 randomized participants were included.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 accept ITT analysis for assignment effects; missing follow-up is assessed separately in D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6 = Y.
guidance: Box 6: answer 2.7 only if 2.6 = N/PN/NI.

evidence: Trial follow-up was incomplete for 25 semaglutide and 40 placebo participants (A p36, Fig. S1A). Although 98.0% completed follow-up and 99.6% had known vital status (M p4), vital status does not establish complete nonfatal MI/stroke ascertainment. Sixty-five incomplete records relative to 254 primary events cannot confidently be considered immaterial under every possible outcome pattern.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 defines “nearly all” by whether missing outcomes “could have made no important difference,” not a fixed percentage. §6.1.5 treats premature censoring as missing outcome data.

evidence: Sensitivity analyses produced similar estimates (A p40, Fig. S2), but varied analysis populations, exposure windows, stratification and eligibility (A pp31–33). None reported a range of assumptions about unobserved cardiovascular events after loss to follow-up or consent withdrawal.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7 require analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome; agreement among other sensitivity analyses does not establish robustness to informative missingness.

evidence: Follow-up ended at consent withdrawal or last direct contact for those lost (A p28). Withdrawal/loss could be associated with health status; individual reasons excluding such a relationship are unavailable.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: if loss or withdrawal “could be related to participants’ health status,” outcome-dependent missingness is possible.

evidence: Incomplete follow-up was somewhat higher with placebo: 2.4% versus 1.5%; loss to follow-up was 32 versus 18, while consent withdrawals were similar, 8 versus 7 (A Fig. S1A). This supports concern, but the small absolute imbalance and absence of documented health-related causes do not establish that outcome-dependent missingness was likely. Primary follow-up was not censored simply upon treatment discontinuation (M p2; A pp28–29).
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could depend” from “likely” dependence and identifies differential missingness as evidence to consider. §§6.1.4–6.1.5 require interpretation of proportions, reasons and censoring circumstances together.

evidence: Prespecified clinical definitions used biomarkers, ECG/clinical evidence, neurological criteria and cause-of-death classification (A Table S4, pp63–78). Events underwent independent adjudication (M p3). These are appropriate methods for this composite.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for unsuitable measurement methods. §7.1 requires considering the influential components of composite outcomes.

evidence: Both groups had scheduled quarterly visits and the same outcome definitions and adjudication procedures (M p3; A Table S4). Treatment discontinuation could lead to telephone rather than site follow-up (P p162), but no systematic difference in ascertainment of this cardiovascular composite is demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 considers “same measurement methods and thresholds” at comparable times and differential opportunities for detection.

evidence: Outcomes were adjudicated “in a blinded fashion by an external, independent event-adjudication committee” (M p3). The protocol confirms blinded review of supporting medical records (P p200, §12.7.3).
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded.” This applies separately from participant awareness in D2.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 = N. MI, stroke and cardiovascular cause-of-death classification can involve judgement, but assessors were blinded.
guidance: Box 10: answer 4.4 only if 4.3 = Y/PY/NI.

evidence: Not reached because 4.4 is NA.
guidance: Box 10: answer 4.5 only if 4.4 = Y/PY/NI.

evidence: The 19 May 2014 protocol specifies this composite, pooled comparison, FAS, stratified Cox model and noninferiority margin (P p208, §17.3). The final SAP dated 16 March 2016 specifies the reported analysis (P pp262, 269–273), with blinding maintained until database release (p272). Actual lock/unblinding dates are absent; nevertheless, pre-unblinding finalization is probable.
guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires a plan finalized before unblinded data were available. §8.3.1 permits confidential monitoring-committee analyses and requires consideration of dates and amendments.

evidence: The reported first-event composite matches the protocol and SAP (P pp208, 273; M pp3, 5). The 109-week observation strategy is documented in the SAP (P p268). Other cardiovascular composites and individual components are also reported (M Table 2; A Table S9). No result-dependent selection of this measurement is evident.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N when reported measurements correspond to intended measurements; §8.3.1 allows changes made while blinded.

evidence: The reported HR comes from the specified primary FAS/in-trial stratified Cox analysis (P p273; A p29). Alternative analyses are displayed in Fig. S2. Superiority testing and two per-protocol analyses were explicitly post hoc (M p3; A p33), but they did not replace the prespecified analysis producing the target HR and noninferiority result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 concerns selection “on the basis of the results,” not merely the existence of multiple analyses; §8.1.2 restricts assessment to the particular eligible result.

evidence: P p188, §11 specifies stratified randomization through IV/WRS in a 1:1:1:1 ratio. The actual sequence-generation method remains unreported. Centralized randomization in this large multicentre trial supports probable random generation, without claiming documented computer-generated numbers.
guidance: §4.3.1.1 and Box 4 permit PY despite missing generation details in an appropriately conducted large trial. §1.1 permits inference instead of NI when justified.

evidence: “A randomisation session will be carried out by using the IV/WRS”; treatment codes were subject to controlled emergency disclosure (P p188, §§11–11.1). No evidence indicates recruiters could access forthcoming assignments.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: centrally administered telephone/internet allocation supports Y.

evidence: Groups contained 1648 and 1649 participants. M p4, Table 1 shows broadly comparable prognostic factors; its only conventionally significant difference was diabetes duration, P=0.048. This does not suggest failed randomization.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences “compatible with chance,” including a small number significant at 0.05, do not establish bias.

evidence: Volume-matched placebo supported blinding (M p2). Nevertheless, discontinuation attributed to “Suspicion of placebo” occurred in 6 semaglutide and 25 placebo participants, alongside differential gastrointestinal intolerance (A pp79–80, Table S5). Some inferred assignment remains probable, although suspicion is weaker evidence than confirmed unblinding.
guidance: Box 6, 2.1 considers awareness, including recognizable effects. §5.1.3 cautions that guessing may reflect outcomes or adverse effects and does not itself demonstrate bias.

evidence: Double-blind treatment and products “identical with regard to appearance, taste and smell” support probable personnel blinding (M p2; P p184). Participant suspicions recorded in Table S5 do not establish personnel knowledge. Actual blinding-success data are absent.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses carers’ knowledge separately. §1.1 supports PN when the available evidence permits a reasonable inference.

evidence: “Suspicion of placebo” and “Trial fatigue” caused treatment discontinuation in respectively 6 versus 25 and 10 versus 26 participants (A Table S5). These reasons identify trial-context departures. Conversely, toxicity-related stopping and additional standard-care treatment were permitted (P p162; M p3). Disallowed-medication use is reported, but its connection to trial-induced behaviour is not established.
guidance: Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence of deviations arising from the trial context and excludes protocol-consistent toxicity management. §5.1.2.1 excludes ordinary non-adherence unrelated to that context.

evidence: The identified contextual discontinuations involved 16/1648 semaglutide participants and 51/1649 placebo participants (A Table S5). Fewer than 1% therefore stopped active treatment for these reasons; most such discontinuations stopped placebo. Material influence on this cardiovascular effect estimate is unlikely, although individual timing and replacement treatment are unavailable.
guidance: Box 6, 2.4 asks whether these deviations affected the outcome; §1.2.1 specifies “risk of material bias.”

evidence: Not reached because 2.4=PN. The imbalance in A Table S5 has already informed the assessment of likely impact.
guidance: Box 6: 2.5 is reached only when 2.4=Y/PY/NI.

evidence: M p3 specifies all randomized participants analysed according to planned treatment. A pp27–29 identifies the FAS, analysis “as randomized,” and the in-trial observation period. Treatment discontinuation did not determine exclusion from the primary analysis.
guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1 accept ITT analysis for assignment effects; incomplete outcome follow-up belongs in D3.

evidence: Not reached because 2.6=Y; the documented primary analysis preserves randomized groups (M p3; A pp27–29).

The latter does not establish complete nonfatal-event ascertainment. The number of non-completers already experiencing a first composite event is unavailable; thus the exact number with missing first-event outcomes is uncertain, but negligible potential impact is not established.
guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires missing outcomes to be too few to make an “important difference.” §6.1.3.2 rejects a universal percentage threshold; §6.1.5 treats premature censoring as missing follow-up.

evidence: Similar estimates across sensitivity analyses support general robustness (A p40, Fig. S2), but those analyses vary exposure windows, populations, stratification and eligibility (A pp31–33). They do not test plausible outcome-dependent missingness after withdrawal/loss.
guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7 require sensitivity analyses addressing the relationship between missingness and the true outcome. Agreement among other analyses is insufficient.

evidence: Follow-up ends at consent withdrawal or last direct contact for participants lost to follow-up (A p28). Their underlying reasons are not sufficiently described to exclude health-related missingness.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: withdrawal or loss that “could be related to participants’ health status” supports possible outcome-dependent missingness.

evidence: Non-completion was 1.5% versus 2.4%; consent withdrawals were 7 versus 8 and losses to follow-up 18 versus 32 (A Fig. S1A). The imbalance supports concern, but its small absolute size and lack of documented outcome-related reasons do not make such dependence clearly likely. Primary follow-up continued after treatment discontinuation (M p2; A pp28–29).
guidance: Box 8, 3.4 distinguishes “could” from “likely” dependence and identifies differential missingness as evidence to weigh. §§6.1.4–6.1.5 require consideration of proportions, reasons and censoring circumstances.

evidence: Clinical definitions used biomarker, ECG, neurological and cause-of-death evidence, with independent adjudication (A pp63–78, Table S4; M p3). No unsuitable measurement method is demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 concerns inappropriate measurement methods. §7.1 requires considering the components contributing to a composite outcome.

evidence: Quarterly visits, common definitions and common adjudication procedures applied across groups (M p3; A Table S4). Telephone follow-up could replace visits after discontinuation (P p162), but systematic differential ascertainment of this composite is not demonstrated.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2 considers comparable methods, thresholds and timing, including differences in detection opportunities.

evidence: Outcomes were adjudicated “in a blinded fashion by an external, independent event-adjudication committee” (M p3). P p200, §12.7.3 confirms blinded review of supporting medical documentation.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3: “Answer ‘No’ if outcome assessors were blinded.” Participant awareness does not automatically establish assessor awareness.

guidance: Box 11, 5.1 requires pre-unblinding finalization. §8.3.1 requires examining dates and allows confidential monitoring-committee analyses without invalidating prespecification.

evidence: The reported first-event composite matches the protocol and SAP (P pp208, 273; M pp3, 5). The 109-week strategy is documented in P p268. Other cardiovascular composites and components are also reported (M Table 2; A Table S9).
guidance: Box 11, 5.2 supports N when reported measurements correspond to intended measurements; multiple outcomes alone do not establish result-dependent selection.

evidence: The target HR uses the specified FAS/in-trial stratified Cox analysis (P p273; A p29). Alternative analyses are shown in Fig. S2. Post hoc superiority testing and per-protocol analyses are disclosed (M p3; A p33), but did not replace the primary analysis producing this target result.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 requires selection “on the basis of the results.” §8.1.2 focuses on the particular eligible result rather than unrelated reporting choices.

evidence: M, pp.2–3: centrally generated “minimization algorithm” using four stratification variables. S1, p.218, §6.6 confirms this; the random component is not explicitly described.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random.” §1.1 permits PY when inference is required.

evidence: S1, p.218, §6.6: allocation followed consent and baseline collection through a “password-protected encrypted website”; the master list was restricted to authorized data-management staff.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: answer Y for centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel.

evidence: M, p.5, Table 1: groups numbered 257/246; median eGFR 56.1/59.0 and proteinuria 1.99/1.93. Other differences show no convincing non-chance pattern. Differences between dose-era cohorts in S2, eTable 3, are not imbalances between randomized treatments.

guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo blinding can prevent awareness; PY requires side effects participants knew were intervention-specific. §5.1.3 cautions that apparent guessing need not demonstrate broken blinding.

evidence: M, p.3 and S1, p.219, §6.7 explicitly describe blinded site personnel. S1, pp.218–219 allows clinical emergency unblinding and central safety unblinding, but does not establish widespread awareness among treating personnel.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 assesses awareness among carers and intervention providers. §1.1 supports a probability judgement rather than NI when circumstances permit inference.

evidence: Not reached because 2.1 and 2.2 are PN. M, pp.2,4 documents safety-directed cessation in 23 participants with scheduled follow-up continued; this does not itself establish an inappropriate trial-context deviation.
guidance: Box 6: ask 2.3 only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Y/PY/NI. §5.1 and Box 6 distinguish toxicity-related treatment cessation from relevant deviations.

evidence: Not reached; no affirmative 2.3 response. M, p.4, Figure 1 documents discontinuations but does not activate this branch.

guidance: Box 8, 3.1 requires data for this outcome from all/nearly all participants. §§6.1, 6.1.6 include missing repeated measurements and warn about trajectories after the last measurement.

guidance: Box 8, 3.2 and §6.1.7 require correction for bias or robustness under plausible relationships between missingness and true outcomes; using available data alone does not establish this.

evidence: S1, p.220, §6.9: follow-up ends at the earliest of final visit, “Death or ESKD,” or withdrawal. Thus loss of subsequent kidney-function measurements can depend directly on kidney deterioration.
guidance: Box 8, 3.3: health-related loss permits dependence on the true outcome; §6.1 explicitly includes missing measurements following death.

evidence: Outcome-related truncation is likely: the protocol stops follow-up at ESKD, which occurred in 50/257 versus 67/246 participants (M, p.6, Table 2). This is substantial and differs by assignment. Earlier measurements remain informative, and later declining counts partly reflect differing follow-up durations, but neither resolves this specific mechanism.
guidance: Box 8, 3.4, reasons 1, 2 and 4: differing missingness proportions, outcome-related reasons, and trial circumstances support likely dependence. §6.1.6 requires attention to the subsequent outcome trajectory.

evidence: S1, p.223, §7.8 specifies creatinine methods traceable to IDMS; p.231 specifies CKD-EPI calculation. M, p.5, Table 1 footnote confirms CKD-EPI use. No evidence establishes an unsuitable measurement instrument.
guidance: Box 10, 4.1 screens for inappropriate measurement methods, not whether a surrogate outcome was a sensible choice.

evidence: M, p.3 and S1, pp.221–223 specify common visit schedules and laboratory procedures. Laboratories varied geographically, but methods were calibrated and not assigned by treatment. Outcome-dependent absence of measurements is addressed in D3.
guidance: Box 10, 4.2: comparable measurement uses the same methods at comparable time points. §7.3 addresses systematic differences in ascertainment between groups.

evidence: S1, p.219, §6.7 explicitly blinds site personnel and endpoint adjudicators; M, p.3 confirms masking. Laboratory staff’s individual blinding status is not separately reported, but site masking supports probable assessor unawareness for this laboratory-derived outcome.
guidance: Box 10, 4.3 asks whether assessors knew treatment status; §1.1 permits PY/PN inference when details are incomplete but circumstances are informative.

evidence: Not reached because 4.3 is PN. The laboratory-derived measurement is described in S1, pp.223,231.

evidence: Annual eGFR slope was specified in the protocol and both SAPs (S1, pp.230,277,295). Table 2 reports all-visits and both treatment-period exclusion variants; S2, p.13 also reports the trajectory. There is no indication that a favorable measurement window alone was selected.
guidance: Box 11, 5.2: N/PN when reported measurements correspond to intended measurements; multiplicity alone does not establish results-based selection.

evidence: The intended t-test analysis and Table 2’s adjusted model are inconsistent (S1, pp.277,295; M, pp.3,6). No explanation or separately identified unadjusted slope estimate establishes which analyses generated the target row or why this version was reported. Reporting all three slope variants weighs against selection, but does not resolve the model discrepancy.
guidance: Box 11, 5.3 permits NI when available information cannot establish selection among analyses. §8.3.2 notes that discrepancies may have legitimate explanations; Y/PY requires evidence of likely results-based selection.

evidence: M, p.3 describes a centrally generated “minimization algorithm”; S1, p.218, §6.6 confirms it. The random component is not separately specified.
guidance: Box 4, 1.1: minimization “should generally be considered to be random.” §1.1 permits PY for a supported inference.

evidence: S1, p.218: consent and baseline collection preceded allocation through a “password-protected encrypted website”; access to the master list was restricted to authorized data-management staff.
guidance: Box 4, 1.2: centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel supports Y.

evidence: M, p.5, Table 1: 257 versus 246 participants; median eGFR 56.1 versus 59.0 and proteinuria 1.99 versus 1.93. No convincing pattern of non-chance imbalance. Differences between recruitment-era cohorts are not randomized-treatment imbalances.
guidance: Box 4, 1.3 and §4.3.3.1: differences “compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias.”

evidence: M, p.3 explicitly reports patient masking and matching placebo. Safety events and disclosure of the suspension could prompt guessing, but individual allocation awareness is not demonstrated (M, pp.2–3).
guidance: Box 6, 2.1: placebo can prevent awareness; intervention-specific effects known to participants would support Y/PY. §5.1.3 cautions against equating guessing with failed masking.

evidence: M, p.3 and S1, p.219, §6.7 explicitly mask site personnel. Emergency and central safety unblinding were permitted (S1, pp.218–219), but these provisions do not establish general awareness among treating personnel.
guidance: Box 6, 2.2 addresses carers and intervention providers. §1.1 supports PN when circumstances permit a reasoned inference despite incomplete reporting.

evidence: Both awareness questions are PN. Safety-directed treatment cessation with continuing follow-up is documented in M, p.4, Figure 1; it does not itself establish a relevant trial-context deviation.
guidance: Box 6: 2.3 is reached only after Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2. Its elaboration excludes protocol-consistent changes such as toxicity-related cessation.

guidance: Box 6, 2.6 and §5.3.1: ITT and analyses excluding only missing outcomes are appropriate here; missing-outcome bias is assessed separately.

evidence: M, p.4 reports “negligible missing data” and inclusion of all available observations; Figure 1 records only 10 participants lost/withdrawn. The 98% figure concerns vital status, so it is corroborative rather than a slope-specific denominator. Together, the evidence supports probable near-complete slope availability.

evidence: Figure 1 reports early termination/toxicity before PK sampling in 0, 2 and 5 participants across ascending-dose arms (M p.659). Against this concern, participants were asked to continue evaluations and known AEs were followed to resolution (S E62, E93); however, complete ascertainment of new SAEs after withdrawal is not established. Known recorded SAEs are not being counted as missing.

evidence: My earlier answer overinterpreted the 0/2/5 early-termination/toxicity exclusions from PK analysis as evidence of informative missing SAE outcomes (M p.659, Figure 1).
